en: The Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya of Haribhadra with Guṇaratna’s Commentary, the Tarkarahasyadīpikā,
based on the Śuali and Jain editions.
Input by Muneo Tokunaga, December 2004.
First Chapter [Introduction]:
The illustrious Mahāvīradeva, who has performed service for the Lord of the Gods.
P: In this peerless and timely work, which possesses exquisite profundity, the entire collection of philosophical systems attains the state of a single drop. //1//

P: May that Victorious One, the illustrious Vīra, be for our prosperity—he by whom, in the forest fire of the *syād-vāda*, the entire mass of wood that is false reasoning has been reduced to ashes; and by whom, alas, all [doctrines] characterized by doubt, worldly convention, greed, confusion, non-finality, and contradiction are likewise consumed.
P: Objections such as sublation, possibility, and confusion have been leveled against [the definition] by others. //2//
May the Goddess of Speech be ever present as our consciousness, she who bestows the objects of thought upon all embodied beings here, like a cultivated wish-fulfilling creeper. //3//
Having bowed with devotion to my own gurus, I shall compose a concise commentary on the *Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya* for the benefit of myself and others. (4)
For here in this world, those great beings possessed of noble minds consider that the accomplishment of the welfare of others alone is the supreme fulfillment of one's own purpose; thus,
he whose very essence consists in being solely intent upon benefiting others—
He who brought benefit to the beings of the world through the composition of one hundred and fourteen treatises;
he who was like the sun causing the dawn of the glory of the illustrious Jina’s teaching;
and he who was beautiful with the awakening attained through the words of the Mahattarā Yākinī.
The venerable Śrī Haribhadrasūri [composed] the *Ṣaddarśanasamuccaya* for all those seekers who desire to know the nature of the objects of discourse,
yet lack the capacity to master the extensive treatises of each respective system.
Desiring to bestow favor upon those to be trained, [the author],
commencing this treatise titled *Ṣaddarśanasamuccaya*, which is concise in words yet vast in meaning and possesses a name reflecting its true nature, says:
P: At the commencement of the treatise, he states this first verse in order to explicitly express the auspiciousness and the subject matter, and to indicate the relationship and the purpose.
Having bowed to the Victorious One, the hero who teaches the doctrine of *syād-vāda* and who possesses true vision, the meaning expressed by all philosophical systems is here stated in brief. (1)
P: "Sat" means eternal or existing; or, with respect to knowledge belonging to those still in the state of spiritual development (*chādmasthika-jñāna*), it means praiseworthy.

He whose vision (*darśana*)—that is, perception or knowledge—is called "absolute" (*kevala*), is one who possesses right vision (*sad-darśana*). Alternatively, "sat" means praiseworthy; thus, "right vision" refers to absolute vision (*kevala-darśana*), because of its infallibility.
And he who possesses *kevalajñāna* is one of right vision (*saddarśana*), meaning he is omniscient (*sarvajña*) and all-seeing (*sarvadarśin*); [the author refers to] him.
By this qualification, the excellence of the knowledge of the Blessed One Śrī Vardhamāna is indicated.
He manifested himself.
Or alternatively: he whose view (darśana) is considered true (sat), being honored by all the lords of men, asuras, and gods—him, the one of true vision (sad-darśana).

P: By this, while declaring that his [the Jina’s] vision is worthy of worship by the three worlds, he further reveals the supreme worshipfulness of Śrī Vardhamāna, the Lord of the three worlds; thus, he has manifested the excellence of his worship.
P: Likewise, he is a *jina* because he conquers enemies such as passion (*rāga*) and hatred (*dveṣa*);
by this, he manifested the excellence of having departed from the miserable states of existence (*apāya*).
P: It might be so; *syādvāda* would be the statement of those parts of real entities that are accepted as such by all philosophical systems, insofar as they are mutually dependent.
P:

The meaning is that [reality] is a non-absolutism (anekānta) consisting of both existence and non-existence, permanence and impermanence, universals and particulars, the expressible and the inexpressible.

Objection: How could those portions of reality desired by all philosophical systems— which speak to one another in contradiction— possibly exist as real entities, such that they could constitute the *syād-vāda* through their mutual dependence?

If it is argued that there would be a contradiction among the true doctrines, it is said in reply: although the various philosophical systems (darśanas) maintain mutual opposition due to their respective differences in opinion, [they do not contradict the truth].
Nevertheless, among those things asserted by them, there are also portions of reality which, being mutually dependent, attain correctness.
As it has been said: "The Buddhists [assert] impermanence, while the Sāṃkhyas [assert] permanence."
By the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas, eternal and non-eternal, existence and non-existence, and universals and particulars are held to be mutually distinct;
by the Mīmāṃsakas, however— with the exception of the word "syāt"— they are both different and non-different.

The eternal and non-eternal aspects, the existent and non-existent portions, the universal and the particular, and the eternality of sound; furthermore, by some, time, inherent nature, necessity, karma, and the person (puruṣa) are cited as the causes of the world.

And by those who maintain the non-duality of the knowledge of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahma-jñānādvaitavādin*), as well as the non-dualities of the knowledge of the Word-Brahman and so forth— whatever such constituent elements of reality are accepted by others, [they are all subsumed].
All of these, being dependent, attain the status of ultimate truth; however,
when independent, they cancel one another out like a lotus in the sky— so enough with this elaboration.

"Teacher of the *syād-vāda*": he who correctly speaks the *syād-vāda* is the teacher of the *syād-vāda*; by this [epithet], he described his excellence of speech. Thus, the author of the treatise has explicitly declared these four excellences herein.
The relationship of cause and effect between these [attributes] is to be understood as follows:
because he is the conqueror of the enemies that are all faults without exception, for that very reason he is omniscient;
because he is omniscient, for that very reason he is a speaker of things as they truly are.
Precisely because he is a speaker of the truth as it truly is, for that very reason he is worthy of worship by the three worlds.
Thus, having bowed to the Hero, the Great Hero, the preeminent among those possessing the fourfold excellence, the current Lord of the Tīrtha, also known by the name Śrī Vardhamāna—

The meaning is: having made a formal resolve (*praṇidhāya*) through the mind by reflecting upon its excellence, through speech by uttering [the name], and through the body by placing the head upon the ground.
By this, he has expressed the initial auspicious invocation;
however, the intermediate auspicious invocation is expressed by the passage beginning with: "The deity there is the Lord of Victors (Jinendra), who is free from passion and hatred."

P:41.p.4) By praising the doctrine of the Victor (jinamata), he will proclaim [the final benediction]. Furthermore, regarding the ultimate meaning of the subject matter (*abhidheya-tātparyārtha*), which should be reflected upon by those of superior intelligence (*subuddhi*), he will state this by employing the term "those of superior intelligence."
The fruit of these three types [of auspiciousness] is as follows: at the beginning,
middle, and end of the treatise,
the first [type of auspiciousness] is prescribed for the purpose of reaching the completion of the treatise without obstacles.
For that very purpose, [he taught] the middle and final [recensions] so that there would be no obstacles;
and for the sake of the non-interruption of the lineage of disciples and grand-disciples, he taught that very same [tradition].
It was stated, "having bowed to the Hero" (vīram natvā).
Since the suffix -ktvā requires a subsequent action, the verbal phrase "is being proclaimed" (nigadyate) must be connected here. Who is it that is being proclaimed?

The meaning expressed by all philosophical systems (*sarva-darśana-vācya-artha*). All the philosophical systems, such as Buddhism and others, taken collectively with respect to their fundamental divisions; the meaning expressed or denoted by them, or by those [systems], is precisely this.

The definitions of reality, the means of valid cognition, and so forth, are being stated—expressed—in brief, that is, in summary, by me. Although not explicitly stated here, it is understood through the sense of the context; by this [it is implied].
He stated the direct subject matter.
The connection and the purpose, however, are to be understood by implication:

knowledge of the reality of the gods and other matters to be taught in all philosophical systems (*darśana*) is the goal (*upeya*), and this treatise is the means (*upāya*) to that; thus, the connection characterized as the relationship between the means and the goal is indicated.
It is to be seen.
Furthermore, the purpose is twofold: that of the author and that of the listener.
Each of these two is also twofold: immediate and remote.
Furthermore, having understood the perceptions of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, and having abandoned that which is to be abandoned while adopting that which is to be adopted,
there is success consisting of the infinite fourfold set through a continuous succession.

[Objection: Surely this author of the treatise, having thoroughly mastered all the treatises connected with every philosophical system (*darśana*), composed this present work for the benefit of others; why then did he not explicitly state here which specific system was to be rejected?
If it is argued that "a certain [view] is to be accepted," it is replied: here, all philosophical systems have been introduced as subjects to be discussed;
therefore, one who describes them with impartiality does not overstep what is appropriate in this context.

But one who says, "This is to be abandoned" and "this is to be accepted," on the contrary, becomes subject to censure for his words, which are unacceptable to both the virtuous and all philosophical systems.
[Objection: "In that case, then, the activity of this teacher is not for the sake of benefiting others.
Why do you speak thus? [Response: Listen, I shall demonstrate this: those listeners who are like me, by virtue of their own limited intelligence..."

Those who do not know the distinction between what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted might, upon hearing the true nature of all philosophical systems (*sarvadarsana-satattva*), instead form this understanding:
"All philosophical systems, for their part, propound mutually contradictory claims."
Furthermore, among those [views], it cannot be determined which one is ultimately real; therefore, what is the use of these views that are so difficult to discern?
For whatever is pleasing to oneself is precisely what should be practiced.
In this way, at this time, many such people who do not understand the distinctions are encountered.

Thus, the activity of the wise author of the treatise, though undertaken for the sake of helping others, has instead resulted in the activity of bringing harm to the majority; and from that, [what] gain?

If it is argued that "the destruction of the very root has occurred for one who desires [this]," we say no; for since the author of the treatise proceeded solely for the benefit of all, no harm whatsoever can be established against anyone, by means of the qualifiers.
Because even the distinction between what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted is indicated by being perceived by a few who possess aesthetic sensitivity (sahṛdaya).
For instance: "Having bowed to the Jina, the true vision; and to the true, that which exists as reality. (P:651.p.5)
Based on the statement in the *Anekārthanāmamālā*, "praśasta" means "praised" or "good";

thus, "sat" means "truth," and not "untruth. He whose view is considered to be such [truth]—that is the one to be qualified as "the Jina" (the Victor), referring here to any one among the twenty-four Jinas.

Having bowed to one among the Victors (*jina*)— who is called "Victor" (*jinam*) because he has conquered the enemies such as passion (*rāga*) along with their lineage, and who is "free from passion" (*vītarāgam*)— by means of these two words, [the author pays homage] to all twenty-four Victors.

It has been indicated that there is no difference of opinion among them. If it is asked, "In that case, how is it that there is a mutual difference of opinion between the Śvetāmbaras and the Digambaras? it is said in reply:
P:61.p.6) "Fundamentally, there is no mutual distinction among these; rather, it is merely subsequent.
What kind of Victor? One who is not a hero (avīra). "Āḥ" is the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū); "Aḥ" is Kṛṣṇa; "U" is the Lord of the Moving (urīścara).
By the combination of the three vowels *ā*, *a*, and *u*, the form *oḥ* is established. (P. 61. p.
6) [The term] *anīra* means "he does not set in motion," but rather "he impels by means of removing that [false] opinion. Thus, the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule *avīra*.
This refers to those who hold the views of the creator of creation and so forth—namely, Brahmā, Kṛṣṇa, Īśvara, and Devatā.
The meaning is "devoid of a Lord."
Likewise, there is the teacher of *syād-vāda*.
[The word] *syād-vāma* means "they cut" (*dyanti*); by applying the suffix *ḍa* according to the rule "in some cases *ḍa*," it becomes *syād-vāda-dāsa*.
[He is so called] because of his proclamation of refutations such as the contradiction between reality and appearance.

The meaning of "of the cutter of the *syād-vāda*" is as follows: that which sharpens (*śyati*)— that is, diminishes (*tanūkaroti*)— their mark (*lakṣmī*) or greatness (*mahiman*) by means of refuting their respective doctrines, is the locus of *syād-vāda*.
*Kai* (kai gai rai śabde); *kāyati* means "it speaks. By the rule *kvacid ḍaḥ*, the suffix *ḍa* is applied, resulting in the word *kam*.
[The term refers to] that whose teaching is the doctrine of *syād-vāda* (*kam-vacana*).
By this qualification, all previously mentioned [schools], such as the Buddhists and others, [are excluded].
The meaning is that this statement brings about the destruction of the views of those who maintain *sambhava* and *aitihya* as valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), headed by Caraka and others.
Having bowed to the Jina, by me... [P:61.p.6]
The author of the treatise has stated that "the meaning expressed by all philosophical systems (darśanas) is here being declared.
Furthermore, in this context, the action of bowing (*namana-kriyā*) is connected to a prior time,
because the suffix *ktvā* denotes a preceding temporal sequence.

The act of articulation (*nigadana-kriyā*), however, belongs to the present; and these two are not untenable when being performed by the single author of the text. Furthermore, in the Buddhist view, it is possible for the agency of all conventional discourse to belong to a single [momentary] cognition; therefore—
Because of the acceptance of momentary entities.

P:61.p.6) Therefore, someone might consider the Buddhist doctrine to be worthy of adoption because it was stated at the beginning of this present work. To prevent that [misconception], [the author says]: P:71.p.7) tan-nivāraṇāya.
Although the refutation of the Buddhist system was already included among the previously mentioned qualifications, it should be understood that it is indicated here once again.
The manner of refuting these other philosophical systems is to be learned from another work.
Thus, by means of these specific qualities, [the author], while declaring the Jina’s vision of the truths and his status as the speaker who conquers all other philosophical systems, [refutes] all...
The fact that non-Jaina systems are to be abandoned and the Jaina system is to be accepted is indicated [here] and should be understood;
therefore, it is not from this author [that such a view follows].

"Even for those who do not recognize the distinction between the true and the false, some degree of harm is possible," because that distinction is also manifested [to them]. Regarding this, another person says:

[Objection: But what is the fate of those for whom there will be no correct adherence to the words of the author of the treatise, which reveal the distinction between the true and the false views? [Response: It is said: For those...
Those who are to be cultivated [as objects of reliance] are of two kinds:

some possess a neutral mind due to the absence of attachment and aversion; others, however, have minds difficult to penetrate because they are turbid with the defilements of attachment, aversion, and so forth.

P:71.p.7) For those whose minds are difficult to enlighten, even for an omniscient one it is difficult to effect the comprehension of the distinction between truth and falsehood, let alone for anyone else.
Thus, disregarding them and addressing those with impartial minds, [the author] proceeds by means of the repetition of qualifiers.
He states the means for knowing the distinction between the true and the false: "right vision" (*saddarśana*). How is right vision? It is the vision—that is, the knowledge—of the *sat* (the good).
That is to say, the *sat* are the virtuous ones whose minds are impartial. Their vision is their knowledge.

That is to say, he is the "True Vision" (saddarśana) because from that Hero arises the knowledge of the distinction between true and false doctrines, by virtue of his being capable of correctly examining the status of a trustworthy authority (āpta).
By this, the very nature of the illustrious Vīra as a trustworthy authority and so forth is established.

It is indicated that [this] must be examined. Alternatively, he is "one who possesses right vision" (*saddarśana*) because his vision of the virtuous (*satām*)— that is, of the good people— is characterized by faith in the meaning of reality (*tattvārtha*).

Alternatively, "existent" (*sat*) refers to existing categories such as the living being (*jīva*) and so forth; "vision" (*darśana*) is the correct observation of these. He from whom [this vision proceeds] is *saddarśana*. Why is he of such a nature?
Because he is the teacher of the doctrine of "may-be" (*syād-vāda*).
This is the discourse on non-origination (*advaya-bhāṣaṇa*) previously mentioned. To the question "Why is it even of such a kind?", he says:
Because the *Jina*—one whose nature is the conquest of passion, hatred, and so forth—is free from passion, he does not speak what is untrue, for that cause is absent; such is the meaning.
The explanation of the remaining verses is as before.

And thus, it is said here as follows: for those who will perform a proper examination of Śrī Vīra’s status as a trustworthy authority (*āpta*) and so forth, and who, having impartially and correctly observed the *syād-vāda* propounded by him, subsequently [examine] even the doctrines of others—
They will behold [the truth],
and they themselves will realize even the distinction between what is true and what is false; for what is the use of paying or not paying heed to our words?

By this, it should be understood that the author of the work has demonstrated complete impartiality regarding this matter; furthermore, the means for thoroughly discerning the distinction between what is true and what is false has been stated here with a view toward [others'] welfare, and it was indeed in this very manner that it was taught by the ancients as well.
Because it effects the distinction between seeing what is true and what is false.
As it was said by the venerable Śrī Haribhadra Sūri himself in the *Lokatattvanirṇaya*:
"That Blessed One is not our kinsman, nor are others our enemies."
Not even one among these has been directly encountered by us;
yet, having heard their words and their various distinguished deeds, we have taken refuge in the Hero out of a longing for his preeminent virtues. (1)
I have no partiality for the Hero (the Buddha), nor do I harbor hatred toward Kapila and the others;
one should accept the words of whoever possesses logical reasoning. //2//
The venerable Hemasūri also stated in the *Vīrastuti*:
"O Vīra, our partiality toward you is not due to mere faith, nor is our lack of taste for others born of mere hatred;
rather, it is because we have examined your status as a truly authoritative teacher and have taken refuge in you alone, O Lord."
We are. //1//
Objection: Here, the subject matter denoted by "all philosophical systems" (sarva-darśana) has been introduced for exposition, and that [subject] exceeds all numerical limits.
How, then, can it be expressed by this very brief treatise?
Because non-Jaina systems of thought—also known by the name *parasamaya* (other doctrines)—are innumerable;
as it has been said: [P:91.p.9]
In the *Sammati-sūtra*, the venerable Siddhasena Divākara states:

(P:91.p.9) "As many as are the paths of speech, so many indeed are the systems of viewpoints (*nayavāda*); as many as are the systems of viewpoints, so many indeed are the heterodox doctrines (*parasamaya*). //1//"

Commentary: Regarding an entity that consists of infinite attributes (*anantadharmātmaka*), the determination of one part of it while being independent of other parts is an impure perspective (*apariśuddhanaya*). That very thing is called a path of speech (*vacanamārga*).

Thus, for an entity that consists of infinite properties (*anantadharman*), as many modes of determination as there may be regarding its individual parts— each considered independently of the other parts— are all *nayās* (standpoints), and they are impure. Furthermore, these are paths of speech (*vacanamārga*).
It is said: Therefore, this is the meaning of the verse:

In every entity, however many and of whatever number the paths of speech (*vacanapatha*)—that is, the ways of expression consisting of the various linguistic paths of words that denote mutually distinct parts [of that entity]—there are modes of determination (*avadhāraṇaprakāra*).
There are exactly as many *nayavādās*— that is,
discourses (*vādāḥ*) or expositions (*pratipādakāḥ*)— as there are modes of determining specific partial aspects (*tat-tad-eka-deśa-avadhāraṇa-prakārāḥ*) of the *nayās*.

Types of words: (P:91.p.9) As many as there are types of words that express the definitive determination of each individual part of the various doctrinal systems (*nayavāda*), so many indeed are the heterodox systems (*parasamaya*) or other philosophical schools (*paradarśana*).
Because the systems of others are based on conceptual constructions fashioned by one's own desires, and because such conceptual constructions are innumerable;
this is the point: however many there may be among people who [grasp] various partial aspects of this or that distinct entity...
There would be as many types of words expressive of restriction as there are systems of other schools;
therefore, those [systems] are indeed infinite, being conceptual constructions fashioned by the craftsmen of one’s own imagination.
Because they are indefinite, the various doctrines arising from them are likewise limited to that same number; thus, the systems of other schools transcend all calculation.

Alternatively, in the second limb known as the *Sūtrakṛta*, three hundred and sixty-three heterodox teachers are enumerated. This verse summarizes their meaning: P:101.p.10) Or else, in the second limb called the Sūtrakṛta, three hundred and sixty-three proponents of other doctrines are enumerated.
This verse summarizes their meaning:

There are eighty-four types of proponents of action (kriyāvādins), sixty-seven types of proponents of non-action (akriyāvādins), and thirty-two types of proponents of agnosticism (ajñānavādins) and conventionalism (vainayikas). //1//

The explanation of this [verse] is as follows: "One hundred and eighty" refers to the Kriyāvādins. Among them, those whose character is such that they assert *kriyā*—namely, the existence of the soul (*jīva*) and so forth—are the Kriyāvādins, such as Marīci Kumāra, Kapila, Ulūka, Māṭhara, and others.
Furthermore, these [categories] should be understood as numbering one hundred and eighty by means of the following method:

having arranged the nine categories— namely, living beings (*jīva*), non-living beings (*ajīva*), influx (*āsrava*), bondage (*bandha*), restraint (*saṃvara*), dissociation (*nirjarā*), merit (*puṇya*), demerit (*apuṇya*), and liberation (*mokṣa*)— in their proper sequence on a tablet or similar surface.
Below the category of the living being (jīva), the distinctions between self and other (sva-para-bheda) should be set forth.

Below those two, the distinctions between eternal and non-eternal (nitya-anitya-bheda) should be placed. Furthermore, below those, the fivefold distinctions of time (kāla), the Lord (īśvara), the self (ātman), necessity (niyati), and inherent nature (svabhāva) should be arranged.
And then, the following conceptual analyses (vikalpa) should be performed, as follows:
P:101.p.10) There is one alternative view: that the living being exists inherently and eternally in terms of time.
And this is the meaning of this conceptual construction: indeed, this self exists in its own form and is eternal in terms of time, according to the view of those who propound time (*kālavādin*).
And those who maintain that the entire world is produced by time alone are to be considered proponents of time.
They hold this view, and thus they say:
"Without time, there would be no blooming of flowers or the production of fruit in plants such as the *campaka*, *aśoka*, and *sahakāra*."
The onset of the rains, marked by the conception of stars through the falling of cold showers clinging to droplets of frost; the divisions of the seasons brought about by these changes;
and the arrival of childhood, youth, old age, wrinkles, and grey hair.
These specific states are possible because they are perceived precisely according to their respective temporal divisions; otherwise, everything [would occur at once].
[The effect] would arise without a fixed order;
however, this is neither observed nor accepted. Furthermore, even the cooking of mung beans is not seen to occur in the world without the passage of time, but rather through a temporal sequence.
Otherwise, when the conjunction of the causal complex consisting of the pot, fuel, and so forth is possible, its existence would occur even at the first moment;
yet it does not occur. Therefore, whatever is produced is all brought about by time.
And so it has been said:
"Whatever arises in the world—whether it be the embryo, the infant, or auspicious events and the like—it does not occur apart from time; indeed, that [time] is the cause. (1)
Furthermore, even the cooking of mung beans is not observed in the absence of time;
therefore, even when a pot and other such factors are present, that [cooking] is held to depend upon time. //2//

And in the absence of time, everything beginning with conception would occur without any fixed order, because that [conception] would arise merely from the existence of the causes desired by the opponent. //3//
Time ripens all beings; Time destroys all creatures.
Time remains awake while others sleep, for Time is indeed difficult to overcome. (As is the staff [of punishment] while others sleep.)
In the Epic (e.g., MBh. 3.148.8d, etc.), [the word] *jāgarti* [is used].
Here, "merely from the existence of the cause desired by the opponent" means merely from the existence of the cause consisting of the union with a woman or a man as conceived by the opponent.
"Because it arises from that" means because it arises from [the seeds of] Garga and others.
Likewise, time cooks— that is, it brings to maturity, it brings to transformation— the elements, such as earth and the rest.
Likewise, Time destroys living beings; having displaced them from their previous state, Time establishes living beings in other states through subsequent transformations.
Likewise, Time remains awake while others sleep; it is Time alone that [overcomes] sleeping people with calamities.
The meaning is that it protects.
Therefore, it is clear that time is difficult to overcome; it is impossible to cast it off.
In the very same manner as previously stated, the second alternative should also be formulated; however, where it was said "of those who propound time," one should say "of those who propound Īśvara.
For example: "The soul exists, is eternal by its own nature, and is devoted to Īśvara."
Furthermore, the proponents of Īśvara maintain that the entire world was created by Īśvara,
and that Īśvara possesses the fourfold nature consisting of innate knowledge, dispassion, dharma, and sovereignty.
And [He is] the impeller of living beings toward heaven and liberation. As it has been said:
"Whose knowledge is unimpeded, whose dispassion belongs to the Lord of the World, and who possesses sovereignty and virtue—this fourfold set is innate. (1)

P:121.p.12) "This ignorant creature is not master of its own pleasure and pain; impelled by Īśvara, it goes either to heaven or indeed into the abyss. [Verse 2] And so forth. The third alternative concerns those who maintain the existence of a self (*ātman*) and so on. Among them, the proponents of the self (*ātmavādin*) maintain that the person (*puruṣa*) alone is this [self].
They have understood [the teaching] beginning with "all," and so forth.
The fourth alternative belongs to those who maintain the doctrine of necessity (*niyativādin*). For they say:
"There exists a distinct reality called necessity (*niyati*), by the power of which all these existents attain manifestation in a strictly determined form, and not otherwise."
For instance: whenever something arises from something else, it is perceived as arising from that very source in a strictly determined form;
otherwise, neither the established relationship between cause and effect nor the established distinction of specific forms would be possible.

It would [not] be so, because there is no restrictive factor (*niyāmaka*). Therefore, who indeed— being skilled in the path of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)— would be able to subvert this necessity (*niyati*), which is perceived precisely through the certainty of the effect?
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the path of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be obstructed elsewhere as well. And so it has been said:
Since all entities exist only in a determined form, they are born of necessity (*niyati*), because they are permeated by that very nature. //1//

Whatever arises from whatever cause, at whatever time, and in whatever manner—at that very time, from that very cause, and in that very manner—it is necessarily produced by logical necessity; who is capable of subverting this? //2//
The fifth alternative belongs to the proponents of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavādin*). For the proponents of intrinsic nature say this:
"In this world, transformation occurs from the very self of a thing; that is its intrinsic nature. All entities arise by the power of their intrinsic nature."

For instance: from clay a jar arises, not a cloth or the like; likewise, from threads a cloth is produced, not a jar or the like. And this restricted manner of arising would not be possible without such an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
It is like the arrangement of pots and jars.
Therefore, all this should be understood as produced by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). And so they have said:
"Who creates the sharpness of thorns? Who creates the diverse forms of beasts and birds?"
And: "All this has proceeded by way of its own nature; there is no acting according to one's will—how then could there be effort? (1)
The thorn of the jujube tree is sharp, straight, single, and curved;
its fruit is round—tell me, by whom was this fashioned? (2)
And so forth.
Furthermore, let alone other sets of effects, even the cooking of mung beans here cannot occur without an inherent nature (*svabhāva*). To explain:
Even when the collection of conditions such as a pot, fuel, and time is present, the cooking of *kaṅkadhuka* beans is not observed; therefore,
whatever does not occur in the absence of something else follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that thing.

If that were produced [by something else], then even the cooking of mung beans would have to be admitted as produced by an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, it must be understood that this entire collection of things has its cause in intrinsic nature alone.
Thus, five alternatives are obtained by the term "from itself" (*svataḥ*). Likewise, five are also obtained by the term "from another" (*parataḥ*).
"From another" means that the self exists as a form distinguished from others, because—
This is well known:

the determination of the intrinsic nature of all things occurs in dependence upon the intrinsic nature of other things, just as [the determination of] length and so forth occurs in dependence [upon its opposite].

The determination of shortness and so forth [occurs in this way]: having thus perceived pillars and other objects within the self, a cognition distinct from them arises. Therefore, that which is the essential nature of the self is determined only through something else, not by itself.
Thus, ten conceptual alternatives are obtained by not abandoning permanence.
Likewise, by means of the final term as well, all combined amount to twenty. And these are obtained through the category of the living being (*jīva*).

P:141.p.14) Thus, regarding each of the eight categories beginning with non-living entities (ajīva), twenty variations are obtained for each. Therefore, twenty multiplied by nine results in one hundred and eighty variations for the proponents of action (kriyāvādins).

P:141.p.14) Likewise, for those who assert that action is impossible for any entity that persists even for a single moment because it perishes immediately after its arising— they are proponents of non-action (*akriyāvādins*), meaning they are proponents of the non-existence of the self (*ātman*) and so forth.
And they [are] Kokrula, Kaṇṭhevid, Viromaka, Sugata, and so forth;
likewise, some say:
"All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary; how can there be activity in things that are unstable?"
For those [who hold this view], existence itself is the action, and that very same thing is called the cause. //1//
These amount to eighty-four. This should be understood by the following method:
one sets out the seven categories of entities, beginning with the living and the non-living, excluding merit and demerit;
beneath each of these, one applies the conceptual distinctions of self and other.
Because the self (*ātman*) does not exist, the conceptual constructions of permanence and impermanence do not apply to it.
Below the five [categories] beginning with time (*kāla*), the sixth, *yadṛcchā* (chance), is placed.
Here, all proponents of *yadṛcchā* are, consequently, proponents of non-action (*akriyāvādin*).
Previously, chance (*yadṛcchā*) was not proposed.

Therefore, there is this conceptual expression (*vikalpābhilāpa*): "The living being (*jīva*) does not exist by itself from the perspective of time"—this is one conceptual alternative (*vikalpa*). This is the meaning.

P:141.p.14) Here, the existence of categories is ascertained either through their defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) or through their effect (*kārya*). Now, there is no such defining characteristic of the self (*ātman*) by which we might establish its existence; nor...
"The production of mountains and the like occurs from atoms, just as effects [arise];
therefore, there is no self (*ātman*).
Thus it is argued by those who maintain doctrines such as [the existence of] a Lord (*īśvara*), up to those who advocate for chance (*yadṛcchā*).
The conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are to be expressed.
All of them together constitute six conceptual constructions. Furthermore, the meaning of these conceptual constructions is to be contemplated as before.

The only difference is that [it arises] "by chance" (*yadṛcchātaḥ*), according to the view of those who propound chance (*yadṛcchāvādinaḥ*); for chance is the attainment of an object not preceded by intention (*anabhisandhipūrvikā*).

Now, who are those proponents of chance (*yadṛcchāvādins*)? It is said: here, those who do not accept a fixed causal relationship among entities in terms of their continuity, but rather [accept it] by chance, they are [the proponents of chance].
The proponents of chance (*yadṛcchāvādinaḥ*) speak thus:
"Indeed, there is no fixed causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) among things, because it is not apprehended by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in that way. For instance:"
From a lotus root (*śālūka*) a lotus root is born; from cow dung also a lotus root is born;
from fire fire is born, and also from the wood of the fire-drill (*araṇi*).
From smoke smoke is born, and also from the contact of fire and fuel.
From a bulb, too, a kandalī plant arises; from a seed as well.
Banyan trees and others arise from seeds, and even from a single part of a branch.
From a seed of *go-dhūma* grass, *go-dhūma* grass arises, and also from a seed of bamboo.
Consequently, there would be no fixed causal relationship whatsoever;
one must therefore conclude that anything arises from anything else by mere chance.
Indeed, it is not possible for those who perceive the existence of things in one way to represent themselves as perceiving them otherwise.
The discerning ones cause [the world] to suffer. As it has been said:
"All the various kinds of pleasure and pain that arise for people occur unexpectedly;
like the striking of a crow by a palm fruit, they do not exist as preceded by conscious intent."
"Fruitless pride" (vṛthābhimāna), and so forth;
[it is said that] "everything seen in the world, such as birth, old age, death, and so on, is like a crow... (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya 151.15).
Regarding the phrase "by means of the two [sets of] palm-claps": thus, six alternatives are obtained from the perspective of self;
likewise, six alternatives are also obtained from the perspective that time does not exist from another.
P:161.p.16) All twelve permutations combined are obtained under the category of "living being" (*jīva*).
Likewise, twelve permutations are obtained for each of the six categories, beginning with "non-living being" (*ajīva*).
Then, twelve multiplied by seven result in eighty-four;
these are the conceptual constructions of those who propound non-action (akriyāvādins).

Similarly, "ignorance" (*ajñāna*) is contemptible knowledge; those who possess this are the *Ajñānikas*. Thus, from the word *ajñāna*, the suffix *ikap* is added in the sense of possession according to the rule *tato 'nekasvarāt*. Alternatively, they are called *Ajñānikas* because they act through ignorance (*ajñānena caranti*).
Sākalya, Sātyamugri, Maudgalya, Phālguṇi, Bādarāyaṇa, Jaimini, Vasu, and others were characterized by the realization that the bondage of karma performed unintentionally is fruitless and so forth.

For they speak thus: "Knowledge is not the highest good; because when that [knowledge] exists, there is the proliferation of errors, and due to the occurrence of mental turbidity and so forth arising from the state of dispute, there is the further prolongation of saṃsāra."
Furthermore, when ignorance is relied upon, then there is no arising of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*), nor is there the state of mental turbidity toward another; consequently, there is no arising of bondage.
Moreover, that karmic bondage which is performed intentionally has a terrible maturation (*vipāka*). Therefore—
This [karma] must necessarily be experienced because it is produced through an intense mental resolve (*tīvra-adhyavasāya*).
However, that which is performed merely through the activity of body and speech without the operation of the mind—
since there is no mental attachment (*abhiniveśa*) therein— it does not necessarily have to be experienced.
Nor does it have a harsh ripening; rather,
that attachment to karma— consisting merely of the dust and grime upon walls whitened with plaster-paste that has become utterly dry— is itself dispelled by the wind of pure resolve.
Furthermore,
the absence of mental clinging arises from the acceptance of ignorance,
because clinging is possible only when there is knowledge. Therefore, it is precisely ignorance that must be [abandoned] by one seeking liberation.

P: (17161.p.17) It must be accepted by one who has set out upon the path to liberation, not mere knowledge. Furthermore, the acceptance of knowledge would be appropriate only if it were possible to achieve certainty regarding that knowledge.
To the extent that this very [cognition] cannot be established— for indeed, all those who hold philosophical views have each maintained that cognition is strictly distinct from one another—
it is therefore impossible to reach a certainty as to whether "this is correct" or "that is correct."

P: (171.17) Now, if it is argued that the knowledge which arises from the teaching of the Blessed Vardhamāna— who directly perceives the totality of all things— is correct and not otherwise, because [other knowledge] is rooted in one who is not omniscient;
P:

(171.17) This is true; however, how is it to be understood that he alone is the direct perceiver of the entire multitude of things, and not the Sugata or others as accepted by the Buddhists and other schools?
P:171.p.17) Since there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend that [object], the doubt remains as it was.
P:171.p.17) But surely, he from whom the gods came down from heaven and performed worship and so forth— he alone [is the one].

If it is argued that Vardhamāna is omniscient, whereas the others such as Sugata and so forth are not, we say no; for Vardhamāna is long past, and there is currently no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend his existence.
If it is argued that [the truth of the matter] is determined from tradition (*sampradāya*), then one must ask:
how is it to be known whether that very tradition was initiated by a deceitful person or by a truthful person?

Because there is a lack of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). Nor are we capable of accepting that which lacks a valid means of cognition; let there be no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)! Furthermore:

Just as magicians, though themselves not omniscient, desiring to manifest their own state of omniscience in the world, display through the power of such sorcery gods moving here and there and performing worship and other rites for them;
P:171.p.17) Furthermore, how can his omniscience be ascertained even from the sight of the arrival of the gods?
Thus said Samantabhadra, the Jaina author of hymns:
"The splendors such as the arrival of the gods, celestial chariots, and yak-tail whisks..."
They are seen even among magicians; therefore, you are not great to us. //1//
Or, let it be that Vardhamānasvāmin was omniscient; nevertheless,
this instruction consisting of the *Ācārāṅga* and so forth belongs to him, and not to anyone else.
How is it to be determined that [this teaching] was composed and set in motion by a deceiver?
Because there is a lack of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding an object that transcends the senses.
Or, even if this instruction were indeed his [the Buddha's], nevertheless, its meaning is as follows:
It is not possible to understand that [the word] refers to nothing else,
for words function in the world with multiple meanings, as is observed to be the case.
P:181.p.18) Therefore, if there is the possibility of another meaning [being intended], how can there be certainty regarding the intended meaning?
For, since the mental states of others are not perceptible to one who is still under the veil of ignorance (*chadmastha*), how could it be known that "this [person]..."?
"The intention of the Omniscient One is such that this word was employed with this specific intention and not with any other intention.
Thus, because it is a cause for a very long cycle of existence and because there is an absence of correct certainty, [it is not the case].
It is established that knowledge is not the highest good; rather, it is ignorance alone.
And those sixty-seven types of agnostics are to be understood by this method:
here, having [placed] the categories (padārtha), such as the living (jīva) and the non-living (ajīva), somewhere on a tablet or similar surface...
Having established the limit, origination is set forth.
Below each of those nine [factors], beginning with the living being (jīva), seven [factors] starting with existence (sattva) are placed. For example:

Existence (1), non-existence (2), both existence and non-existence (3), inexpressibility (4), existence and inexpressibility (5), non-existence and inexpressibility (6), and both existence and non-existence and inexpressibility (7).
Among these, existence is the state of being present by way of its own nature (1); non-existence is...

2. Non-existence by way of another form; 3. Existence and non-existence, which is existence and non-existence by way of its own form and another form respectively. (P:181.p.18) Likewise, that very same existence and non-existence [is so called] when they are to be expressed simultaneously by a single word.
4. When it is held that no word whatsoever exists to denote that [entity], there is "ineffability" (*avācyatva*).
5. But when one part is existent while another part is ineffable, and both are intended to be expressed simultaneously, there is "existence-and-ineffability" (*sad-avācyatva*).
6. But when one part is non-existent while another part is ineffable...
Regarding that state of being existent, non-existent, and inexpressible (sad-asad-avācyatva):
when one part is existent, another is non-existent, and yet another is further inexpressible, then there is [the state of being existent,
non-existent, and inexpressible].

P:191.p.19) Or rather, "it is to be expressed" (vācya-vat). And no alternative beyond these seven alternatives is possible, because everything is included within these very ones. Therefore, seven alternatives have been presented.
The seven conceptual constructions, when multiplied by nine, become sixty-three. Regarding origination, there are only the first four conceptual constructions, namely:
existence, non-existence, both existence and non-existence, and the inexpressible. The remaining three conceptual constructions [apply to the other categories].
Because it depends on the parts of the object after its production has occurred, it is not possible in this case; therefore, it was not mentioned.
These four alternatives are included within the sixty-three [possibilities].
Then, sixty-seven [alternatives] arise.
Among them, the first alternative is: "Who knows that the soul exists? The meaning is that no one knows this, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend it.

Or what is the use of that which is already known? For that which is known serves as a cause for dogmatic attachment and thus stands as an obstacle to the next world. In this same way, the conceptual constructions such as "non-existent" and so forth should also be cultivated.
P:191.p.19) Furthermore, who knows whether origination belongs to that which exists, that which does not exist, that which both exists and does not exist, or that which is inexpressible?
And even if it were known, there would be no purpose whatsoever in knowing it.
Likewise, those who act according to discipline (*vinaya*) are called *vainayikas*,
such as Vasiṣṭha, Parāśara, Vālmīki, Vyāsa, Ilāputra, Satyadatta, and others.

These should be understood as characterized by the practice of discipline and the realization of the Vinaya, even though their signs and conduct are not fixed. They are to be seen as numbering thirty-two through this method:
appearing in the forms of gods, kings, ascetics, elders, and the eight [types of] parents, beginning with the lowliest.
Discipline (*vinaya*) should be practiced through body, mind, speech, and giving that is appropriate to the place and time;
thus, the four [factors] beginning with the body are established.
When these four are multiplied by eight, they become thirty-two.
Thus, these three hundred and sixty-three (or sixty,
according to the text) systems of other views come to be.
Alternatively, even regarding the nature of the world, many proponents dispute in various ways;
for instance,
some declare that the world is born from Nārī and Īśvara, while others say it originates from Soma and Agni.
The Vaiśeṣikas [assert] the sixfold categories, beginning with substance and quality; some say it was created by Kaśyapa, others by Dakṣa Prajāpati;
some say it was created from the single form of the triad beginning with Brahmā; and the Vaiṣṇavas say it consists of Viṣṇu.
The followers of the Purāṇas [hold that caste] was born from the mother produced by Brahmā, who himself was born from the lotus from Viṣṇu’s navel; some [of them] hold it to be without [such origin].
Others [hold that it] was created by Brahmā through [the application of] colors and so forth; still others [hold it] to be produced by time.
Some say it was created by the Lord whose eight forms are earth and the rest;
others say it arose from the birth of the Brahmins and other castes from the mouth and other parts of Brahmā; the Sāṃkhyas say it originated from primordial nature (prakṛti).

The Śākyas [assert] that it is representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*). Others [hold it to be] of the nature of a single living soul; some [hold it to be] of the nature of multiple living souls; others [hold it to be] produced by past karma;
still others [hold it to be] born of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); some [hold it to be] arisen from the elements composed of imperishable atoms (*akṣarajātabhūta*). Some...
Aṇḍaprabhava [asserts] that it arises from an egg; Āśramin, however, [asserts] it is without cause; Pūraṇa [asserts] it is produced by destiny; Parāśara [asserts] it arises through transformation.
Some hold that [the world] is accidental; others are proponents of non-unity, asserting that it possesses a manifold nature.
There exist various proponents of such views, such as the Turuṣkas, who maintain that the lords of the earth (*gosvāmin*) originate from a single divine being, and so forth.
The essential nature of these [categories] should be understood from the *Lokatattvanirṇaya* by Haribhadra.
Thus, there are no dissenting views regarding the nature of the soul as being omnipresent and so forth, nor regarding the nature of the movement of the celestial spheres and so forth.
Likewise, among the Buddhists there exist eighteen divisions of schools,
or distinctions such as the Vaibhāṣikas, Sautrāntikas, Yogācāras, Mādhyamikas, and so forth.

And there are many divergent views regarding Jaimini’s [work] composed by his disciples: "Ombeka knows the *Kārikā*, Prabhākara knows the *Tantra*, Vāmana knows both, but Revana knows nothing at all. (1)
There are also many other internal divisions, such as the Bahu-udaka, Kūṭīcara, Haṃsa, Paramahaṃsa, Bhāṭṭa, Prabhākara, and others; and among the Sāṃkhyas, there are the Cakraka and so forth.
Differences:
Regarding the nature of the deities, the principles, the means of valid cognition, liberation, and so forth, there are also differences among all other philosophical systems.
P:1.p.2 There exist many differences of opinion, composed by various lineages of disciples or by various authors of treatises.
Thus, in this way, many philosophical systems (darśanas) are spoken of in the world.

P:1.p.2 And since it is impossible to describe all of those [deities] here in this brief introductory treatise due to the distinctions among the principles of the deities (*devatā-tattva*) and the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how then has the Teacher [proceeded] in this regard?

"Since the objects denoted by all philosophical systems (sarva-darśana) are being declared," thus it was promised that an object impossible to speak of would be spoken of— [an object] as utterly [unfathomable] as the measurement of a finger-breadth in the sky, or like the counting of every grain of sand on both shores of the ocean.
If it is argued that "this matter undertaken is difficult to accomplish," [we reply:
this is true, provided that this matter were introduced with reference to its internal subdivisions.

However, since it was only with respect to the primary divisions that all these philosophical systems were intended as the subject matter here, and the promise to speak concerning them alone was made— not with respect to their subsequent subdivisions— therefore, there is no fault whatsoever.
P: We, while explaining all these words, have indeed already demonstrated this meaning previously; however, because you are prone to forgetfulness, you have caused it to be forgotten.
The author of the treatise also states this very same point directly:

"In this system, there are exactly six philosophical systems (darśanas) when considering the fundamental divisions; these should be understood by the wise according to the distinctions among the deities and the principles (tattvas). (2)

P:1.p.2 Regarding this subject at hand, in this treatise, only six philosophical systems (darśanas) are to be known by the wise and intelligent, with respect to their fundamental divisions— that is, depending on their primary distinctions—
and not otherwise.

With respect to their intermediate subdivisions, there are more; however, because they are ultimately included within these very ones, the word "only" (*eva*) is used with restriction to state that there are exactly six. For what reason do the root divisions consist of six?
Having raised this doubt, he says: "By means of the distinction of the reality of the deities" (*devatā-tattva-bhedena*).
Here, "deities" (*devatāḥ*) refers to the gods themselves; the suffix *-tā* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*).
"Realities" (*tattvāni*) are objects established by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaiḥ*), which exist in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha-santaḥ*). [This occurs] in a *dvandva* compound.
The *devatā-tattvas*, by their differentiation—that is, by their distinctness. Therefore, this is the meaning here:
(P:22) by way of the differentiation of the *devatā-tattvas*, there are exactly six root divisions of the systems of vision (*darśana*).
"Therefore, only six systems of philosophy will be discussed here, and not more, even in consideration of further subdivisions.
By this, it is shown that although the word "all" was used in the preceding verse, only six systems of philosophy are intended here.
It should be understood that this indicates they have been promised to be spoken.

Now he states the names of the six philosophical systems: "The Bauddha, the Naiyāyika, the Sāṃkhya, the Jaina, the Vaiśeṣika, and likewise the Jaiminīya—these, indeed, are the names of the philosophical systems. (3)
P:22) Those Buddhas, the Sugatas, are seven: Vipaśyin (1), Śikhin (2), Viśvabhū (3), Krakucchanda (4), Kāñcana (5), Kāśyapa (6), and Śākyasiṃha (7).
This is their Buddhist doctrine.

Those who know or study the *nyāya*, that is, the treatise on logic (*nyāyatarka*) composed by the sage Akṣapāda, are called *naiyāyikas*; this is their philosophy, the *Naiyāyika* system. Those who know *saṃkhyā*, consisting of the twenty-five principles beginning with *prakṛti*, [are the Sāṃkhyas].
Or rather, the Sāṃkhyas study [this];
or else, according to the tradition of the elders, there is also a sound "śāmkhya" beginning with the palatal [sibilant].

In this regard, there was a certain primordial distinguished person named Śaṅkha; his descendant, such as a grandson or later progeny—by applying the suffix *yañ* according to the rule for the *garga*-class—the term is *Śāṅkhyas*.
The philosophical system belonging to them is called *Sāṃkhya*, or alternatively *Śāṅkhya*.
P:22) The Jinas are the twenty-four Arhats, such as Ṛṣabha and the others; this is their doctrine, the Jaina.
By this it is shown that even among the twenty-four Jinas, there arose but one single doctrine, and not—
Furthermore, it is made known that there was some mutual disagreement among them.
The ultimate particularities (*antyaviśeṣas*) are those that reside in eternal substances. [The term] *vaiśeṣika* is derived from *vinayādibhyaḥ* with the suffix *ikaṇ* in its own sense (*svārthe*).
Those who know or study that *vaiśeṣika* [system], or who know or have studied it, [are called Vaiśeṣikas] by the addition of the suffix *aṇ*.
The Vaiśeṣikas [derive their name] from this *vaiśeṣika* [treatise].
Jaimini was the first distinguished person; this is his doctrine, the *Jaiminīya*, which has the alternative name *Mīmāṃsaka*.
The words *tathā* and *ca* here have the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). It should be understood in this same way elsewhere as well.
These six are the names of the [six] philosophical systems (*darśana*).

P:23) "Aho" is used as an address to the disciples. This address is presented here for the purpose of turning the disciples' attention toward listening to the treatise by removing their mental distractions. [Introduction] [End]
Bauddha B43: Now, according to the maxim that the explanation follows the enumeration, he first describes the Buddhist doctrine:
"In that Buddhist doctrine, the deity is said to be the Sugata."
B: It is the expositor of the four noble truths, beginning with suffering. //4//
B: Here, the word *tatra* has the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), while the word *tāvat* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*).
The meaning is: "Let other systems of philosophy remain aside for now; the Buddhist doctrine alone is first selected and stated.
Furthermore, at the outset, in order to characterize the Buddhist system and to favor the ignorant students, the nature of the Buddhists' dress, appearance, conduct, and so forth is demonstrated.
B: "The final mark [of our asceticism] consists of shaven heads, skins, and water-pots.

A soft bed in the morning, rice-gruel upon rising, a meal at midday, a drink in the afternoon, a piece of grape in the evening, sugar at midnight, and liberation at the end—this was envisioned by the son of the Śākyas. (1)
B: Having eaten pleasant food and used pleasant bedding and seating, the sage meditates pleasantly in a pleasant dwelling.
(3) [B45] Thinking that everything fallen into the alms-bowl is pure, they eat even meat.
B: On the road, they walk while wiping [the ground] for the sake of compassion toward living beings; B:
and they become exceedingly firm in their own practices, such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*);
B: such is their conduct.
B: The Three Jewels consist of the Dharma, the Buddha, and the Saṅgha. B: The goddess Tārā destroys obstacles within the Teaching.
B: The seven Buddhas, beginning with Vipaśyin, are marked with three lines on their throats; they are omniscient deities.
B: "The Buddha is the Sugata, the *dharmadhātu*," and so forth—these are his names. B:
Their temples are circular and are designated as *buddhāṇḍaka*.
B: The Buddhists are known by the names Bhikṣu, Saugata, Śākya, Śauddhodani, Sugata, Tāthāgata, and Śūnyavādin.
B: Their teachers, the authors of treatises, are headed by Śauddhodani, Dharmottara, Arcaṭa, Dharmakīrti, Prajñākara, Dignāga, and others.
B46: Now, the verse at hand is explained first:
In the Buddhist system—that is, in the Buddhist philosophy—the Sugata, the Buddha, is the deity, the god.
B: "Kila" refers to the report of a reliable authority.
B: "Of what kind is he?
B: "Of the four," and so forth.
B: They are called *āryas* because they have gone far away (*ārāt*) from all dharmas that are to be abandoned; the formation of the word follows the *pṛṣodarādi* rule.

B: They are "truths" (*satyāni*) because they are beneficial (*hitāni*) to the virtuous (*satām*), to holy persons, or to entities, as the case may be—either by bringing about liberation or by reflecting upon the true nature of things as they actually exist.
Alternatively, they are "truths" because they are beneficial to the virtuous (*sadbhyo hitāni*).
B: "Noble truths" (*āryasatyāni*) means the truths of the noble ones (*ārya*).
[He is] the one who elucidates and teaches the four realities characterized by suffering, origin, path, and cessation.
Among these, "suffering" refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandhā�*), beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*), which constitute the result and will be explained hereafter.

B: These very [factors], accompanied by craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and acting as the cause, are the "origin" (*samudaya*), based on the etymological derivation that "the suffering characterized by the five aggregates arises from this.
B: The "path" (*mārga*) is a specific state of mind having the aspects of the cause of cessation, selflessness, and so forth. B:

The suffix *al* is applied with the causative (*ṇij*) form of the root *mārg*, belonging to the *cur*-class, in the sense that it is "sought," "searched for," or "requested" by those desiring cessation.

B: Cessation is the state of the mind free from afflictions (*niḥkleśāvasthā*). [The suffix] *ghañ* is used here in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), as in: "by this, saṃsāra—characterized by a mind afflicted by passion and hatred—is ceased. Thus, the meaning is liberation (*mukti*).

Regarding the phrase "of suffering and so forth" (*duḥkhādīnām*), although the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) has many meanings, it should be understood here in the sense of "classification" (*vyavasthā*). As it has been said:
B: "The wise man should recognize that the word 'ādi' (beginning) is used in four senses: proximity, arrangement, manner, and part. (1)

B: Here, the word *ādi* (beginning) has several senses. It denotes proximity, as in "the hamlet near the village"; it denotes a fixed order or classification, as in "the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas"; it denotes a type or likeness, as in "the wealthy ones beginning with Devadatta," meaning those who are like Devadatta are wealthy; and it denotes a part, as in "the houses beginning with the pillars. In this context, however, the sense of fixed order or classification is appropriate. The term is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those for whom suffering is the first [or initial]," i.e., those whose first [experience] is suffering. //4//
B: Now, wishing to explain the truth of suffering, he says:
B48: Suffering consists of the aggregates of those in saṃsāra, and they are proclaimed to be fivefold:
consciousness, sensation, perception, mental formations, and form. //5//

B49: What is suffering? It is the reality of suffering (*duḥkha-tattva*). He says: those who wander—that is, those whose nature is to go from place to place or from existence to existence—are the *saṃsārin* aggregates (*skandhas*), whether conscious or unconscious, which are specific aggregations of atoms (*paramāṇu-pracaya-viśeṣa*).
And these aggregates are declared to be exactly five, because the statement is restrictive; there is no other aggregate called a "self" (*ātman*).
B: What are those aggregates?
B: They are proclaimed to be five.
Thus he says: "Consciousness," and so forth.

B: [They are] the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*), the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*), the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), and the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
B: The word *eva* is used for the sake of completion, and the word *ca* is used for conjunction.
B: Among these, non-conceptual cognition—such as the cognition of form, the cognition of taste, and so forth—which is specific knowledge, is the aggregate of consciousness.

B: And knowledge free from discursive thought (*nirvitarka*) should be understood as being of this nature: "For there is first a non-conceptualizing sensory perception (*ālocana-jñāna*), which is like the cognition of infants, the mute, and so forth, and consists of the pure object itself" (Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika, Pratyakṣa 112).
B50: Pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant—this is the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*).
B: For feeling arises from the ripening (*vipāka*) of karma performed in the past.
B: Likewise, once while wandering for alms, the Sugata was pierced in the foot by a thorn and said:
B: "In the ninety-first aeon from now, a man was killed by me with a spear; through the ripening of that karma, O monks, I have been pierced in the foot. Thus [he spoke].

B51: The aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is a cognition whose nature consists in the grasping of the signs of perception. In this context, "perception" refers to [notions] such as "cow," and the basis for their application is the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth. The grasping of these two is their conjunction; the meaning is that the cognition whose nature consists in such a conjunction—namely, conceptual knowledge (*savikalpaka-jñāna*) consisting in the conjunction of names, universals, and so on—is the aggregate of perception. B52: The aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is the collection of factors such as merit and demerit, through the awakening of which recollection and other such states arise regarding an object previously experienced.
B53: The aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) consists of the earth element and so forth, as well as visible form and so forth.

B54: Furthermore, no entity called the "self" (*ātman*), which is distinct from these [aggregates] such as consciousness and which serves as the substratum for pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and cognition, is apprehended by direct perception.
Nor is it [apprehended] by inference, because there is no perception of an unerring logical mark (*liṅga*).
B: Furthermore, there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) distinct from direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) that is non-contradictory with respect to its object.
B: And those five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) should be understood as lasting for only a single moment (*kṣaṇa-mātra*), and not as permanent, nor as persisting for some duration of time.
B: This will be demonstrated in the verse: "All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary" (Kārikā 7). //5//
B55: Having explained the truth of suffering through its fivefold division, he now explains the truth of origination, which is the cause of the truth of suffering:
"That from which the entire host of passions, such as attachment and the rest, arises in the world—consisting of the notions of 'self' and 'mine'—is declared to be origination. (6)

B56: Because, from the origin (*samudaya*)—that is, from within the world—the entire multitude, the complete collection, of faults such as passion and so forth (*rāgadveṣādi-doṣagaṇa*), arises and comes into being. B: What kind of multitude? He says: that which is called the state of "self" and "mine" (*ātmātmīyabhāva*). B: "Self" (*ātman*) is oneself; "mine" (*ātmīya*) is one's own. The state (*bhāva*) of those two is their essential nature (*tattva*).
B: The state of "self and what belongs to the self" (*ātmātmīya-bhāva*) means a relationship such as "this is the self" and "this is what belongs to the self.
Since this is an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), relationships such as "this is another" and "this belongs to another" are also to be understood.
That very thing is its designation (*ākhyā*); thus, it is called "the state of self and what belongs to the self."

B: This is the meaning: that from which attachment, aversion, and so forth arise—whether through the relationship of self and what belongs to the self, or through the relationship of "other" and "belonging to another"—is called the truth of origination (*samudaya*) as propounded in the Buddhist doctrine. Regarding this, one should not consider the fault of metrical breakage (*chando-bhaṅga-doṣa*) due to the presence of two quarters with seven and nine syllables respectively in the second half-verse; for this treatise is of *ārṣa* (sage-like) origin. //6//
B57: Now, elaborating upon the truths of the path and cessation, which serve as the antidotes to the truths of suffering and its origin—the causes for the progression of cyclic existence—he says:
“The habitual tendency that all conditioned phenomena are momentary—this should be understood here as the path; cessation is called liberation. (7)
B58: The most minute unit of time is a *kṣaṇa*; "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*) means existing for only a single moment.
B: "All conditioned phenomena" (*sarvasaṃskārāḥ*) refers to all things (*padārthāḥ*); the meaning is that all things perish in every moment.
B: And thus the Buddhists declare: "When a thing arises from its own causes, does it arise with a perishable nature?"
B: Or [it has] an indestructible nature.

B: If it has an indestructible nature, then, because causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)—which pervades that [nature]—is absent both successively and simultaneously, the absence of the entity (*padārtha*) itself, which is the pervaded, would follow as a logical consequence.
For it is said: "That alone is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*) which performs causal efficiency."
B: Furthermore, that eternal entity, when engaging in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), would have to act either successively or simultaneously.
It cannot act successively; for at the time of performing one causal efficiency, does its nature to perform other causal efficiencies exist or not?
If it exists, why does it perform them successively?
B: If it is argued that [the cause] depends on auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), then does some excellence (*atiśaya*) produced by that auxiliary factor affect that eternal entity, or not?
If it is produced, is it produced through the abandonment of its prior nature, or without such abandonment?
If it is through abandonment, then because its state has changed, it follows that it is non-eternal.

B: Now, if [the cause] does not abandon its prior nature, then since that eternal thing lacks any benefit produced by those [auxiliaries], what could be accomplished by depending on them? B: Or, if even something that contributes nothing is required as an auxiliary for the sake of a specific effect, that is incorrect; because— B: "If some other [factor] were required, it would have to perform some function."
B: If it performs no action whatsoever, why would it depend on anything at all? (PV 3.279) B:
Now, if at the time of performing its first causal function (*arthakriyā*), that [permanent entity] lacks the nature of performing other causal functions, then its permanence is clearly lost. B:

Alternatively, if this permanent entity were to perform its causal functions simultaneously, then because it would have performed all its causal functions in the very first moment, it would be a non-agent in the second moment.
B: And thus, that very same consequence of impermanence follows.

B: Now, if it were argued that because the entity possesses that nature, it would perform those same causal functions again and again even in the second and subsequent moments—that is incorrect; for there is no performing of what has already been performed.

B: Furthermore, all the sets of purposes to be accomplished in the second and subsequent moments would be attained in the very first moment, because the entity possesses that nature; and if it did not possess that nature, its impermanence would follow.
B: Thus, since a permanent entity lacks causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)—both successively and simultaneously—it does not arise from its own causes.

B59: Now, if it arises with a perishable nature (*vinaśvarasvabhāva*), then, in that case, because there is no obstacle, our previously stated momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) of the entire collection of entities follows. And so it has been said: "The very birth of entities is held to be the cause of their destruction."
B: "That which has been born and is not yet destroyed—by what means could it be destroyed later?

(1) B60: Now, even though impermanence exists, it is understood that for a thing such as a jar, it is perishable only at the very moment it encounters the causal complex of a mallet or similar factors, and not at every single moment.

B: [Objection: Therefore, even for impermanent entities that depend upon a cause of destruction, there is no momentariness. This is the speech of one who has not served a teacher. For when a hammer or similar instrument is present, does that nature of destruction which belongs to this jar or other object exist at its very time of production, or not? B: If it exists, then it follows that it must perish immediately after its production.
B: On the other hand, if that nature does not exist at the time of production, how could it come into being later?

B: If it is argued that such is its very nature—that having remained for some time, it must perish—then even in the presence of a hammer or other such causes, this would remain its nature; consequently, it would have to persist for that same duration once again, and thus there would be no destruction even after a hundred blows from a hammer or similar instruments. In this way, the pot and other objects would possess a lifespan lasting until the end of an aeon (*kalpa*), and thus one would be stained by the sin of destroying the established order of worldly affairs.
Even one who does not wish to accept it must concede that things are momentary (*kṣaṇakṣayitva*).

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever has a perishable nature (*vinaśvarasvabhāva*) possesses that very nature even at the time of its arising, just like the nature of a jar existing in its final moment; and since form, taste, and so forth, possess a perishable nature from the very moment they arise—this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Thus, because there is no efficacy in a cause of destruction, and because things arise from their own causes as being [already] final [in their duration], their momentariness is established.
B61: Now, if entities perish moment by moment, how then can there be the cognition "this is that very same thing"?

It is said: due to the arising of consciousness that perceives a continuous succession of similar preceding and succeeding moments, and because of the bondage of ignorance (*avidyā*), at the very moment of the dissolution of the preceding moment, another similar moment arises—just as one flame of a lamp gives rise to another—due to the uninterrupted emergence of a long-lasting stream of cognitions with identical forms. Consequently, even though the preceding moments have been utterly destroyed, the firm conviction (*adhyavasāya*) that "this is that very same [thing]" forcefully manifests.

B: Furthermore, observe that just as in the case of nails, hair, and the like, which grow back after being cut, there arises the recognition "this is that very same thing," why do you not consider this possibility here as well, O good sir?
Therefore, it is established that whatever exists is momentary.
For this very reason, it has been rightly said: "All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary."

B62: Now that which is at hand is introduced: "In the statement 'all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are momentary,' by the word 'iti' (thus), which has the sense of 'in this manner,' such [views] as 'this [person] has no self whatsoever, but there exist only continuums of moments of cognition' are also included here."

B: Therefore, the meaning is as follows: that mental cognition (*mānasī pratīti*)—which has the form "all things are momentary, there is no self," and so forth; which consists of such a latent impression (*vāsanā*) formed by a prior cognition and existing as a potency in a subsequent cognition through a succession of moments; and which is derived from the suffix *ka* in the sense of its own object—that is what is called the Noble Truth of the Path (*mārga-āryasatya*). In this Buddhist system, it is to be known and understood as a specific state of mind (*cittaviśeṣa*) characterized by the momentariness of all things, selflessness, and so on. Furthermore, it should be regarded as the cause of cessation (*nirodha*).
B63: Now he states the fourth noble truth: cessation (*nirodha*), the reality named cessation, is called liberation (*mokṣa*) or final emancipation (*apavarga*).
The meaning is that cessation, which consists of the state of the mind being free from afflictions (*niḥkleśāvasthā*), is declared to be liberation.

It should be understood that these four noble truths, beginning with suffering, which were just mentioned here by the author of the treatise, are according to the system of the Sautrāntikas alone. //7//

B64: Now, without specifying the distinctions such as those of the Vaibhāṣikas and others, but according to the Buddhist view in general, he speaks this verse with the intention of explaining those twelve categories (padārtha) that exist:
B: The five sense-faculties, the five objects beginning with sound, the mind, and the sphere of phenomena—these are the twelve spheres (āyatana). //8//
B: Explanation—the sense-faculties (*indriya*) are five in number, consisting of hearing, sight, smell, taste, and touch.
Sound and the rest—namely, sound, form, taste, odor, and touch—are the five objects (*viṣaya*), which are the domains of the sense-faculties.
The mental faculty (*mānasa*) is the mind (*citta*), which has another name, "the sphere of sound" (*śabdāyatana*).

B: "Phenomena" (*dharmāḥ*) refers to pleasure, pain, and so forth; their "abode" (*āyatana*) means their home, that is, the body. These twelve abodes just mentioned are the realities designated as "abodes. The word "and" (*ca*) is used in a conjunctive sense: not only are there the four previously mentioned [truths] such as suffering and so on, but these twelve abodes also exist. Furthermore, these abodes should be understood as being momentary.
B: For the Buddhists here argue as follows:
existence, characterized by causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), by the logic previously stated, excludes non-momentary things and remains restricted to momentary things alone.
This being the case, the inference of momentariness is easily obtained: whatever exists is momentary, just like a flame of a lamp and so forth.
B: And there are twelve sense-bases (āyatana).
By this inference, since no other object exists apart from the twelve sense-bases, momentariness is established as residing within those very twelve sense-bases. Thus it is said.

B66: Thus, having established in this way the four truths beginning with suffering according to the Sautrāntika school, and the twelve truths in the form of the sense-bases (*āyatana*) according to the general Buddhist view, it is now necessary to state here the specific definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Since that [specific definition] is inseparable from its general definition, the general definition of the means of valid cognition is stated first: "The means of valid cognition is non-discrepant knowledge" (Pramāṇavārttika 1.3). That is to say: a means of valid cognition is non-discrepant knowledge.
