B: Non-contradiction (*avisamvādakatva*) is pervaded by the capacity to bring about the attainment of the object, because that which does not bring about the attainment of the object lacks non-contradiction, as in the case of the cognition of a mass of hair (*keśoṇḍuka-jñāna*).

B: Furthermore, the capacity to bring about the attainment of the object is pervaded by the capacity to incite activity (*pravartakatva*), because that which does not incite activity does not bring about the attainment of the object.
B: Likewise, the capacity to incite activity is itself pervaded by the capacity to present the object (*viṣayopadarśakatva*).
B: For knowledge does not impel a person by seizing him by the hand; rather, it is called "impelling" and "attaining" because it prompts action by presenting its own object.
B: There is no other mode of attaining [the object] than the presentation of its own object.
B: And that [presentation] consists in the nature of a capacity.
And it has been said: "The capacity for attainment is validity (*prāmāṇya*), and that alone is the state of being an attainer (*prāpakatva*).

Furthermore, only perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) demonstrate their own objects, not any other type of cognition. Therefore, these two alone are worthy of definition, and non-contradiction (*avisamvādakatva*) is the defining characteristic common to both of them.

B: For by perception, an object that accomplishes purposeful action is presented as being apprehended through direct observation; whereas by inference, it is presented as being determined through the non-deviation of the observed mark (*liṅga*). Thus, for these two, "means of attainment" (*prāpaka*) consists precisely in their capacity to present their own respective objects.

B: Although the momentary particular (*kṣaṇa*) is the object of apprehension for perception, and since that has already ceased it is not reached [in the present], nevertheless, its continuum (*saṃtāna*) is the object of determination; and since that is reached upon practical engagement, the validity of perception consists in its being a means of attaining the indicated object by having the continuum as its domain.

In the case of inference, however, the object of apprehension is the internal form (*svākāra*) conceptualized through the observation of the mark (*liṅga*), and not the external object; whereas the external object is what is reached, having been determined as non-different from the internal form.
Thus, the validity of this [inference] also consists in its being a means of attaining the indicated object by having that [external object] as its domain.

B: As it has been said: "For one who acts after having determined an object by means of these two [perception and inference] is not deceived regarding purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). And since the object being reached is obtained with its specific place, time, and form, validity belongs only to perception and inference, which reveal such an object as it truly is, and not to other types of cognition. Therefore, there is no consequence of validity for cognitions apprehending a yellow conch-shell and the like, because they do not lead to the attainment of the object as it was presented; for those [cognitions] fail to cause one to reach the object that was displayed.

B: For the object with its specific place, time, and form that is presented by those [cognitions] is not obtained as it was presented; and that which is obtained is not presented by them in that way, because a difference in the object is established through differences in place and so forth. Thus, they do not possess the capacity to cause one to obtain the object they have presented, and consequently, they lack validity (*prāmāṇya*).

Nor is verbal testimony (*śabda*) and the like valid as a means of cognition distinct from the two [perception and inference], on the grounds that it causes one to obtain the object it presents; for since the object presented by it is not restricted by place and so forth, it is non-existent and impossible to obtain.

B: Furthermore, the non-ascertainment of the object indicated by that [cognition] is due to the impossibility of the intended object—whether directly or through a lineage of transmission—being established.
Therefore, it is established that for both [types of cognition], validity consists in non-contradiction, which has as its essential nature the capacity to reach the object indicated.

Furthermore, the capacity to lead [to the object] (*prāpaka-śakti*)—which is the cause for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) being inseparable from the object—is ascertained by the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that follows upon perception. For instance, it is said that perception—which is synonymous with "seeing" (*darśana*)—because it arises from an object, determines itself as the "seer" by producing a determinative judgment (*avasāya*) corresponding to itself; thus, it intrinsically (*svataḥ*) ascertains its validity, which consists in its inseparability from the object and its capacity to lead [to it]. It does not, however, depend on another cognition to ascertain this, just as it does not depend on another cognition to experience the object itself.
B: Therefore, it is logical that non-contradictoriness alone is the defining characteristic of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). //8//
B69; Now, desiring to describe the specific characteristics of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [the author], first establishing the number of such means, says:
"In the Buddhist system, two means of valid cognition are to be known:
perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*), because correct knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) is of two kinds. (9)

B70; Explanation: The word *tathā* (thus) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*) with respect to the principles mentioned previously, while the word *ca* (and) is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*).
B: Therefore, this is the meaning: in the Buddhist system (*saugata-darśana*), only two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are to be known, and not one, three, four, five, or six.
B: By this, it is made known that the Buddhists do not accept any other number of means of valid cognition as imagined by the Cārvākas, Sāṃkhyas, and others.

B: To the question "What are those two means of valid cognition? he says: perception and inference. B: To the question "Why are there exactly two means of valid cognition? he says: because right knowledge—that which is non-erroneous and free from contradiction—is of two kinds. B: According to the principle that "every sentence implies a restriction," it is of two kinds only, and not one kind or three kinds.

B71; Here, some say: "Just as when it is stated 'in two ways' (*dvidhā*), it means 'only in two ways' and not 'in one way' or 'in three ways,' thus excluding connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*); likewise, in cases such as 'Caitra is an archer,' Caitra would possess only archery and not heroism, generosity, fortitude, and so forth. This is incorrect; for even according to the maxim that "every sentence is restrictive" (*sāvadhāraṇam*), exclusion applies only to what is suspected [to be otherwise].
B: For a statement is indeed uttered for the sake of another; it serves only to exclude that which has been wrongly apprehended by another due to delusion.

In such cases as "Caitra is an archer," since the impossibility of Caitra being an archer is what is suspected by others, it is only that [misconception] which is excluded, and not any other property.

Here, however, the Cārvākas, Sāṃkhyas, and others have asserted that right knowledge is both unitary and manifold in various ways; therefore, by demonstrating its fixed duality, [the author] rejects both the unity and the multiplicity of right knowledge.

B: And thus, this very particle *eva*, when uttered together with a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), a qualificand (*viśeṣya*), and a verb (*kriyā*), becomes threefold respectively by virtue of its function of excluding non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*), connection with others (*anya-yoga-vyavaccheda*), and absolute non-connection (*atyanta-ayoga-vyavaccheda*). As stated in the *Viniścaya*: "The particle that functions as an exclusion (*vyatirecaka*) excludes the non-connection of a property (*dharma*), its connection with others, and indeed its absolute non-connection. (Verse 1)
B: The particle *eva* is indeed an exclusionary [particle], a restrictor.
That which is uttered together with a qualifier, a qualificand, or an action—its meaning is understood from the speaker's intention even when it is not explicitly employed. (2)
B: A statement has exclusion as its result, as for example: "Caitra is an archer," "Pārtha is an archer," or "The lotus is blue. (Pravā. 4.190–92;
B72); Furthermore, the twofold nature of correct knowledge is to be understood from the twofold nature of its objects: the perceptible and the imperceptible.

B: Since everything other than the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) here is an object that is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*), there are therefore exactly two types of objects; consequently, there are also exactly two kinds of correct cognition (*samyag-jñāna*) that apprehend them, neither fewer nor more. Among these, that correct cognition which has an imperceptible object as its domain consists in the comprehension of the imperceptible object through a general form (*sāmānya-ākāra*) derived from something else that is connected with the property-bearer (*dharmin*) to be established by it; therefore, that [cognition] is included within inference (*anumāna*). Thus, there are only two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), characterized as direct perception and inference.
B: For instance—an object that is remote (*parokṣa*) is not perceived directly by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because that would entail the consequence that it is non-remote (*aparokṣa*).

Furthermore, an independent conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) alone, like the conceptualization of kingship and so forth, lacks validity; for since it is not necessarily tied to a remote object, there is no absence of deviation (*avyabhicāra*) from it.
Nor can an object that does not exist without its own probandum (*sādhya*) be an indicator of a remote object, because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasakti*).

B: Furthermore, if that which is not even connected to the subject (*dharmin*) were a means of cognition, then, because there would be no distinction between proximity and remoteness, it would become a cause for cognition everywhere. Therefore, whatever is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that serves as the basis for the cognition of such an object is nothing other than inference (*anumāna*), because its definition is precisely this. And thus is the formal argument (*prayoga*): whatever is a means of valid cognition that is not perception is included within inference, just like [cognition] arising from the power of a logical mark (*liṅga*); and verbal testimony (*śābda*) and the rest, which are accepted as distinct means of valid cognition, are indeed means of valid cognition that are not perception. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāva-hetu*).

B: Whatever is included within something else cannot exist outside of it, just as nothing that is established as being included anywhere can exist elsewhere. And this means of valid cognition called inference is included within perception; thus, there is the "perception of what is incompatible with its own nature" (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*), because inclusion and exclusion are contradictory by virtue of being defined as mutually exclusive states.

The opponent says: "Granted that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whose object is imperceptible may be included within inference (*anumāna*), but it is not logical for those such as verbal testimony (*śabda*) whose objects are different things to be included therein. [Reply: No; because there exists no object of knowledge (*prameya*) other than the perceptible and the imperceptible, and because a means of valid cognition devoid of an object of knowledge cannot possess the status of a *pramāṇa*. For, according to the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) that "it is a *pramāṇa* because by it an object is correctly measured (*pramīyate*)," its status as a *pramāṇa* is established only when it possesses an object of knowledge.

B: For instance—whatever lacks an existing object of cognition (*prameya*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as the cognition of a [non-existent] circle of fire (*alātacakra*) and the like; and that which is accepted as another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) because its object is distinct from the two [accepted] means of valid cognition likewise lacks an existing object of cognition. This is a non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*), because an object of cognition is either directly or indirectly a cause for a means of valid cognition.
As it has been said: "That whose positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is not replicated is not a cause; and that which is not a cause is not an object."
Furthermore, it is established by perception itself that there is no other object of cognition distinct from the perceptible and the imperceptible.

B: For perception (*adhyakṣa*), arising through the power of an object standing before it, becomes the cause for the conventional usage of "perceptual" for that object precisely by manifesting as a determinate appearance whose nature is restricted to that [object]. Furthermore, by excluding from it the nature of other objects and establishing the entire collection of other objects—that is, those which are indirect (*parokṣa*)—as a separate category, it establishes the absence of a third possibility; this is because the entire collection of objects not apprehended by perception is established as being "other" and thus indirect.

B: Otherwise, if its exclusion from having the form of other objects were not established, there would be no determination of it even by way of its own form; thus, nothing at all would be apprehended through perception. For the specific nature of entities is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Otherwise, because of the consequence that everything would be perceived in every way and so forth, there would follow the destruction of all conventional usage based on specific determinations.

B: If [it is argued that] the specific nature [of an object] is not apprehended by perception, what other form of it could possibly be apprehended? Thus, by means of perception—which manifests the very nature of the object—the absence of any other object of cognition is already established.

Furthermore, the absence of such [other objects] is also understood through inference, because things whose natures consist of mutual exclusion are established as being of one particular mode precisely by the exclusion of other modes.

B: And the formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: Wherever there is the determination of one category through the exclusion of another category, there is no possibility for a third category; for example, in the case of yellow and so forth, when there is the determination of the non-blue category through the exclusion of the blue category. Now, in the case of the perceptible and the imperceptible, there is the determination of one category through the exclusion of the other, with respect to every object of knowledge (*prameya*) that is not made the object of the excluded category. This is the perception of a contradictory [property], because those two categories—being "that" and "not that"—are characterized by their existence through mutual exclusion.
B: Therefore, because there is no other object of cognition (*prameya*), there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

And it has been said: "Since no other object of cognition is possible apart from the perceptible (*pratyakṣa*) and the imperceptible (*parokṣa*), the twofold nature of the means of valid cognition is accepted on account of the twofold nature of the objects of cognition" (Pravāraṇa 2.63).

B: Here, the refutation of other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) such as verbal testimony, analogy, presumptive implication, and non-existence, or their subsumption under perception and inference, should be understood from Buddhist texts such as the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* or from [Jaina] texts such as the *Sammati-tarka*. However, it is not stated here for fear of excessive length of the work. Therefore, this remains established: there are only two means of valid cognition, namely perception and inference. //9//

B76; Now he states the definition of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*): "Direct perception is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*); let it be understood therein. B77; Explanation: "Therein" means between those two, namely direct perception and inference; "let it be understood" means let it be known. Regarding that: "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*) is that which has gone toward (*pratigata*) the sense organ (*akṣa*).
B: Of what kind?

B: Free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*). Conceptual construction is a cognition associated with the association of words; that from which conceptual construction has departed or is absent is "free from conceptual construction."
B: But surely, in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, that which ends in a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) is placed first; therefore, it should be "kalpanāpoḍha" (free from conceptual construction).

B: No, because of the rule "in *vahitāgni* and so forth," or because of the mention of the word "or" (*vā*), and because *āhitāgni* and the like belong to the class of *ākṛtigaṇa* (open-ended groups), there is no requirement for the prior placement [of the participle].

B: Alternatively, by way of etymological analysis (*kalpanā*), "apoḍha" means devoid or abandoned; thus, "kalpanāpoḍha" means devoid of conceptual constructions such as name (*nāman*), genus (*jāti*), and so forth. This is the meaning.
B: In that regard, conceptualization of a name (*nāma-kalpanā*) is, for example, "Ḍittha. Conceptualization of a genus (*jāti-kalpanā*) is, for example, "cow.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*kriyā*), and substances (*dravya*).
Among these, conceptualization of a quality (*guṇa-kalpanā*) is, for example, "white."
B: Conceptualization of action is, for example, "a cook"; conceptualization of substance is, for example, "one with a staff" or "standing on the ground.
Perception is devoid of these conceptualizations, because it arises from the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) which is itself devoid of words.
B: And it has been said: "For there are no words that are identical in nature to objects, such that they would appear when that object appears," and so forth.

By this, he rejects the status of perception for conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*) which grasps external objects such as stable, gross pots and cloths. Furthermore, what kind of perception is it?
B: It is non-erroneous (*abhrānta*), because of the statement: "Error is the apprehension of that in what is not that. B:
It does not apprehend a non-existent or unreal entity; rather, it discerns the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) characterized by momentary atoms that are mutually distinct exactly as they are.
B: By this, he rejects the status of perception for non-conceptual cognitions that are erroneous, such as the visual perceptions of those with cataracts.
B78; This direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is fourfold: sensory cognition (*indriya-jñāna*), mental cognition (*mānasa*), self-reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), and yogic cognition (*yogi-jñāna*).
B: Among these, sensory direct perception is the cognition that arises based on the five sense organs, such as the eye, and has the five external objects, such as form, as its objective support.

B: Mental cognition is the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) produced by sensory cognition acting as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), with the assistance of the object immediately following its own [sensory] object.

B: Mental cognition (*mānasa*) is that which is produced by sensory cognition—acting as the material cause (*upādāna*) and designated as the "immediately preceding condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*)—in conjunction with its immediate object, namely the second moment of the object such as a jar that was the object of the sensory cognition.

By the qualification "immediately preceding condition," the unwanted consequence that the cognition of a yogi is mental is excluded. The term "immediately preceding condition" is well-established through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) for a cognition existing within one's own continuum that acts as a material cause.
B: Therefore, with respect to the yogic cognition existing in a different continuum, there is no designation of "immediately preceding" for the minds of ordinary persons.
Self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is the self-cognition (*ātmasaṃvedana*) of all minds and mental factors (*caitta*).

Mind (*citta*) is the cognition that grasps the mere thing (*vastumātra*); mental factors (*caitta*) are those which arise in the mind and grasp the specific forms of the thing, characterized by pleasure, pain, and equanimity. That by which their own nature is cognized is self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).

B: Yogic cognition arises from the ultimate limit of the intensification of the cultivation of the real object (*bhūtārtha*). B: The "real object" is an object established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); "cultivation," moreover, is the repeated mental application [of that object].
B: Yogic cognition is that which is born from the ultimate limit of the intensification of the cultivation of the real object.

B79; [Objection: If atoms that perish moment by moment are indeed the only ultimate realities, then what is the cause of this appearance of gross objects such as pots, cloths, mats, carts, and clubs? [Reply: This appearance of gross objects is entirely without an external basis (*nirālambana*). It is set in motion by beginningless, false habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and is devoid of an objective referent (*nirviṣayatva*), like the perception of hair in the sky or like dream-cognition. As it has been said: "No external object exists in the way it is conceptualized by the ignorant;
the mind, stirred by habitual tendencies, proceeds toward the appearance of an object. (Verse 1)
B: "There is nothing else to be experienced by the intellect, nor is there another experience of it;
because it is devoid of the distinction between the grasped and the grasper, it manifests by itself.
(PV II.327) Now, one might ask: how can the *svalakṣaṇa*—the nature of atoms that perish moment by moment—be cognized through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)?
B: It is said: perception indeed perceives only the present, proximate form of an object, and not its future or past state, because those are not proximate (*asannihitatvāt*).
If it is asked: "In that case, why does a determination of momentary destruction not arise immediately after perception, just as there is a determination of the blue form?
It is said: At that very time, memory—which determines the object's connection with a previous place, time, and condition—prevents the arising of a determination of momentary destruction.

B: For this very reason, the Buddhists state this: because perception makes an object its content regardless of whether that object is momentary or non-momentary, even if non-momentariness is superimposed due to some cause of error, perception is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding non-momentariness; on the contrary, it is invalid (*apramāṇa*) because it is overcome by a contrary determination (*viparītādhyavasāya*). Nor is it a means of valid cognition regarding momentariness, because it does not produce a corresponding determination (*anurūpādhyavasāya*). However, it is a means of valid cognition with respect to the blue form itself, because it produces a determination of that very nature.
B: Therefore, it is rightly stated that perception (*pratyakṣa*) is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*).

Here, by the inclusion of the qualification "non-erroneous," and because that [qualification] is not included in the case of inference (*anumāna*), it indicates that inference is erroneous. For instance: inference is erroneous because it manifests a universal (*sāmānya*); and since a universal is untenable—being excluded by the dilemmas of whether it is distinct or non-distinct from the external particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)—inference conceptualizes the universal as having the nature of a particular.

B: Because the apprehension of that [object] within what is not its own specific characteristic (*asvalakṣaṇa*)—that is, the determination of it as a specific characteristic—is characterized by error. Furthermore, the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of inference is due to its being indirectly dependent upon the power of external specific characteristics (*bāhya-svalakṣaṇa*).

B: For instance—without an object, there is no presence of a logical mark (*liṅga*) bound by a relationship consisting of identity (*tādātmya*) or origination from that (*tadutpatti*); without that [mark], there is no cognition having that as its object; without that cognition, there is no recollection of the previously ascertained relationship; and in the absence of that recollection, there is no inference. Thus, because it is not non-deviant with respect to the object, even an erroneous [cognition] is celebrated as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

As it has been said: "For two people running toward the light of a jewel and a lamp, respectively, while perceiving them as a jewel—though there is no difference in their false cognitions, there is a difference regarding purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). (1)

B: Whether [the object] is as it appears or not as it appears, the status of being a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) for both inference and its fallacy is established in accordance with causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*). (PV 2.57–58) B82;
Now he states the definition of inference: "The cognition of the inferable (*liṅgin*) from a mark (*liṅga*) possessing the three characteristics is designated as inference. (PV 2.10)
B: "From a mark possessing three forms," and so forth.

That which has three forms—namely, the properties of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and the others that will be explained later—is "three-formed" (*tri-rūpa*); the meaning is that it possesses a triple nature.

From that three-formed mark, i.e., from the reason (*hetu*), when correctly understood, that cognition of the hidden object (*liṅgin*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) designated as inference (*anumāna*).

B: "Anu" means after; immediately following the perception of the mark (*liṅga*), the cognition that measures an imperceptible object is inference (*anumāna*); such is the meaning of the word *anumāna*.
B: Although the last quarter of this verse contains nine syllables, there is no fault, as it is due to the archaic style (*ārṣatva*). B:

This is the essential point here: just as a person is determined to be the king—the possessor of the mark—by seeing marks such as an umbrella, so too, by means of a three-featured mark (*liṅga*) such as smoke perceived in some place, the imperceptible object—the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) such as fire—is known to exist there.
B: Furthermore, this cognition of the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) based on the mark (*liṅga*) is designated as inference (*anumāna*).
And that is of two kinds: for one's own sake (*svārtha*) and for the sake of others (*parārtha*).
When one, by means of a mark possessing the three characteristics, personally realizes the probandum (*sādhya*), which is the possessor of the mark, that is inference for one's own sake.

B: But when there is the statement of a three-featured reason (*tri-rūpa-hetu*) for the sake of another's comprehension of the probandum (*sādhya*), then that is inference for others (*parārthānumāna*).
Regarding the phrase "but the cognition of the mark" (*liṅgi-jñānaṃ tu*), here the word *tu* (but) serves as a qualifier;

it distinguishes this [inference for others] from the following: that which was stated as the three-featured mark (*liṅga*) which makes the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) known, that mark is of exactly three kinds, due to the division into non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), essential nature (*svabhāva*), and effect (*kārya*).

B: Therein, non-apprehension (anupalabdhi) is described as fourfold, depending on its fundamental divisions. Namely: apprehension of the contradictory (viruddhopalabdhi), apprehension of the effect of the contradictory (viruddhakāryopalabdhi), non-apprehension of the cause (kāraṇānupalabdhi), and non-apprehension of the essential nature (svabhāvānupalabdhi).
Among these, apprehension of the contradictory is, for example: "There is no sensation of cold here, because of fire."
B: Perception of a contradictory effect is, for example: "There is no cold touch here, because of smoke.
B: Non-perception of a cause is, for example: "There is no smoke here, because of the absence of fire.
B: Non-perception of an essential nature is, for example: "There is no smoke here, because that which meets the conditions for perception is not perceived."

B: As for the remaining seven types of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) propounded in treatises such as the *Dharmabindu* and the *Nyāyabindu*, they are included within these very four divisions; thus, because they are merely sub-divisions, they are not mentioned here separately. B:
An example of a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) is: "This is a tree, because it is a *śimśapā*.
B: An example of a reason based on an effect (*kāryahetu*) is: "There is fire, because there is smoke."

In these three reasons—non-apprehension and so forth—invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) exists by virtue of the relationship of identity (*tādātmya*) or origination (*tadutpatti*): because of the existence of identity in the first and last types of non-apprehension as well as in the reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), and because of the presence of origination in the two middle types of non-apprehension as well as in the reason of effect (*kāryahetu*). Furthermore, invariable concomitance is pervaded solely by identity and origination;
and identity and origination exist only in non-apprehension, essential nature, and effect, and nowhere else.

B: Therefore, all objects other than non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), essential nature (*svabhāva*), and effect (*kārya*)—which lack the constraints of identity (*tādātmya*) or origination therefrom (*tadutpatti*)—must be understood as nothing but fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).
Consequently, reasons such as "conjunction" (*samyoga*) and others imagined by the Vaiśeṣikas and others are not valid reasons, because deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is possible.
Furthermore, inference of an effect from a cause is not accepted precisely because it is subject to deviation.

B: Furthermore, even that inference of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth from taste (*rasa*) at the same moment which is accepted by the Buddhists, as well as the inference of the production of an effect from a complete cause, these too are intended as inferences based on essential nature (*svabhāvānumāna*). To explain: "The preceding moment of color-form is capable of producing such a subsequent color-form, because it generates such a taste, just like the previously perceived color-form. This is the inference of the capacity for the production of a subsequent color-form.

B: This causal complex of seeds and so forth, being free from obstacles, is capable of producing its own effect because it is complete, just like the previously observed causal complex of seeds and so forth; this is the inference of capability (*yogyatā*).
Therefore, these two [inferences] arise solely from the reason of essential nature (*svabhāva-hetu*), and not from the inference of an effect from a cause. //10//
B87; Now, he states those very three characteristics which belong to each of the three types of logical mark (*liṅga*)—namely, non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), and so forth:

"The characteristics of the reason (*hetu*) are its being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), its presence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), and its absence in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*); thus should the three be understood. (11)

Commentary: The subject (*dharmin*) qualified by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is the *pakṣa* (the thesis-subject). A property of that [subject] is the *pakṣadharma*. The state of being such is *pakṣadharmatva* (the property-ness of the thesis-subject). Here, by the word *pakṣa*, only the subject itself is denoted, because the term for the whole is applied metaphorically to its part. If, on the other hand, the *pakṣa* were taken in its primary sense as the subject qualified by the property to be proven, then inference would be entirely useless, because the property to be proven, like the subject, would already be established. Consequently, *pakṣadharmatva* is the existence of the reason (*hetu*) in the subject, which is the *pakṣa*.
B: And that [existence] is cognized either through perception or through inference.
In this regard, perception consists in the observation of smoke in a certain place;
and inference consists in the ascertainment of the quality of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) in the case of sound.
B: This is the first characteristic.
Likewise, that which is similar to the subject is the "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*); the existence of the reason in that similar instance, the example, means its presence in a general sense.
This is the second characteristic, and its second designation is "positive concomitance" (*anvaya*).

B: Likewise, the contrary side is the "dissimilar instance" (vipakṣa), which is devoid of both the probandum and the probans; the non-existence of the reason in that dissimilar instance is its absolute absence there. This is the third characteristic (rūpa) of the reason, and its second designation is "negative concomitance" (avyatireka).

These three characteristics of the mark—the reason—consist of being a property of the subject (pakṣadharmatva), presence in similar instances (sapakṣasattva), and absence in dissimilar instances (vipakṣāsattva).
B: "In this way, because the word 'iti' has the meaning of the word 'evam' (thus), let it be reflected upon and correctly understood by the heart. B89;

In that regard, if the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) were not a form [of the reason], then smoke observed in a kitchen or similar place would cause fire to be inferred elsewhere, such as on a mountain; yet it does not so cause inference. Therefore, the property of being a characteristic of the subject is indeed a form [of the reason].

B: Likewise, if "presence in the similar class" (*sapakṣasattva*) were not a defining characteristic [of the reason], then even for a person who has not grasped the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between the probandum and the probans, the mere sight of smoke would cause them to cognize fire; yet it does not so cause cognition. Therefore, presence in the similar class is a defining characteristic. B: Likewise, if "absence from the dissimilar class" (*vipakṣāsattva*) were not a defining characteristic, then smoke would lead one to infer fire even in the dissimilar class—such as water—which is devoid of the probandum; yet it does not so lead to inference. Therefore, absence from the dissimilar class is a defining characteristic.

B: Alternatively, in the case of "Sound is impermanent, because it is black like a crow," there is no property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*). In the case of "Sound is impermanent, because it is audible," there is neither presence in the similar instances (*sapakṣasattva*) nor absence from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣāsattva*), precisely because of the non-existence of both similar and dissimilar instances.

B: "Sound is impermanent because it is knowable, like a cloth; [it is] pierceable by iron, because it is earthen, like trees and so forth; the frog has hair because it moves by leaping repeatedly, like a deer; or the deer is hairless because it moves by leaping repeatedly, like a frog"—in these cases, even though the reasons occur where the probandum, such as impermanence, is absent (i.e., in the counter-example), they lack non-existence in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).
Therefore, only that reason which possesses all three of these combined characteristics is a prover of its own probandum, and no other.
B90: If it is asked, "In that case, how many are these reasons characterized by such definitions?
B: It has already been stated previously that there are only three types of reasons, namely those called non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), essential nature (*svabhāva*), and effect (*kārya*).

B: Examples of these have already been shown previously; nevertheless, the reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) is illustrated once more: "All things are momentary" is the thesis (*pakṣa*); "because of existence" (*sattvāt*) is the reason (*hetu*). This reason exists in all [things]—this is its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*). "Whatever is existent is momentary, such as lightning and so forth"—this is its presence in the similar class (*sapakṣasattva*). "Whatever is not momentary is not existent either, such as a sky-flower."

B: Here, since existence—defined by causal efficiency—is untenable in a permanent entity, which is the opposite of the momentary, there is an exclusion of existence from the permanent; thus, there is "absence in the counter-example" (*vipakṣāsattva*). "And all that exists" is the application (*upanaya*), and "therefore, because of existence, everything is momentary" is the conclusion (*nigamana*). B: This should be understood in the same way for other reasons as well.

B: Although the Buddhists have traditionally taught that inference consists of the three forms—pervasion (*vyāpti*), presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), and application (*upasamhāra*)—nevertheless, for the sake of instructing those of dull intellect, the presentation of inference with five members (*pañcāvayava*) is also not faulty.

This is the intended meaning of the two verses here: there are only three types of logical marks (*liṅga*), characterized by the three features of being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*); namely, non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), essential nature (*svabhāva*), and effect (*kārya*).
Here, some further particulars, though not explicitly mentioned, are also recorded.
B: In that regard, the result of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is precisely the apprehension of the object, which is non-different from the valid cognition itself.
Reasoning (*tarka*) and recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) lack the status of valid cognition.
The ultimate reality, which is the domain of valid cognition, consists of particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) defined as atoms that perish moment by moment and are mutually distinct.
B: Karma is of the nature of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
B: Pleasure and pain consist of merit and demerit (*dharma* and *adharma*).
B: These are merely modalities (*paryāya*), not a substance (*dravya*).
B: Regarding an object, there is only its own existence and not the existence of another; this is the Buddhist position in general.
Alternatively, Buddhists are divided into four schools based on the distinctions of Vaibhāṣika, Sautrāntika, Yogācāra, and Mādhyamika.
Among these, the view of the Vaibhāṣikas—also known as the Āryasammitīyas—is as follows: an object consists of four moments.
B: Birth causes to be born; B: Duration causes to endure;
B: Decay causes to decay.
B: Destruction destroys.
Likewise, the self (*ātman*) is also of such a nature, and it is designated as a person (*pudgala*).
Cognition, though formless, is dependent upon a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that coexists with the object; thus, it is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding that object.
Furthermore, this is the Sautrāntika position: for all embodied beings, these five aggregates—form, feeling, consciousness, perception, and mental formations—exist, but there is no self (*ātman*).
Indeed, it is these very [aggregates] that go to the next world.
And thus is their established tenet: "O monks, these five are mere designations, mere assertions, mere conventionalities, and mere worldly usage."
B: Which five?
B: The past time, the future time, destruction with a cause, space, and the person (pudgala).
B: Here, by the word "person" (pudgala), the self (ātman) imagined by others—which possesses qualities such as permanence and omnipresence—is meant.

B: An external object is always imperceptible; however, its existence is understood through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the forms within cognition. Cognition possessing a form is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Likewise, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary.
B: The particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
As those who advocate this view say: "The reality consists solely of the atoms of form, taste, smell, and touch, which perish at every moment, as well as cognition.
B: The meaning of a word is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).

B: The determination of an object occurs through its arising from that [object] and its having that [object’s] form. Liberation is the cessation of the continuum of consciousness resulting from the cultivation of selflessness.

B: There is no external object, because the non-duality of cognition alone is the ultimate reality;
there are multiple streams of cognition.
B: Cognition possessing an aspect (*sākāra*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
B: The appearances of blue, yellow, and so forth arise from the maturation of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
B: For the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is the substratum for all latent predispositions.
B: "Liberation is simply the purification of the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
However, in the Madhyamaka view—this [world] is empty;
the distinction between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the object of valid cognition (*prameya*) is like a dream.
B: "Liberation, however, arises from the vision of emptiness; for that purpose, there is the cultivation of the remaining [stages]. (Pravā. 1.256) B:
But some Mādhyamikas speak of knowledge as being inherently stable. As it has been said:
B: "The object is endowed with cognition; this is asserted by the wise Vaibhāṣika. (Pravā. 1.7)

those who follow the Yogācāra doctrine hold that cognition possessing an aspect (sākāra-buddhi) is supreme.
Alas! But those of perfected intellect, the Madhyamikas, consider the supreme self-abiding consciousness alone to be ultimate. (1) [Thus it is said.]

B: The ten treatises beginning with the *Jñānapāramitā* are as follows: the *Tarkabhāṣā*, the *Hetubindu*, its commentary by Arcaṭa, the one titled *Tarka*, the *Pramāṇavārttika*, the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, the *Nyāyabindu*, and Kamalaśīla’s *Nyāyapraveśaka*; these and others are their works. B96;

Now, listen—let it be heard—the brief exposition of the Naiyāyika doctrine, which is the Śaiva teaching, as it is being told hereafter.
First, the manifestation of the *liṅga* and other categories of the Naiyāyikas, also known as the Yaugas, is stated.

And they were staff-bearers, wearing mature loincloths, wrapped in blankets, bearing matted hair, devoted to smearing themselves with ashes, wearing sacred threads, holding water-vessels and bowls in their hands, subsisting on tasteless food, mostly dwelling in the forest, carrying gourds at the base of their arms, eating roots, tubers, and fruits, and intent upon the duty of hospitality. They were both with wives and without wives; among them, those without wives were the most excellent.

And they are devoted to the practice of the five fires (*pañcāgni-sādhana*); they bear matted hair on their hands and other parts of their bodies, and they also wear the *liṅga* of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Having attained the supreme state of self-restraint (*saṃyama*), they wander about naked.
Having performed their morning purification, such as cleaning the teeth and so forth, they meditate upon Śiva and touch their limbs three times each with ashes.
The patron, bowing with palms joined in reverence, says: "Om namaḥ śivāya.
The guru likewise replies: "Śivāya namaḥ.
And they speak thus in the assembly:
"Even he who, having practiced the Śaiva initiation for twelve years, eventually abandons it—
even if he becomes a slave or a servant— he too attains liberation.
For them, God is the Lord, the omniscient one, the performer of creation, dissolution, and so forth.

And his eighteen incarnations (avatāras) are these: 1. Nakula, 2. Śoṣyakauśika, 3. Gārgya, 4. Maitrya, 5. Akauruṣa, 6. Īśāna, 7. Pāragārgya, 8. Kapilāṇḍa, 9. Manuṣyaka, 10. Kuśika, 11. Atri, 12. Piṅgala, 13. Puṣpaka, 14. Bṛhadārya, 15. Agasti, 16. Saṃtāna, 17. Rāśīkara, and 18. Vidyāguru.
These are their lords of sacred sites (tīrtheśas), who are to be worshipped.
The procedure for their worship and dedication (praṇidhāna), however, is to be understood from their respective scriptures.
Among them, at all sacred fords (*tīrtha*), only the *bharaṭas* are the worshippers.
Salutation to the gods should not be performed by the *sannyāsins*.
Among them, those who are free from modification (*nirvikāra*) point to this verse found in their own *Mīmāṃsā*:

"Neither the celestial river, nor the serpent-king, nor the garland of skulls; neither a digit of the moon, nor the Daughter of the Mountain, nor matted hair, nor ashes—nor anything else whatsoever do we worship there, but that form of the Lord practiced by the ancient sages.
That alone is to be served by yogins, for any other is merely a partaker of worldly enjoyment."
"He, being meditated upon, is resorted to by those greedy for the pleasures of sovereignty and the like.
And it has been said by them in their own Yoga-śāstra:
"The yogi, remembering the One Free from Passion, attains the state of being free from passion."
For one who meditates with passion, the state of being passionate is certain. //3//
"For by whatever state the driver of the machine is joined,
he attains the nature of that very thing, just like a crystal [reflecting] all forms" (4).
All this— the nature of the *liṅga*, the *veṣa*, the deity, and so forth— is to be understood even according to the Vaiśeṣika system.

For although there is a difference in the number of the principles (*tattva*) among the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas when they are compared with one another, only a very slight difference arises when their respective principles are mutually subsumed; therefore, their views are for the most part identical.
And these [Śaivas] are fourfold according to the divisions of Śaiva and so forth. As it has been said:
"Those who wear the sacred ash as a support, a loincloth, matted hair, and a sacrificial thread..."
Ascetics are of four kinds, distinguished by their respective modes of conduct and other such factors. //1//
"Ṇ: The Śaivas, the Pāśupatas, and likewise those who observe the Great Vow (Mahāvrata-dhara);
Ṇ: the Turyas and the Kālamukhas are the principal divisions of these ascetics (tapasvins).
Ṇ5: Among them, there are internal subdivisions such as the Bharaṭas, Bhaktaras (?), Laiṅgikas, Tāpasas, and so forth."
Regarding the initiation (*vrata-grahaṇa*) of ascetics such as the *bharaṭas*, there is no restriction concerning the social classes (*varṇa*), such as being a Brāhmaṇa or others.

Whoever possesses devotion to Śiva—be they a *bharaṭa* or another—may become an initiate. Furthermore, according to the scriptures, the Naiyāyikas are called *Śaivas* because they are always devotees of Śiva, whereas the Vaiśeṣikas are *Pāśupatas*.
Therefore, the teaching of the Naiyāyikas is called Śaiva, and the Vaiśeṣika system is called Pāśupata.
I shall here state this exactly as it was heard and seen by me;
however, the specific details thereof should be understood from their respective original treatises. //12//
Now, he states the summary of the Naiyāyika position as previously promised:
In the system of Akṣapāda, the Lord Śiva is the creator of creation and dissolution; he is omnipresent, eternal, uniquely omniscient, and the substratum of the final cognition. (13)

Commentary: Since the foundational aphorism (*mūlasūtra*) of the Naiyāyika system was composed by the primordial teacher Akṣapāda, the Naiyāyikas are called Ākṣapādas, and their doctrine is called the Ākṣapāda doctrine. In that Ākṣapāda doctrine, Śiva is the Great Lord (*mahā-īśvara*). "Creation" (*sṛṣṭi*) is the manifestation of the world of moving and non-moving beings; "destruction" (*saṃhāra*) is its dissolution. In a copulative compound, these two are "creation and destruction. He performs these two through the majesty of his inconceivable power; thus, he is the "performer of creation and destruction" (*sṛṣṭisaṃhārakṛt*).

If creation were performed by [Śiva] alone, then the countless multitude of living beings being produced incessantly throughout the three worlds would not suffice; therefore, just as with creation, he must also perform destruction.

Regarding this, the Śaivas state the following formal argument (*prayoga*): "The earth, mountains, moon, sun, ocean, and so forth, are preceded by an intelligent agent (*buddhimat-pūrvaka*), because they are effects (*kāryatvāt*). Whatever is an effect is preceded by an intelligent agent, just like a jar. And these are effects; therefore, they are preceded by an intelligent agent."
The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "And he who is its intelligent creator is indeed Īśvara.
The counter-example (*vyatireka*) is the sky (*gagana*).

Nor is this reason (*hetu*) unestablished (*asiddha*), because it is well-known in the world that the earth, mountains, and so forth are effects (*kāryatva*), either by virtue of being produced by their respective collections of causes or by virtue of being composite wholes (*avayavitva*).

It is neither contradictory nor inconclusive, because it is absolutely excluded from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). Nor is it "mistimed" (*kālatyayāpadiṣṭa*), because the reason operates within a domain of a subject and a property to be proven that is not sublated by perception or scripture. Nor is it "neutralized by the context" (*prakaraṇasama*), because there is no emergence of a counter-inference established by proving the nature of a thing that acts as its own adversary.

If it is argued: "But since a counter-inference arises—namely, that God cannot be the agent of creation and dissolution precisely because He is bodiless like one whose self is in a state of final liberation (nirvṛtātman), how is this not the fallacy of *prakaraṇasama*? It is replied:

In this case, regarding your inference, is the subject (*dharmin*)—God, who is being proven—intended by you as something already cognized or as something uncognized? If it is uncognized, then the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) would attach to the reason (*hetu*) imagined by you.

If [the body] is indeed perceived, then why is it not accepted that by the very same means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through which it is perceived, its own inherent form is also manifested? Thus, how can there be a state of bodilessness?
Therefore, the reason is not subject to the fallacy of being "neutralized by the context" (*prakaraṇasama*).
Consequently, it is well said: "Śiva is the creator of creation and dissolution."
Likewise, [the Lord] is all-pervasive like space, pervading the entire universe.

For if He were restricted to residing in one specific location, it would be impossible for Him to fashion objects that reside in various indefinite locations according to their respective fixed requirements.
Indeed, even a potter situated in one place does not exert himself toward the production of pots and other items located at a great distance; therefore, [the Lord] is all-pervasive.

Likewise, [the term] "eternally one and omniscient" (*nityaikasarvajña*) is a compound of three qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇatrayasamāsa*). It is "eternal" (*nitya*) and it is "one" (*eka*), thus "eternally one" (*nityaka*); and he is that "omniscient" (*sarvajña*).
In this context, "eternal" means unchanging, unarisen, stable, and of a single nature—immovable like a mountain peak (*kūṭastha*).

For if Īśvara were impermanent, he would necessarily be subject to being produced by something else, due to his dependence on another for his own arising. Indeed, an entity that requires the operation of another for its own production is accepted as being "produced" (*kṛtaka*). If the creator of the world were himself produced, then he too would have to have another creator, precisely because of his impermanence.
It must be eternal, precisely because it is impermanent [otherwise].
Furthermore, if one agent were to be produced by another agent, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), like a river difficult to cross.
Therefore, it must be accepted as being indeed eternal.

ṇ11: Although eternal, He alone should be understood as being without a second. For if many were accepted as the creators of the world, then because each would be separately and individually occupied with various dissimilar tasks, the creation of each individual object would be dissimilar; thus, everything would fall into inconsistency. Therefore, the qualification "one" is appropriate. ṇ12: Although one, He is omniscient—the knower of all objects in their entirety.

For in the absence of omniscience, it would be impossible to create things exactly as they are, because one would lack the capacity to bring together the complete collection of scattered atoms dispersed throughout the universe that are necessary for the intended objects.

Furthermore, in His omniscience, while fashioning objects as effects in accordance with the totality of appropriate causes that have converged for all living beings, and by way of inferring (or according to) the merit and demerit they have themselves acquired, He bestows the experience of pleasure and pain in heaven and hell; thus, He never transcends what is entirely fitting. And so it has been said by His devotees:
"O Lord of the World, whose knowledge is unimpeded, and who possesses both dispassion, sovereignty, and virtue—this fourfold set is innate. (1)

"This living being is ignorant and not master of its own pleasure and pain; impelled by the Lord, it goes either to heaven or indeed to the abyss. (Mahābhārata, Vanaparvan 30.28) Alternatively, the single qualification "eternally and uniquely omniscient" is to be explained.
Ṇ: He is eternal (*nityaḥ*), always one and without a second; he is the omniscient one, the eternally unique omniscient one (*nityaikasarvajñaḥ*).
Ṇ: By this it is indicated that, apart from the one Lord (*īśvara*) who is omniscient from the beginningless past, no other person has ever been omniscient at any time.

Ṇ: Since the cognitions of other yogins—though they may know all other supersensible objects (*atīndriya-artha*)—do not know their own selves, how then could they be omniscient? This is what is being made known.

Likewise, "the locus of eternal cognition" means the abode of eternal cognition or knowledge; for one who possesses momentary cognition lacks primary agency due to dependence on external factors for the accomplishment of effects, which would result in the undesirable consequence of his not being the Lord (Īśvara).
Thus, in the system of the Naiyāyikas, the god Śiva is characterized by such attributes. //13//
Now, desiring to explain those principles (*tattva*), he first declares their number and names:
"In this system, there are sixteen principles, beginning with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); namely:
the means of valid cognition, the object of valid cognition, doubt, and purpose. (NS 1.1.1)
The example (dṛṣṭānta), the established conclusion (siddhānta), the members of the syllogism (avayava), deliberation (tarka), and ascertainment (nirṇaya);
debate (vāda), wrangling (jalpa), cavil (vitaṇḍā), fallacies of the reason (hetvābhāsa), and quibbles (chala). //15//
The classification of these [categories] consists of the types of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). Now follows their detailed exposition:
"The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which is the cause for the apprehension of an object; it is fourfold. (Verse 16, with three *viśeṣaka*s).

Commentary: In this context, within the system of the Naiyāyikas under discussion, there are sixteen principles (*tattva*), beginning with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of valid cognition (*prameya*).
ṇ: *Tad-yathā* is used in the sense of "for example.
ṇ: *Pramāma*, *ca*, and so forth.

ṇ: In that context, valid cognition (*pramiti*) is apprehension (*upalabdhi*), which is knowledge; that by which this [knowledge] is produced is the cause (*kāraṇa*) that generates such knowledge, namely, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The term *pramāṇa* is derived from the etymology: that by which knowledge (*jñāna*) is measured, or produced, is a means of valid cognition.
And the producer of knowledge is of two kinds: the non-conscious (*acetana*) and consciousness (*jñāna*).

Among these, the non-conscious—such as the sense organs, the contact between the object and its sense organ, lamps, logical marks (*liṅga*), words, and so forth—is a means of valid cognition because it serves as a cause for knowledge.
1. Furthermore, that which functions toward the production of another cognition is also a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it generates a cognition;
however, that which does not generate a cognition would be the fruit (*phala*) of the means of valid cognition, but not itself a means of valid cognition.
2. The object of cognition (*prameya*) is the entity to be grasped by the cognition produced by the means of valid cognition.
Doubt (*saṃśaya*) is a cognition that oscillates between alternatives.
The three *ca*-particles serve the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*), indicating that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the other categories are mutually dependent.
Purpose (*prayojana*) is the desired result to be accomplished. 3–4.
*Ṇ*: An example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is an illustration agreed upon by both the proponent and the opponent. *Ṇ*: The particle *api* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
*Ṇ*: The word *atha* signifies immediate succession (*ānantarya*).
6. Siddhānta (established conclusion) refers to the scriptures and so forth accepted by all philosophical systems.
7. Avayava (member of a syllogism) refers to the constituent parts of inference, such as the thesis (pakṣa) and the others.
8. Tarka (reasoning) is the consideration of the property of concomitance following doubt, such as: "A post is possible here at this moment."
The ascertainment that "this is indeed a post" is *nirṇaya* (conclusion).
In a *dvandva* compound, *tarka* and *nirṇaya* [are mentioned].
Dialogue with a teacher for the purpose of ascertaining the truth is *vāda* (debate).
11. *Jalpa* (wrangling) is speech characterized by a desire for victory over an opponent. 12. *Vitaṇḍā* (cavil) is mere verbiage that fails to touch upon the true nature of the subject matter. 13.
*Hetvābhāsas* (fallacious reasons) are those which appear to be reasons but are not valid reasons; this is the meaning.
14. *Chalas* (quibbles) are the production of sophistical distinctions for the purpose of refuting the arguments of others.
15. *Jātis* (futile rejoinders) are improper refutations.
16. *Nigrahasthānas* (points of defeat) are those [faults] by which, when stated, the speaker is defeated.
ṇ: There is thus this exposition—that is, the demonstration of the essential nature—of these aforementioned categories beginning with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

ṇ15: Among those, wishing first to provide an exposition of the means of valid cognition, [the author] states its general definition and its number at the outset: ṇ: "The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which is the cause of the apprehension of an object."

The apprehension of an object—whether external and graspable, such as a pillar, a jar, or a lotus, or internal, such as cognition and pleasure—is "knowledge" (*jñāna*), and thus "apprehension of an object" (*arthopalabdhi*).

According to the maxim that "the specific meaning is understood from the explanation," what is to be understood here is an apprehension of an object that is non-erroneous, non-verbalizable, and determinate in nature, and not mere apprehension in general.
That which is the cause or instrument of this [apprehension] shall be the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The attainment of the object (*arthopalabdhi*), however, is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The intended meaning here is as follows: the totality of conditions (*sāmagrī*) that produces the attainment of an object characterized by qualifiers such as non-deviation, or a single part of that totality—such as the eye, a lamp, or cognition, whether of the nature of consciousness (*bodha*) or not—is the *pramāṇa* because it is the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*).
And its status as a *pramāṇa* consists in its being the generator of that [attainment of the object].
The result, however, is the apprehension of the object produced by that [instrument].

Since it is that very apprehension which arises as qualified by specific attributes such as being produced by the sense organs (*indriya-ja*) or being produced by signs (*liṅga-ja*), those alone will be stated as the specific definitions of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as perception (*pratyakṣa*).
However, the qualification "inexpressible" (*avyapadeśya*) here should not be connected to verbal cognition (*śābda*), because that [verbal cognition] is expressible, since it is produced by words.
Regarding this, he states the divisions of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): "That is fourfold. That means of valid cognition is fourfold, meaning it has four divisions. //14-16//
Now, he states that very fourfold division:
perception, inference, comparison, and likewise verbal testimony.
Among these, [perception] is that which arises from the contact of the sense organs with their objects and is non-erroneous.
Knowledge that consists of ascertainment, which is free from verbal designation, is perception;
inference, however, is preceded by that [perception] and is of three kinds. //18//
The "pūrvavat" and "śeṣavat" [types of inference] have been seen as such through generalization;
among them, the first is here proclaimed as the inference of the effect from the cause. (16)

Commentary: *Pratyakṣa* means direct perception (*adhyakṣa*). *Anumāna* means inference based on signs (*laiṅgika*). The word *ca* (and) has the sense of conjunction. *Upamāna* means comparison (*upamiti*). Because the word *tathā* (so) also has the sense of conjunction, *śābdika*—meaning that which arises from words (*śabda*)—refers to verbal testimony (*āgama*). Now, he defines the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) with the passage beginning "In that regard, [the contact] of the sense-organ with the object," and so forth.
Among those means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), perception (*pratyakṣa*) is stated first.

Herein is this sūtra composed by Akṣapāda: "Perception is knowledge produced from the contact of a sense-organ with its object, which is non-verbal, non-erroneous, and of a determinative nature" [NS 1.1.4].

A sense-organ (*indriya*) is that beginning with the eye and ending with the mind (*manas*). Its object (*artha*) is the thing to be determined; it is the object of the sense-organ, such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, because of the statement: "Form and the rest are their objects."

ṇ: Proximity (*saṃnikarṣa*) is the close connection of the sense organ; that is to say, its attainment or relation. ṇ: And that is sixfold: 1) in the case of a substance, it is simply conjunction (*saṃyoga*) with the sense organ;
2) in the case of qualities such as color (*rūpa*), it is inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyukta-samavāya*), because they inhere in the substance [with which the sense organ is conjoined].
3. In the case of [qualities] such as color-ness (*rūpatva*), which are inherent in qualities, there is indeed inherence-in-what-is-inherent-in-the-conjoined (*samyuktasamavetasamavāya*).
4. In the case of sound (*śabda*), there is indeed inherence (*samavāya*) alone, because space is established as the sense of hearing (*śrotra*), and sound is inherent therein as its quality.
5. In the case of sound-ness (*śabdatva*), there is indeed inherence-in-what-is-inherent (*samavetasamavāya*), because it is inherent in that which is inherent in sound.
The meaning is as follows: for inherence (*samavāya*) and non-existence (*abhāva*), there is only the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*).

That is to say, among things connected by the five kinds of relations previously described, inherence—such as [the inherence of] a cloth—and perceptible non-existence function either as qualifiers or as qualificands. For example: "The threads possess the inherence of the cloth," or "The inherence of the cloth resides in the threads."

The sixfold contact (*ṣoḍhā sannikarṣaḥ*) is as follows: [contact between] the sense organ and the object (*indriya-artha*), [contact between] the sense organ and the qualifier (*indriya-viśeṣaṇa*), [contact between] the sense organ and the qualified (*indriya-viśeṣya*), [contact between] the sense organ and the negation (*indriya-abhāva*), [contact between] the object and the qualifier (*artha-viśeṣaṇa*), and [contact between] the object and the qualified (*artha-viśeṣya*). For example: "the ground is empty of a jar," or "there is no jar here on the ground.

Now, one might argue that the inclusion of the term *saṃ* (in *saṃnikarṣaḥ*) is redundant, and that only the term *nikarṣa* (contact) should suffice. This is not correct, because the inclusion of the word *saṃ* is intended to indicate these six types of contact. It is understood from the inclusion of *saṃ* that this very sixfold contact alone is the efficient cause for the production of knowledge, and not [other types of contact] such as *samyukta-samyoga* (conjunction with what is conjoined). Thus it is obtained from the inclusion of *saṃ*.
ṇ19: "Arisen" means produced from the contact of the sense organ with its object.
ṇ: The inclusion of the term "production" (utpatti) is for the purpose of indicating its status as an efficient cause (kāraka).
ṇ: The intended meaning here is this: the sense organ is connected with the object due to proximity, and from the connection between the sense organ and the object, cognition arises.
Regarding what was said: "The self moves together with the mind; the mind [moves] with the sense organ, and the sense organ with its own object—this sequence is rapid.
What is there inaccessible to this very yoga of the mind? Wherever the mind goes, there the self has gone.

(Verse 11) The inclusion of the term *jñāna* (cognition) is for the purpose of excluding pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth, because pleasure and the like are not of the nature of cognition (*ajñāna-rūpa*).

For pleasure and the like are experienced as objects of apprehension, having the nature of delight and so forth, whereas cognition is experienced as the subject of apprehension, having the nature of the comprehension of an object; thus, the difference between cognition and pleasure and the like is indeed established by direct perception.
That which is "inexpressible" is devoid of the conceptual construction of names; for if there were a conceptual construction of a name, it would be verbal (conceptual).

ṇ: For, in the absence of the inclusion of the term "non-verbal" (*avyapadeśya*), verbal designation (*vyapadeśa*) is [defined as] speech; thus, the cognition produced by both that [designation] and the contact between sense-organ and object would also be a result of perception (*pratyakṣa*). To exclude that, the term "non-verbal" is employed. ṇ: Even though it is produced by both that [word] and the sense-organ, because the word is predominant due to its having a vast range of objects, it is accepted as verbal knowledge (*śābda*), and not, on the other hand, as perception (*adhyakṣa*).

The term *avyabhicāri* (non-erroneous) is employed for the purpose of excluding the cognition of water in a mirage produced by the sense organs, as well as the cognition of silver in a piece of mother-of-pearl and the like.
That cognition which arises as "that" in what is "not-that" is erroneous; by its exclusion, the cognition that [arises] as "that" in what is "that" is non-erroneous.
The term *vyavasāya* refers to a specific determination (*viśeṣa*), in the sense that "by this, something is determined."

[The cognition] produced by a particularity (*viśeṣa*) is of the nature of ascertainment (*vyavasāyātmaka*). Alternatively, "of the nature of ascertainment" means of the nature of certainty (*niścayātmaka*).
By this, it is indicated that doubtful cognition (*saṃśaya-jñāna*), because it has multiple objects as its basis and because it is not of the nature of certainty, is not the fruit of perception.

[Objection: But even so, the word "cognition" (*jñāna*) is redundant, since cognition is already obtained through the two final qualifiers; [Response: No, because this [word] serves to indicate the subject (*dharmin*). For it is the subject, introduced by the word "cognition," that is qualified by such properties as being produced from the contact of the sense organ with its object. Otherwise, in the absence of a subject, where would those words [denoting] properties such as non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) convey their respective attributes?

Furthermore, some explain it as follows: by the two terms "indescribable" (*avyapadeśyam*) and "of the nature of determination" (*vyavasāyātmakam*), he states the twofold division of perception according to the distinction between non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) and conceptual (*savikalpaka*); the remaining [terms], however, are qualifiers of cognition (*jñāna*).
In this Sūtra, three possibilities exist regarding the qualification of the result, the essential nature, and the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
Among these, the position that they are qualifiers of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is not tenable.
The meaning there would be that perception is knowledge possessing the aforementioned qualifications.

And in that case, the status of perception would accrue to knowledge that is not an instrument (akāraka); yet it is not logical for that which is not an instrument to be perception, because it is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) alone that constitutes a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, it would follow that scales, gold, lamps, and so forth—as well as proximity, the sense organs, and other factors—which are non-cognitive in nature, would also be perceptions.

Furthermore, the author of the Sūtra intends for these [cognitions] to be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, the position that takes the nature of the cognition itself as the qualifier is not tenable, nor is the position that takes the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) as the qualifier. For if the causal complex were the qualifier, the meaning of the Sūtra would be as follows: "The causal complex consisting of the knower, the object of knowledge, the eye and other sense organs, light, and so forth—which generates knowledge—is metaphorically called 'direct perception' because it produces a knowledge qualified by such attributes as 'being produced from the contact between the sense organ and the object,' since it is distinguished by those very attributes."

Thus, the fact that the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) possesses the qualifiers mentioned in the Sūtra is due only to metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), because it produces such a result, and not by its own nature.
However, even that position is not tenable;
rather, the position that the result is the qualifier is consistent with reason.
In this view, the word "yataḥ" (from which) must be supplied.

Therefore, the meaning is as follows: that from which knowledge—characterized by such attributes as being produced by the contact of the sense organ with its object—arises, namely that contact of the sense organ with the object and so forth, is the means of valid cognition (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*);
and knowledge is the result of the means of valid cognition (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa-phala*).

But when cognitions of avoidance, acquisition, and so forth arise from that knowledge, then, with respect to those cognitions of avoidance and so on, knowledge is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the cognitions of avoidance and so forth are the result (*phala*).
This is because of the statement: "When knowledge is the means of valid cognition, then the cognitions of avoidance and so forth are the result" (Nyāyabhāṣya 1.1.3).

And just as in the case of memory—which arises from the continuum of a prior experience of knowledge—so too this cognition, "This is that," is a result of perception (*pratyakṣa-phala*), since it is produced by the contact of the sense organ with its object.
But that [recollection] is indeed perception;

for the recollection of the connection between pleasure and pain, because it acts as a cooperative factor for the contact between sense-organ and object, produces a cognition of similarity (*sārūpya*) in the form "this is such-and-such," and thus possesses the status of the means of valid perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, that cognition of similarity possesses the status of the means of inference (*anumāna-pramāṇa*), because it produces an inferential result in the form "this is a means to pleasure."

Furthermore, the cognition of the capacity for pleasure to be a means [to happiness] is not produced by the contact between a sense organ and its object, because that capacity is not present [in the object].
When there is contact of the self with the mind (the internal organ), the resulting cognition of pleasure and so forth is the fruit;
the mind as the sense organ and that contact constitute the instrument of perception (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*).

Thus, in other cases as well, the distinction between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) should be understood according to what is appropriate. Regarding this very point, the author of the treatise has stated it in this way, following the requirements of metrical composition, beginning with the words: "That which arises from the contact of the sense-faculties and their objects," and so forth.
Here, *samparka* means connection (*sambandha*).
In the phrase "and non-deviant" (*avyabhicāri ca*), the word *ca* (and) serves to conjoin the qualifier.
In the reading *avyabhicārikam*, however, *avyabhicāry evāvyabhicārikam*; the suffix *kapratyaya* is used in its own sense (*svārthe*) to form the derivative *avyabhicārikam*.
"Designation" (vyapadeśa) means conceptual construction (nāmakalpanā).
Here too, in the commentary, the word "because" (yataḥ) must be supplied. The meaning of the term (bhāvārtha) is entirely as explained previously. Thus [ends the section].
Now, with the intention of not distinguishing between perception and its result, the varieties of perception are stated:
perception is twofold, namely, non-yogic perception (*ayogi-pratyakṣa*) and yogic perception (*yogi-pratyakṣa*).
That knowledge which arises for people like us from the contact of the sense-faculties with their objects is non-yogic perception.
That [perception] is also of two kinds: non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) and conceptual (*savikalpa*).
Among these, non-conceptual perception is that which manifests only the essential nature of the object, such as the cognition produced by the initial contact of the sense organ.

Conceptual perception is the cause for the arising of cognition through the delineation of the relationship between a name and the named, such as "This is Devadatta" or "He is the one with the staff," and so forth.
Yogic perception, however, is that which grasps objects remote in space, time, and nature.
It is of two kinds: the perception of those who are "joined" (*yukta*) and that of those who are "disjoined" (*viyukta*).

Among these, the perception of those who are "joined"—who possess one-pointedness through meditative absorption (*samādhi*)—is the apprehension of all objects independent of contact with external things, arising solely from the conjunction of the self and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), aided by the merit born of yoga (*yogaja-dharma*), the Lord (*īśvara*), and so forth.
And this [perception] is indeed non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), because one-pointedness of concentration (*samādhy-ekāgrya*) is impossible through conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

Furthermore, this should be understood as belonging only to the most advanced yogins, since it is impossible for ordinary yogins. During the state of non-concentration, the perception of forms and so forth by yogins arises from the contact of the fourfold basis consisting of the self, the mind, the external sense organs, and the objects such as form; the perception of sound arises from the contact of the triad consisting of the self, the mind, and the ear; and the perception of pleasure and so forth arises from the contact of the dyad consisting of the self and the mind. This is the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of those who are detached.
And that [perception] should be understood as being both non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) and conceptual (*savikalpaka*).
One who desires a detailed account, however, should consult the *Nyāyasāra-ṭīkā*.
Now, he states the section on inference (*anumāna*): "Inference, moreover, is preceded by that [perception]; it is of three kinds, namely *śeṣavat*," and so forth.
And here, the words *eva* and *ca* indicate the multiplicity of meanings of the preceding [terms], as before;
the word *tathā* has the sense of the particle *ca*, serving as a conjunction for accumulation (*samuccaya*);
the remainder, however, will be explained by the commentary on the sūtra itself.

The sutra, however, is this: "Inference is preceded by that (perception) and is of three kinds: pūrvavat, śeṣavat, and sāmānyatodṛṣṭa. Some explain it thus: here, due to the general nature of the term *sāmānya*, one instance of the word *pūrvaka* is to be understood as being elided. In the expression *tat-pūrvakam*, the word *tat* (that) refers back to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The meaning is that the knowledge of the mark (*liṅga*) has perception as its antecedent;
the knowledge of the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) has that [knowledge of the mark] as its antecedent.
This is the point here: from perception, the knowledge of smoke and so forth arises, and from the knowledge of smoke and so forth, the knowledge of fire and so forth arises.
