The qualifiers "produced from the contact of a sense-organ with its object" (*indriyārthasannikarṣotpanna*) and so forth, as well as [the other] qualifiers of cognition mentioned in the *pratyakṣa* sūtra, should be connected here as well.
The things to be excluded by these [qualifiers] should be reflected upon by oneself according to what was stated previously.

Likewise, the term "apprehension of an object" (*arthopalabdhi*) must be included in order to exclude the status of inference from that which produces [cognition] preceded by the recollection of an inseparable relation (*avinābhāva-sambandha*) based on the prior observation of a second mark (*liṅga*), because such [recollection] is preceded by that [observation]; however, this is not necessary for recollection itself, since it occurs even without an object.
Therefore, this is the meaning:

inference (*anumāna*) is that knowledge which arises from a mark (*liṅga*) and so forth, preceded by that [two-fold perception]—knowledge which is non-erroneous, inexpressible, and of a determinative nature, and which consists in the apprehension of an object.

Thus, by resorting to a specific analysis of the compound *tat-pūrvaka*—meaning "that which has those two perceptions as its antecedent," namely the perception of the relationship between the mark and the marked (*liṅga-liṅgin*) and the perception of the mark—it should be understood that inference is shown to be preceded by the two types of direct perception (*adhyakṣa*).

Thus, by resorting to the specific analysis of the compound as *tat-pūrvakam*—"that which has those [means] as its antecedent"—it is established that inference is preceded by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as perception and the rest.
Nor should it be objected: "Since those [means] were not previously under discussion, how can they be referred to by the word *tat* (that)?
For even though they were not directly under discussion, they were introduced in the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa-sūtra*) as the objects to be excluded.
In this explanation, there is no defect whatsoever, such as under-extension (*avyāpti*).

However, for those who do not accept the indication of a single elided word "pūrva," there would follow the consequence that perception (*pratyakṣa*) is inference (*anumāna*), because its result is preceded by the means of valid cognition that is perception.

Now, if it is argued that since that which is not a causal factor (*akāraka*) lacks the status of a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇatva*), the status of being a causal factor is thereby obtained—and thus the meaning [of inference] is this: "Inference is the cognition of a mark (*liṅga-jñāna*) which, as the fruit of perception, produces an apprehension of an object that is non-erroneous (*avyabhicārin*), non-designatable (*avyapadeśya*), and of a determinative nature (*vyavasāyātmika*)"—then it is replied: even so, it follows that inference would be nothing other than a specific kind of cognition (*viśiṣṭa-jñāna*).

Furthermore, it is not the case that cognition (*jñāna*) alone constitutes inference, because of the statement: "Memory, inference, scripture, doubt, intuition, dream-cognition, deliberation (*ūha*), the perception of pleasure and so forth, and desire and the like are the marks (*liṅga*) of the mind" (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.16). Since everything—whether of the nature of consciousness or unconsciousness—that produces a specific result would then be an inference, this would constitute the fault of being under-extensive (*avyāpti*) as a definition.

Therefore, the correct interpretation is: "Inference is that from which [knowledge] preceded by that [perception] arises, wherein the apprehension of an object is qualified by such attributes as non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) and so forth. This alone is logical.
If it is objected that even here the mention of "threefold" is redundant, we say no; for it is intended to classify inference.
Furthermore, the mention of "pūrvavat" and so forth is for the purpose of making known the scope of "pūrvavat" and the rest by way of excluding the scope of "svabhāva" and the rest.
Thus, the first explanation is that it is precisely "pūrvavat" and the others that are intended to be divided into three types, not "svabhāva" and the rest.
Others, however, explain the sūtra in this way: "That which is preceded by that"—meaning preceded by perception—is inference, which is of three kinds, thus having three divisions.
To ask what these divisions are, he says: "pūrvavat," and so forth.

By the word *pūrva* (prior), the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is designated; since it is determined prior to the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), the positive concomitance is "prior. That [inference] which possesses this is *pūrvavat*, namely, the purely positive inference (*kevalānvayy-anumāna*). //1//

The "remainder" (śeṣa) is the negative concomitance (vyatireka); that which possesses this as its only [probans] is "the remainder-like" (śeṣavat), which is the purely negative inference (kevalavyatirekin). //2//

That which is observed in general through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), which are the two modes of proof, is "observed in general" (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*), and it is also the "possessing positive and negative concomitance" (*anvaya-vyatirekin*). Thus [ends the commentary on Sūtra 1.1.35].
Alternatively, "threefold" means having three forms (*tri-rūpa*). What are these three forms? He says: "the former" (*pūrvavat*), and so forth.

Because it was previously taken up, it is the "former," namely the subject (*pakṣa*); that which possesses this is "the former-like" (*pūrvavat*), which is the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*).

The "remainder" (*śeṣa*) is the example based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), because it is other than what has been employed; that which exists here is "the remainder-like" (*śeṣavat*), which is presence in the similar class (*sapakṣe sattvam*).

"Seen generally" (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*) means that which is not seen even slightly in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*); this non-existence in all dissimilar instances is the third characteristic (*rūpa*).

Furthermore, by the word "and" (*ca*), the two characteristics of being uncontradicted by perception and scripture (*pratyakṣāgamāviruddhatva*) and having no counter-argument (*asatpratipakṣatva*) are also included.

Thus, that inference which is preceded by a mark (*liṅga*) possessing these five characteristics is the inference based on both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireki-anumāna*). (i.e., *vyatireki-anumāna*)

Because it lacks connection with either of the two forms—absence from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) and presence in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*)—inference based on a four-featured mark (*catur-rūpa-liṅga*) consists of the purely positive (*kevalānvayi*) and the purely negative (*kevalavyatireki*).
Among these, "Sound is impermanent, because it is a product, like a pot and unlike space" is a reason that possesses both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatirekī*). //1//

In the argument: "Unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth are perceptible to someone, because they are objects of cognition (*prameya*), like the palm of the hand," this is a *kevalānvayin* [reason] precisely because there is no dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*)—that is, no object whatsoever that is not perceptible to someone—when "perceptibility to someone" is the property to be proven. //2//
Every effect is preceded by an omniscient creator, because it is occasional; for whatever is not preceded by an omniscient creator is not occasional, such as space and so forth.

Here, since every effect is made the subject (*pakṣa*) of the argument, there is no similar instance (*sapakṣa*); therefore, this is a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*). Alternatively, it is a purely negative inference by way of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*).

ṇ: For example, [the argument]: "This living body is not soulless, because that would entail the consequence of its lacking breath and so forth, like a clod of earth"—this is the *prasaṅga* (reductio). The formal application (*prayoga*), however, is as follows: "This living body possesses a self (*sātmaka*), because it possesses breath and so forth; for whatever lacks a self does not possess breath and so forth, like a clod of earth. This is a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*) preceded by a *prasaṅga*. //3//

Having thus explained the divisions and the essential nature of inference, they spoke as follows in order to establish the threefold nature of its object: "Alternatively, inference preceded by that [perception] is of three kinds, i.e., of three types.

As for what those three types are, he says: "pūrvavat," etc. That inference in which a prior cause exists is *pūrvavat*—that is, where the effect is inferred from the cause, such as when one infers that rain will occur from the rising of specific clouds. Here, by the word "cause" (*kāraṇa*), the property of the cause (*kāraṇadharma*), such as height and so forth, is to be understood.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: These clouds are producers of rain, because while possessing deep thundering and flashes of lightning (or, despite the absence of flashes of lightning), they are exceedingly high; whatever possesses these qualities is a producer of rain, just like the clouds that preceded the current rain; and these [clouds] possess those qualities; therefore, it is so.
[Objection: But since it is observed that even clouds endowed with properties such as height do not produce rain, how can the inference of an effect from a cause be considered certain?
No; for it is intended that a specific property, such as "elevatedness" (*unnatatva*), serves as the indicator (*gamaka*).
Nor can it be said that its distinction cannot be ascertained by one who is not omniscient, because that would entail the destruction of all inference.

For instance, it could certainly be said that even smoke and the like—which are distinguished from mosquitoes and other such things—cannot have their non-deviation (*avyabhicāritva*) from their respective probanda be ascertained by one who is not all-knowing.

Now, according to the principle that "a well-discriminated effect does not deviate from its cause," smoke and the like possess the capacity to indicate [their causes]; if that is so, then the same applies here as well.

For only one who is capable of discerning a specific feature such as elevation—which is non-deviant with respect to future rain—infers it from that [feature], not one who has not grasped the specific feature. As it has been said: "This is the fault of the inferrer, not of inference."

The "effect" (kārya) is that which has an effect; that which possesses this [effect] is called *śeṣavat* (the inference based on the effect). It is that case where the cause is inferred from the effect, such as rain being inferred from the observation of a river in flood. Here, by the word "effect," the mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the property of the effect is to be understood.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: The river connected to the region above the rainfall is characterized by recent rain, because, while possessing rapid currents and carrying masses of fruit, foam, wood, and so forth, it is full, like other rivers [known to have such characteristics when raining].

Inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*) is that in which the object of inference (*liṅgin*) is apprehended through a mark (*liṅga*) that is neither its effect nor its cause, yet is invariably concomitant with it, such as [inferring] water from a crane.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) for this is as follows: "The location where cranes reside possesses water, because it contains cranes, like a location commonly recognized [as having water].
Or, for example, the cognition of motion [in the sun] occurs by observing the sun, which was seen above one tree, appearing above another mountain.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: The observation of the sun elsewhere is invariably concomitant with motion, because it is an observation elsewhere, like the observation of Devadatta and others elsewhere.

In this regard, just as the observation of Devadatta and others elsewhere is preceded by walking, so too is that of the sun. Furthermore, observation elsewhere is not the effect of motion, because conjunction and the like are the effects of motion.
Others, however, describe it in this way:
The cognition of a simultaneous tactile sensation from a visual form—which is neither its effect nor its cause—arises from inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*).
Here is the formal argument (*prayoga*): "This garment possesses such a tactile sensation, because it has such a visual form, like another garment of that same kind.

Or, having seen one mango tree bearing fruit, there arises the cognition that "all mango trees in the world are flowering"; the formal argument for this is: "All mango trees in the world are flowering, because they are mango trees, like the mango tree [seen] before," and so forth.

Alternatively, [the term] *pūrvavat* means "similar to the former," because it is similar to the perception that previously apprehended the pervasion (*vyāpti*). Since there is a similarity in the object with respect to the perception that apprehends the relation (*sambandha*), there is also a certain degree of similarity here in the act of determination (*pariccheda-kriyā*) within this inference. Thus, the application of the suffix *-vat* in the sense of "possessing similarity of action" (*kriyā-tulyatva-vat*) is established; therefore, that inference from which a cognition arises that is similar to a previous cognition is *pūrvavat* inference. For example: "Desire and so forth are dependent on something else (*paratantra*), because they are qualities (*guṇatvāt*), like color and so forth."

§44: *Śeṣavat* means "by elimination" (*pariśeṣa*). It occurs when, after the negation of all possible alternatives, there is no possibility for it to apply elsewhere, resulting in the cognition of that which remains. For example, because desire and so forth are qualities, they must depend on something else; and when [possible substrata] such as the body have been negated, [the soul is understood].

[The reason is: desire and so forth are not qualities of the specific types of bodies, because there is a difference in nature (*vaidharmya*): while the qualities of those [bodies], such as color and so forth, are perceptible by both oneself and others, desire and so forth are perceptible only by oneself.
Nor do the qualities belong to the sense organs or their objects, because we observe the recollection [of them] even when those [organs or objects] have been impaired.
Nor is there any possibility for another [substratum], and therefore, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), the self (*ātman*) is established.
Furthermore, the formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: that which is the "other" is denotable by the term "self," because it is the substratum of desire and so forth.
Those things which are not denotable by the word "self" are also not the substrata of desire and so forth, just like the body and other such things.

Here, having grasped the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) through perception, the cognition of the self arises by the force of pure negative concomitance (*kevala-vyatireka*); this is the result of the *śeṣavat* inference.

Where the subject (*dharmin*) and the probans (*sādhana-dharma*) are perceptible, but the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*) is always established as imperceptible, that is the *sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa* [inference].
For example: "Desire and so forth are dependent on another [cause], because they are qualities, like color.
Or: "Apprehension is accomplished by an instrument, because it is an action, like the action of cutting.

Or: "The diversity of the world is preceded by a non-common cause, because it is variegated, like the variegation of a painting," and so forth—one should consider that there are many such examples of the *sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa* [type of inference].

If it is objected: "Since the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*) is not always perceptible, how can the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the probans (*hetu*) with that which is to be proven be apprehended?", it is replied as follows:

The subject (*dharmin*), such as desire and so forth, is indeed apprehended through perception; likewise, the probans—such as being a quality (*guṇatva*) or being an effect (*kāryatva*)—is also certainly apprehended as a property of that [subject].
Furthermore, its pervasion with its own probandum by way of dependence is indeed understood through direct perception (*adhyakṣataḥ*) in the case of color-form (*rūpa*) and other such things.
Through the exclusion of the probandum (*sādhya*), the exclusion of the probans (*sādhana*) is also understood solely from another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).
[Objection: But if this is so, what is the distinction between *pūrvavat*, *śeṣavat*, and *sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa* from one another?

It is said: when there is the apprehension of mere dependence on another in the case of desire and so forth, their status as a quality or their being an effect is as previously described. That very [status], being determined by a subverting means of knowledge (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*)—namely, that it must have a specific substratum due to the exclusion of other possible substrata—is the result of the *śeṣavat* [inference]. Even though that property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*) is perceptible in another locus, its perpetual imperceptibility in that particular locus is the basis for the designation "generally observed" (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*). Therefore, all three [types of inference] have one and the same example.

Thus, because the causes and so forth are threefold, the mark (*liṅga*) produces a threefold valid cognition; being preceded by that [mark], it is inference (*anumāna*). This is the second explanation.
Among these two explanations, only the first explanation is favored by many, beginning with those who study the text.
And regarding that, the fourfold explanation of *pūrvavat* and the others which was stated in the second explanation is precisely what should be understood here.

Now, the author of the treatise himself, for the sake of preventing confusion among beginners, sets aside the remaining modes of explanation and, in order to make known the objects of the threefold inference, explains the terms beginning with *pūrvavat* and says: "Among those," and so forth.

Among those [terms] beginning with *pūrvavat*, what is the first, *pūrvavat* inference? He says: from a cause (*kāraṇa*) as a mark (*liṅga*), the inference—meaning the cognition—of the effect (*kārya*) which possesses that mark, is *kāryānumāna*. This is proclaimed—that is, stated—in this context of the discussion on inference.
Alternatively, there is the reading: "Inference of the effect from the cause is declared here."
In that context, because of the ellipsis of the word "exists" (*asti*), there is the inference that "the effect exists because of the cause.
Here, in this discussion of inference, it is stated—that is, declared—that the knowledge "the effect exists because of the cause" is inference.

Furthermore, regarding the fact that the knowledge of the mark (*liṅgijñāna*) was expressed by the term "inference" in both readings, that is according to the opinion of those who provide the second explanation, and not according to the opinion of those who provide the first explanation.
According to the opinion of the first commentator, the very cause of knowledge would be what is denoted by the term "inference" (*anumāna*).
The same should be understood for the *śeṣavat* [type of inference] as well.
Where there is the cognition of an effect from a cause qualified by its own cognition, that is *pūrvavat* inference.

In this context, since it is stated that "the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the cause for the apprehension of an object," the result of inference is the knowledge of the effect, while the cause of that [knowledge] is inference as the means of valid cognition.

Therefore, in this case, "inference based on what has occurred before" (*pūrvavad-anumāna*) is so called because it makes known the effect—whether by way of the cause, or by the knowledge of that [cause], or by the recollection of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between cause and effect. //17–18–19//
An example of this is as follows:
"Clouds such as these, possessing a dark luster like that of bees, buffalo-horns, serpents, and *tamāla* trees, do not fail to bring rain here. (20)
Commentary: The word "yathā" (as) is used for the purpose of providing an illustration.
*Rolambas* are bees; *gavalas* are wild buffaloes born in the forest; *vyālas* are rogue elephants and serpents; and *tamālas* are the *tāpiccha* trees.
Likewise, those whose splendors or lusters (*tviṣaḥ*) are dark or blackish (*malināḥ śyāmalāḥ*) are described as such.

By this statement regarding the beauty of the clouds, a certain indescribable and extraordinary darkness is suggested. Regarding the term *evam-prāyāḥ*: the word *evaṃ* expresses "of this kind," while the word *prāyaḥ* denotes "abundance.

Therefore, the meaning of *evam-prāyāḥ* is "those in which there is an abundance (*prāya*)—that is, a preponderance—of such kinds (*evaṃ-idam-prakārāṇām*)," signifying a great frequency of this particular type.
By this, the abundance of qualities such as deep thundering and long-lasting radiance in clouds is indicated.
The meaning is that clouds endowed with the aforementioned specific attributes do not fail to produce rain for people in this world; they invariably become rain-makers.
Furthermore, the formal application (*prayoga*) should be stated here exactly as it was explained during the occasion of the commentary on the [relevant] Sūtra. //20//

Now he states the explanation of *śeṣavat* (inference by elimination): "The inference of a cause from an effect is considered *śeṣavat*; for example, from such a rise in a river, one infers that it has rained upstream. (21)

Commentary: The inferential knowledge (*anumāna*) which consists in the cognition of the sign-possessor (*liṅgin*), the cause, from the sign (*liṅga*), the effect—the particle *ca* being used for conjunction with what was previously mentioned as *pūrvavat*—that is considered *śeṣavat*.
This is the essential meaning here: where the cognition of the cause arises from the effect, that is *śeṣavat* inference.

Here too, as before, the cause of the cognition of the cause—namely, the effect, the perception of the effect, and the recollection of their relationship—is to be understood by the term "inference" (*anumāna*).
The particle *ṇ* [is used] as follows: first, it should be applied here for the purpose of introducing an example.

*ṇ*: "In such a manner"—that is, from the mark (*liṅga*) of a river flood characterized by the properties of having a very rapid current, carrying fruit, foam, and so forth, and extending across both banks, there arises the cognition that "it has rained in the upper region" [due to the cloud]. Here, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as before. //21//

And as for that which is "inferred from general observation" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), it is as follows: "The attainment of another location in a person is preceded by motion; so too is it in the case of the sun. (22) Commentary: The word *ca* has the sense of "moreover. Furthermore, that mark (*liṅga*) which is observed elsewhere than in the relation of cause and effect, by the force of a general inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), is "inferred from general observation" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*). That is as follows: [text continues]

He asks: "How so? and replies: Just as for a person, the arrival at another location from one location is preceded by motion, so too for the sun, that arrival at another location is likewise preceded by motion.
Here, by the term "arrival at another location," "perception of another location" is to be understood.
Otherwise, since arrival at another location is an effect of motion, this [perception] would not be distinct from the inference based on the remainder (*śeṣavat*).

Even though the motion of the sun as it traverses the sky is not perceived due to the absence of the range of visual observation by the eye, nevertheless, its appearance at the peak of the western mountain (astācala) after a certain interval from the eastern mountain (udayācala) makes known its motion. Furthermore, the formal argument (prayoga) has already been stated above.

Alternatively, the world does not perceive that reaching another location is an effect of motion; thus, this example is presented here without the intention of expressing a causal relationship (*kārya-kāraṇa-bhāva*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: "The sun’s reaching of another location is preceded by motion, because it is a reaching of another location, like Devadatta’s reaching of another location.
(22) He states the definition of analogy (*upamāna*):
"The establishment of an unknown thing through its similarity to a well-known thing. (23)
The means of comparison (upamāna) is declared to be as follows: "As is a cow, so is a gavaya. //23//
Commentary: The aphorism is: "Comparison (upamāna) is the means of establishing that which is to be established (the object of proof) through similarity with something well-known" (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.6).

Here, the word "from which" (*yataḥ*) must be supplied; therefore, comparison is defined as that knowledge of similarity from which the establishment—that is, the comprehension—of the relationship between a name and its bearer occurs. This establishment pertains to the object to be proven (*sādhya*), namely the gavaya, which is not yet well-known, based on the similarity (*sādharmya*)—that is, the possession of common properties—with a well-known entity, such as a cow. That knowledge of similarity is what is designated as comparison.
Furthermore, the establishment of similarity is preceded by traditional authority (*āgama*). Therefore, for the purpose of indicating that authority, he says: "As is a cow, so is a *gavaya*.
Here, a *gavaya* is a wild ox (*araṇya-gavaya*).
The meaning here is this: someone sent by his master to bring back a gavaya, not knowing its nature for that purpose, asked him, "What is a gavaya like? He replied, "It is like a cow."

Then, as he wanders in the forest and perceives an object similar [to a cow], there arises from the contact of the sense organ with the object—assisted by the recollection of the meaning of that [previously heard] sentence—a cognition of similarity (*sārūpya*) in the form "This is similar to a cow. This is the fruit of perception. That very cognition, when characterized by qualifiers such as non-erroneousness (*avyabhicārin*) and so forth, produces the comprehension of the relationship between the name and the named in the form "This is what is denoted by the word *gavaya*"; this is *upamāna*.
Furthermore, the comprehension of the relationship between the name and the named is the fruit of *upamāna*.
Furthermore, it is not derived from scripture (*āgamika*), because at that time the word that produces such knowledge is absent.

Moreover, the knowledge regarding the object—the individual buffalo (*gavaya*)—that arises as something to be avoided and so forth, is the fruit of perception (*pratyakṣaphala*), since it is produced by the contact of the sense organ with its object. //23//
Now he states the fourth [means of knowledge], verbal testimony (śābda): "Verbal testimony is the instruction of a reliable person; thus, the means of knowledge are fourfold.
The objects of knowledge, however, are the self, the body, and so forth, as well as the intellect, the senses, pleasure, and so on. (24)
Commentary: "Verbal" (śābda) means that which is produced by words; its meaning is "scriptural tradition" (āgama).
The particle "tu" (but/and) is used for the sake of a different sequence: verbal means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), however, is the instruction of a reliable person (*āptopadeśa*).
A reliable person (*āpta*) is one who speaks exclusively the truth and is well-wishing; his instruction—that is, his speech—is "instruction of a reliable person."
The knowledge produced by that [word] is the result of verbal [cognition].
Valid cognition (*māna*), which is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), is thus said to be fourfold according to the method described.

Having thus explained the first reality, that of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa-tattva*), he now speaks in order to explain the second reality, that of the object of valid knowledge (*prameya-tattva*):

"But the object of cognition (*prameya*) consists of the self, the body, and so forth. The object of cognition, moreover, is that which is to be grasped by the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-phala*); it is the self, the body, and so on. "Self" (*ātman*) refers to the living being (*jīva*), and "body" (*deha*) refers to the physical form (*vapu*); that which has these two as its first [members] is "the self, the body, and so forth" (*ātma-dehādyam*). Furthermore, the intellect (*buddhi*), the sense organs (*indriya*), pleasure (*sukha*), and so on are also objects of cognition. "Intellect" (*buddhi*) is knowledge (*jñāna*); "sense organs" (*indriya*) range from the eye up to the mind; "pleasure" (*sukha*) is satisfaction (*sāta*); and that which has these as its first [members] is "the intellect, the sense organs, pleasure, and so forth" (*buddhi-indriya-sukhādi*).
The particle *ca* (and) serves as a conjunction (*samuccaye*) with respect to the self, the body, and so forth.
Here, by the two qualifiers—the first word "ātma" and the word "ādi"—the inclusion of the remaining seven objects of knowledge (*prameya*) should be understood.

Thus, the Nyāya Sūtra states: "That [object of knowledge] is of twelve kinds, distinguished as: self, body, sense organs, intellect, mind, activity, defects, rebirth, fruit, suffering, and liberation" (NS 1.1.9).

In that regard, everything from the body down to suffering is to be abandoned (*heya*), while liberation (*apavarga*) is to be accepted (*upādeya*). As for the self (*ātman*), it is in some sense to be abandoned and in some sense to be accepted: it is to be abandoned as the experiencer of pleasure, pain, and so forth, but to be accepted as being liberated from those. In this context, the self is the substratum (*āśraya*) of desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, knowledge, and the like.
The self is recognized through such attributes as consciousness, agency, and omnipresence.
1: The body is the locus for the experience of those [objects].
2: The five sense organs are the nose, tongue, eye, skin, and ear.
3: The five objects are visible form, taste, odor, touch, and sound.

ṇ: Among those, fragrance, taste, color, and touch are the four qualities of earth; color, taste, and touch are the three qualities of water; color and touch are the two qualities of fire; touch alone is the quality of air; and sound is the quality of space. 4.
ṇ: Intellect (*buddhi*) means apprehension or knowledge; it is momentary, and because its nature is experience, it is the cause of saṃsāra and must therefore be abandoned. 5.

[NS 1.1.16] Since cognitions do not arise simultaneously even when there is contact between the sense organs and their objects, and since internal objects such as pleasure are perceived—just like the perception of external objects such as odors—the internal instrument, the mind (*manas*), is inferred; for it is accomplished by means of an instrument. It has all things as its object, and it is atomic, possesses velocity, moves rapidly, and is eternal.

[NS 1.1.17] Activity (*pravṛtti*) consists of the operations of speech, mind, and body, and it bears auspicious or inauspicious fruits. [NS 1.1.18] Attachment, aversion, and delusion are the three defects (*doṣa*); envy and other such states are included within these very [three], and this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) is produced by them.
The primary fruit is pleasure and pain, consisting of the defects produced by worldly activity; however, the means to that [fruit] is secondary.

Pain, which is by nature affliction and torment, is indeed implied by the mention of "fruit," yet it is taught here for the purpose of cultivating the realization of pain, since even pleasure is inseparable from pain.
Liberation (apavarga) is the absolute cessation of pain, the abiding of the self in its own essential nature, divested of all qualities.
Because it is impossible to abandon pleasure through the discrimination of pleasure and pain, one who desires to abandon pain should abandon pleasure as well;
for the supreme human goal, liberation (*apavarga*), consists in the severance of the continuous cycle of birth, old age, and death, and that is attained through the knowledge of reality. 12 //24//
He states the essential nature of doubt (*saṃśaya*) and purpose (*prayojana*):
"Doubt is considered to be a cognition characterized by uncertainty, such as 'What is this?';
and because one desires that [object], the purpose is that which is to be accomplished. (25)

Commentary: This word *kim* exists in the sense of censure, as in "he who betrays is no friend at all" (*akiṃsakhā yo 'bhidruhyati*); it exists in the sense of inquiry, as in "what is dear to you? (*kiṃ te priyam*); it exists in the sense of prohibition, as in "what is the use of your weeping? (*kiṃ te ruditena*); it exists in the sense of denial, as in "what do I owe you? (*kiṃ te 'haṃ dhārayāmi*); it exists in the sense of conciliation, as in "what can I do for you that is pleasing? (*kiṃ te 'haṃ priyaṃ karomi*); it exists in the sense of contempt, as in "who is making you prattle on? (*kas tvām ullāpayate*); and it exists in the sense of deliberation, as in "what is this that is seen in the distance? (*kim idaṃ dūre dṛśyate*). Here, however, [it is used] in the sense of deliberation, by means of seeing from afar, one perceives the general nature of the object.
Doubting its specific nature, one reflects: "Is this perceptible object standing upright a post or a person?
That reflective inquiry which, being perceptual, involves the consideration of multiple alternatives while remaining in doubt, is considered and accepted as *saṃśaya* (doubt).

Now, as for the purpose (*prayojana*): because of the desire for something—that is, because of the longing for a particular result—one engages in activity and exerts effort toward the means for that [result]. That which is desired as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is the purpose, the fruit; the meaning is that it is the purpose for the sake of which one engages in actions.

Furthermore, because the undertaking of presenting the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is rooted in the purpose, the purpose, although included within the objects of cognition (*prameya*), is taught separately. //25//
Now, wishing to explain the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the tenet (*siddhānta*), he says: "But the example is that which is not a subject of dispute.
The tenet, however, is of four types, according to the divisions of *sarvatantre* and so forth. (26)

Commentary: "The end (anta) is seen" means that certainty (niścaya) is found here; thus, this is an example (dṛṣṭānta). Furthermore, what is this? He says: it is that which, being presented, does not become the object (viṣaya) or domain (gocara) of dispute (vivāda)—where "dispute" refers to a mutually contradictory argument between the proponent and the opponent. The meaning is that an example must be presented in inference and so forth as something agreed upon by both the proponent and the opponent.

Although the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) will be discussed among the five members [of the syllogism] that are to be mentioned later, it is taught here separately because it is the locus for grasping the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the proving property (*sādhana*). For an argument endowed with positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) falters only so long as it lacks the support of a clearly perceived example. And it has been said: "An object that has entered the range of the thinker's mind wavers only so long..."
"ṇ: As long as [the system] is not supported by the illustration of the 'prop' (uttambhana) itself. ṇ64: "But the established tenet (siddhānta), moreover, is of four kinds.
Why? He says: 'By the division of the *sarvatantropadiṣṭa* and so forth,' that is, by the distinction between the *sarvatantropadiṣṭa* and the other types."

The first is the *sarvatantrasiddhānta* (tenet common to all systems); from the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it should be understood that the *pratitantrasiddhānta* (tenet specific to a particular system), the *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (tenet established by the context of the discussion), and the *abhyupagamasiddhānta* (tenet accepted for the sake of argument) are also included.
Here, by the word *tantra*, a treatise (*śāstra*) is to be understood.

Among these, a tenet that is not contradicted by any system and is accepted within its own system is a *sarvatrantrasiddhānta* (tenet established for all systems), which is the object of agreement among all treatises; for example, that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are the instruments for establishing the objects of cognition (*prameya*), that the sense organs are the olfactory organ and so forth, that their respective objects are smell and so forth, and that the determination of an object of cognition occurs through a means of valid cognition, and so on. A tenet established in one system but not established in another system is a *pratitantrasiddhānta* (tenet established in specific systems); for example, that the sense organs are composed of material elements (*bhautika*) according to the followers of Yoga and Kaṇāda, whereas they are non-material (*abhautika*) according to the Sāṃkhyas.

Likewise, for the Sāṃkhyas, everything arises as only existent and not non-existent; for the Naiyāyikas and others, everything arises as only non-existent due to the power of the causal complex (sāmagrī); but for the Jains, both existent and non-existent arise, and so forth.

*Adhikaraṇasiddhānta*: That is an *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* when, upon the establishment of one thing that is being processed as a thesis, there follows the establishment of something additional by way of implication; for example, when through [the reason] "being an effect" and so forth, the general existence of an intelligent cause is established in relation to the earth and other things, there follows the establishment of another cause capable of producing them—namely, a substratum of eternal knowledge, will, and effort.

When those who engage in mature debate, desiring to proclaim the excellence of their own intellect, accept some matter without prior examination and then examine its specific qualities, that is an *abhyupagama-siddhānta* (a tenet accepted for the sake of argument). For example: "Let sound be a substance; however, is it eternal or non-eternal? Here, having provisionally accepted the unestablished fact that sound is a substance, one examines the specific quality of its being eternal or non-eternal. Thus, the *siddhānta* is of four kinds. //26//
§65: He explains the nature of the three principles, beginning with the members [of a syllogism]:

"The thesis (pratijñā), the reason (hetu), the example (dṛṣṭānta), the application (upanaya), and likewise the conclusion (nigama)—these are the five members (avayava). Reasoning (tarka) occurs when doubt has been resolved. (27)
After [the initial inquiry], conviction through doubt and reasoning is considered to be the final determination (nirṇaya). (28) [Couplet]

Commentary: There are five members [of a syllogism]. Which five? He says: the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the application (*upanaya*), and by the word "conclusion" (*nigama*), the conclusion (*nigamana*) itself.

Among these, the proposition is the thesis; it is the statement of the property and the subject, such as "this mountain possesses fire," "it has smoke," and so forth. The reason is the means of proof; it is the statement of the logical mark (*liṅga*), such as "because of possessing smoke," and so forth.

The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is the statement of an illustration; it is of two kinds: by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). By way of positive concomitance, for example: "Whatever possesses smoke possesses fire, such as a kitchen," and so forth. By way of negative concomitance, for example: "Whatever does not possess fire does not possess smoke, such as water," and so forth.
The application (upanaya) is the statement that brings the reason to bear upon the subject, such as "and this [mountain] possesses smoke," and so forth.

The conclusion (nigamana) is the application of the property to be proven by means of the instruction of the reason, such as "because it possesses smoke, it has fire," and so forth. Now, the principle of reasoning (tarka): "Reasoning occurs when doubt has been stilled."

When the true nature of an object is not correctly understood, there arises a doubt (*saṃśaya*) such as, "Is this a post or a person? Upon the cessation—that is, the removal—of that doubt, there occurs *tarka* (reasoning), which consists in the investigation of positive concomitances (*anvaya-dharma*).
To explain how this is so, he says: "Just as by crows, etc. The word "just as" (*yathā*) serves to illustrate; [the reasoning is] that it must be a post (*sthāṇu*), meaning it must be a wooden stake.
Here, the particle *hi* should be understood as having the sense of a certain conjecture (*niścayotprekṣaṇa*).

ṇ: For at present, since a human being is impossible here in the forest and because only things possessing the characteristics of a *sthāṇu* (a trunk or post) are observed, it follows that a *sthāṇu* alone is appropriate here. ṇ: As it has been said: "This is a forest; the sun has set, and no human being can possibly exist here now. Therefore, this must certainly be one who shares the nature of a bird or similar creature, and whose name is equal to 'Smārārāti' (the Enemy of Smara, i.e., Śiva). This is the *tarka* (logical reasoning).

Now, he states the true nature of *nirṇaya* (ascertainment): "After [the aforementioned]," and so forth. Following immediately after doubt (*saṃśaya*) and reasoning (*tarka*), which have the previously described natures, that cognition—such as the realization "this is certainly a post" or "this is certainly a person"—is considered and intended to be *nirṇaya*, that is, certainty (*niścaya*).
Since the terms "that" (*yat*) and "which" (*tat*) are understood from their connection with the meaning even when not explicitly stated in certain cases, they are explained here [by implication].
The same should be understood in other instances as well. //27-28//

Now, he states the true nature of *vāda* (debate): "That discourse which arises from the adoption of a position and a counter-position by a teacher and a student, and which serves as the cause for the practice [of logic], is declared to be *vāda*. (29)

Commentary: Discussion (*kathā*) is the adoption of a thesis and a counter-thesis by the proponent and the opponent. It is of two kinds: discussion between those free from passion (*vītarāga-kathā*) and discussion between those seeking victory (*vijigīṣu-kathā*).

In that [discussion] where a disciple, together with a teacher who is free from passion, employs proof (*sādhana*) and refutation (*upalambha*) for the sake of determining the truth—where he provides proof for his own position and refutation (which is the critique of the opponent's inference) against the opposing position—that is called "discussion between those free from passion" by the technical name *vāda*.
One may conduct a *vāda* even if it lacks the formal establishment of a counter-position (*pratipakṣasthāpanā-hīna*).

By way of the door of inquiry (*praśna-dvāra*), that discourse in which one desirous of victory (*vijigīṣu*) engages with another desirous of victory—seeking gain, honor, and fame for the sake of victory or defeat—or where one free from passion (*vītarāga*) engages for the sake of favoring others and for the sake of protecting the sprout of knowledge (*jñānāṅkura*), is called *vijigīṣu-kathā*. It consists of four members (*catur-aṅgā*): the proponent (*vādī*), the opponent (*prativādī*), the chairman of the assembly (*sabhāpati*), and the assessors (*prāśnika*). It is designated by the terms *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā*.

And so it has been said: "Wrangling (*jalpa*) and cavil (*vitaṇḍā*) are for the purpose of protecting the determination of truth, like the covering of thorny branches for the protection of the growth of seeds" (NS 4.2.50). "Wrangling (*jalpa*) is a debate characterized by the previously stated definitions, wherein there is the employment of quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), as well as proof and refutation; that same [debate], when devoid of the establishment of a counter-position, is cavil (*vitaṇḍā*)" (NS 1.2.2–3). This concludes the clarification of *vāda*, *jalpa*, and *vitaṇḍā*. Now, let us proceed with the subject at hand: the teacher (*ācārya*) is the instructor and preceptor; the student (*śiṣya*) is the learner and disciple.

"Of those two"—namely, the teacher and the student—"due to the adoption of a thesis and a counter-thesis": a *pakṣa* (thesis) is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), which is the collection of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth; a *pratipakṣa* (counter-thesis) is the subsequent position (*uttarapakṣa*), meaning a position that opposes the prima facie position. Because of the adoption—that is, the acceptance—of these two, that discourse which is the cause of practice, the cause for repeated training, and which constitutes authoritative discussion (*vārttā*), such discourse is called, or celebrated as, *vāda* (debate). The teacher accepts the prima facie position and explains it, while the student adopts the counter-position and refutes the prima facie position.

Thus, when a teacher and a student hold a discussion for the sake of practice—comprising the presentation of a position and its counter-position, while disregarding the role of the moderator, the chairman of the assembly, victory or defeat, quibbling, futile rejoinders, and so forth—that should be understood as *vāda* (debate). //29//
Now he explains *jalpa* (disputation) and *vitaṇḍā* (cavil):

"That which is a debate among those seeking victory, characterized by the refutations of quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and so forth, is *jalpa*. That same [debate], when devoid of a counter-position, is *vitaṇḍā*. (30)

Commentary: Furthermore, that which is a debate (*vijigīṣu-kathā*) initiated by two disputants (*vāda-prativādin*), desiring victory—that is, a formal discussion (*pramāṇa-goṣṭhī*)—of what nature is it? It is one characterized by "quibbles" (*chala*) and "futile rejoinders" (*jāti*), whose definitions will be stated hereafter; by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the "points of defeat" (*nigrahasthāna*) and so forth are included. That in which there is refutation (*dūṣaṇa*)—the production of faults—in the thesis or other positions proposed by the opponent, through these [means], is "refutation by quibble, futile rejoinder, etc. This is *jalpa*, which takes the form of a debate for the sake of victory. The word "illustrated" (*udāhṛta*) is to be connected from the preceding verse.

If it is objected that it is not proper for the virtuous to produce refutations of an opponent’s position through means such as *chala* (quibble) and *jāti* (futile rejoinder), we say no; for the production of such refutations is permitted as a means for attaining the true path (*sanmārga*). Indeed, by establishing one's own position, the production of refutations against an opponent’s argument—even through the employment of *chala*, *jāti*, and so forth—is permitted as a means for attaining the true path. And thus it has been said:
"O, how else could those whose mouths are made to chatter by fragments of ill-taught and fallacious reasoning, and who are adorned with the arrogance of cavil (*vitaṇḍā*), be refuted? (1)

"The world follows what it has already followed; thus, having been led astray onto a wrong path, the compassionate Sage spoke of *chala* (quibble) and the other [fallacies] as deviations from the path" (*Nyāyabhūṣaṇa*, p.
11). Therefore, when a difficult situation arises, the establishment of one's own position even by means of *chala* and the like is permitted.

For in the victory over another, there arises the possibility of faults such as the destruction of *dharma*; therefore, victory even by means of quibbles (*chala*) and the like is better. As for the passage beginning with "But that [is] *vitaṇḍā*," the word "but" (*tu*) has the sense of restriction and its position is displaced. That [is] precisely that same debate of those seeking victory (*vijigīṣu-kathā*), devoid of a counter-position—that is, lacking the opponent's presentation which would oppose the proponent's stated position; the meaning is that it is devoid of a proof for a counter-position. This is what is called *vitaṇḍā*.
The meaning is this: for a caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*), not establishing a position even when one has been accepted by his own master, merely refutes what is said by the opponent through debate. //30//
Now, he elucidates the nature of the three principles beginning with the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*):

The fallacies of the reason are those such as the "unestablished" (*asiddha*) and so forth; quibble (*chala*) is like a well containing new water; and the "futilities" (*jāti*) are the semblances of refutations (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*), by which the thesis (*pakṣa*) and other members of the argument are not actually refuted. (31)

N77: There are five fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa): the unestablished (asiddha), the contradictory (viruddha), the inconclusive (anaikāntika), the mistimed (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa), and the counter-balanced (prakaraṇasama).

Among these, that which lacks the property of being a characteristic of the subject (pakṣadharmatva) is the unestablished; for example: "Sound is impermanent because it is visible" (1). That which exists in the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) but does not exist in the similar instances (sapakṣa) is the contradictory; for example: "Sound is permanent because it is a product" (2).
ṇ: The inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) is that which occurs in all three [times] of the [logical] period. For example: "Sound is impermanent because it is knowable" (3).

ṇ: The time for the application of a reason (*hetu*) is the occasion of adopting a thesis (*pakṣa*) that is not sublated by perception or scripture. When a reason is applied having passed beyond that time, it is called "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), meaning it exists in a thesis that is contradicted by perception or scripture. Examples: "Fire is not hot because it is produced," and "Wine should be drunk by a Brāhmaṇa because it is a liquid substance, like milk" (4).

The *prakaraṇasama* (neutralized by the context) is a reason that possesses the three characteristics not only for establishing one's own position but also for establishing the opposing position; the meaning is that it is equal with respect to both the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*).

When one person says, "Sound is non-eternal, because it is one or the other of the subject and the similar instance (sapakṣa), like the similar instance," the second person replies: "If non-eternality is established by this method, then let the establishment of eternality also be possible—namely, that sound is eternal, because it is one or the other of the subject and the similar instance, like the similar instance. Or alternatively: "Sound is non-eternal, because the properties of the eternal are not perceived, like a jar"; or "Sound is eternal, because the properties of the non-eternal are not perceived, like space."

Furthermore, none of these is a stronger proof such that it could be said to subvert the other. Although these fallacies of reason (*hetvābhāsa*) are included within the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), they are stated separately because, by effecting a discernment of logic (*nyāyapraviveka*), they bring about the purification of the subject matter (*vastuśuddhi*) in debate.

Regarding "quibble" (*chala*): "The well has new water. Quibble is the obstruction of speech through the imposition of one's own intended interpretation upon a statement presented by another in a debate.
That [quibble] is threefold: quibble regarding speech (*vāk-chala*), quibble regarding a general term (*sāmānya-chala*), and quibble regarding metaphorical usage (*upacāra-chala*).
Quibble regarding speech is the imagining of a different meaning in what has been stated by another.

For example, when someone says "the boy has a new blanket" (*nava-kambala*) with the intention that he possesses a *navya* (new) blanket, the opponent who employs the quibble asks: "How does he have nine (*nava*) blankets? //1//

§71: *Sāmānyacchala* (quibble regarding the general) is the refutation of a general term by attributing to it the status of a cause, even though that term leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) through mere possibility. For example, in the context of praising a Brāhmaṇa, someone says: "Oh, what a truly excellent Brāhmaṇa he is, endowed with both learning and conduct! To this, another person, who employs quibbling, attributes causality to the property of being a Brāhmaṇa and objects, saying: "It is possible for a Brāhmaṇa to possess the excellence of learning and conduct.
[In doing so, he challenges the original speaker by falsely imputing that the word "Brāhmaṇa" functions as the logical reason.]

[The opponent says: This [argument] is inconclusive because of the *vrātya*. For if the perfection of knowledge and conduct exists in a Brāhmaṇa, it would also exist in a *vrātya*; for a *vrātya* is indeed a Brāhmaṇa. //2//

N80: When a figurative usage is employed, the denial [of its literal sense] by imagining it to have its primary meaning is "quibble regarding metaphorical usage" (*upacāra-chala*). For example, when it is said, "The platforms cry out," the proponent of the quibble says: "It is the persons standing on the platforms who cry out, not the platforms themselves, because they are insentient. //3//

Now, the author of the treatise, wishing to explain "quibble" (*chala*), states an example of the first type, quibble regarding speech (*vāk-chala*): "The well has new water. In this case, when the word *nava*, meaning "new," has been employed, the quibbler objects: "How can there be nine (*nava*) waters in a single well?
By this, the examples for the remaining two types of quibble should also be understood as being indicated.
Regarding the passage beginning with "jātayaḥ": *jātayaḥ* are fallacious refutations (*dūṣaṇābhāsāḥ*).

They are called "fallacious refutations" because, although they are not actual refutations, they appear as such. By means of these, the thesis and so forth—the thesis, the reason, and so on—are not actually refuted; because they are mere appearances, they cannot be refuted. Rather, when a valid reason or a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) has been employed by the proponent, a certain kind of counter-position (*pratyavasthāna*)—which consists primarily of a reflection of the reason (*hetupratibimbanaprāya*)—is a *jāti*. This occurs when, at that very moment, the true nature of the fault [in the opponent's argument] does not manifest.

And that [refutation] is of twenty-four varieties, distinguished by the counter-objections such as "the similar" (*sādhya*) and so forth. For example: similarity (*sādharmya*), dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), superiority (*utkarṣa*), inferiority (*apakarṣa*), the commendable (*varṇya*), the non-commendable (*avarṇya*), the optional (*vikalpa*), the attainment of the probandum (*sādhyaprāpti*), the non-attainment (*aprāpti*), the consequence (*prasaṅga*), the counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*), non-arising (*anutpatti*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), the point of the discussion (*prakaraṇa*), the non-reason (*ahetu*), implication (*arthāpatti*), non-distinction (*aviśeṣa*), perception (*upalabdhi*), non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), permanence (*nitya*), impermanence (*anitya*), and the effect (*kārya*).
Among these, the counter-objection based on similarity is the fallacy of "similarity through similarity" (*sādharmyasama*).

When the argument "Sound is non-eternal because it is produced, like a jar" has been stated using a similarity-based formulation (*sādharmya-prayoga*), an opposition is raised by means of that very similarity:

"If sound is held to be non-eternal because of its similarity to the non-eternal jar due to its being produced, then it follows that it must be eternal because of its similarity to the eternal ether (*ākāśa*) due to its being incorporeal (*amūrta*).

(1) §83: An opposition based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is the "balancing-by-dissimilarity" (*vaidharmya-sama*) fallacy; it is an opposition raised when the aforementioned argument—"Sound is non-eternal because it is produced, like a jar"—is stated using a dissimilarity-based formulation (*vaidharmya*).
Ṇ: Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal; for that which is corporeal is seen to be non-eternal, such as a jar and the like.

Ṇ: If, on account of its dissimilarity to the eternal ether, sound is held to be non-eternal due to being produced, then, by virtue of its dissimilarity to non-eternal things like jars—namely, its incorporeality—it follows that it must be eternal, since there is no distinction [between the two cases].
Ṇ84: Objections based on exaggeration and depreciation constitute the two fallacies known as *utkarṣasama* (balancing the addition) and *apakarṣasama* (balancing the subtraction).

In that very same argument, [the opponent], while attributing some similarity with the example (*dṛṣṭāntasādharmya*) to the subject of the thesis (*sādhya-dharmin*), employs the fallacy (*jāti*) of "balancing the addition" (*utkarṣasama*):

"If sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a jar, then, like a jar, it must also be corporeal (*mūrta*). If it is not corporeal, then let it not be impermanent either, just as the jar is not. Thus, he attributes the addition of another property (*dharmāntara-utkarṣa*) to the sound. 3.
ṇ: But as for the "reduction" (apakarṣa): a jar, being produced, is seen to be non-audible; let sound be the same.

ṇ: If not, then like a jar, let it also not be impermanent—thus one reduces audibility to the case of sound. ṇ85: The two fallacious rejoinders (jāti) known as "equal by the describable" (varṇyasama) and "equal by the non-describable" (avarṇyasama) consist in opposition based on what is to be described and what is not to be described.

That which is to be described (*varṇya*) is to be praised, while its opposite is not to be praised (*avarṇya*). When one employs two fallacies (*jāti*), namely *varṇyasama* and *avarṇyasama*, by reversing these two properties of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), it is as follows:

"The property of sound, such as being produced (*kṛtakatva*), is not like the property of a jar; and the property of a jar is not like the property of sound. For indeed, the property of the probandum and the property of the example ought to be made equivalent.

But here there is a reversal: for the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth, which belongs to a jar, is not the same as that which belongs to sound. For the "producedness" of a jar is of one kind, being generated by a potter and the like; whereas the "producedness" of sound is generated by the operation of the palate, lips, and so forth. (5–6) ṇ86: *Vikalpasamā* (the equalizing by alternative) is a futile rejoinder (*jāti*) consisting in an opposition based on the variation of another property.

[Objection: Just as some produced things are seen to be soft, such as cotton beds and the like, while others are hard, such as axes and the like; so too, some produced things will be impermanent, such as jars and the like, while others will be permanent, such as sound and the like. [Response:
*Sādhyasama* (the "equal-to-the-probandum") is a futile rejoinder (*jāti*) consisting in an opposition based on establishing an equality with the probandum (*sādhya*).

[For instance: If it is the case that as the jar is, so is the sound, then it follows that as the sound is, so is the jar. And since the sound is the probandum (*sādhya*), the jar would also become a probandum. Consequently, the probandum could not serve as an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) for the probandum.
If it is not thus, nevertheless, because of their dissimilarity, it is even more so not a valid example. (8) ṇ88:
Opposition by means of the alternatives of "reaching" and "not reaching" constitutes the *jāti* [fallacy] called "equivalence through reaching and non-reaching.
(ṇ: As for this "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) which has been put forward as the probans (*sādhana*), does it establish the probandum (*sādhya*) by reaching it, or without reaching it?

If [it is argued that] there is attainment (*prāpti*), then attainment occurs only between two things that both exist, not between what exists and what does not; and since both exist, what is to be established (*sādhya*) and what is the means of establishment (*sādhana*)? Furthermore, being a means of establishment without having attained [the object] is illogical, as it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). (9–10)

§89: The sophistical refutation (*jāti*) known as "the equal-to-the-consequence" (*prasaṅgasama*) consists in opposing [the argument] by means of drawing out an unwanted consequence (*prasaṅga*). For example: "If 'being produced' (*kṛtakatva*) is the proof for impermanence, then what is the proof for 'being produced'? And what is the proof for that proof? §90: The sophistical refutation known as "the equal-to-the-counter-example" (*pratidṛṣṭāntasama*) consists in opposing [the argument] by means of a counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*).
When it is stated, "Sound is non-eternal because it follows immediately upon effort, like a jar," the proponent of the genus (*jāti-vādin*) says:

"Just as a jar is seen to be non-eternal because it follows immediately upon effort, so too is the counter-example, space (*ākāśa*), seen to follow immediately upon effort even though it is eternal, since it is perceived immediately after the effort of digging a well. This is not an instance of pointing out inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*), because it is a counter-argument (*pratyavasthāna*) by means of a different category (*bhagya-antara*). 12.
§91: An opposition based on non-arising is the *anutpatti-sama* futile rejoinder (*jāti*).
[Objection: Since the subject (*dharmin*) called "sound" has not yet arisen, where could the property (*dharma*) of "being produced" reside?
Thus, because the reason (*hetu*) is non-existent, there is no proof for impermanence. (13)

§92: That same *jāti* (futile rejoinder), whether it be *sādharmyasamā* (balancing the homogeneity) or *vaidharmyasamā* (balancing the heterogeneity), when presented as a doubt, becomes the *saṃśayasamā* (balancing the doubt) *jāti*.

For example: "Is sound impermanent because of its similarity to a jar through its being produced (*kṛtakatva*), or is it permanent because of its dissimilarity to that [jar] through its similarity to space (*ākāśa*) by virtue of being incorporeal (*amūrtatva*)? §93:
When that same *sādharmyasamā* or *vaidharmyasamā* *jāti* is employed with the intention of establishing a second alternative, it becomes *prakaraṇasamā* (balancing the point at issue).
In that very context, when the argument is "Sound is non-eternal because it is produced, like a jar," [one might object]: "Sound is eternal because it is audible, like sound itself.
The diversity of *jāti* (futile rejoinders) should be understood as arising merely from differences in the manner of their presentation.
(94) The *jāti* called "Equivalence through the Reason" (*hetusama*) consists in an opposition to the reason based on its impossibility across the three periods of time.
The reason (*hetu*) is the means of proof (*sādhana*); it must exist either before, after, or simultaneously with that which is to be proven (*sādhya*).
If it exists before, then while the *sādhya* is non-existent, for what would it be a means of proof?
If the means of proof exists later, then the *sādhya* must exist beforehand; and if that is already established beforehand, what is the use of a means of proof?
[Objection: If the probandum and the probans are simultaneous, then, like the left and right horns of a cow, there could be no relationship of probandum and probans between them at all. [Response:
*Arthāpattisama* (the equalization by implication) is a futile rejoinder based on an implication.

If it follows by implication that sound is impermanent because of its similarity to the impermanent—namely, its being produced—then it follows by implication that it must be permanent because of its similarity to the permanent.

Furthermore, there is a similarity between this [sound] and eternal things such as space, namely, the quality of being incorporeal (*amūrtatva*); thus, this is merely a different mode of presentation. (17) The *aviśeṣasamā* (the "equalization of non-distinction") is a futile rejoinder (*jāti*) consisting of an objection based on the induction of non-distinction.

(18) If a single property, such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), is admitted for both sound and a jar, then, due to their connection with that common property, they would be non-distinct; and consequently, by that same logic, the non-distinction of all categories of entities would follow. (18)
N97: A counter-argument based on a logical justification (*upapatti*) is the *upapattisama* futile rejoinder (*jāti*).

When it is argued that sound is impermanent because of its being produced (*kṛtakatva*), [the opponent] objects: "In that case, why does it not also become permanent because of its being incorporeal (*amūrtatva*)? This intends to result in a lack of definitive determination due to the justification for both positions; thus, this is merely a difference in the manner of pointing out [the fallacy]. N98: A counter-argument based on perception (*upalabdhi*) is the *upalabdhisama* futile rejoinder. When it is stated, "Sound is impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort," [the opponent] objects as follows: [text continues]
Ṇ: Indeed, being immediately subsequent to an effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) is not the proof for impermanence.
Ṇ: For that by which the probandum (*sādhya*) cannot be apprehended in its absence is called a "proof" (*sādhana*).

Ṇ: And impermanence is apprehended even in the absence of being immediately subsequent to an effort, as in the case of lightning and so forth; and it is likewise in the case of sound when it is produced by trees being shattered by the force of the wind. (20)
§99: The "equal to non-apprehension" (anupalabdhisamā) futile rejoinder (*jāti*) consists in opposing [the argument] by means of non-apprehension.
Thus, when the reason "being produced immediately after effort" has been put forward, the proponent of the rejoinder says:
"Sound is not an effect of effort; it certainly exists even prior to its utterance, but it is not apprehended because of its connection with an obstruction."
If it is argued that even when an obstruction is not perceived, the sound does not exist prior to its utterance because it is not perceived, we say no.
For in this case, does that non-perception reside within itself or not?

If it resides [within itself], then just as there is a non-perception of the obstruction in which the non-perception resides, so too there would have to be a non-perception of the non-perception of the obstruction itself.
Since there is no perception of an obstruction due to its non-perception, it must be non-existent.

And since that [obstruction] is absent, the existence of the obstruction follows from its perception. Consequently, just as in the case of a wooden peg or similar object hidden by earth, the non-apprehension of sound prior to its utterance is caused precisely by the perception of an obstruction.
Furthermore, if non-perception does not apply to itself, then non-perception would not exist even in its own nature.
Nevertheless, since non-existence consists in non-perception and existence consists in perception, it follows that sound must exist even prior to its utterance.
Thus, because it lacks the quality of being produced by effort in either of these two ways, sound is eternal.

This is the *nityasama* (balancing the eternal) fallacy, which establishes the eternity of sound by means of a dilemma concerning the permanence or impermanence of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).
When it is proposed that "sound is impermanent," the proponent of the *jāti* (fallacy) raises a dilemma:
"Is this impermanence which is predicated of sound itself impermanent or permanent?
If it is impermanent, then it must necessarily perish; thus, because impermanence perishes, sound would be permanent.

[Objection: Now, even if impermanence (*anityatā*) were itself eternal (*nitya*), nevertheless, because a property (*dharma*) must have a substratum (*āśraya*) and cannot exist without one, the sound (*śabda*) which serves as its substratum would also necessarily be eternal; for if that [sound] were impermanent, it would be impossible for its property to be eternal. Thus, in both cases, sound is eternal.
(22) [Response: An objection raised by establishing the impermanence of all entities in this manner is the fallacy known as "balancing the impermanent" (*anityasama*).

If it is argued that "the jar has a similarity with sound by way of impermanence," and on that basis the impermanence of sound is established, then since every other entity indeed possesses some kind of similarity with the jar, they too would necessarily be impermanent. Alternatively, if other entities do not become impermanent despite having such a similarity, then let sound likewise not be impermanent. Because this [fallacy] arises from pointing out a specific distinction after first establishing mere impermanence, it is distinct from the *aviśeṣasama* (balancing the non-distinction). 23.
The *kāryasama* (equal-to-the-effect) futile rejoinder (*jāti*) consists in an objection based on the presentation of the diversity of effects produced by effort.
When it is stated, "Sound is non-eternal because it follows immediately upon effort," the proponent of the futile rejoinder says:
"A twofold nature of effort is observed: some [effort] produces something that was previously non-existent, such as a jar."
[Objection: Something already existent is merely manifested through the removal of obstructions and so forth, just as a peg buried beneath the earth or a child within the womb [is revealed].
[Reply: Thus, because there is a diversity of effects produced by effort, there arises the doubt whether this sound is manifested by effort or produced by it.

Furthermore, the fallacy of "balancing the effect" (*kāryasama*) is distinguished from "balancing the doubt" (*saṃśayasama*) due to the difference in the manner in which doubt is induced. 24 (28 ṛrong).

Thus, although the varieties of *jāti* (futile rejoinders) are infinite due to the differences in the conceptualizations regarding the objects of their manifestation, these twenty-four types of *jāti* have been demonstrated with the intention of providing unmixed examples. However, the refutation of all *jāti*s consists precisely in the examination of the definition of inference, such as the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth;
for such "dust-throwings" do not prevail against a reason whose definition is unimpaired.

Because the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "occurring immediately after an effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) is firmly established, the non-perception of sound is not caused by a screen or the like, but rather is caused solely by its impermanence (*anityatva*). Furthermore, when an opponent employs a futile rejoinder (*jāti*), one must state only a correct response; one should not counter-argue with futile rejoinders in return, as that would lead to the undesirable consequence of total incoherence. //31//

Now he states the points of defeat (nigrahasthāna): "The point of defeat is declared as that by which an opponent is defeated, through its various divisions such as the abandonment of the proposition (pratijñā-hāni), renunciation (saṃnyāsa), contradiction (virodha), and so forth. [Verse 32]

Commentary: By whatever means—such as by the violation of a thesis (*pratijñā-hāni*) or other such contradictions—the opponent, the adversary, is defeated and cast into a state of defeat (*vacana-nigraha*); that is a "point of defeat" (*nigrahasthāna*). The meaning is that it is the place of defeat, its locus, or its cause. It has been explained—that is, stated—from what specific categories? He says: "violation of the thesis," and so forth.

*Hāniḥ* means loss; *samnyāsaḥ* means abandonment or denial; *virodhaḥ* means contradiction or the state of being contradictory to the reason (*hetu*). In a copulative compound (*dvandva*), these form *hāni-samnyāsa-virodhāḥ*.

Then, by the word "pratijñā" (thesis), the following connections are established: *pratijñā-hāni* (loss of the thesis), *samnyāsa* (relinquishment), and *virodha* (contradiction) are the "pratijñā-hāni-samnyāsa-virodhas"; those which have these as their beginning are "pratijñā-hāni-samnyāsa-virodhādayaḥ. By the word "ādi" (etcetera), he refers to the remaining varieties as well. "From their differentiation" (*vibhedataḥ*) means from their specific distinctions. The meaning is that a "point of defeat" (*nigrahasthāna*) is that by which an opponent is defeated through the web of fallacies such as the loss of the thesis and so forth.
Point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) is generally of two kinds: misconception (*vipratipatti*) and non-comprehension (*apratipatti*).
Among these, misconception is the cognition of a fallacious proof as a valid proof, and the cognition of a fallacious refutation as a valid refutation.
Non-comprehension, however, is the failure to refute a proof and the failure to rescue a refutation.

For a proponent is defeated in two ways: namely, by failing to establish what ought to be established, or by establishing the opposite. And because of this distinction between misapprehension (*vipratipatti*) and non-apprehension (*apratipatti*), there are twenty-two points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).

Namely: abandonment of the proposition (*pratijñā-hāni*), shifting the proposition (*pratijñā-antara*), contradiction of the proposition (*pratijñā-virodha*), renunciation of the proposition (*pratijñā-saṃnyāsa*), shifting the reason (*hetu-antara*), the irrelevant (*artha-antara*), the meaningless (*nirarthaka*), the unintelligible (*avijñātārtha*), the incoherent (*apārthaka*), the mistimed (*aprāpta-kāla*), the deficient (*nyūna*), the redundant (*adhika*), the repetitive (*punar-ukta*), failure to restate (*ananubhāṣaṇa*), lack of understanding (*ajñāna*), inability to respond (*apratibhā*), distraction (*vikṣepa*), admission of the opponent's view (*matānujñā*), neglecting what should be censured (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*), censuring what should not be censured (*niranuyojyānuyoga*), deviating from one's own tenet (*apasiddhānta*), and fallacious reasons (*hetv-ābhāsa*).

In this case as well, non-reproduction [of the opponent's argument], ignorance, lack of ingenuity (*apratibhā*), evasion (*vikṣepa*), and overlooking what is worthy of censure (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*) are types of non-comprehension (*apratipatti*); the remaining ones are varieties of misconception (*vipratipatti*).

Among these, when a reason has been rendered inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), for one who accepts the property of the counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*) in their own example (*svadṛṣṭānta*), there occurs the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) called "abandonment of the thesis" (*pratijñāhāni*).

The proponent stating the proof, "Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses, like a jar," has the reason rendered inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) by an opponent who points out that universals (*sāmānya*), though perceptible by the senses, are seen to be eternal. If the proponent should then say, "In that case, let the jar also be eternal like a universal," he who speaks thus would abandon his proposition (*pratijñā*) that sound is impermanent;
for sound itself would consequently become eternal. Thus, he is defeated through the fallacy of abandoning the proposition (*pratijñā-hāni*). 1.

N109: When the opponent has refuted the point asserted in the thesis, for one who then states another property (*dharmāntara*) to be proven regarding that very same subject (*dharmin*), there occurs the point of defeat called "shifting the thesis" (*pratijñāntara*).

For example, when it has been stated, "Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses," and a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) has been pointed out on the grounds of [the case of] the universal (*sāmānya*), if one should say: "It is correct that the universal is perceptible by the senses and eternal, for it is all-pervading (*sarvagata*); however, sound is not all-pervading."

2. Ṇ: He who, having previously asserted the proposition (*pratijñā*) "this sound is impermanent," then asserts another proposition—"sound is not all-pervading"—is defeated by that change of proposition (*pratijñāntara*).

Ṇ110: Contradiction between the proposition and the reason (*pratijñā-hetv-avirodha*) is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) called "contradiction of the proposition" (*pratijñāvirodha*). For example: "Substance is distinct from its qualities, because no object other than [the qualities] such as color is perceived. This is a contradiction between the proposition and the reason.
ṇ: If indeed substance (*dravya*) is distinct from its qualities (*guṇa*), then there is no non-perception of an object other than color and so forth.

ṇ: But if there is no non-perception of an object other than color and so forth, how can substance be distinct from its qualities? Thus, this [proponent] is defeated because he has stated something contradictory to his own thesis (*pratijñā*). ṇ111:

When the proof of one's position has been refuted by an opponent and, being unable to rescue it, one simply withdraws the thesis itself, that constitutes the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) called "renunciation of the thesis" (*pratijñā-saṃnyāsa*).

When it has been stated, "Sound is non-eternal because it is perceptible by the senses," and the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) based on the generality [of the reason] has been pointed out in that very manner, if he should say, "Who said that sound is non-eternal?", he becomes defeated due to the abandonment of his proposition (*pratijñā-saṃnyāsa*).
