§112: When a reason has been stated without qualification and is refuted, the statement of a qualification for that [reason] constitutes the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) called "another reason" (*hetvantara*).

In that very same argument, when the generality has been refuted by such a deviation, one who employs a qualification such as "provided it possesses a genus" becomes defeated by means of a different reason (*hetvantara*). A "different point" (*arthāntara*) is a ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) consisting in the statement of a matter other than the subject at hand, which is irrelevant to the purpose. For example: "Sound is non-eternal because it is produced"—this is the reason (*hetu*). [If one then says something else entirely unrelated, such as "A pot is made of clay," that is *arthāntara*.]
The word *hetu* (cause) is a nominal stem (*kṛdanta*) derived from the verbal root *hi* with the suffix *tu*.

Having introduced the fourfold division of words (*pada*)—nouns, verbs, prefixes, and particles—the [opponent], while attempting to explain nouns and the others, is defeated by introducing an irrelevant point that does not contribute to the subject at hand. Nirarthaka (the meaningless) is a ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) consisting merely in the employment of a sequence of phonemes devoid of any denotable meaning. 6/114.

"Sound is non-eternal because it possesses *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *pa* sounds, like *gha*, *jha*, *ḍha*, *dha*, and *bha*. This [argument] also constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) because it is entirely devoid of meaning, either due to its lack of utility for the thesis (*sādhya*) or because it is unintelligible.

§115: When a statement of proof (*sādhana*) or a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*), though stated three times, cannot be understood by the assembly (*parṣat*) and the opponent (*prativādin*), it is a point of defeat called "unintelligible meaning" (*avijñātārtha*), characterized by such features as obscure terminology, the use of unestablished conventions, or being uttered too rapidly.

ṇ: This is indeed defined as a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) called "incoherence" (*apārthaka*), because it is a manner of concealing one's lack of competence; for it consists in the employment of a collection of words whose preceding and succeeding parts are disconnected, resulting in a sentence-meaning that is not established. ṇ116:
For example: "Ten pomegranates, six cakes, a bowl, a goat-skin, a ball of minced meat," and so forth. 9.

N117: An inferential statement that transgresses the sequence of the propositions—thesis, reason, example, application, and conclusion—and is employed with the members of the syllogism in reverse order, constitutes the point of defeat called "untimely" (*aprāptakāla*). This is because, like one's own internal realization, the generation of realization in another depends upon the sequence of the inference for others (*parārthānumāna*); by deviating from this sequence, the purpose is not achieved. N118: When a five-membered statement ought to be employed, employing it lacking even one of those members constitutes the point of defeat called "deficient" (*nyūna*).
[Ṇ]: [This is so] because all five members, beginning with the proposition (*pratijñā*), are useful for the arising of another's understanding.

Ṇ119: When a matter has already been established by one reason or one example, for one who states another reason or another example, there occurs the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) called "redundancy" (*adhika*), because it is a statement devoid of purpose. Ṇ120: Furthermore, the repetition of words or meanings constitutes the point of defeat called "repetition" (*punarukta*), except in the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*).
Ṇ: Verbal repetition (*śabdapunaruktam*) is that in which the same word is uttered again, such as "Sound is impermanent, sound is impermanent.

Ṇ: Semantic repetition (*arthapunaruktam*), however, is that in which a certain meaning is first expressed by one word and is then expressed again by another synonym, such as "Sound is impermanent, [it is] perishable, [it is] resonance.

Ṇ: But repetition in the context of restatement (*anuvāda*) is not a fault, as for example, the restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) by means of the instruction of the reason (*hetu*), which is called the conclusion (*nigamana*). 13.

When a proponent has been understood by the assembly and has stated his position three times, the opponent's failure to repeat it constitutes the point of defeat for the respondent known as "non-reproduction" (*ananubhāṣaṇa*).
Without repeating [the argument], upon what basis could he state a refutation?

ṇ122: Even when the meaning of the proponent's statement has been understood by the assembly, if the opponent lacks knowledge of it, that is the point of defeat called "ignorance" (*ajñāna*). For how could one who does not know the subject matter of the reply provide a reply? Nor is this merely a case of "non-reproduction" (*ananubhāṣaṇa*), because even when the matter is known, one may be observed to lack the capacity for reproduction. ṇ123: Even when the opponent's position has been grasped and reproduced, the failure to conceive of a reply is the point of defeat called "lack of ingenuity" (*apratibhā*).

N124: The interruption of the discussion due to preoccupation with one's own affairs is the point of defeat called "distraction" (*vikṣepa*). Having concluded that the matter one intends to prove is impossible to establish, one interrupts the discussion by saying things such as, "This duty of mine is being neglected," or "My throat is choked by a cold," and by thus interrupting the discussion through distraction, one is defeated. N125: When one fails to remove a fault attributed to one's own position and instead projects that very same fault back onto the opponent's position, it is the point of defeat called "admission of the opponent's view" (*matānujñā*).

When it is said, "You are a thief because you are a man, like a well-known thief," if one replies, "You too are a thief because you are a man," one is defeated by the *matānujñā* (admission of the opponent's position), for one has thereby accepted the defect of thievery as imputed to oneself by the other. 18.

§126: "Overlooking the one who deserves censure" (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*) is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) consisting in the failure to censure one who has reached a state of defeat. One who "deserves censure" (*paryanuyojya*) is one who must necessarily be challenged because of the occurrence of a defeat, being addressed with the words: "This point of defeat has come upon you; therefore, you are defeated. He who overlooks such a person and does not censure them is himself defeated by the fault of overlooking the one who deserves censure. 19/

ṇ127: To urge a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) where there is no point of defeat is the point of defeat called "urging one who should not be urged" (*niranuyojyānuyoga*). If one were to say to a speaker who has argued correctly, who is not negligent, and who does not deserve defeat, "You have been defeated," then that person is himself defeated by the exposure of a non-existent fault. 20/

N128: Having accepted a tenet (*siddhānta*), the occurrence of a discourse without restriction constitutes the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) called "contradiction of tenets" (*apasiddhānta*). One who, having first accepted some tenet, begins a discourse, and then—either for the sake of establishing the matter he intends to prove or for the sake of refuting an opponent—states something contrary to that tenet, is defeated by the charge of contradiction of tenets. For example, someone, having accepted the Mīmāṃsā [tenet], says: "The Agnihotra is a means to attain heaven. How [could this be]?

When questioned as to how the performance of the *agnihotra* sacrifice, once performed, becomes the means for attaining heaven, he replies: "The Great Lord (*mahā-īśvara*), being propitiated by this ritual, bestows the fruit, just like a king. Because he accepts an *Īśvara* not favored by the *Mīmāṃsā*, this constitutes the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) called "the discarded" (*apaviddha*).
(21) The fallacies of reason (*hetv-ābhāsa*), such as the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), and so forth, as previously described, are also points of defeat.
(22) Thus, although there is an infinity of other subdivisions, twenty-two root types of points of defeat have been set forth. (23)

Thus, one who understands the specific definitions of quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), avoiding these in his own speech while properly countering those employed by others, attains the proof of the thesis as intended. [These verses are absent in the *Ṣuali* edition. Regarding the summary verses for the futile rejoinders and points of defeat, they are as follows: "Similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), increase (*utkarṣa*) and decrease (*apakarṣa*)," and so forth.
Furthermore, there are the alternatives regarding what is to be described and what is not to be described, as well as the attainment and non-attainment of the goal to be established. //1//
Regressus ad infinitum, the counter-example, non-arising, as well as doubt; likewise, the [infinite] regress, the [unestablished] reason, presumption, and the non-distinction. (2)
Likewise, origination, perception, and non-perception,
as well as the eternal and the non-eternal, are proclaimed in due order as the fallacies of the "equal to the effect" (*kāryasama*).
Immediately following those are the loss of the proposition (*pratijñāhāni*), its abandonment (*saṃnyāsa*), and contradiction (*virodha*).
That which consists of a reason, a different meaning, a redundant meaning, or an unintelligible meaning is *apārthaka* (meaningless). //4//

Deficiency is that which lacks [a point] at the improper time; excess is that which is redundant or repetitive. Furthermore, there are those known as non-reproduction, ignorance, lack of comprehension, [inability to respond], and distraction. //5//

"By [admitting] the opponent's view, you become one who should not be censured; therefore, [the opponent's] indifference and further questioning constitute a departure from tenets and a failure to prove. These are the summary verses on the *jātis* (futile rejoinders) and *nigrahasthānas* (points of defeat).
ṇ131: Here, something not previously mentioned is also stated: the cause of the apprehension of an object is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Knowledge that is to be known by another knowledge inhering in the same self is the result (*phala*), which is distinct from the means of valid cognition; the former is the means of valid cognition, while the latter is the result.

1. Non-validity of memory; 2. Universals and particulars are mutually distinct, as are the eternal and the non-eternal, and the existent and non-existent aspects; 3. The object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is ultimately real; 4. Darkness and shadow are not substances; 5. Sound is a quality of space and is non-material (*apaudgalika*); 6. The comprehension of meaning from a word occurs solely by virtue of convention (*saṃketa*), and not through its inherent capacity to convey that meaning; 7. There is a distinction between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*); 8. A universal (*sāmānya*) resides in many [individuals]; 9. Action (*karman*) is characterized by the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the self (*ātman*).

In the *Nyāyasāra*, liberation is defined as the abiding of the self through the annihilation of the body, objects, sense faculties, cognitions, pleasure, and pain; furthermore, it is stated thus: "Liberation for the person is the absolute cessation of suffering characterized by eternal, experienced happiness."

The treatises on logic (*tarka-grantha*) for these [schools] are the *Nyāyasūtra-bhāṣya*, *Nyāyavārttika*, *Tātparya-ṭīkā*, *Tātparya-pariśuddhi*, and *Nyāyālaṃkāra-vṛtti*. Composed respectively by Akṣapāda, Vātsyāyana, Uddyotakara, Vācaspati, Śrī Udayana, Śrīkaṇṭha, Abhaya, and Upādhyāya, they comprise 54,000 [verses]. (The term *pramitāḥ* is absent in the Śuali edition.)

Regarding the *Nyāyasāra* composed by the omniscient Bhāsarvajña, there are eighteen commentaries (*ṭīkā*s). Among them, the principal commentary is the one called *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa*, composed by that very same author; also [the works] *Nyāyakalikā* composed by Jayanta, and the *Nyāyakusumāñjalitarka*. //32//
Now, concluding that view and introducing the next view, he says:
"This summary of the Naiyāyika doctrine has been stated directly;
now this [summary] of the existents favored by the Sāṃkhyas is being declared. (33)

Commentary: This summary—that is, the concise exposition—of the system of the Naiyāyikas, which was just described, has been stated directly and swiftly. Now, this summary of the categories favored by the Sāṃkhyas—the followers of Kapila—namely the twenty-five principles (*tattva*) and other such entities, is being set forth. (The second chapter, titled "The Revelation of the Nature of the Naiyāyika System") Now begins the third chapter: The Sāṃkhya.
Now, first of all, for the sake of identifying those who have adopted the Sāṃkhya doctrine, their insignia and other characteristics are described:

they may carry three staffs or a single staff; they wear loincloths or garments dyed with ochre; they maintain a topknot, wear matted hair, or have shaved heads; they sit on deer skins; they eat at the houses of the twice-born; they are intent on consuming only five mouthfuls; or they are reciters of the twelve-syllable mantra. These include the wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*) and others.
Their devotees, when offering salutations, say "Oṃ, obeisance to Nārāyaṇa," while they themselves say "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa."
And among them, in the *Mahābhārata*, there is mentioned a wooden mouth-cloth known as a *bīṭā*, which serves to block the breath from the nose out of compassion for living beings. As they say:
"O Brahmin, by a single breath following after [the scent] drawn in through the nose, hundreds of creatures are killed by those who profess the doctrine of the subtle atoms and syllables. (1)
And they themselves wear a water-strainer (*galanaka*) for the sake of compassion toward aquatic creatures, and they instruct their devotees as well:
"One should make a firm water-strainer thirty-six finger-breadths in length and twenty finger-breadths in width; furthermore, one should purify [the water] of living beings. (1)
Oṣṭhas: Pūtanas born of alkaline matter die from sweet water;
others, however, die from alkaline water. Therefore, one should not cause a mixture of these two. //2//
"O Ṣ! Within a drop fallen from the thread of a spider's web, there are creatures;
O Ṣ! so minute that they are the size of bees, yet they would not even fit within the triple heaven. Thus ends the investigation of the "dripping" (galana) in the Mīmāṃsā.
3: Some Sāṃkhyas [accept] God as a deity, while others are atheistic.
And for those who are without a Lord (nirīśvara), their deity is Nārāyaṇa.
Their teachers, who perform the installation of Viṣṇu, are designated by such terms as Caitanya and others.
Those who expound their doctrine include Kapila, Āsuri, Pañcaśikha, Bhārgava, Ulūka, and so forth; therefore, they are designated by names such as Sāṃkhya and Kāpila.

Furthermore, since "Paramarṣi" is the second name of Kapila, they should also be known by the name "Pāramarṣas. In Vārāṇasī, they are numerous; many Brāhmaṇas who fast for a month follow the path of smoke (dhūmamārga), which is contrary to the path of light (arcirmārga). The Sāṃkhyas, however, follow the path of light.
Therefore, the Brāhmaṇas who are fond of the Vedas and follow the path of sacrifice [are one group],
while the Sāṃkhyas— who abstain from the Veda which abounds in violence— are proponents of the inner self (*adhyātma*).
They proclaim the greatness of their own system in this way, as it is stated in the *Māṭharavṛtti*:
"Laugh, drink, play, eat, rejoice constantly, and enjoy pleasures according to your desire!
If you understand the doctrine of Kapila, you will attain the bliss of liberation before long.
It is also stated in another treatise:

"One who knows the twenty-five principles, regardless of which stage of life he is devoted to—whether he wears a topknot, is shaven-headed, or has matted hair—is liberated; of this there is no doubt. (2) //33//
Now the author of the treatise presents the Sāṃkhya doctrine:
"Some Sāṃkhyas are non-theistic, while others have God as their deity;
for all of them, however, there are twenty-five principles. (34)

Commentary: Some are "without a Lord" (*nirīśvara*), meaning those from whom the Lord has departed; they consider themselves solely devoted to the inner self (*adhyātma*). Others have the Lord as their deity (*īśvara-devatā*)—that is, those for whom the Lord is the presiding deity.
For all of them, both those without a Lord and those with a Lord, there are twenty-five principles (*tattva*).
Indeed, according to the Sāṃkhya doctrine, in a person afflicted by the threefold suffering, there arises a desire to know the principles that serve as the cause for its cessation.
There are three types of suffering: internal, celestial, and elemental.
Here, the internal is twofold: physical and mental.

Of these, that suffering which arises with respect to the self—the body—caused by the imbalance of wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*śleṣman*), such as fever, dysentery, and so forth, is physical. Mental suffering is based on desire, anger, greed, delusion, envy, and the non-perception of desired objects.

All of this is internal suffering (*ādhyātmika-duḥkha*) because it is to be accomplished through internal means. External suffering (*bāhya-duḥkha*), which is to be accomplished through external means, is twofold: that caused by other beings (*ādhibhautika*) and that caused by divine or celestial forces (*ādhidaivika*). Among these, *ādhibhautika* is caused by humans, domestic animals, birds, wild beasts, reptiles, and stationary objects; *ādhidaivika* has its cause in possession by *yakṣas*, *rākṣasas*, planetary spirits (*graha*), and so forth.

By this threefold suffering, which consists of the various transformations of *rajas* and resides within the intellect (*buddhi*), the living being who is afflicted develops a desire to know the principles (*tattva*) for the sake of destroying that suffering. And the principles are twenty-five in number. //34//

Now, desiring to explain the twenty-five principles (*tattva*), he first states the nature of the qualities (*guṇa*) such as *sattva* and the rest: First, it should be known that there are three qualities: *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
These are characterized respectively by their effects, namely clarity (*prasāda*), distress (*tāpa*), and dejection (*dainya*). (35)

The word "tāvat" (firstly) introduces the subject; and it should be understood as follows: among those twenty-five principles (*tattva*), *sattva* is characterized by pleasure (*sukha*), *rajas* is characterized by pain (*duḥkha*), and *tamas* is characterized by delusion (*moha*). Thus, first of all, these three qualities (*guṇa*) are to be known. He asks: what are the marks (*liṅga*) of those three qualities? He says: "clarity" (*prasāda*), and so forth.
That triad of qualities beginning with *sattva* has, respectively, clarity, heat, and dejection as its characteristic effects (*kārya-liṅga*).

*Prasāda* is clarity or serenity; *tāpa* is distress; *dainya* is dejection, the cause of wretched speech and so forth. In a *dvandva* compound, these are *prasāda*, *tāpa*, and *dainya*. Those effects for which these are the primary types are "those beginning with clarity, distress, and dejection" (*prasāda-tāpa-dainyādīni*). That which has these effects beginning with clarity, distress, and dejection as its *liṅga*—that is, its indicator, signifier, or mark—is "that which has effects beginning with clarity, distress, and dejection as its mark" (*prasāda-tāpa-dainyādi-kārya-liṅgam*). The meaning is this: clarity, intelligence, proficiency, lightness, productivity, non-attachment, absence of aversion, affection, and so forth are the effects that serve as the mark of *sattva*.
Heat, emaciation, piercing pain, mental instability, rigidity, and agitation are the effects and marks of *rajas*.
Dejection, delusion, death, exhaustion, loathsomeness, ignorance, lack of respect, and so forth are the effects and marks of *tamas*.

These effects allow one to know *sattva* and the other qualities. For instance, whoever in the world experiences happiness becomes a locus for straightforwardness, gentleness, truthfulness, purity, modesty, intelligence, forbearance, compassion, serenity, and the like; that is *sattva*.
Whoever experiences suffering at any time becomes a locus for hatred, malice, envy, censure, deception, bondage, torment, and so forth; that is *rajas*.
Whoever at any time experiences delusion becomes a locus for ignorance, pride, laziness, fear, dejection, incapacity, nihilism, despair, insanity, sleep, and so forth; that is *tamas*.

The entire world exists pervaded by these three qualities—sattva and the others—which mutually assist one another. However, in the upper world, among the gods, there is generally an abundance of *sattva*; in the lower world, among animals, there is an abundance of *tamas*; and in the middle world, among humans, there is an abundance of *rajas*, which is why human beings are characterized by suffering. As it has been said: "The creation is expansive with *sattva* at the top, and expansive with *tamas* at its root."
In the middle, the realm of passion (rajo-viśāla) extends from Brahmā down to a blade of grass (stamba).
[ṢK 54] Here, the phrase "from Brahmā down to a blade of grass" refers to the eightfold creation, beginning with Brahmā and ending with the Piśācas. [35]
The state of equilibrium of these [guṇas] is indeed called *prakṛti*;
it is denoted by the terms *pradhāna* and *avyakta*, and its nature is eternal. (36)

Commentary: That state or condition of these qualities—sattva and the rest—which is equal, meaning of equivalent measure, is called the "equilibrium state" (*samāvasthā*) of sattva and the others; such is what is termed *prakṛti*.

The word *kila* indicates a traditional report from earlier sources. The meaning is that even when there is a predominance of one among the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas in certain states such as those of the gods, their equilibrium state—considered in terms of their relative proportions—is proclaimed as *prakṛti*.
It is denoted by the terms *pradhāna* and *avyakta*; furthermore, this *prakṛti* is spoken of by the alternative names *pradhāna* and *avyakta*.

The meaning is as follows: "Possessing an eternal nature" (*nityasvarūpikā*) means that her nature is eternally immutable, stable, and of a single essence, never falling away nor arising anew; she is *kūṭastha* (unchanging). For this very reason, she is said to be without parts (*anavayavā*), unique (*asādhāraṇī*), and devoid of sound, touch, taste, form, and smell, and is called imperishable (*avyayā*). Regarding the primary Sāṃkhya school, they maintain that for each individual self (*ātman*) there is a separate, distinct primordial matter (*pradhāna*); however, the later Sāṃkhya thinkers have concluded that there is one eternal *pradhāna* common to all selves. //36//
From the conjunction of primordial nature (prakṛti) and the self (ātman), creation arises. Therefore, he describes the very sequence of creation:
"From that, the intellect (buddhi) is born, which is called the Great One (mahat). From that, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) arises; from that, the group of sixteen. (37)

Commentary: From that, *buddhi* (the intellect) is born—that is, it arises from *prakṛti*. And this [intellect], which consists of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) and ascertainment (*niścaya*) of objects—such as, when a cow or the like is seen before one, [thinking] "this is indeed a cow, not a horse," or "this is indeed a post, not a person"—is called "the Great One" (*mahat*) and is designated by the name *mahat*. Furthermore, that *buddhi* has eight forms: four are *sāttvika*, consisting of virtue (*dharma*), knowledge (*jñāna*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), and sovereignty (*aiśvarya*); while the four beginning with non-virtue (*adharma*) are *tāmasa*, being the opposites of those.
From that [intellect] as well, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) arises;
and that [ego-sense] consists of the form of self-conceit such as "I am fortunate," "I am handsome," and so forth. From that ego-sense, the group of sixteen—the aggregate—is produced. //37//
Now, he describes the group consisting of sixteen with two verses:
"Touching, tasting, smelling, seeing, and hearing as the fifth—these are the five organs of perception (buddhīndriya) here, as well as the organs of action (karmendriya). (38)
The six [organs] are those called the anus, the generative organ, speech, the hands, and the feet, as well as the mind;
the other five are the subtle elements (tanmātras) of form and so forth—thus there are sixteen. (39) [This is a pair of verses.]

Commentary: Touching is the skin; tasting is the tongue; smelling is the nose; seeing is the eye; and hearing is the ear as the fifth. These five are the organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*) within this group of sixteen. They are called "organs of cognition" because they cognize their respective objects. To illustrate: the organ of touch cognizes the object of touch; likewise, the tongue [cognizes] taste, the nose [cognizes] smell, the eye [cognizes] form, and the ear [cognizes] sound.
The word "tathā" (likewise) serves to draw forward the term "five.
[They are] five in number, and because they are the instruments of action (*karmakāraṇa*), they are the organs of action (*karmendriya*).
To the question "Which are they?", he says: they are known as the anus, the generative organ, speech, the hands, and the feet.

Among these, the anus is the rectum; the generative organ (*upastha*) refers to the two sexual organs of male and female; and speech (*vacaḥ*)—so called because one speaks by means of it—is that which utters words through the eightfold locations such as the chest and throat. The hands and feet are well known. By means of these, the functions of excretion, sexual enjoyment, speaking, grasping, and locomotion are accomplished; thus they are called the organs of action (*karmendriyāṇi*).

The word "tathā" (likewise) is used for conjunction. And the eleventh is the mind (*manas*); for the mind is both a cognitive faculty (*buddhīndriya*) among the cognitive faculties and a motor faculty (*karmendriya*) among the motor faculties; and it functions through volition even without [the presence of] the true nature of reality (*tattvārtha*).

For example: suppose a certain young brahmin hears that "there is a feast in another village," and he forms a mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) regarding it, such as: "I shall go there; and there I will obtain a meal consisting of molasses and curds, or perhaps curds, or else nothing at all. This is what is meant by *manas*. Similarly, from the *ahaṃkāra*, five other subtle entities known as the *tanmātras*—form and the rest—are produced.

Among those, the subtle element of form (*rūpa-tanmātra*) consists of specific forms such as white, black, and so forth; the subtle element of taste (*rasa-tanmātra*) consists of specific tastes such as bitter and so forth; the subtle element of smell (*gandha-tanmātra*) consists of specific smells such as fragrant and so forth; the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*) consists of specific sounds such as sweet and so forth; and the subtle element of touch (*sparśa-tanmātra*) consists of specific touches such as soft, hard, and so forth—thus there are sixteen. This is the meaning of "this group of sixteen. (38–39)

Now, he says that the five elements arise from the subtle elements (tanmātras): "From form comes fire, from taste comes water, from smell comes earth, from sound comes space, and from touch comes air; thus, from the five [subtle elements] arises the pentad of elements. (40)

Commentary: From the subtle element of form (*rūpa-tanmātra*), known as the subtle, fire (*tejas*) arises; from the subtle element of taste (*rasa-tanmātra*), water (*āpas*) is born; from the subtle element of smell (*gandha-tanmātra*), earth (*pṛthivī*) is produced; from the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*), known as *svara*, space (*ākāśa*) emerges; likewise, from the subtle element of touch (*sparśa-tanmātra*), air (*vāyu*) manifests. Thus, from these five subtle elements, the five gross elements (*bhūta-pañcaka*) come into being. //40//
Thus, in the Sāṃkhya system, *pradhāna* has been described as consisting of twenty-four principles (*tattva*).
On the other hand, the *puruṣa* (the person) is another principle; he is a non-agent, devoid of the *guṇas*, an enjoyer, and endowed with eternal consciousness.
(41) [Commentary: Thus, in the manner stated, in the Sāṃkhya system, *pradhāna* consists of twenty-four principles.

Prakṛti, Mahat, and Ahaṃkāra—these three; the five sense organs, the five action organs, and the one mind; the five subtle elements (tanmātras) and the five gross elements—thus the twenty-four principles constitute its form or nature. That which has these twenty-four principles as its form is the Pradhāna, which is declared to be Prakṛti.
As it has been said: "From Prakṛti comes Mahat, from that Ahaṃkāra, and from that the group of sixteen; from five among those sixteen come the five gross elements" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 22).

In this context, primordial matter (*prakṛti*) is not a modification (*vikāra*), because it is unproduced. Furthermore, the seven principles beginning with intellect (*buddhi*) are called both *prakṛtis*—by virtue of being causes—and *vikṛtis*—by virtue of being effects—for those who hold the opposing view.
The group of sixteen, however, is only a modification, because it consists of effects.
The person (*puruṣa*), on the other hand, is neither *prakṛti* nor *vikṛti*, because he is neither a producer nor is he produced.
And likewise, Īśvarakṛṣṇa states in the *Sāṃkhyasaptati*:

"The root-primal nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) is not a modification; the seven, beginning with the Great One (*mahat*), are both primal natures and modifications; the group of sixteen is a modification; and the person (*puruṣa*) is neither a primal nature nor a modification. (SK 3)

Likewise, the Great One (mahat) and the others, which are transformations of primordial nature (prakṛti), being manifest, may again become unmanifest; thus they fall away from their own essential nature due to their impermanence.
Primordial nature, however, is accepted as unmodified and eternal;
therefore, it never falls away from its own essential nature. And so the Sāṃkhyas have described the essential nature of the Great One and the rest, as well as that of primordial nature, in this way.
"The manifest is caused, non-eternal, non-pervasive, active, manifold, dependent, composite, and subordinate;
the unmanifest is the opposite. [Sāṃkhyakārikā 10] Thus it is said.

In that context, "possessing a cause" means having a causal basis; "the Great One" (*mahat*) and so forth are "impermanent" because they have the nature of arising, as is the case with the intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest. They are "non-pervasive," meaning they are restricted and not omnipresent. "Active" means they exist together with activities such as determination (*adhyavasāya*) and so on; thus they are "active"—that is, possessing function, up to the point of being characterized by the activity of movement. "Many" means consisting of twenty-three varieties. "Dependent" means existing by relying upon *pradhāna* (primordial matter) as something that assists the Self (*ātman*). "The mark" (*liṅga*) refers to that which...
That from which something has arisen goes to dissolution and destruction within that very thing; this is the mark (*liṅga*).

In this regard, the gross elements (*bhūta*) dissolve into the subtle elements (*tanmātra*); the subtle elements, the sense organs, and the mind dissolve into the ego (*ahaṃkāra*); that [ego] dissolves into the intellect (*buddhi*), and that [intellect] dissolves into the unmanifest (*avyakta*). But that [unmanifest], because it is unproduced, does not dissolve anywhere. It is "possessing parts" (*sāvayava*) because it is endowed with parts consisting of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell; it is "dependent on another" (*paratantra*) because it is contingent upon a cause. Such is the manifest (*vyakta*), beginning with the Great One (*mahat*).
The unmanifest (avyakta), however, is called *prakṛti*; it is the opposite of this [purusha]. In that regard, its "oppositeness" is indeed easy to apply.

Furthermore, since the *pradhāna* exists everywhere—pervading heaven, earth, and the intermediate space—it possesses pervasiveness (*vyāpitva*). Likewise, because the unmanifest lacks action in the form of movement due to its pervasive nature, its "actionlessness" (*niṣkriyatva*) is to be understood; thus, only a mere indication has been shown. A detailed explanation, however, is to be understood from its own scriptures, such as the *Sāṃkhyasaptati*.
Now he states the twenty-fifth principle, the *puruṣa-tattva*, beginning with: "But the other is a non-agent," and so forth.

Distinct from *prakṛti*—which consists of the twenty-four principles—the *puruṣa* is the principle known as the person (*pumān*), who is moreover a non-agent, devoid of the *guṇas*, an enjoyer, and endowed with eternal consciousness.

In that regard, he is a "non-agent" because he does not perform the objects of experience such as pleasure, nor their causes such as meritorious karma; for the self is incapable of even bending a blade of grass.

The agent, however, is primordial matter (prakṛti) alone, because its very nature is activity. Likewise, [the Self] is devoid of qualities (viguṇa), being free from the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest, since these qualities are attributes of primordial matter and are absent in the Self.

Likewise, the enjoyer is the experiencer. Even though the enjoyer does not directly enjoy, he is nevertheless designated as the enjoyer because, through the mere arising of a reflection within his own stainless self, he experiences the pleasure, pain, and so forth that have been transferred to the intellect (*buddhi*)—which, though consisting of both primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and its transformations, is like a mirror with two faces—according to the statement: "The *puruṣa* perceives the object determined by the intellect."

Just as redness and so forth are attributed to a crystal by virtue of the proximity of a hibiscus flower or similar objects, so too, because it possesses the influence of *prakṛti*, it is entirely appropriate to attribute to the *puruṣa* the status of an enjoyer (*bhojaka*) with respect to objects consisting of pleasure, pain, and so on.

Vādamahārṇava also says: "The reflection of an object transferred to the mirror of the intellect ascends onto the *puruṣa*, who is like a second mirror; that alone constitutes his state of being an enjoyer, but there is no transformation of the Self. Likewise, Āsuri says:

It is said that his experience (*bhoga*) occurs when the intellect (*buddhi*), having transformed into the form of the object in a state of isolation, arises as a reflection, just as the moon appears in clear water. (1)
Vindhyavāsin, however, explains experience in this way:

"The Puruṣa, whose nature is indeed unchanging, causes the mind—which is insentient yet reflects its own [form]—to become conscious through its proximity, just as a crystal [is colored by a proximate object]. (Verse 2)

Likewise, he is "endowed with" that eternal consciousness (*cit*, *cetanā*). By this it should be understood that what is taught is that consciousness alone is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the *puruṣa*, and not knowledge (*jñāna*), because knowledge is a property of the intellect (*buddhi-dharma*).

The pure Self merely identifies its own nature as non-different from the intellect (*buddhi*). Objects such as pleasure and pain enter the intellect through the gateway of the senses; and since the intellect has the form of a mirror facing both ways, the power of consciousness (*caitanya-śakti*) is reflected in it. Consequently, one metaphorically designates oneself as "I am happy," "I am suffering," or "I am the knower. As Patañjali said: "Though the Puruṣa is pure, it observes the mental modification (*pratyaya*) of the intellect; observing that, although it is not of the nature of that [intellect], it appears as if it were of that nature" (Yogasūtrabhāṣya 2.20).
"Even though the intellect (*buddhi*) is insentient, it appears as if sentient due to the proximity of the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*).

(SK 20) Regarding the term "the person" (*pumān*), the singular number is used with reference to the genus; therefore, the self (*ātman*) must be accepted as being manifold, because of the observed regularity of birth, death, and the sense organs, and because of the diversity in the engagement with *dharma* and other factors.
All these selves are to be understood as all-pervading (*sarvagata*) and eternal (*nitya*). And it has been said:
"In the Sāṃkhya system, the Self is formless, conscious, an enjoyer, eternal, omnipresent, inactive, a non-doer, devoid of qualities, and subtle. (1) //41//
Summarizing the principles (*tattva*), he says: "The principles are thus twenty-five in number;
and here the interaction between primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and the Spirit (*nara*) is like that between the lame and the blind. (42)
Commentary: The letter *ca* is displaced [in the verse]. Thus, by this enumeration, there are twenty-five principles (*tattva*).

Now, one might ask: "Since both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* are all-pervading and joined together, how do they exist? Anticipating this objection, he says: "The *pradhāna*... and so forth. Here, the functioning or mode of existence of *pradhāna* and *puruṣa* is like that of a lame man and a blind man.

For example, a certain blind man set out for the city of Pāṭaliputra together with a caravan, and that caravan was attacked by robbers. The blind man was left behind right there, running hither and thither; he was seen by a cripple and addressed thus: "O, O blind man, do not fear! I am a cripple, inactive due to my deficiency in the capacity for actions such as walking, yet I see everything with my eyes. You, however, possess the capacity for actions such as walking, yet you do not see."
Then the blind man said: "This is excellent; I shall carry you on my shoulder, and let our conduct be thus."

Then, just as a lame man, having been placed upon the shoulders of a blind man—who possesses the quality of sight—reaches the city, beholds plays and the like, and experiences joy upon perceiving the objects of the senses such as songs and other things; even so, the Puruṣa, whose nature is pure consciousness and who resembles the lame man, resting upon the active Prakṛti which resembles the blind man, experiences joy by being conscious of sound and other objects determined by the intellect (buddhi) as they are reflected within himself, and while thus experiencing joy...
Out of delusion, considering primordial nature (prakṛti) to be of the nature of happiness, one dwells in saṃsāra. //42//
Then, he explains how liberation for that [puruṣa] might occur:
"Liberation is the disjunction from primordial nature (prakṛti) for the puruṣa; indeed, this occurs through knowledge of the distinction between them.
And here, the three means of valid cognition are perception, inference, and verbal testimony. (43)

Commentary: The word *bata* is an address to those who inquire. Through the knowledge of that "interval"—the discrimination (*viveka*) between these two, primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the person (*puruṣa*)—there occurs for the person a separation from nature; that is liberation (*mokṣa*). For it is said:
"This person is, in the ultimate sense, of the nature of pure consciousness.
Not knowing the interval [from] nature, he has resorted to transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) through delusion. (1)

Therefore, as long as there is no apprehension of Nature—which is by nature pleasure, pain, and delusion—through discriminative discernment, so long is there no liberation. However, when Nature ceases its activity upon the vision of discriminative discernment, the abiding of the Puruṣa in its own essential form is liberation. And liberation occurs through the severance of bondage; furthermore, bondage is threefold, distinguished as being of the nature of Nature (*prākṛtika*), of the modifications (*vaikārika*), and of merit (*dākṣiṇa*). To explain: for those who worship Nature out of a lack of knowledge regarding the Self, their bondage is of the nature of Nature.

Those who worship the transformations—namely the elements, the senses, the ego, and the intellect—as the Self, for them there is the *vaikārika* (evolvent) creation. Sacrifices and charitable works (*iṣṭā-pūrta*) belong to the *dākṣiṇa* (southern) path; for one who performs sacrifices and works while ignorant of the reality of the Puruṣa is bound, his mind being afflicted by desire. As it is said: "The fools who consider sacrifice and works to be the highest, and who do not rejoice in any other excellence..."
"Having reached the back of the firmament by means of their good deeds, they enter this world or one even lower. [Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.10].
And from bondage proceeds *saṃsāra*, which consists in transmigrating after death.

Furthermore, according to the Sāṃkhya doctrine, since the *puruṣa* is devoid of the nature of both *prakṛti* and its transformations (*vikṛti*), there is no bondage, liberation, or *saṃsāra* for the *puruṣa*; rather, these belong to *prakṛti* alone. Thus say the followers of Kapila:
"Therefore, no one is bound, nor is anyone liberated, nor does anyone transmigrate;
rather, it is *prakṛti*, which has various substrates, that transmigrates, is bound, and is liberated" (SK 62).
However, these states of bondage, liberation, and transmigration are metaphorically attributed to the *puruṣa*.

Just as victory and defeat, though occurring in the servant, are attributed to the master because the fruit thereof—the acquisition of wealth and so forth—is connected to the master, so too, although enjoyment and liberation reside in *prakṛti*, they are attributed to the *puruṣa* due to the failure to grasp their distinction.

Here, the general definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is stated: "A means of valid cognition is the cause of the apprehension of an object. Now, in the latter half [of the verse], there is the triad of measures and the triad of means of valid cognition; this refers here to the Sāṃkhya system.

What are these? He says: perception (*pratyakṣa*), that which is recognized, inference (*laiṅga* = *anumāna*), and verbal testimony (*śābda* = *āgama*). The word "and" (*ca*) should also be connected here.
Therein, the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*) is stated: "Perception is the non-conceptual functioning of the ear and the other [senses].
Regarding this, it is said: "The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth.

The ear and so forth are the sense organs; their "functioning" (*vṛtti*) means their activity or transformation (*pariṇāma*). For their established doctrine is that the sense organs themselves, when transformed into the form of the object, constitute perception.

[Ṣ: "Non-conceptual" (avikalpikā) means being devoid of conceptual constructions such as name, genus, and so forth; it is to be explained like the perception [of the Sāṃkhya] school according to the Śākyas.
Ṣ31: Īśvarakṛṣṇa, however, says: "Perception is a determinate cognition arising from the ear and other [senses].
Ṣ32: But this is the definition of inference: inference is threefold—namely, *pūrvavat*, *śeṣavat*, and *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*.
Among these, that which is "based on what has been previously perceived" (*pūrvavat*) is when, upon seeing the rising of a river, one infers that it has rained upstream;

that which is "based on the remainder" (*śeṣavat*) is when, by tasting a drop of ocean water, the rest of the water is known through inference to be salty, or when, from the movement of a single grain of boiled rice in a pot, the rest of the food is known to be cooked or uncooked; and that which is "based on general observation" (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*) is preceded by the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*), such as when, upon seeing a triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*), it is understood—even though not directly seen—that the bearer of the mark, a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*), exists. Thus, [inference] is of three kinds.
Alternatively, the Sāṃkhyas define the characteristic of inference (*anumāna*) as simply "that which is preceded by the mark (*liṅga*) and the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*).

As for verbal testimony (*śābda*), it is the word of a reliable person (*āpta*) and sacred revelation (*śruti*). Reliable persons (*āpta*) are those free from passion, hatred, and other defects, such as Brahmā and Sanatkumāra; *śruti* is the Veda; and the word of these [reliable persons] is verbal testimony (*śābda*).

In this regard, even that which has not been stated is here briefly mentioned: consciousness (*cit-śakti*), being devoid of the delimitation of objects, does not know an object; and the intellect (*buddhi*), being insentient, does not perceive. Due to the proximity of these two, there occurs an appearance otherwise than [their true nature]. From the conjunction of *prakṛti* and the self, creation arises. Action is the very nature of the transformations of *prakṛti*. Likewise, the universal is of the nature of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*). Thus, the object of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is real.

Here, there are three qualities (*guṇa*): *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. From that, by the rule "after *ananta* and others, *ṇya* is added in the sense of the base itself" (though not in Pāṇini), we have *ṇya*: just as the three worlds are *trailokya*, and six qualities are *ṣāḍguṇya*, so too that universal whose form or nature (*rūpa*) consists of the three qualities is *traiguṇyarūpa*. And the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: each preceding stage is the means of valid cognition, while each subsequent stage is the fruit. 34: Likewise, the effect exists even while in the cause; it arises from reasons such as "because the non-existent cannot be produced," and so forth. As it has been said:

"Because of the non-production of the non-existent, because of the grasping of the material cause (*upādāna*), because of the impossibility of everything arising from everything, because the potent produces only that which is possible for it to produce, and because of the nature of the cause—the effect exists [in the cause].

[SK 9] Regarding this, "because of the impossibility of everything arising from everything": if the effect were non-existent, then everything would arise from everything. Consequently, gold and other such things would also arise from grass and the like; yet they do not so arise. Therefore, the effect must already exist in the cause.

[S]: Likewise, [the opponent claims] that only substances (*dravya*) exist, and there are no modes (*paryāya*) whatsoever characterized by the properties of arising and passing away, because those [modes] are merely manifestations and disappearances.

[Ṣ36]: The logical treatises of the Sāṃkhyas include the *Māṭharabhāṣya*, which is an exposition of the *Ṣaṣṭitantra* titled *Sāṃkhyasaptati*; the *Tattvakaumudī*; the *Gauḍapāda*; the *Ātreyatantra*; and so forth. //43//
Desiring to conclude the Sāṃkhya doctrine and intending to explain the Jaina doctrine hereafter, he says:
"Thus, the summary of the Sāṃkhya doctrine has now been told; next, the concise presentation of the Jaina system is being stated with thorough deliberation. (44)

Commentary: By the method thus stated, this applies not only to the Bauddha and Naiyāyika systems, but also to the Sāṃkhya system; such is the meaning of the word "api" (also). "Summary" (*samāsa*) means a concise exposition is now being declared. The summary of the Jaina philosophy is being told. Of what nature is it? It is "possessed of excellent inquiry" (*suvicāravān*). "Excellent inquiries" (*suvicārāḥ*) are those inquiries which are "excellent" (*suṣṭhu*) because their nature is uncontradicted by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); that which possesses these is "possessed of excellent inquiry. It does not, however, possess inquiries that are merely "delightful when not investigated" (*avicāritaramaṇīya*).
By this, it should be understood that other philosophical systems are charming only when left unexamined. As has been stated by the opponents themselves:

"The Purāṇas, the Dharma of Manu, the Veda along with its supplements, and medical science—these four are established as authoritative commands and are not to be undermined by logical reasoning. (Manu Smṛti 12.110)
For others, indeed, out of the apprehension of faults, do not pay heed to the investigation of their own doctrine; as it has been said:
"There is something that must be said [by others], and for that reason this is not investigated by them.
If gold were truly faultless, why would it fear examination? (1)
For this very reason, the Jains, being fearless due to the faultlessness of the Jina’s doctrine as established through investigation, teach as follows:

"Having completely abandoned partiality toward one's own school, all philosophical systems should be examined again and again with impartiality by means of hundreds of logical arguments. Among them, that system alone which appears to be consistent with reason, and in which not even a trace of internal contradiction is perceived—that alone should be accepted by the wise, and nothing else. Thus it has been said:
"I have no partiality for the Hero (Vīra), nor do I harbor hatred toward Kapila and others.
Whosever speech is endowed with reason, that one’s words should be accepted. [Lokatattvanirṇaya, verse 38] (This verse appeared in the introduction).
(The Third Chapter, titled "The Revelation of the Secrets of the Sāṃkhya Doctrine") [End]
Now begins the fourth chapter.
First, the dress, conduct, and so forth according to the Jaina doctrine are explained.
The Jains are of two kinds: the Śvetāmbaras and the Digambaras.

Among them, the insignia (*liṅga*) of the Śvetāmbaras consists of the *rajo-haraṇa*, the mouth-cloth (*mukhavastrikā*), and the plucking out of hair (*locana*); their attire includes the waist-cloth (*colapaṭṭa*) and the upper garment (*kalpa*), and their conduct (*ācāra*) comprises the five *samitis* and the three *guptis*.
These are known as: vigilance in movement (*īryā*), speech (*bhāṣā*), seeking alms (*eṣaṇā*), taking up and putting down objects (*ādāna-nikṣepa*), and the disposal of bodily waste (*utsarga*).
"Five *samitis* and three *guptis* are said [to constitute conduct] through the restraint of the three-fold yoga. From this statement:

the Guru is one who possesses non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and possessionlessness; who has conquered anger and the other passions; who is self-controlled in his senses; who is free from bonds (*nirgrantha*); and whose food is always purified by the "honey-gathering" (*mādhukarī*) mode of livelihood according to the nine-fold purity (*navakoṭi-śuddhi*). He wears robes, bowls, and other requisites solely for the sake of maintaining self-restraint (*saṃyama*). When being honored, he declares, "May there be the attainment of Dharma. (The *madhukaravṛtti* is the benediction bestowed by a Jaina ascetic.)
Furthermore, the Digambaras are characterized by nakedness as their emblem and using their hands as alms-bowls.
They are divided into four groups based on the distinctions between the Kāṣṭhāsaṅgha, the Mūlasaṅgha, the Mathurāsaṅgha, and the Gopyasaṅgha.

In the Kāṣṭhāsaṅgha, the broom (picchikā) is made from the hair of a yak; in the Mūlasaṅgha, it is made from peacock feathers; in the Mathurāsaṅgha, the broom is not even accepted from its very root; and in the Gopyasaṅgha, the broom consists of peacock feathers.

The first three *saṅghas*, when being saluted, declare an increase in the Dharma; yet they do not consider there to be liberation for women, nor enjoyment for the *kevalins*, nor liberation even for one who possesses the vows and the monastic robes (*sacīvara*). But the *gopyas*, when being saluted, declare the attainment of Dharma; they consider there to be liberation for women and enjoyment for the *kevalins*. The *gopyas* are also called *yāpanīyas*. (In the Drāviḍa tradition, they are called *yāpanīyakas*.
Furthermore, for all of them, during the begging of alms and the eating of food, thirty-two obstacles and fourteen impurities (*mala*) must be avoided.

In matters of conduct toward the teacher and the deity, everything is identical to that of the Śvetāmbaras; there is no other difference between them regarding their scriptures or logic. (That is all!
Now, he states the definition of the deity:
The Lord of Jinas is the deity therein, free from attachment and aversion.
Having slain the great wrestler of delusion, he possesses exclusive knowledge and vision. //45//
Worshipped by the lords of the gods and asuras, the illuminator of the true nature of reality, having brought about the total destruction of all karma, he has attained the supreme state. (46)

Commentary: In this regard, according to the Jaina doctrine, "Jinas" are those who have conquered passion and the like; they are the ordinary *kevalins*. Their "Lord" (*indra*) is the Master endowed with supreme sovereignty accompanied by thirty-four such incomparable excellences (*atiśayas*). He is the deity, the God, who, having brought about the destruction of all karma, has attained the supreme state—this is the grammatical connection.

"What is he like? he asks, and says: "Free from attachment and aversion" (*rāga-dveṣa-vivarjitaḥ*). Attachment consists of delusion and greed; aversion consists of anger and deceit. "Free from attachment and aversion" means specifically devoid of them, being separated from them through repeated practice; the meaning is that he is one who has transcended passion (*vītarāga*). For attachment and aversion are well-known in the scriptures as difficult to conquer and as obstacles to liberation, because they are the causes for falling into the endless cycle of existence. As it is said:
"Who would undergo suffering? And who would be amazed by pleasures?"*1* *1 This verse is cited from the *Ācārāṅga-sūtra* 1.2.3.3.*

"Who would encounter suffering, and who would be amazed by pleasures? Who would not attain liberation, were it not for passion and hatred? (1) [Who would experience pain, and who would be astonished by joys?
And who would not obtain release, if passion and aversion did not exist?]

Then, their separation is described: "One by whom the great wrestler of delusion has been slain. Delusion (*moha*) is the bewilderment arising from the activation of the *mohanīya* karma, which consists of the desire for liberation even from scriptures whose nature is violence and so forth. That very delusion is like a "great wrestler" (*mahāmalla*) because it is difficult for the entire world to conquer. He is "one by whom the great wrestler of delusion has been slain.

By these two epithets, it should be understood that the excellence of the Lord’s freedom from the states of misery (*apāya*) is manifested; furthermore, it is made known that the Arhat alone is the Lord, being devoid of passion, hatred, and great delusion. As it has been said:
"Passion is to be inferred from the desire for union with women; hatred is to be known by the weapon used to wound an enemy;
delusion is established by the faults found in the study of evil conduct—he in whom these do not exist is a God, and he is likewise an Arhat.

(1) Likewise, "one who possesses *kevala*" means one whose knowledge and vision are solitary (*asahāya*)—in that they do not depend on other forms of cognition—or complete (*sampūrṇa*). For the Blessed One consists of absolute knowledge and absolute vision; like an amalaka fruit held in the palm of the hand, he knows and perceives the entire nature of the world, consisting of both substance and modification, incessantly.

The term *kevalajñānadarśana* is intentional (*sābhiprāya*); for in the case of one still under the veil of ignorance (*chadmastha*), vision arises first and then knowledge, whereas for the omniscient one (*kevalin*), it is knowledge first and then vision.

In this regard, with respect to every object of cognition (*prameya*) which consists of both the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*), that cognition (*jñāna*) which apprehends the universal in a subordinate state and the particulars in a predominant state is "cognition"; whereas that which apprehends the universal in a predominant state and the particulars in a subordinate state is "vision" (*darśana*). By this distinction, the excellence of cognition (*jñānātiśaya*) should be understood as being directly stated.

Likewise, "all the gods" refers to the *suras* and the *asuras*, the *daityas*. Although the term *sura* includes the *asuras*, their separate mention should be understood according to worldly convention (*lokarūḍhi*). For in the world, one designates the *dānavas* separately from the gods because they are their adversaries.
Their lords are the masters; he is to be fully honored and worshipped by them or for them.

ñ: Even for one so worthy of worship, being served by multitudes of humans, animals, celestial beings, *kinnaras*, and others is merely incidental; by this, the excellence of his worship is expressed. ñ8: Likewise, he is the illuminator and instructor of those things that exist as they truly are—the categories of reality such as living beings (*jīva*) and so forth; by this, the excellence of his speech is stated.
ñ9: Furthermore, "all" means complete *ghāti* and *aghāti* karmas, specifically the *jñānāvaraṇa* [karmas]; their destruction is their total dissolution.
Having attained that supreme state, he has reached perfection (*siddhi*).
By this, the stage of perfection, characterized by the total exhaustion of all karma, is described.

Other [teachers], such as the Sugatas and others, even after attaining liberation, descend again into existence when there is the possibility of insults from rival sects (*tīrtha*) and so forth. As others have said:
"Those who are knowers and founders of the ford of Dharma, though they have gone to the supreme state,
return once more to worldly existence due to their disparagement of the ford.
Thus, they do not truly possess the path to liberation in the ultimate sense, because of the absence of the destruction of karma.

For in reality, when karma is exhausted, there is no further entry into rebirth. As it has been said: "Just as a sprout does not emerge at all once the seed is burnt, so too, when the seed of karma is burnt, the sprout of existence does not grow. (Tattvārtha Sūtra Bhāṣya 10.7)

And it has been said by the venerable Siddhasena Divākara as well, describing the powerful manifestation of delusion (*moha*) among those intent on worldly existence: "Having violently shaken off even Nirvāṇa—which is undesired by one who fears what is not yet understood—he returns to existence once his fuel is consumed; though he is himself liberated, having fashioned a body for the sake of others, here in this world, the kingdom of delusion prevails over those who oppose your teaching. [Siddha-dvātriṃśikā] Enough with further elaboration.

Thus, that deity who is endowed with these four excellences and is free from defects is alone to be resorted to as a deity; he alone brings about supreme accomplishment, and not any other god who possesses passion or is subject to rebirth—this is what must be understood from what has been explained.
[Objection: Surely, let there be no such deity as the Sugata and so forth; why is Īśvara, the creator of the world, not accepted?
[Response: We say it is because there is a lack of valid means of proof (*pramāṇa*) for his existence.
Now, there indeed exists a proving means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): the earth and so forth have an intelligent creator because they are effects, like a pot.

Nor is this reason unestablished, since the fact that the earth and so forth are effects is established by their possessing parts. For instance: everything, such as the earth, mountains, and trees, is an effect because it possesses parts, like a pot.
Nor is it contradictory (*viruddha*), because we observe the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) in things such as jars, which have a determined creator.
Nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because it is excluded from things such as space (*vyoman*), which are determined to be without a creator.
Nor is it mis-timed (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), because its subject matter is not sublated by perception or scripture.

Nor should it be argued that the reason (*hetu*) is contradictory because it proves the opposite of the probandum (*sādhya*)—which is qualified by attributes such as omniscience—as observed in the examples of the potter and so forth; and that the example is deficient in the probandum because such an intelligent agent does not exist in the case of a pot and the like. For if the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the probandum and the probans were grasped through their specific particulars, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of all inference. Rather, pervasion is determined through generalization by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
Furthermore, because they are infinite and because of their variability, these two [attributes] cannot be apprehended in specific instances.
Therefore, the pervasion of "being an effect" by "having an intelligent antecedent" should be understood solely on that basis, and not by means of [attributes] such as "possessing a body.

Indeed, a body is not required in the causal complex for agency; for even in its absence, one is observed to exercise agency in the production of one's own body by virtue of being the substratum of knowledge, desire, and effort.
If something were considered a cause merely by its concomitance, even though it is incapable of producing an effect, then the heat of fire would also result in being a cause for smoke.
For indeed, even when the body is present, if there is an absence—either collectively or individually—of cognition and the other factors, agency is not observed even in a potter and the like.

First, there is the cognition of the collection of causes that produce the effect; from that, the desire to act; from that, effort; and from that, the accomplishment of the result. Thus, since the agency regarding the effect belongs only to these three combined, there is no deviation anywhere.
And his omniscience is established because he is the agent of all effects.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: God is omniscient because he is the agent of all effects, such as the earth and so forth.

For whoever is the agent of something is necessarily cognizant of its material cause and other factors; just as a potter, who produces a jar, is cognizant of the lump of clay and so on; and this [God] is the agent of the universe; therefore, he is omniscient.

For the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world consists of four kinds of atoms characterized by earth, water, fire, and air; the instrumental cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) consists of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth; the enjoyer is the Self (*ātman*); and the object of enjoyment consists of the body and other such things.
Furthermore, it is not possible for one who lacks knowledge of these [causes] to be the agent of the earth and so forth, just like ourselves and others.
Moreover, those qualities of His, such as knowledge and the rest, are eternal, because they are distinct from the knowledge and other qualities of potters and the like.

§14: Furthermore, the oneness of the creator of earth and the other elements is established because the activity of multiple agents is logically possible when they are regulated by a single supervisor.
For it is well known that the activity of architects and others in the construction of great palaces and similar works proceeds under the dependence of a single master builder.
§15: Nor should it be argued that the occasional nature and diversity of effects are contradicted by the singularity and eternity of God.
Since the occasional and diverse nature of effects is established through the acquisition of occasional and diverse auxiliary causes, no contradiction is possible.

[Objection: But surely, if the earth and so forth have an intelligent cause, then even when no activity is observed—as in the case of old wells and the like—the cognition that they were "made" would arise; yet such a cognition is not seen to arise here. Therefore, because the reason observed in the example is absent from the subject (*dharmin*), the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*). [Reply: That too is incorrect, for this [objection] is stated either with respect to what is authoritative (*prāmāṇika*) or otherwise.
If it were otherwise, then the same consequence of being unestablished (*asiddha*) would apply even to smoke and the like.

However, for that which is established by valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*), there is no lack of establishment; for the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*), whose inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with an intelligent agent has been recognized, is well-established in the case of the earth and so forth, just as smoke is in the case of mountains and the like. Nor is there a rule that all things that are produced necessarily manifest the cognition of having been made within themselves, since the cognition of something being "made" does not arise in one who has not witnessed the action in the case of ground that was dug up and then filled back in.
Furthermore, you seek to establish here that the existence of an intelligent cause is not perceived;
this, however, is incorrect, because it is only the non-perception of something perceptible that can logically prove non-existence.
And this [non-perception] is not possible in this case, because the creator of the world is imperceptible.
Furthermore, if non-existence were to be proven by means of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), it would follow that even things such as *piśācas* could be established in that manner.

To this, the following response is given: Regarding that proof of "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) which was stated to establish that the earth and so forth have an intelligent cause—would that consist of (1) having parts (*sāvayavatva*), or (2) the inherence (*samavāya*) of its own cause's existence in what previously did not exist, or (3) being the object of the cognition "it has been made," or (4) being subject to modification (*vikāritva*)?

If [the reason] is "having parts" (*sāvayavatva*), then what is this? Is it (1) existing in parts, (2) being produced by parts, (3) having spatial extension (*pradeśavattva*), or (4) being the object of the cognition "that which has parts"?

Regarding these, in the first position, this reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because of the generality of parts (*avayavasāmānya*); for that [generality], although it exists in parts, is said to be partless and not an effect. In the second position, however, the reason is equivalent to the probandum (*sādhyasama*); for just as the fact that earth and so forth are effects is the probandum, so too is the fact that they are produced by parts such as atoms.

The third [reason] is also inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because of space (*ākāśa*), since space, despite possessing spatial dimensions (*pradeśavattva*), is not an effect. Its possession of spatial dimensions will be established further on. Even in the fourth stage [of the argument], there is an inconclusiveness for that very same reason; moreover, it does not lack parts (*niravayavatva*), because that would contradict its omnipresence (*vyāpitva*), as in the case of an atom (*paramāṇu*).

Nor is "being an effect" the inherence (*samavāya*) of its own cause's existence (*sattā*) in what was previously non-existent, because since that [inherence] is eternal, it cannot logically possess such a definition.

Alternatively, if [the world] possesses those characteristics, then since effects such as the earth and so forth would likewise follow as being eternal, for what could it be proven that they have an intelligent cause? Furthermore, this reason is partially unestablished (*bhāgāsiddha*), because it does not apply to the case of yogis when their karma is entirely exhausted; for that exhaustion, being of the nature of a non-existent destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), lacks both existence and inherence in its own cause.

Ñ21: Furthermore, the status of being an object of the notion "it has been made" (*kṛtam*) should not be [taken as] a probans; for since this notion applies even to space—which is not a product—due to such acts as digging or filling it up, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Ñ22: Moreover, if mutability (*vikāritva*) were itself a product, it would follow that even the Great Lord (*maheśvara*) is a product. For mutability is indeed the alteration of an existing entity.

Since that [alteration] exists in the case of the Lord as well, there would be the undesirable consequence of his having another intelligent cause, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). And if he were immutable, his capacity to produce effects would be extremely difficult to establish.
This reason—"because of being an effect"—is unestablished (*asiddhi*), because when the nature of an effect is investigated, it is found to be untenable.

Furthermore, in the world, a thing that exists only occasionally is well known to be an effect; however, since the universe exists eternally, like the Great Lord (*maheśvara*), how could it be an effect?

If it were an effect because the young grass and other things contained within it are effects, then by the same logic, since the intellect and so forth contained within the Great Lord are effects, and since the forms produced by heat (*pākaja-rūpa*) contained within atoms and so forth are effects, it would follow that the Great Lord himself is also an effect.

Furthermore, if one were to postulate that this [world] also has another intelligent being as its cause, an infinite regress and a departure from established tenets would follow. Or, let it be granted in some way that the world is an effect; nevertheless, what is intended here as the reason is either "effect-hood" in general or a specific instance of it. If it is the former, then no specific intelligent agent can be established on that basis, because a necessary concomitance (vyāpti) with such a specific agent is unproven; rather, it would establish only a general agent. In that case, the reason is either ineffective or contradictory, because it proves something contrary to the probandum.
Therefore, being an effect (*kāryatva*) is that which produces the cognition of having been made; it is the indicator of an intelligent agent, but not everything [is such an indicator].

If something were an indicator merely by virtue of similarity (*sārūpya*), then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that steam and the like would also be indicators of fire. Furthermore, because of the similarity [of the self] to the Great Lord (*maheśvara*), there would follow the inference of [the Lord's] being a transmigrating being (*saṃsārin*), being a knower of only a little (*kiñcijjña*), and not being the creator of the entire world, since the objections and their resolutions are identical in both cases.

ñ: Therefore, although there is some degree of similarity between steam and smoke, smoke leads one to infer fire due to certain specific characteristics it possesses that steam lacks; likewise, some specific distinction must be admitted between the earth and other effects [of an intelligent agent] as well.

ñ25: Now, if the second [alternative] is accepted, then the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*) because of the absence of a specific effect; or, if such a specific effect were present, it would follow that even someone who has never seen a construction would form the cognition that it was made, just as one does upon seeing an old well or a palace.

If it is argued that [the agent] does not exist because of superimposition (*samāropa*), why should that [superimposition] not also occur in both cases without distinction? For there is no difference between the two cases regarding the fact that the agent is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*).

If you say, "In this case, for one who possesses valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*), there certainly exists the cognition that [the action] has been performed," then how does he come to understand its having been performed there—either by this very inference or by another?

First, there is a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). For instance, the emergence of this [inference] depends upon a reason whose qualification is already established, and once it has emerged, the qualification of the reason is established by it.

In the second case, another inference would likewise emerge only from a reason possessing a qualification; if that [qualification] were established through yet another inference, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Therefore, the qualification consisting in the nature of "producing a cognition of what has been done" is not established. Consequently, the reason suffers from the fallacy of being unestablished in its qualification (*viśeṣaṇāsiddha*).

As for what is said—that "there is no rule that the sight of ground being filled after having been dug necessarily produces the cognition of something made in the mind regarding things that are made"—that too is incorrect. For in that case, there exists a similarity to an unmade portion of ground and so forth, which prevents that [cognition] from arising; thus, the non-arising of that cognition is logically accounted for. Furthermore, even in the case of the earth and so on, there is no similarity to an unmade configuration by virtue of which the cognition of being unmade would arise, because such a thing is not admitted at all. And if it were admitted, it would result in the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets (apasiddhānta).
[Ñ: Because the qualification "having the nature of producing a conscious intellect" is unestablished, the reason is unestablished in its qualification (*viśeṣaṇāsiddha*). [Ñ27:

Or, even if it were established, it would nevertheless be contradictory (*viruddha*), because here one is proving an intelligent agent characterized by a body and so forth, just as in the case of a jar and other such things. [Ñ28:

If it is objected that, in this way, if one searches for a commonality between the example and the subject of the example, reasons would be untenable in all cases—[we reply] no; for in an inference from smoke and the like, fire is understood as something common to both the kitchen and other places.

In this regard, it is also incorrect to claim that there is no contradiction because the generality of "intelligent agents" is well-established; for the reason of being an effect is established only for that generality which has a perceptible particular as its locus, not for one whose locus is imperceptible, since such a thing is not perceived even in a dream, just like the generality of a donkey's horn.

Therefore, from whatever kind of cause a particular kind of effect is observed, from that very same kind [of cause] must that very same kind [of effect] be inferred. Just as the production of smoke possessing such-and-such properties from fire possessing such-and-such properties has been established through highly firm means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), so too is there an inference of fire possessing those very same properties from smoke possessing those very same properties.

By this, the objection beginning with "If pervasion were grasped through the specificities of the probandum and the probans, it would follow that all inference is destroyed" should be seen as refuted.
This reason is inconclusive because of such things as trees and grasses that arise without being drawn forth [by an agent].

Two kinds of effects are observed: some are preceded by an intelligent agent, such as jars and the like; others, however, are the opposite of that, such as grasses and the like that arise without being drawn forth.

If [the opponent argues that] there is no deviation because those [instances] are made into the subject (*pakṣīkaraṇāt*), then even such arguments as "He is dark-skinned because he is his son, like other sons of his" would result in being valid proofs (*gamaka*). Consequently, no reason (*hetu*) would ever be deviant, since it would always be possible to make the very object of deviation the subject in every case.

Furthermore, there is deviation with respect to the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth of God (*īśvara*); for although these are effects, they do not have a preceding intelligent agent distinct from God as their inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*). And if one were to accept such a [distinct agent], there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Likewise, this [reason] is also "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), because the absence of an agent in the case of sprouts and so forth that grow without being ploughed is determined by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). It is like [the reason] "being a substance" when one intends to prove that fire is not hot.

If it is argued: "In that case too, the agent is simply an invisible God," we say: no. Because the existence of such a [God] there would have to be established either from this very [inference] or from some other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

In the first case, there is a circular argument (*cakraka*): for only when its existence is established is the non-perception of it due to its invisibility established; when that is established, the fallacy of "being set aside by lapse of time" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*) is absent; and from that, its existence is established once again.
In the second case as well, it is untenable, because there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) that could inform us of its existence.
Or, even if that [soul] exists there, nevertheless, its non-perception is caused by the absence of a body, or by the power of knowledge (*vidyā*) and so forth, or by a specific birth (*jāti-viśeṣa*).
In the first case, agency is untenable because of the lack of a body, just like a liberated soul (*muktātman*). [Objection:

But surely, even in the absence of a body, agency is possible in creating one's own body by being the substratum of cognition, desire, and effort; [Response: this too is an unconsidered statement, because such instigation is possible only through a connection with a body, and in the absence of a body, that is impossible, just as in the case of a liberated soul.
