Furthermore, in the absence of a body, it is impossible for [the self] to be the substratum of cognition and so forth, because the body is the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) for their production; otherwise, it would follow that they could arise even in the case of a liberated soul (*muktātman*). Moreover, if the power of knowledge (*vidyā*) and so forth were the cause of invisibility, then that [power] might at some time become visible. Indeed, a permanent invisibility is not observed in those who possess knowledge, as is the case with *piśācas* and the like.
Nor is a specific genus (*jāti-viśeṣa*) the cause of invisibility, because such a genus cannot belong to a single individual, since it must reside in multiple individuals.

Whether that [cause] be visible or invisible, it must nonetheless be the cause of the earth and so forth by virtue of either (1) mere existence, (2) possessing knowledge, (3) possessing knowledge, desire, and effort, (4) activity preceded by those, or (5) sovereignty.

Regarding these, in the first case, it would follow that even potters and the like are the creators of the world, since there is no difference in their state of existence. In the second case, however, it follows that even yogins would be creators.
The third [alternative] is also untenable, because it was already refuted that one who is bodiless can be the substratum of knowledge and so forth.
The fourth is also impossible, because it is impossible for one who is bodiless to possess activity performed by body or speech.

Sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) may consist in being a knower, being an agent, or something else. If it consists in being a knower, is that merely being a knower or omniscience? In the first case, he would be merely a knower and not the Lord (*īśvara*), like other knowers such as ourselves. In the second case, he would possess only omniscience and not sovereignty, like the Sugata and others. If, on the other hand, it consists in being an agent, then it would follow that potters and others—who produce many effects—would also possess sovereignty.
Nor is it anything else, because there exists nothing other than desire and effort that could serve as the basis for the sovereignty of Īśvara. Furthermore,

regarding the creation of the world, does Īśvara act according to his own whim (1), through dependence on karma (2), out of compassion (3), for the sake of sport (4), for the purpose of inflicting punishment and bestowing grace (5), or by his very nature (6)?
Regarding this, in the first alternative, there might sometimes be a creation of a different nature altogether;
in the second, there would be a loss of sovereignty; and in the third, He would make the entire world exclusively happy.

Now, what does Īśvara do? If beings experience suffering because they are governed solely by their previously accumulated *karma*, then what is his human effort (*puruṣakāra*)? And if he acts while depending on the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), what is the point of postulating him? Let the world simply be dependent upon that [unseen force]; what is the use of this useless internal tumor?
In this regard, for the fourth and fifth [alternatives], it follows that he would be devoid of passion and hatred.

For instance: "God possesses passion because he engages in play, like a child; likewise, he possesses passion because he bestows favor, like a king; and likewise, he possesses hatred because he inflicts punishment, just like him.
Now, if it is by way of inherent nature (*svabhāva*), then let the activity of the insentient world itself proceed by way of its own inherent nature; what is the use of postulating a creator for it?

The reason "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) does not establish an intelligent creator, namely Īśvara. Likewise, [reasons] such as "possessing a specific configuration," "having insentient material causes," and "coming into being from what did not previously exist" should also be raised by oneself, since the objections and their resolutions are identical.

Furthermore, when it is to be proven that the earth and so forth are preceded by an intelligent agent, all the reasons (hetu) presented are indeed contradictory (viruddha), because—by virtue of the support of the examples—they prove that they are preceded by an agent who possesses a body, is non-omniscient, and is not an omnipotent creator.

Nor does this same fault apply even to the inference of fire from smoke; for in that case, smoke is observed to be pervaded by fire in its mere generality, regardless of specific substrates such as grass or leaves.

In this case, there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) of "being an effect" by the general property of having an agent characterized by the distinction between being omniscient or non-omniscient, because an omniscient agent is not established prior to this inference.

Furthermore, these [reasons] are inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*), since the manifestation of lightning and the like is observed even without an intelligent agent, and because effects are seen even when preceded by what is non-intelligent, as in states such as dreaming.

And these [reasons] are "mistimed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa), because they are employed immediately after a thesis that has been sublated by perception and scripture; and that sublation has already been demonstrated previously.
These are "equivalents by counter-argument" (*prakaraṇasama*), because there exist other reasons that initiate an inquiry into the matter.

For instance: "God is not the creator of the world, because he lacks instruments, like a potter who is devoid of instruments such as a staff, a wheel, and a cloth; likewise, [he is not the creator] because he is all-pervasive, like space, and because he is one, like that [space]," and so forth.

However, qualifiers such as "eternality" and so forth, when brought forward to establish that [nature], are simply not worth hearing—much like a description of physical beauty addressed to a eunuch by a lustful woman.
Nevertheless, something is said here for the sake of demonstrating its inability to withstand critical analysis. First, eternality is examined; and that does not hold true in the case of Īśvara.

For instance: God is not eternal, because He is the agent of effects such as the earth and so forth precisely through a differentiation of His own nature (*svabhāva-bheda*), since the definition of eternity is accepted as that which is "immutable, unarisen, stable, unitary in nature, and immovable" (*kūṭastha*).
Furthermore, if a differentiation of nature were not admitted, His performance of contradictory actions such as creation and dissolution would be utterly impossible.

Nor can it be asserted that His knowledge and other qualities are eternal, because that contradicts direct experience and because it is contradicted by the following inference: "The knowledge and other qualities of God are not eternal, because they are knowledge and so forth, like the knowledge and other qualities of ourselves and others."
By this, that which was asserted—namely, that his knowledge and so forth are eternal—is refuted; this should be inferred.

Furthermore, by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is his omniscience to be apprehended? It cannot be by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because, being produced from the contact of the sense faculties with their objects, it lacks the capacity to apprehend objects that transcend the senses.

Nor [is it known] by inference, because there is no non-deviant logical mark (*avyabhicāri-liṅga*). If it is argued that such a mark certainly exists in the form of the impossibility of the world's diversity arising otherwise, we say no; for there is no necessary concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with that [omniscience], since the diversity of the world can be accounted for even without omniscience, by virtue of the ripening of wholesome and unwholesome karma and so forth.

Furthermore, if he were omniscient, why would he create—asuras and others who act with license to bring calamity upon the world, and people such as ourselves who revile him—beings for whom he must later exercise restraint? Therefore, he is not omniscient.

Likewise, when many individuals act toward a single purpose, the fear that discord may arise leads to the postulation of a single Great Lord; this is comparable to a miser’s resorting to a desolate wilderness by abandoning his most beloved sons, wife, friends, and so forth, out of fear for the expenses of food and other necessities.

This is because even though the effects such as Indra’s head, honeycombs, and honey are produced by hundreds of various insects and bees, they are nevertheless perceived as being uniform, undifferentiated, and without variation.
Furthermore, if the Lord's status as the creator of the entire world were accepted, the established distinction between valid and non-valid scriptures would be destroyed.

For instance: "Every scripture is valid because it was composed by the Lord, just like other scriptures composed by Him. Moreover, there would be a collapse of the distinction between opponents and others, since it would be impossible for anyone to act contrary to His command—given that all would be following the Lord's instructions—and this would result in the absence of any opponent. Thus, the existence of a Great Lord who is the creator of the universe cannot be established in any way whatsoever.

Therefore, because he reveals the true nature of reality, it is established that only the God who is free from passion (*vītarāga*) is worthy of being accepted as a deity, and no other; this is the conclusion.

On this point, the followers of Jaimini (*Jaiminīyas*) argue: "Indeed, there exists here no deity whatsoever characterized by such attributes as omniscience and so forth that you favor, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend such a being."

For instance: first of all, perception is not the means of apprehending that [omniscience], because of the statement: "That which is connected and present is indeed grasped by the eye and other [senses]" (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra-bhāṣya, Pratyakṣa-sūtra, verse 84).

Nor is it inference, because inference operates only upon an object already perceived through perception. Nor is it scripture, because since an omniscient being is not established, his scripture is likewise a subject of dispute.
Nor is there comparison (*upamāna*), because there is no other being similar to an omniscient one.
Nor is there presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), because no fact is observed that is otherwise inexplicable (*anyathānupapanna*) and thus necessitates the existence of an omniscient being.

Therefore, since the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) do not apply to him, the omniscient one is indeed the object of the means of valid cognition consisting in non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*). As it has been said:

"Where the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) do not arise with respect to the nature of an object, there the status of non-existence (*abhāva*) as a means of valid cognition exists for the purpose of understanding the non-existence of that object. (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra-vārttika, Abhāva-pariccheda, Verse 1).
The formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: "An omniscient being does not exist, because he is not apprehended by the five means of valid cognition, like the horn of a donkey."

Furthermore, one might think: "Just as even beginningless impurity in gold becomes pure through processes such as alkaline treatment, clay, and *puṭapāka* (a specific method of preparing medicinal substances), why should omniscience not likewise belong to the self, since its impurities are removed by the constant practice of knowledge and so forth? This too is not correct; for through practice, there may indeed be a gradual degree of purification, but not a supreme perfection. For a human being cannot [attain] flight [merely through practice].
Even that which is perceived as possessing degrees of excellence through practice (*abhyāsatas tāratamyavat*) is observed to have the entire world as its object. And it has been said:
"Even one who, by leaping, might travel ten cubits (*hasta*) through the air, would not be able to go a hundred *yojana*s even with hundreds of practices. (Cf. Ṭīkā on Ślokavārttika 826, etc.)

Furthermore, by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does he know the entire range of objects? Is it through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), or rather through all the means of valid cognition as far as possible?
It cannot be through direct perception, because that [ordinary perception] grasps only proximate and specific objects.
Nor can it be through supersensuous direct perception, because there is no proof for its existence.

Nor can it be by means of all the instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because all of them are preceded by perception (*pratyakṣa-pūrvaka*), and because [if they were not], it would follow that everyone is omniscient. Furthermore, if he perceives things exactly as they are, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of experiencing the taste of impurity and so forth, because he would perceive them in their actual state. And it has been said:
"And the consequence of experiencing the taste of impurity and so forth is unavoidable.
Furthermore, does he know past and future objects in their own respective natures, or only as being present?
In the first case, it follows that such cognition would not be perception, because it apprehends a non-present object, like memory and so forth.
In the second case, however, it follows that such cognition is erroneous, because it apprehends an object as being otherwise than it actually exists, like the cognition of two moons and so forth.

To this, the following reply is given: First, regarding the proof stated—namely, "because there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends it"—that is incorrect, because there do exist inferential means of valid cognition (*anumāna-pramāṇa*) that establish it.
For instance: "The gradation of knowledge must rest upon some ultimate limit, because it is expressed by the terms 'more' and 'most,' just like measurement.
This reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*), since we perceive a gradation in knowledge in the form of the proficiency of qualities such as wisdom and intelligence in every living being.

Therefore, it must necessarily reach its ultimate limit of excellence, just as [the limit of] dimension is reached in space. And that [limit]—which consists in the capacity of knowledge to illuminate all things—is where the Blessed One rests; he is the Omniscient One.

If it is argued that this reason is inconclusive because we do not observe the attainment of a state of ultimate fire-form through the gradation of heat in water being heated, even though such a gradation exists, we say no.

Since that which is an innate property of a substance—not dependent on auxiliary causes—and which, though innate, initiates a modification in its own substrate, reaches the ultimate limit of excellence through the process of repeated practice, as is the case with the purity of gold produced by a continuous series of smelting and heating;

yet heat is not an innate property of water, but rather depends on auxiliary causes such as fire—how then could heat, when practiced upon it, reach the highest degree? On the contrary, through extreme heating, there is only the total evaporation of the water.

Knowledge, however, is an innate property of the soul (*jīva*), and it imparts a specific excellence (*viśeṣa*) to its own substrate. Therefore, because it bestows ever-increasing excellence through continuous practice, it is not unreasonable that it reaches the ultimate limit of excellence.

By this, the argument beginning with "the practice of jumping" (*laṅghanābhyāsa*) is refuted; for jumping is not an innate property, it does not impart excellence to its own substrate, and on the contrary, it results in the exhaustion of one's capacity.

Likewise, [the weight] of a drop of ocean water and so forth are perceptible to someone, because they are objects of knowledge (*prameya*), like the specific qualities such as color residing in a jar or similar objects.

Nor is "being an object of knowledge" unestablished, for that would entail the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the means of non-apprehension (*abhāvapramāṇa*); for you yourself accept that an entity which transcends the five means of valid cognition falls within the scope of the means of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, if the nature of the objects of knowledge—such as the measure of the waters of the ocean and so forth—were to transcend the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then even those would fall within the scope of the means of valid cognition known as non-existence (*abhāva*). Yet, since that is not possible here, the Blessed One, for whom these things are directly perceived, is omniscient.

Likewise, there exists someone who directly perceives the multitude of objects that transcend the senses, because he provides instructions on the apprehension of the moon and other such things, which consist of specific directions, locations, times, and measures, and which are non-contradictory even in the absence of verbal instruction or logical marks (*liṅga*). Whatever person provides non-contradictory instructions regarding a particular object in the absence of verbal instruction or logical marks is a direct perceiver of that object, just as we and others are; and since there is indeed someone who provides such non-contradictory instructions, he must be a direct perceiver of them. And such a person is none other than the venerable Omniscient One (*sarvajña*).

As for what was said—that because the five means of valid cognition do not operate, the omniscient being falls within the scope of the means of valid cognition known as non-existence—that too is mere words, because the non-operation of the five means of valid cognition is impossible. For that [non-operation] would have to function as a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), yet no subverting factor is possible with respect to an omniscient being. To explain: such a subverting factor would have to be either perception, inference, scripture, comparison, or presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

Among these, the first position is not tenable; for if perception were either the cause or the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of an object, then its cessation would logically entail the cessation of the object as well—just as the cessation of fire (the cause) or "tree-ness" (the pervader) entails the cessation of smoke or "śimśapā-ness.
However, perception is not the cause of an object, because the object exists even in its absence when there is a spatial or other obstruction.
Nor is it the pervader, because objects remote in space and so forth do not cease to exist even when perception of them ceases.

Nor is it logical that the non-occurrence of what is neither an effect nor pervaded [by the reason] follows from the occurrence of what is neither a cause nor a pervader, because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Nor is inference a sublater of that [thesis], because the nature of the subject (*dharmin*), the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), and the means of proof (*sādhana*) are unestablished (*svarūpāsiddhi*).
For in that case, as for the subject, is it intended to be (1) the omniscient one, (2) the Sugata and others, or (3) all persons?
If he is omniscient, then what is to be proven there: (1) his non-existence, or (2) his non-omniscience?
If it is his non-existence, what is the proof for that: (1) non-perception, (2) the affirmation of a contradictory property, or (3) [the presence of] being a speaker and so forth?
If it is non-perception, is it the non-perception of the omniscient one himself, or (2) of his cause, or (3) of his effect, or (4) of his pervader?

If [the reason] belongs to the omniscient one, is that [non-perception] related to himself (1) or related to all things (2)? If it is related to himself, is it without qualification (1) or qualified by the condition of being perceptible (2)? In the first case, the reason—"because of non-perception"—is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the specific states of another's mind and so forth, for it is not admitted that those [states] are non-existent even though they are not perceived.

Nor is there the qualification of "having attained the conditions for perception," because that would entail the non-existence of the proof for the absence of an omniscient being at all times and in all places.

For it is not possible for that which is absolutely non-existent to attain the conditions for perception, since such attainment is invariably concomitant with the existence and perception [of the thing] at some place and at some time.
By this, the position regarding all possible relations is also rejected.
Furthermore, the non-perception of all related [conditions] is unestablished, because it is impossible for one who is not omniscient to realize it.
Indeed, as long as the nature of all things and their cognitions are not realized, the non-perception of an omniscient being—which would be related to them—cannot be realized.
Nor is there a non-perception of the cause, because that cause—the destruction of karma such as the obscuration of knowledge—is perceived through inference.
And this is the inference that establishes [the point], while the logical arguments will be stated further on.
(ñ61) The non-perception of the effect is also unestablished, because its effect—an authoritative scripture—is indeed perceived.
(ñ62) The non-perception of the pervader is also unestablished, because its pervader—the state of directly perceiving all objects—is understood through inference.

For instance: There exists someone who directly perceives all objects, because, while having the nature of apprehending them, the obstructing conditions have been destroyed. Whatever has the nature of apprehending something and has its obstructions destroyed is a direct perceiver of that thing; for example, an eye from which obstructions such as cataracts have been removed is a direct perceiver of form. Thus, the proof [based on] non-perception does not establish the non-existence of an omniscient being.
Furthermore, even the affirmation of the contradictory (*viruddhavidhi*) could establish the non-existence of an omniscient being, either directly or indirectly.
In the first case, because non-omniscience—which is directly contradictory to omniscience—is established either at some place and at some time, or everywhere and at all times:
regarding that, in the first sub-case, it would not be established that there is an absence of an omniscient being everywhere and at all times;
for wherever that [non-omniscience] is established, only there is its presence, and not elsewhere.
For nowhere and never has the absence of cold—which is contradictory to and pervaded by fire—been observed when fire is present.

The second [alternative] is also untenable, because it is impossible for one with limited vision to observe the presence of non-omniscience—which is contradictory to omniscience—everywhere and at all times; and if such observation were possible, that very observer would himself have to be omniscient, which establishes our desired conclusion.

Ñ64: Even by way of a logical sequence (*paramparā*), could the affirmation of any of these—(1) that which is contradictory to its pervader, (2) that which is contradictory to its cause, or (3) that which is contradictory to its effect—indicate (or bring about the cognition of) the non-existence of an omniscient being? Ñ: First of all, it cannot be the affirmation of that which is contradictory to its pervader; for the pervader of an omniscient being is the direct perception of all objects. Contradictory to that is either the lack of such direct perception or the grasping of only limited objects.

Furthermore, the prescription of that [contrary cause] would establish the absence of that [omniscience] only in some cases and at some times, but not everywhere or at all times; for example, from the prescription of fire—which is excluded by cold that pervades the sensation of frost—there follows the negation of the sensation of frost only in some cases and at some times.
Likewise, even the prescription of a cause contrary [to omniscience] would establish the absence of an omniscient being only in some cases and at some times, but not everywhere.

For the cause of omniscience (*sarvajñatva*) is the total exhaustion of all karma (*aśeṣakarmakṣaya*). A prescription for the non-exhaustion of karma—which is the opposite of that—can prove the absence of an omniscient being only at a particular time and place, just as the prescription of fire, which is opposed to the cold that causes horripilation and the like, results in the negation of the effects of cold, such as horripilation, only at a particular time and place. It does not, however, do so universally, because the universal exhaustion of all karma is impossible, and because we shall later demonstrate that such exhaustion does not exist in any self whatsoever.

Nor is there the formulation of a contradictory effect (*viruddhakāryavidhi*). For that which is contradictory to omniscience is limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva*); its effect is speech whose object is restricted to specific things, and the formulation of that [speech] would not establish the non-existence of an omniscient being in its entirety. This is because, just as the formulation of that [effect] is capable of proving the absence of that [omniscience] only in that very [particular] instance—just as smoke, the effect of fire which is contradictory to cold, proves the negation of the sensation of cold only in a place specifically characterized by that smoke—it follows that even the formulation of a contradictory effect is not a subverter of the existence of an omniscient one.

Nor can [the reason] such as "being a speaker" (vaktṛtva) and so forth [establish the non-existence of an omniscient being], because if the existence of an omniscient being is not admitted, that [reason] is unestablished due to its impossibility; yet, if its possibility is admitted, there is a contradiction with one's own words, namely: "There is no omniscient being, and yet he is endowed with properties such as being a speaker. Therefore, the non-existence of an omniscient being cannot be proven by any reason whatsoever.
Nor can "non-omniscience" be established as the probandum in the form "The omniscient one is non-omniscient," because the contradiction here is likewise no different.

Furthermore, when proving non-omniscience, is it intended as a reason that the Omniscient One speaks of matters contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which is the opposite of that [omniscience], or is it merely "the state of being a speaker"?

In the first case, the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*), because it is impossible for an omniscient being to speak of such [contradictory] matters. In the second case, however, the reason is contradictory (*viruddha*), because the state of speaking of matters not contradicted by what is seen or accepted is possible only if one is indeed omniscient.

Even in the third alternative, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because there is no contradiction between the mere fact of being a speaker and omniscience. By this, the position that takes Sugata and others as the subject (*dharmin*) is also refuted, as the aforementioned defects apply without distinction. Furthermore, if the omniscience of a specific individual such as Sugata is denied, the affirmation of it for others necessarily follows, because the negation of a particular implies the permission of the remainder, as in the case of "This person is not a Brāhmaṇa."

Therefore, it is argued that by taking all persons into account, their non-omniscience is established on the grounds of their being speakers and so forth; but this is not so, because since its exclusion from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) is unestablished, its exclusion from the subject (*pakṣa*) is doubtful. Thus, one might be both omniscient and a speaker. Consequently, this is not an inference that subverts the existence of an omniscient being.

Nor is there scriptural authority (*āgama*), for such scripture must be either of human origin or not of human origin. First of all, it cannot be of non-human origin, because that lacks intrinsic validity (*aprāmāṇya*); for the validity of words is established only through their dependence upon a speaker endowed with excellence.

Furthermore, since its status as a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) is accepted only with respect to its specific object (its own meaning), it would not possess validity regarding the universal negation of intrinsic nature.

Nor is there any Vedic statement that establishes the absence of all-encompassing knowledge (*aśeṣajñāna*), for we hear many Vedic passages, such as "Hiraṇyagarbha is omniscient," which establish that very point. Nor can analogy (*upamāna*) serve as a sublater of that [omniscience], for analogy occurs—like that of a cow and a gavaya—only when both the object of comparison and the thing compared are perceptible.

Furthermore, neither all persons nor any omniscient being have been seen by anyone, such that there could be an analogy like "the omniscient being is like all persons" or "those [persons] are like the omniscient being. Moreover, if all persons were seen, it would follow that he himself is omniscient. Nor is presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) a subverter of that [omniscience], because there is no fact whatsoever that is unaccountable except for the non-existence of an omniscient being; indeed, the authority of the Veda is only established if an omniscient being exists.

For the validity of words is not possible in the absence of a speaker possessing [excellent] qualities; thus, there is no subverting evidence against the existence of an omniscient being. Furthermore, the non-operation of the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in his absence is itself unestablished. Likewise, that which was stated—that [the omniscient being] is the object of the "proof of non-existence" (*abhāvapramāṇa*) due to the non-operation of the five means of valid cognition—is also inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). This is because things such as the weight of Mount Himavat or piśācas are not within the scope of the proof of non-existence, even though the five means of valid cognition do not operate regarding them. Thus, the argument beginning with "where the five means of valid cognition... should be regarded as refuted.

As for what was stated—namely, "By what means of valid cognition [is] the entire collection of things [known]? and so forth—that too is incorrect, because the Omniscient One knows all things, such as the entire world and the non-world, by means of the complete light of absolute knowledge (*kevalajñāna*) arising from the total destruction of all veils of knowledge.

As for what was said, namely, "the tasting of the flavor of impurity and so forth," that too merely reveals malice toward the Supreme One. Since the Omniscient One is beyond the senses, he is independent of the operation of the sense organs; his cognition is a perception of things exactly as they are, through a state of detached neutrality, without depending on the operation of the tongue-organ. It is not, however, a cognition dependent on such operations, as yours is. Furthermore, as for what was asserted, "saṃsāra is beginningless and endless in terms of time" and so forth, that too is incorrect because of simultaneous cognition. Nor is that impossible, for it is observed [to be so].

For instance: just as the meaning of all the scriptures, having been thoroughly mastered, appears simultaneously in a general way, so too does it appear even when characterized by every particular detail. As it has been said:
"Just as the meaning of all the scriptures, having been well-mastered, appears in the mind in a single moment, so too is the knowledge of the infinite and so forth. [Pravārttika 2.227].

As for what was said regarding "the past and the future" and so forth—that too merely demonstrates the ignorance of its own author. For although those two entities, the past and the future, are non-existent in relation to the present time, nevertheless, just as the past existed in the past time and just as the future will exist, there is no fault whatsoever in [the Buddha's] direct perception of them. Thus, it is established that he is omniscient, because—like pleasure and other such states—he possesses a well-ascertained cognition for which no subverting means of knowledge is possible.

Now, the Kṣapaṭas argue: "Granted that the existence of an omniscient being is established because there is no valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) that can definitively refute it; however, we do not accept that he takes food in morsels (*kavalāhāra*).

For instance, the omniscient one (*kevalin*) does not take food in morsels because of the absence of its causes; and in the absence of causes, an effect cannot arise, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasakti*).

Nor is the absence of its causes unproven; for among the six factors beginning with sensation (*vedanā*), which constitute the primary cause for taking food, not even one of them exists in the omniscient one."

For instance: first of all, no sensation arises for him, because that which would produce such sensation has become like a burnt rope. Even if a sensation were present, he would not experience suffering caused by it, owing to his infinite power (*anantavīrya*).

Furthermore, the failure to perform services for the Blessed One, who is worthy of worship by the three worlds, is simply impossible for him. Moreover, he perceives the modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*) perfectly through the destruction of the veil of omniscience (*kevalajñānāvaraṇa*).

As for his self-restraint (*saṃyama*): because one whose conduct is as described has achieved the ultimate goal and possesses infinite power (*anantavīrya*), it does not become a cause for taking food.
Furthermore, even his maintenance of the vital breaths (*prāṇavṛtti*) is established otherwise, due to the non-decline of his lifespan and his infinite power.

The occasion for reflection on *dharma*, however, has passed, because he has achieved the ultimate goal. Thus, in this way, the consumption of solid food (*kāvalikāhāra*) is not possible for the Kevalin, as it is corrupted by many defects.

To this it is replied: First, as for the proof stated there—“because of the absence of its cause”—that is unestablished (*asiddha*); for the cause of food, namely *vedanīya* karma, exists in exactly that same way for the *kevalin*. And thus, why should that former bodily state not persist? Here the formal argument (*prayoga*) would be: the eating of the *kevalin* occurs because the complete causal complex is present, just like previous eating.

And this collection consists of: sufficiency, the karmas to be experienced (*vedanīya*) and so forth, the fiery body (*taijasa-śarīra*) which is the cause for the digestion of food, and long life. And although this collection is complete, it exists in the Kevalin. As for the claim that the karma to be experienced has the status of a "burnt rope" (*dagdharajju-sthānikatva*); that too is unscriptural and illogical, because the scripture establishes the existence of the absolute intensity of its fruition (*atyantāsātoda*) in the Kevalin.

There is also a logical argument (*yukti*): if the beginninglessness of his knowledge (*jñānānādya*) were due to the destruction of destructive karma (*ghāti-karma*), what would happen to the hunger arising from the *vedanīya* karma, such that it would not occur?

There is no contradiction between the two—pleasure (*sāta*) and pain (*asāta*)—characterized by their non-coexistence like shadow and heat, or by their mutual exclusion like existence and non-existence. Since pleasure and pain alternate every *antar-muhūrta*, even as there is the experience of pleasure, there is also the experience of pain. Thus, even while possessing infinite power (*anantavīryatva*), there certainly occurs a decline in physical strength and the affliction arising from hunger.
And it is not the case that there is any deficiency in his taking of food; it is merely a matter of personal preference (*āho-puruṣikā*).

As for what is said—"Because of the absence of the activation (*udīraṇā*) of karma to be experienced (*vedanīya*), there is an absence of the arising of a great quantity of *pudgala*; and because of that absence, there is an absolute absence of suffering"—that is incorrect. This is because in the fourth and subsequent stages of spiritual development (*guṇasthānaka*), there exists the "ladder of qualities" (*guṇa-śreṇī*) of karma to be experienced; furthermore, even when there is the arising of a profuse amount of *pudgala*, we observe only a minimal degree of suffering caused by it; and finally, as in the case of the Victor (*Jina*) during the subsidence of anger (*sāta*), we see that intensity [of experience] is manifested even in the absence of the arising of a profuse amount of *pudgala*.

As for the claim that "desire for food is hunger, and that is the notion of possession, which is a transformation of deluding karma (*mohanīya*); since that has been eliminated, the Kevalin does not eat," this is incorrect. For hunger does not arise from the fruition of deluding karma, because such fruition is being ceased through the cultivation of its antidotes, as is observed in the case of anger and the other passions.
As it is said: "One should destroy anger through tranquility" (*Daśavaikālika Sūtra* 8.39), and so forth.

Furthermore, hunger is not seen to be something that can be turned back by the cultivation of its opposite, as is the case with [other] sensations; therefore, hunger has the nature of being a maturation of delusion.
By this, it is refuted that which is said:
"The lifespan, knowledge, and so forth do not diminish when the [karma] that has achieved its purpose is exhausted."

[The objection that] "infinite vigor is for the benefit of the world, so why would there be enjoyment for one whose thirst has ceased? (Kevalibhukti-śloka 16), and so forth, is refuted. For, given the presence of such a collection of factors as grossness and the like, it would follow that even in the state of being a *chadmastha* (one still under the veil of karma), the *kevalin* (omniscient one) would not enjoy food. If it is argued that the *chadmastha* enjoys food because of the absence of the destruction of all *vīryāntarāya* (obscuration of vigor) karma, that is incorrect.

For what reason would there be a reduction of his lifespan there, or why would there be any loss of the four types of knowledge, such that he would eat? Therefore, just as food is a cause for the long-term duration of the lifespan, so too is it a cause [for the maintenance of the body]; and just as the final moment of meditative concentration, in which activity has ceased, is the cause for the attainment of perfection, so too is right speech and the like. Thus, even his possession of infinite vigor is not contradicted by his taking of food.

Likewise, for him, activities such as eating, as well as walking and sitting, occur by his own will (*devacchanda*) and other causes of rest; thus, the act of eating also occurs because there is no contradiction. Furthermore, hunger does not diminish for one who is more powerful and possesses great vigor, because such a rule has exceptions. Moreover, scripture also establishes that the *kevalin* eats; for instance, the *Tattvārthasūtra* states: "The eleven [faculties] exist in the Jina" (TS 9.18).

Commentary: Eleven hardships—namely hunger, thirst, cold, heat, gadflies and mosquitoes, wandering, lodging, violence, disease, contact with grass, and dirt—occur in the Jina who possesses omniscience (*kevalin*); this is because their cause, the *vedanīya* (feeling-producing) karma, still exists even now.
Furthermore, it is not possible for the effect to be destroyed while its cause remains unextinguished, for that would lead to an over-extension of the principle.

Therefore, it is indeed possible for the pain of the feeling of hunger to occur in the omniscient one; however, due to his infinite power (*anantavīrya*), he does not become overwhelmed by it, nor does he, having accomplished his purpose, endure suffering without any necessity.
Nor can it be asserted that "the body of the Blessed One is exactly such that it is not afflicted by the pain of hunger," because that [affliction] is established therein through inference.
For instance: "The body of an omniscient one (*kevalin*) is afflicted by hunger and so forth, because it is a body, like the bodies presided over by people such as ourselves.

Likewise, the claim that "just as his body is naturally devoid of perspiration and the like, so too it is devoid of food taken by mouth" must certainly be rejected, as it lacks any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*).

Thus, in this manner, just as the intake of food is a cause for the duration of the gross body according to one's lifespan—since there is no possibility of a "prior limit" (pūrva-koṭi) to the time of the existence of a Kevalin—so too is the "supplementary food" (prakṣepāhāra).

For it is thus: when that which has been made soft by the fiery body (taijasa-śarīra), ingested, and transformed by its own capacity for digestion, undergoes a successive process of transformation, hunger arises for those possessing gross bodies in this way.

[Objection: For what reason, then, does he not eat? [Response: Furthermore, the four destructive karmas (*ghāti-karma*) do not possess the status of auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*) with respect to the sensation of hunger; such that, because of their absence, one could say that [eating] is absent due to their absence. Thus, the eating of the *kevalin* is established. Likewise, the formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: the *kevalin* possesses food consisting of morsels (*prakṣepāhāra*), because there is no contradiction between being a *kevalin* and consuming morsel-food (*kavalāhāra*), just like the experience of pleasant sensation (*sāta-vedanīya*). This concludes the section establishing the eating of the *kevalin*.
Now he states the principles (tattvas):

"The soul (jīva) and the non-soul (ajīva), as well as merit (puṇya), demerit (pāpa), influx (āsrava), restraint (saṃvara), bondage (bandha), dissociation (nirjarā), and liberation (mokṣa)—these are the nine principles. //47//

Commentary: The soul (jīva) is characterized by consciousness (cetanā); that which is characterized by the opposite of that is the non-soul (ajīva). This [non-soul] is established as fivefold through the divisions of dharma, adharma, space (ākāśa), time (kāla), and matter (pudgala).
All entities existing within the world are included within these two alone.

For knowledge and so forth, as well as color, taste, and so forth—the qualities of substance—and the actions such as upward throwing, as well as generality, particularity, and inherence, do not obtain their own existence apart from the living (jīva) and the non-living (ajīva); because they are absolutely not perceived as distinct from those [two categories], and because they are apprehended as being of the nature of those [categories]; otherwise, it would follow that they are non-existent.

The principles (tattvas) such as suffering (duḥkha) and so forth, postulated by the Bauddhas and others, should not be stated as being of a different genus (jāty-antara) distinct from living beings (jīva) and non-living beings (ajīva); for the entire world is pervaded by the two aggregates of jīva and ajīva, and that which is not pervaded by them is equivalent to a hare's horn.

If it is argued that the separate mention of merit (*puṇya*), demerit (*pāpa*), influx (*āsrava*), and so forth would not be based on logic because everything is already encompassed by the two categories [of the auspicious and the inauspicious], we say no; for the purpose is to dispel misconceptions regarding merit and the rest. There is no fault in the separate mention of influx and the others, as they are intended to demonstrate transmigratory existence along with its causes and liberation.

Furthermore, one should understand from scripture how restraint (*saṃvara*) and the wearing away of karma (*nirjarā*) are the causes of liberation; how influx is the basis for bondage; and how bondage, which is divided into the two types of merit and demerit, is the cause of transmigratory existence.

In this context, merit (*puṇya*) consists of auspicious (*śubha*) karmic entities (3); however, those same [entities] when inauspicious (*aśubha*) are demerit (*pāpa*) (4). That from which karma flows is an influx (*āsrava*), namely the activity of body, speech, and mind; it is twofold because it has the nature of being a cause for both merit and demerit (5). Restraint (*saṃvara*) is the cessation of influx, so called because practices such as the guptis, samitis, dharmas, and anuprekṣās act as obstacles to the influx; it too is twofold, based on the distinction between total and partial [restraint] (6).

§92: Bondage (*bandha*) is a specific kind of cohesion of the soul (*ātman*), which is accompanied by passions (*sakaṣāya*), with the matter-particles (*pudgala*) of the karma-aggregates (*karmavargaṇā*). Although it is generally of one kind, it is fourfold through the distinctions of nature (*prakṛti*), duration (*sthiti*), intensity (*anubhāga*), and quantity (*pradeśa*). Furthermore, each of these is eightfold according to the distinction of the root-natures (*mūlaprakṛti*), such as knowledge-obscuring (*jñānāvaraṇa*) and so forth. Moreover, each of those is manifold according to the distinction of the secondary natures (*uttaraprakṛti*), such as the obscuration of sensory cognition (*matyāvaraṇa*) and so forth.

And this [karma] is of two kinds: one is commendable because it brings about results such as those of a *tīrthaṅkara*, and the other is non-commendable because it brings about results such as those of a denizen of hell. This is because karma, which arises from commendable and non-commendable transformations of the self (*ātmapariṇāma*), brings about results to be experienced as pleasure and pain. (7) Nirjarā is the cause for the wearing away of karma associated with the self; it consists of twelve kinds of austerity (*tapas*).

And that [nirjarā] is supreme when it takes the form of pure meditation (*śukladhyāna*), according to the scriptural statement: "There is nirjarā through austerity" (*Tattvārtha Sūtra* 9.3); for meditation is itself a form of internal austerity. (8)

Liberation (*mokṣa*) is the abiding of the self—whose all bonds have been completely severed and who has attained the nature of a Jina—at the end of the world (*lokānta*); for there is the statement: "Liberation is the dissociation from bondage. (9) These nine numbered principles (*tattva*) are to be known in this system, the Jaina doctrine. (93) Now, the author of the treatise himself explains the principles in sequence; therein, according to the maxim that "explanation follows the enumeration," he first states the principle of the living being (*jīva-tattva*):
"In that regard, [the soul] is distinct-and-non-distinct from attributes such as knowledge, and it possesses motion..."
The agent of wholesome and unwholesome karma, and the one who is liberated from the fruit of karma. //85//

The soul (*jīva*) is characterized by consciousness (*caitanya*); that which is the opposite of this is declared to be the non-soul (*ajīva*). Merit (*puṇya*) consists of the *pudgala* particles of virtuous action. (Verse 49, a pair). Commentary: The word "therein" (*tatra*) has the sense of specification. Those internal and external modes (*paryāya*) belonging to the soul—namely, knowledge, perception, conduct, pleasure, pain, energy, the state of being capable of liberation (*bhavyatva*), existence (*sattva*), knowability (*prameyatva*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), the possession of vitalities (*prāṇa-dhāritva*), transformation into anger and so forth, the state of being in *saṃsāra*, the state of being a perfected one (*siddhatva*), and exclusion from other substances—and such qualities as these are called the attributes (*dharma*) of the soul, beginning with knowledge.
The soul (*jīva*) is neither different from those [qualities] nor non-different; rather, it is both different and non-different by virtue of being a distinct category (*jāty-antara*).

For if the soul were different from qualities such as cognition (*jñāna*), then there would be no appearance of non-difference such as "I know," "I see," "I am the knower," "I am the seer," "I am happy," or "I am capable"; yet this appearance of non-difference exists for all living beings. Likewise, if it were non-different, then the cognition of difference—"this is the substratum (*dharmin*); these are the qualities (*dharmas*)"—would not exist; yet that cognition does exist.

Alternatively, if there were non-difference [of the Self], there would be identity among all attributes such as knowledge and so forth, because they are non-different from the single soul. And in that case, there would be no mutual cognition of difference among the attributes such as knowledge, as in "I have knowledge" or "I have perception," and so on.
Yet such cognition does exist. Therefore, it must be admitted that the [Self] is both different and non-different from its attributes such as knowledge.

By this [verse], he refutes both the absolute distinction between the property and the property-possessor (*dharmin*) as maintained by the Vaiśeṣikas and others, and the absolute non-distinction accepted by the Buddhists; for even the Buddhist accepts the self (*ātman*), in the form of a succession of moments of consciousness, as the property-possessor.
(ñ95) Likewise, "transformation" (*vivṛtti*) is various modes of existence, the following after other states such as human or celestial; that which possesses this is "possessed of transformation.

By this, he sets aside the Cārvākas, who are in disagreement regarding a self that migrates to another existence, as well as the Naiyāyikas and others, who maintain a self that is eternally immutable.

Likewise, he performs auspicious and inauspicious actions; thus, he is the doer of auspicious and inauspicious karma. Likewise, he is the direct experiencer (*sākṣād-bhoktā*) of the fruit—such as pleasure and so forth—of the karma performed by himself.

The particle *ca* (and) serves to aggregate the qualifiers. By these two qualifiers, there is the refutation of the Sāṃkhyas, who [erroneously] conceive of the self (*ātman*) as a non-doer through figurative usage (*upacarita-vṛtti*) and as an experiencer.

Furthermore, he is characterized by consciousness (*caitanya-lakṣaṇa*), meaning his defining characteristic or essential nature (*svarūpa*) consists of the functional application (*upayoga*) that is either with form (*sākāra*) or without form (*nirākāra*).

By this, the self (ātman) accepted by the Naiyāyikas and others, which is insentient by nature, is excluded. This should also be connected to the statement: "The living being (jīva) characterized in such a way has been thus described."

The Cārvākas argue as follows: "In this world, it is only the elements themselves, transformed into the shape of the body and serving as the cause of consciousness, that are perceived; there is no self whatsoever—possessing the characteristics previously described—that departs to another existence distinct from them, because there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for its existence.
For instance, regarding the existence of a self distinct from the elements, would a valid means of knowledge such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) operate, or would it be inference (*anumāna*)?"

Nor should it be asserted that in the cognition "I know the jar," the self appears as distinct from the elements by virtue of being the agent of knowledge; for that [cognition] is properly understood to have the body as its object, just like [the cognitions] "I am fat" or "I am thin.
Indeed, that cognition cannot have the self as its objective support, because attributes such as fatness and so forth are impossible in the self.
Likewise, even in the cognition "I know the jar," no self (*ātman*) postulated by you that is distinct from the body is ever perceived as its objective referent (*ālambana*), even in a dream.
Even if one were to postulate such an unperceived entity, it would result in the fault of conceptual over-extension (*kalpanā-gaurava*) and the absence of a fixed determination of specific objects.

Nor should it be said that the cognition "I" is untenable for the body, which is insentient by nature, like a jar or other objects; for the body is endowed with sentience through its connection with consciousness (*cetanā*).

Nor should it be said that this consciousness has the *jīva* as its agent; for since such a [jīva] is not perceived, its agency is untenable, as it would lead to the absurd consequence that even things like sky-flowers could possess it.

Therefore, because it is well-established, it is logical that the body alone is the agent with respect to consciousness. This is also because consciousness conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the body.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: Whatever indeed follows the positive and negative concomitance of something is the effect of that thing, just as a jar is the effect of a lump of clay; and consciousness follows the positive and negative concomitance of the body; therefore, the body is its agent.
For everywhere, the relationship of cause and effect is to be understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
And these two are present here: because consciousness is perceived when the body exists, and it is not perceived when it does not exist.

Nor should it be argued that its conformity to the positive and negative concomitance of the body is unestablished, because consciousness is not perceived in a dead body; for in the state of death, due to the absence of air and fire, the body itself ceases to exist, since the body is established as being nothing other than a specific conjunction of the elements.
Furthermore, it is not logical that consciousness arises from the mere form of the body, for otherwise it would follow that consciousness would arise even in painted horses and the like.

Therefore, it is established that consciousness is indeed an effect of the body. Consequently, it is established that the notion of "I" arises only with respect to the body when it is conjoined with consciousness. Thus, the self is not an object of perception; therefore, it simply does not exist. The formal argument here is as follows: the self does not exist, because it is absolutely imperceptible; whatever is absolutely imperceptible does not exist, just like a flower in the sky.

Whatever exists is indeed apprehended by direct perception, as for example a jar. For although atoms are themselves imperceptible, they attain perceptibility when transformed into effects such as jars and the like. However, the self never at any time attains the state of being perceptible; therefore, the qualification "absolutely" (*atyanta*) is used here, so that there is no deviation [from the rule] due to the case of atoms.

Likewise, inference (anumāna) does not operate toward the existence of a self distinct from the elements, because it lacks the status of a valid means of cognition (pramāṇa); or, even if it were a valid means of cognition, the reason (hetu) would be "mistimed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa), since it is employed immediately after a formal argument for a thesis that has already been sublated by perception. For the thesis of a self distinct from the body is indeed sublated by perception itself.

Furthermore, inference is preceded by the recollection of the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*). For example: having previously perceived through direct perception the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), between fire and smoke—the mark and the possessor of the mark—in a kitchen or similar place; and subsequently, upon observing a column of smoke rising into the sky in some mountain valley or wilderness, one recollects the relationship previously grasped.

For example: "Wherever there is smoke, there I have seen fire, as in the kitchen and so forth; and here smoke is seen; therefore, fire must also be present here. In this way, through the perception of the mark (*liṅga*) and the recollection of its connection, the cognizer perceives the consumer of oblations (*huta-bhuja*, i.e., fire) there.

However, no such connection between any mark and the self (*ātman*), which is the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*), has been established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); for if that were the case, the cognition of the self would arise upon seeing that mark again, even for one who does not recall that connection.

Furthermore, if the relationship between the living being (*jīva*) and the body were established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then, because the living being would also be perceived directly, inference (*anumāna*) would be rendered useless; for that very reason, the living being is not established [by perception].

Nor should it be argued that the living being is established through inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa-anumāna*), as in the case of the sun’s motion—just as the sun possesses motion because its arrival at another location is observed, like Devadatta.

Indeed, in the case of Devadatta, who serves as the subject of the example, the prior arrival at another location is determined by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in a general sense; thus it is logical that the cognizer establishes the same for the sun as well.

However, in this case [of the soul], no reason whatsoever is perceived through direct perception that is invariably concomitant (*avinābhūta*) with the existence of the soul in any instance of an example. Therefore, its cognition cannot be achieved even through inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*).

Likewise, the self (*ātman*) is not established by means of scripture (*āgama*). For the authority of scripture consists in its being composed by a trustworthy person (*āpta*) whose words are non-contradictory. Yet, we do not perceive any such trustworthy person whose self is perceptible, from whom [the scripture] could have originated. And since we do not perceive such a person, how could we deceive ourselves? Furthermore, all scriptures describe [their respective objects] without mutual contradiction.

Consequently, because of the doubt as to what is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and what is not, the authority of scripture (*āgama*) is indeed consumed by the blazing flames of a forest fire of uncertainty. Therefore, the self is not established even through the authority of scripture. Likewise, the self is not an object of comparison (*upameya*) for the means of knowledge known as comparison (*upamāna*). For instance, in cases such as "as is a cow, so is a gavaya," similarity produces a cognition regarding an object that is present before one.
However, in this case, there is no object whatsoever in the three worlds similar to the self, by the perception of which we might understand the self.

[Objection: But surely time, space, direction, and so forth exist as entities equal to the individual soul (jīva). [Response: No; for these too are subjects of dispute and are thus subject to the same refutation. §104:

Likewise, the self (ātman) cannot be established through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti). For there is no perceived or heard object whatsoever that would not be possible without the self, by the force of which we might establish it.

§105: Therefore, since it transcends the scope of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that apprehends existing things, and is instead made the object of the means of cognition called "the absence of any proof establishing it," it is established that the individual soul is indeed negated.

To this, the following reply is given: As for what was stated—that "here, only the primary elements (bhūtas) transformed into the form of the body are perceived, and not a self distinct from them, because there is a lack of evidence for its existence," and so forth—that is an unexamined assertion; for there does exist direct perception as proof of its existence.

To explain: a self-evident cognition arises within every living being, which is experienced as manifesting a distinction between the object of knowledge, the knower, and the act of knowing, such that one thinks, "I experience pleasure."
Nor is this [cognition] false, because there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*). Nor is it doubtful, because there is no contact with both extremes [of existence and non-existence].

Nor is it logical that such a [cognition] should lack an objective support (*anālambanatva*), for that would entail the consequence that even cognitions of form (*rūpa*) and so forth lack an objective support.
Nor does it have the body as its objective support, because it arises through the operation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) independently of the external organs.
Indeed, the body is not cognizable as the object of the notion "I" in this manner, because it is an object of the external senses.

Therefore, one must admit some conscious entity distinct from the body that serves as its objective support, since it alone is logically established as the knower. And that is precisely the *jīva*. Thus, the self (*ātman*), which is characterized by being directly perceived through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*), is proven.

Likewise, that which is also illogical—namely, the claim that "the notion of 'I' belongs to the body alone because the body possesses consciousness through its connection with consciousness," and so forth—is merely empty chatter. For even when there is a connection with consciousness, it is logical that the production of the notion of "I" occurs only for that which is itself conscious; it does not occur for that which is unconscious. Just as it is never observed that a jar—which is by nature non-luminous—becomes a source of illumination even when connected with the light of thousands of lamps, whereas it is the lamp itself that is the illuminator.

Thus, even in connection with volition (*cetanā*), the capacity for knowing belongs not to the body itself—which is inherently insentient—but rather to the self alone; and it is of that [self] alone that the notion of "I" arises.

Even the cognition that manifests as "I am fat," "I am thin," and so forth, is merely figurative (*aupacārika*), arising with respect to the body because it serves the self's interests—just like the cognition "this is indeed I" directed toward a servant who is extremely beneficial.

Furthermore, as for what was asserted by the proponent—that "the agency regarding consciousness belongs to the body alone"—that too is merely the composition of a madman's words; for there is no positive or negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) between consciousness and the body. Indeed, in those who are intoxicated, unconscious, or asleep, such consciousness is not observed despite the presence of a body of that same kind.
Moreover, it is seen that some with very emaciated bodies possess an excellence of consciousness, while others with large bodies possess its deficiency.
Therefore, consciousness does not conform to the positive and negative concomitance of those [elements]; hence, it is not their effect.

Furthermore, we do not perceive any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the claim that consciousness is an effect of the elements. To explain: first of all, there is no direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because perception does not operate upon objects that transcend the senses.

For neither consciousness as already arisen nor as yet unarisen enters the scope of perceptual activity; since perception consists in the grasping of objects suitable to its own nature and present before it, and consciousness, being immaterial, is unsuitable for such [perception].

Nor is it possible to perceive directly that the elements have the self as their effect, in the form "I am the effect of the elements"; for the relationship between cause and effect is to be understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Furthermore, no persisting entity (*anvayin*) distinct from the consciousness of the elements is admitted as the knower of the positive and negative concomitance of those two, because that would entail the proof of the existence of a self (*ātman*).

Likewise, consciousness's being an effect of the elements is not perceived even by inference, because that [inference] is not accepted; for there is the statement: "Perception alone is the single means of valid cognition, and no other.
Even if it were accepted, the establishment of the intended object through that [inference] would not be achieved.

[Objection: "Surely consciousness arises from the elements that have transformed into the form of an effect, because consciousness exists only when those [elements] exist—just as the power of intoxication [arises] from the ingredients of liquor. Thus, through such inference, consciousness indeed exists and the fact that it is an effect of the elements is established. [Response: This is not so; for the reason "because [consciousness] exists only when those [elements] exist" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since even when those [elements] are present in the state of death, consciousness is absent.

It might be argued as follows: consciousness is indeed produced from the collection of the four elements characterized by earth, water, fire, and air; and since there is no air in a dead body, the absence of consciousness there is due to the absence of that [air], so there is no deviation [from the rule] by that case. To this it is replied: when there is a cavity, the presence of air there is all the more likely.

Furthermore, if consciousness were absent there due to a deficiency of air, then consciousness would be perceived there once the air had been restored by means of enemas (*basti*) and other treatments; yet, even when the air has been restored there, consciousness is not perceived.

If it is argued that consciousness is absent there because of the absence of the air characterized as *prāṇa* (inhalation) and *apāna* (exhalation), we say no; since consciousness does not follow the presence or absence of *prāṇa* and *apāna* through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), these airs are not the cause of consciousness.

Since, even when there is the occurrence of extremely long inhalations and exhalations during the state of death and so forth, an accumulation of consciousness reaching its highest excellence is observed in some yogi whose prāṇa and apāna have been suppressed;
if it is argued that there is no consciousness in the state of death due to the absence of heat (*tejas*), then why is consciousness not perceived once heat has been introduced there?

Furthermore: if it is maintained that consciousness is absent in the state of death due to the absence of air and fire, then how is there consciousness in the case of worms and other creatures that arise some time after death in a corpse? Therefore, this [objection] is trivial.

Furthermore, consciousness is not caused by the elements alone. If that were the case, since consciousness would have as its inherent nature being produced from the elements alone, and since those elements would also have as their inherent nature the production of that [consciousness], there would always and everywhere—in jars and so forth—be the manifestation of consciousness, just as it is in persons and the like, because the causal conditions would be no different. And thus, there would be no distinction between a jar and a person.

If it is argued that there is no room for the previously mentioned fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) because of the statement, "Consciousness is perceived from the elements which possess the transformation into the form of a body and the appropriation of inhalation and exhalation," that is not so; for in your view, the very transformation into the form of a body is untenable.

To explain: is that transformation into the form of a body caused solely by the elements such as earth and so forth, or is it caused by some other entity, or is it causeless? These are the three possible alternatives.

In this regard, the first position cannot be accepted; for since the existence of earth and so forth is present everywhere, it would follow that there would be a transformation into the form of a body everywhere as well.

If it is argued that, due to the deficiency of auxiliary causes for the existence of such things as the probandum (*sādhya*) and so forth, that [property] does not necessarily follow everywhere, we say no; because even that state of being similar and so on is not caused by some other entity, for that would entail the consequence of its becoming a different reality (*tattvāntara*). Rather, it is caused merely by the existence of earth and the other elements. Therefore, since that too would result in its presence everywhere without distinction, how could there be a deficiency of auxiliary causes?
Furthermore, the position that it is caused by another entity is also untenable; for if that were accepted, it would entail the proof of a living soul (*jīva*).

If, on the other hand, it were causeless, then there would follow the undesirable consequence that entities must exist eternally or not exist at all, according to the statement: "Because they do not depend on anything else, a cause, there would be either eternal existence or non-existence" (Pravāraṇa 3.34). Therefore, in your view, the transformation into the form of a body is not tenable. In the absence of that [transformation], the possession of inhalation and exhalation by these elements is utterly discarded. Thus, consciousness is not an effect of the elements; consequently, it must be accepted that sentience is indeed an attribute of the living being (*jīva*).

Furthermore: because its qualities are perceptible, the self (*ātman*) is also indeed perceptible. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: the self is perceptible, because specific cognitions which are its qualities—such as memory, inquiry, desire to act, desire to go, doubt, and so forth—are perceptible through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). In this world, it is observed that whatever has perceptible qualities is itself perceptible, just like a jar. And the living being (*jīva*) possesses perceptible qualities; therefore, it is perceptible.

Here the opponent says: "This reason is inconclusive (anaikāntika); for sound, which is a quality of space (ākāśaguṇa), is perceptible, whereas space itself is not. This is incorrect, because sound is not a quality of space, but rather a quality of the person (pudgalaguṇa), since it is perceptible by the senses, like color and so forth. This will be established in the investigation of the person (pudgalavicāra). Regarding this, he says: "Surely, since qualities are perceptible, the possessor of qualities (guṇin) must also be perceptible, because [the quality] is non-different from it."

But rather, it is in the body alone that qualities such as cognition are perceived; therefore, it is logical that the body itself is their possessor (*guṇin*), just as a jar is the possessor of color and other qualities.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: cognition and the rest are indeed qualities of the body, because they are perceived in that very [body], just like whiteness, leanness, or stoutness.

To this it is replied: This fallacious thesis (*pakṣābhāsa*) is sublated by a counter-inference (*pratyanumāna*). And that [inference] is as follows: "The qualities of the body, such as cognition and so forth, do not belong to it, because it is corporeal or because it is visible, like a jar. Therefore, since the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*) is established through the perceptibility of its qualities, the living self (*jīva*) is also perceptible.

Consequently, for one who denies the self—which is perceptible and grasped by the notion of "I"—this is a fallacious thesis known as "contradicted by perception" (*pratyakṣaviruddha*), just like the claim that "sound is inaudible" and so forth.

Furthermore, because there exists the inference for the existence of the self that will be stated later, this [denial] is also contradicted by inference, just like the claim that "sound is eternal" and so forth. Moreover, for one who denies the self—which is well-known even to children, cowherds, and women—there is contradiction with the world, just like saying "the sun, the maker of light, does not exist. And for one who says "I am not I," there is contradiction with one's own words, just like saying "my mother is barren."

Thus, by the reasoning already established, it is settled that the reason—"because the self is not absolutely imperceptible, since it is directly perceived through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*)"—is also unestablished (*asiddha*).

Likewise, the self is also accessible through inference. These [inferences] are as follows: 1. The living body is presided over by one possessing effort (*prayatnavat*), because it is the locus of actions that conform to will, like a chariot.
2. The auditory organ and the others are instruments employed by an agent, because they are instruments (*karaṇa*), like an axe or similar tools.

The body has a creator, because it possesses a beginning and a specific form, like a jar. Furthermore, that which lacks a creator does not possess both a beginning and a specific form, as is the case with the transformations of clouds.

That which is the creator of one's own body is the *jīva*. [Objection: Since even Mount Meru and other such things have a specific form, yet they have no creator, the reason would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) by those examples; therefore, the qualification "having a beginning" (*ādimattva*) must be understood in order to exclude them.

[Objection: Likewise, there exists a controller of the sense organs, because they are instruments, just as a potter is the controller of the stick, wheel, and so forth. Furthermore, the body possesses an existing enjoyer, because it is an object of enjoyment, like food. And he who is the enjoyer is the *jīva*.

[Reply: Now, these reasons are indeed contradictory (*viruddha*), because they establish what is contrary to the point to be proven (*sādhyaviruddha*). For instance, potters and the like, who are the agents of jars and other such things, are observed to be corporeal and of an impermanent nature.
Therefore, the *jīva* would be established as being exactly of that same kind. Yet, the *jīva* is intended to be the opposite of this.

If it is argued that the reasons (hetus) are contradictory because they prove something contrary to the probandum (*sādhyaviruddha*), we say no; for since the transmigrating soul (*jīva*) possesses a body due to being enveloped by the eight types of karmic matter (*karmapudgala*), it is in some sense corporeal (*mūrta*), and thus this fault does not apply.

Likewise, the cognition of form and so forth must be dependent on something, because it is a quality (*guṇatva*), just like color and so forth. Similarly, cognition, pleasure, and the rest must be preceded by a material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*), because they are effects (*kāryatva*), just like a pot and the like.

Nor should it be asserted that this is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because it is accepted that [the self] is dependent upon and has as its material cause (*upādāna*) the body; for the dependence upon and the being the material cause of the body have already been refuted previously.
Furthermore, this word "non-living" (*ajīva*) possesses a counter-correlate (*pratipakṣavat*); because there is a negation of a pure word that possesses etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*).

Wherever a negation of a pure word possessing etymological derivation is observed, that [negation] possesses a counter-correlate, just as "non-pot" (*aghaṭa*) possesses the pot as its counter-correlate.

For here, in the expression "non-pot" (*aghaṭa*), there is a negation of a word that is both pure and understood by those possessing linguistic proficiency. Therefore, there must necessarily be a counter-positive (*pratipakṣa*) characterized as a "pot. However, where there is no counter-positive—as in the case of the word "donkey's horn" (*kharaviṣāṇa*) or "Aḍittha"—there is no negation of a pure word understood by those possessing linguistic proficiency. In the case of "non-donkey's-horn" (*akharaviṣāṇam*), there is a negation of the impure compound word characterized as a "donkey's horn. Here, even though there is linguistic proficiency, because the word is not pure, there is no counter-example (*vipakṣa*).

However, in the case of [the name] "Ḍittha," because it lacks an etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), even though it is a pure word, there is no specific referent characterized as "Ḍittha" that exists as a counter-example like a living being.

(Ñ 126) Likewise, having established the self in one's own body through the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*), it is also established in another's body by means of inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa-anumāna*). That is to say:
there is a self in another's body as well, because engagement with what is desired and avoidance of what is undesired are observed, just as in one's own body.

Furthermore, engagement with and withdrawal from the desirable and undesirable are observed in another's body; therefore, that [body] possesses a self (*sātmaka*), because in the absence of a self, those two would not exist, just as in the case of a jar.
By this, the argument previously stated—that "the self is not established even by inference based on general observation" (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*)—and so forth, should be understood as refuted.
Likewise, this sound which negates the living being, namely "there is no soul," is necessarily concomitant with the existence of a soul, because it is a word of negation.

Just as the statement "there is no jar here" is invariably concomitant with the existence of a jar elsewhere, so too is the formal argument (*prayoga*) here: that which is negated in this context must exist somewhere else, just like a jar or similar objects. And since you negate [the self] by saying "the soul does not exist," it must therefore exist. Furthermore, the negation of that which is absolutely non-existent is never observed, such as a sixth element beyond the five elements.

If it is argued that this reason is inconclusive because negation is observed even for non-existent things such as a donkey’s horn, we say no; for in this context, whatever object is negated, it is only the fourfold relation—characterized by conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), universal (*sāmānya*), and particular (*viśeṣa*)—that is negated with respect to the intended location, provided that the object exists elsewhere.
