It is not, however, its absolute non-existence that is being established.

Just as in expressions such as "Devadatta is not in the house," it is merely the conjunction of Devadatta and the house—which both exist—that is negated, and not their existence altogether; likewise, in expressions such as "the horn of a donkey does not exist," it is merely the inherence of the donkey's horn—which exists [in its material cause]—that is refuted. Similarly, in expressions such as "there is no other moon," because the existing moon itself is negated as being "other," it is merely the universal "moon-ness" that is negated, and not the total non-existence of the moon.

Just as in such cases as "there are no pearls the size of a jar," it is only the specific quality of being the size of a jar that is denied of the pearls, and not their non-existence that is proclaimed;

likewise, here too in the statement "the self does not exist," you must deny only the mere conjunction of an existing self with some place or something else—just as one says, "the self does not exist in this body," and so forth—but not the absolute non-existence of the self.
Here someone says: "But surely, if that which is negated exists, then let my lordship over the three worlds also exist, since it is being negated by you and others.
Likewise, there must also be a fifth mode of negation for the four [modes] beginning with conjunction and so forth, because even that is being negated by you yourself."

That is incorrect. What is being negated for you is merely the specific quality of being the lord of the three worlds—just as the size of a jar is negated for liberated beings—but not lordship in every respect, since you yourself possess lordship over your own disciples and so forth.

Likewise, regarding the negation, it is only its qualification by the number five that is being excluded as non-existent; it is not the total absence of negation, because it exists as qualified by the number four.

[Objection: But surely all of this is incoherent. For instance: first of all, the status of being the lord of the three worlds—which is already non-existent—is what is being negated; and even the fact that the negation itself is qualified by the number five is something non-existent that is being precluded.

Likewise, conjunction, inherence, universals, and particulars are also negated precisely because they are non-existent in the case of [the examples] "house," "Devadatta," "donkey's horn," and so forth. Therefore, how is it not the case that whatever is negated must necessarily exist?

To this it is replied: conjunctions and so forth belonging to Devadatta and others are negated only when they are non-existent in relation to the house and such; however, in relation to other objects, those [conjunctions] certainly do exist for them.
For instance, the conjunction of Devadatta with the house itself does not exist, yet he certainly exists in conjunction with other objects such as a grove.

Just as Devadatta has no connection with the house, whereas he certainly does have one with the bed and so forth; likewise, the horn has no inherence (*samavāya*) with the donkey, whereas it certainly exists in the cow and other such animals. Furthermore, the universal (*sāmānya*) does not exist in the moon itself because of the absence of a second moon, yet it certainly exists in other objects such as jars. Similarly, the status of being the Lord of the Three Worlds does not belong to you [the Buddha], whereas it certainly belongs to the Tīrthaṅkaras and others.

Even the qualification by the number five does not exist among the types of negations [in the case of absolute non-existence], whereas it certainly exists in cases such as the Unsurpassed Celestial Mansions (*anuttara-vimāna*). With this intention, we say that whatever is negated exists in a general sense. However, we do not assert that "whatever is negated here exists in that very place," for if that were so, there would be a logical inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*); thus, while there may be a negation of the existing soul (*jīva*) somewhere, it is not the case that it is negated everywhere.

Likewise, there exists a self (ātman) distinct from the body and the senses, because even when the senses have ceased [to function], there is the recollection of objects previously perceived by them; just as Devadatta, who perceives through five windows, remembers the objects perceived [through them]. Thus, it is established that the self is apprehended by inference.

For once its apprehensibility by inference is established, its apprehensibility by scripture, comparison, and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is also established by virtue of being included within that [category of inference].

Furthermore, as for what was stated, "Because of the absence of the five means of valid cognition," and so forth—that too is like the behavior of one intoxicated by liquor; for even in the case of the measurement of Mount Himavat and the like, or of Piśācas and the like, these exist despite the absence of the five means of valid cognition. Therefore, the claim that "whatever lacks the five means of valid cognition is necessarily non-existent" is inconclusive (anaikāntika). Thus, it is established that the Self is apprehended by perception and other means of valid cognition.

And that [self] possesses transmigration and goes to the next world. Regarding this, the following inference is established: the infant’s desire for the mother’s breast on the day of birth is preceded by a prior desire, because it is a desire, just like the desire for the breast on the second day and so forth.

This inference, by establishing that the initial desire for the breast is preceded by another desire, implies through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) the existence of a transmigrating soul (*jīva*) who goes to the next world; for there is no other desire in that [present] life [to have served as its cause]. Thus it is settled.

Likewise, the immutability (*kūṭasthanityatā*) of the self is also untenable; for if the self were to remain exactly as it was in its prior state even at the time of the arising of knowledge, then, just as before, how could it be the determiner of objects? This is because immutability consists in the non-deviation from a fixed nature. However, if there is the determination of objects, since the self undergoes transformation by becoming a knower where it was previously not a knower, whence can there be immutability?

Likewise, the agency asserted by the Sāṃkhyas is also untenable. To explain: the self is the agent because it is the enjoyer of the fruits of its own actions; for whoever is the enjoyer of the fruits of its own actions is also seen to be an agent, just as a farmer is.
Furthermore, the *puruṣa* postulated by the Sāṃkhyas is not a real entity because it lacks agency, like a flower in the sky.

Furthermore, the self is asserted to be the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*); does it perform the act of enjoying or not? If it performs it, then what fault has been committed by other [actions]? On the other hand, if it does not even perform the act of enjoying, then it must be considered how it can be called an "enjoyer. Here is the formal argument (*prayoga*) for this: the transmigrating self is not an enjoyer, because it is a non-agent (*akartṛ*), like a liberated self. Moreover, if one accepts that it is both a non-agent and an enjoyer, there would follow the faults of the destruction of what was done (*kṛtanāśa*) and the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*), and so forth.

An action performed by *prakṛti* would not be connected with its fruit, which results in the loss of what was done (*kṛtanāśa*). Furthermore, since that [action] was not performed by the self, yet it is connected with its fruit, this results in the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtāgama*); thus, the self must be accepted as the agent.

Likewise, the nature of the self as being insentient (*jaḍasvarūpatva*) is also untenable, because there exist inferential arguments that refute it. For instance: the self, whose nature is devoid of utility, cannot be the agent of the discernment of objects, because it is insentient, like space.

If it is argued that [the self] distinguishes [objects] because of the inherence (*samavāya*) of volition (*cetanā*), then, just as the self possesses the status of a knower due to the inherence of volition, so too would the pot possess the status of a knower; for inherence—being eternal, unitary, and all-pervading—is indistinguishable everywhere. Much could be said regarding this point, but it is not stated here for fear of making the work too voluminous.

Therefore, by those who accept that the self (*ātman*) is the delimiter of categories (*padārtha*), its nature as consciousness (*caitanya*) must also be admitted by the logic of "the rope around one's neck" (*gale pādikānyāya*). Thus it is established that the living being (*jīva*) is characterized by consciousness.
And the living being is of nine kinds, distinguished by earth, water, fire, air, plants, and those possessing two, three, four, or five sense organs.

[Objection: "Granted that earth and the other elements possess the status of living beings because they are endowed with the characteristics of a living being; however, how can their status as living beings be accepted, since no manifest sign of such a being is perceived? [Reply: This is true; even though no manifest sign of a living being is perceived in them, nevertheless, an unmanifest one is indeed clearly perceived.

Just as those who have fainted from drinking liquor mixed with *hṛtpūra* and other substances are designated as being "alive" by means of unmanifest signs even in the absence of manifest signs, so too the state of being "alive" should be designated for the earth and the other elements.

[Objection: But surely, in those who have fainted, breathing and so forth exist as unmanifest signs of consciousness (*cetanā*); however, in earth and the other [elements], there is no such sign of consciousness at all. [Reply: This is not so. First, regarding the body of earth, one must admit consciousness in salt, coral, stones, and the like—which remain in their own respective forms—because they possess the production of sprouts of a similar kind, just as in the case of trees (*vanaspati*), which are assumed to be conscious because they possess a conceivable single sign of consciousness despite having unmanifest consciousness.

The insentience of the tree (*vanaspati*) is clearly evident from its production of specific seasonal fruits, and this will be further established [later]. Therefore, it is established that the earth is endowed with consciousness (*sacitta*), because it possesses characteristics such as the utilization of the unmanifest (*avyakta*).

Now, one might object: "How can the earth consisting of coral, stone, and so forth—which is composed of *pudgala* as described—be sentient? This is not so; it is said in reply: Just as bone, which is inherent in the body, is observed to be both sentient and solid, so too is the body of the earth, which is inherent in the living soul (*jīva*).

Alternatively: Earth, water, fire, air, and plants possess living bodies (*jīva-śarīra*), because they are substances that are subject to being cut, pierced, lifted, enjoyed, smelled, tasted, and touched, like a collection [of parts] such as a dewlap and horns.

For it is impossible to deny that earth and the other elements are observed to be subject to cutting and so forth; nor is it being asserted here that earth and the others have living bodies as something undesired, since it is accepted that all *pudgala* substance constitutes a "substance-body" (*dravya-śarīra*).

The distinction lies in whether it is accompanied by a living soul (*jīva*) or not. Earth and other elements that have not been struck by weapons are sometimes conscious, because they are composite aggregates, like the aggregate of hands and feet. That very same [earth], however, is at times partially unconscious, because it has been struck by weapons, just like the hand or foot; yet it is not absolutely devoid of consciousness.

[Opponent: Now, if it is argued that the body of water is not a living being because it lacks the characteristics [of a living being], like a spring or the like—[we reply] this is not so, because the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*). For just as a body is seen to be possessed of moisture and consciousness when it has recently arisen in the state of the embryo (*kalala*), so too is the body of water; or just as the mere fluid within an egg, before its parts have developed and before the distinctions of the beak and so forth are manifest, is seen to be possessed of consciousness.

This very same analogy applies to living beings as well. And the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: water is endowed with consciousness, because it possesses fluidity while being unimpaired by weapons, like the *kalala* stage that constitutes the material cause of an elephant's body. By the inclusion of the qualification "unimpaired" in the reason (*hetu*), springs and the like are excluded. Similarly: water is possessed of a self (*sātmaka*), because its fluidity is unimpaired, like the *kalala* situated within an egg.
Or rather, this is the proof once it has been established that [water] possesses the nature of a body inhabited by a living being, just as in the previous case.

[Objection: Snow and the like possess consciousness in some instances, because they belong to the water-body (*apkāya*), just like other water. Likewise, in certain places, waters possess consciousness, because they arise naturally from excavated earth, just like frogs. Alternatively, waters originating in the atmosphere possess consciousness, because they fall after having spontaneously coalesced during transformations such as clouds, just like fish.

Likewise, during the cold season when intense cold falls, that warmth which is perceived in rivers and other bodies of water—whether it be slight, moderate, or great—is caused solely by living beings (*jīva*); it is like the slight, moderate, or greater warmth found in the human bodies of few, many, or very many people gathered together.

And the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: The sensation of warmth in waters during the cold season originates from a substance possessing the quality of warmth; because it is a sensation of warmth, just like the sensation of warmth in a human body.
Furthermore, this sensation of heat in water is not innate, because of the statement of the Vaiśeṣikas and others that "the touch of water is exclusively cold.

Likewise, during the cold season when the cold is intense, if one stands in the western direction at dawn looking toward a pond or similar body of water, a mass of vapor emerging from that water is seen; that too has living beings as its cause.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: At the time of cold, the presence of steam in waters arises from a substance possessing hot touch; because it is steam; like the steam from the body of a person sprinkled with cold water during the winter season. In both these arguments, that very substance which is the cause of the hot touch and the steam must be understood as the entity called the "Self" (*ātman*), endowed with a fiery body (*taijasa-śarīra*). This is because there is no other substance in the waters that could serve as the cause for the hot touch and the steam.

Nor can it be argued that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from the [invariable] nature and cause by the case of a cold season where one encounters the sensation of heat on a heap of refuse or a ground covered with debris, accompanied by perspiration emerging from the body; for even in those cases, it is admitted that the cause is the body of a living being or a corpse produced amidst such refuse.

If it is asked, "How can the bodies of the dead and the living serve as the cause for heat-tactile sensation and steam? it is said: just as when water is poured onto fragments of stone burnt by fire, heat-tactile sensation and steam arise even though the fire has been extinguished, so too is it here despite the presence of contact with cold. In this same way, in other cases as well, the cause of steam and heat-tactile sensation—whether sentient or insentient—should be stated according to what is possible.

In this very way, during the cold season, warmth is perceived near the slopes of mountains and beneath trees and such things; that too must be understood as being caused by the living soul (*jīva*), just like the bodily warmth of a human being. Likewise, during the summer season, because the fire in the form of a fiery body is diminished by external heat, the cool touch found in water and other substances must also be accepted as having its cause in the living soul, just like the cool touch of a human body. Therefore, by possessing such characteristics, the bodies of water are possessed of souls.

Just as at night the bodily transformation of a firefly, possessing a power produced by the activity of a living being, manifests clearly; so too, the specific powers of light and so forth in embers and the like are inferred to be manifested through the particular activity of a living being.
Or, just as the heat of a fever does not transcend the activity of a living being; this very same analogy applies to fiery creatures.

Furthermore, those suffering from fever are never found to be dead; thus, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the possession of consciousness by fire is to be known. And the formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: the transformation into light manifested in charcoal and the like has the conjunction with a self (*ātman*) as its cause; because it resides within a body, like the bodily transformation of a firefly.
Likewise, the heat of charcoal and the like is preceded by conjunction with a self; because it resides within a body, like the heat of a fever.
Nor is there an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) due to the sun and so forth, since the hot touch of all these is likewise preceded by conjunction with a self.

Likewise, fire is endowed with consciousness; for, like the human body, it is observed to undergo transformations such as growth through the assimilation of suitable fuel. By such characteristics, beings of fiery nature are to be identified.

Just as, by the power of a god’s own capacity or by means of ointments, sciences, and mantras for humans, a body that has become invisible is determined to exist and to possess consciousness even though it is not perceived by the eye; so too, in the case of wind, there is no form graspable by the eye because of its subtle transformation, like an atom, or like the fire within a piece of stone burnt by fire which is devoid of thought.

And the formal argument is this: wind possesses consciousness, because it possesses a lateral movement that is not directed by another and is not restricted to a single direction, just like cows, horses, and the like.

There is no deviation from the rule regarding atoms (*paramāṇu*), because their movement is restricted to horizontal [directions] and because they are not subject to the aforementioned specific qualification; for it is stated that "the soul (*jīva*) and matter (*pudgala*) move along a linear path (*anuśreṇi*)," as atoms possess restricted motion. In this same way, the wind, when not struck by weapons, should be understood as possessing consciousness (*cetana*). These bodies of various kinds of plants, such as the *bakula*, *aśoka*, and *campaka*, do not possess properties identical to those of human bodies without the activity of a living soul (*jīva*).

For instance: just as a human body is perceived to be presided over by consciousness and to possess manifest consciousness because it undergoes specific transformations through the stages of childhood, youth, adulthood, and old age, so too is this body of a tree; since a *ketaka* tree, once born, becomes a child, a youth, and an adult; therefore, due to its similarity to a human body, the tree is endowed with consciousness.

Likewise, just as this human body grows in a regular manner through specific successive stages such as infancy, childhood, youth, and so forth; so too does this body of a plant grow in a regular manner through specific stages such as the sprout, the tender leaf, the branch, the sub-branch, and so on.

Likewise: just as the human body is accompanied by consciousness, so too is the body of a plant; for that state [of consciousness] exists in the *śamī*, *prapunnāṭa*, *siddhasāraka*, *sundaka*, *babbūla*, *agastya*, *āmalakī*, *kaḍī* (*imalī*, the "tamarind tree"), and others, due to their sleep and awakening.

Likewise, there is the enveloping of a heap of wealth buried underground by its own sprouting. Similarly, there is the emergence of sprouts from the *vaṭa*, *pippala*, *nimba*, and other trees upon contact with the sound of rain clouds in the monsoon and the cool breeze.
Likewise, from the gentle kicking of the feet—adorned with anklets—of an intoxicated woman, there is the bursting forth of sprouts and flowers on the *aśoka* tree;
likewise, from the embrace of a young woman, [the blossoming] of the *panasa* (jackfruit tree); likewise, from the sprinkling of mouthfuls of fragrant wine, [the flowering] of the *bakula*;

likewise, from the sprinkling of fragrant, pure water, [the blooming] of the *campaka*; likewise, from a sidelong glance, [the flowering] of the *tikalā*; and likewise, from the utterance of the fifth musical note (*pañcama-svara*), there is the scattering of flowers from the *śirīṣa* and the *virahaka*.
Likewise, there is the blossoming of lotuses and other flowers at dawn; of *ghoṣātaka* and other flowers at twilight; and of night-lotuses (*kumuda*) and others at the rising of the moon.

Similarly, when rain falls from nearby clouds, there is the oozing of sap from the *śamī* tree. Likewise, there is the climbing of creepers toward their supports, such as trees. Furthermore, in the case of the sensitive plant (*lajjālū*) and others, a clearly manifest action is perceived through the contraction of leaves upon contact with hands and the like.

Alternatively, it is only during specific seasons that all trees bear fruit; and this network of activities related to the tree mentioned immediately above would not be possible without consciousness. Therefore, it is established that the tree possesses sentience.
Likewise, just as a human body withers when its hands or other limbs are severed, so too a tree’s body is observed to undergo dessication when its shoots, fruits, flowers, and so forth are cut away.

Nor is this property [of taking food] characteristic of insentient things. Thus, just as a human body is a consumer of food through the ingestion of breast milk, condiments, boiled rice, and so forth, so too is the body of a plant a consumer of food through the ingestion of earth, water, and so forth. And this quality of being a consumer of food is not observed in insentient things. Therefore, by virtue of that state, [plants] possess sentience.

Likewise, just as the human body has a fixed lifespan, so too does the body of a tree; for its maximum lifespan is ten thousand years. Similarly, just as the human body is subject to increase and decrease through the acquisition of desirable or undesirable food and other such things, so too is the body of a tree.

Likewise, just as in the case of a human body there occurs, due to contact with various diseases, paleness from illness, enlargement of the abdomen, swelling, emaciation, the sinking and drooping of the fingers and nose, and so forth; similarly, in the case of the body of a plant, there occurs, due to such diseases, the alteration and falling away of flowers, fruits, leaves, bark, and so on.

Likewise, just as in the case of a human body there occurs, through the application of medicine, growth, decline, the healing of wounds, and the restoration of what was broken; so it is also for the body of a plant.

Likewise, just as the human body experiences an increase in specific luster, sapidity, strength, and so forth through the application of elixirs (*rasāyana*), oils, and the like; similarly, the body of a plant also possesses specific sapidity, potency, and unctuousness (*snigdhatva*) due to the sprinkling of specific desirable rain, water, and so on. Likewise, just as the birth of a son or other offspring occurs from the fulfillment of such pregnancy-longings (*dauhṛda*) in the female body, so too does the production of fruit and the like occur from the fulfillment of those [longings] in the body of a plant, and so forth. Furthermore, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: plants possess consciousness.

[The body] is characterized by various specific activities such as (1) the states of childhood, desire, and old age; (2) specific growth; (3) expansion and contraction caused by sleep, waking, touch, and so forth; (4) the withering of severed limbs; (5) the intake of food from specific locations; (6) a lifespan as declared in the *Āyurveda*; (7) increase and decrease caused by desirable and undesirable food and other factors; (8) the increase and decrease brought about by the application of specific medicines for those respective diseases mentioned in the *Āyurveda*; and (9) the healing of wounds and the restoration of what was broken or bent.

Because it would otherwise be impossible for [the tree] to possess a body characterized by such specific qualities as taste, potency (*vīrya*), oiliness (*snigdhatva*), dryness (*rūkṣatva*), and the presence of specific cravings (*dauhṛda*) and so forth, just like the body of a particular woman.

Alternatively, these reasons should each be employed together with the subject (*pakṣa*); or rather, this is the formulated syllogism (*prayoga*) which summarizes the stated meaning: "Plants are sentient, because the combined presence of birth, old age, death, disease, and so forth exists in them, just like a woman."

154. Here, because birth and the other states are taken collectively, and because we observe such designations as "that curd has been produced," no deviation [from the rule] can be alleged on the basis of insentient things like curd.

155. Thus, the sentience of earth and the other elements is established; or alternatively, the fact that all things possess a self (sātmakatva) is established through the word of a reliable authority (āptavacana).

Furthermore, regarding those with two sense-faculties and so forth—such as worms, ants, bees, humans, and animals that move in water, on land, or in the air—there is no disagreement among anyone concerning their possession of a self (*sātmakatva*). However, for those who still dispute this point, the following is stated:

The self is distinct from the sense-faculties, because even when the sense-faculties have ceased, there is recollection of objects perceived by them. The formal argument here is as follows: in this world, that which is the recollector of objects perceived by something even after that thing has ceased is distinct from it; for example, Devadatta [is distinct] from the windows even after the windows have ceased, since he recollects the objects perceived through them.
This self likewise recollects at times of blindness, deafness, and so forth, the objects perceived by the sense-faculties; therefore, it is a different entity from them.
Alternatively, the self is distinct from the sense organs, because even when the sense organs are active, there are occasions when one is in a state of non-attention and does not perceive objects.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: the self is distinct from the sense organs, because even when they are functioning, there is no perception of objects.

In this world, whatever person does not perceive objects that are otherwise perceptible even while those [senses] are functioning, is seen to be distinct from them; for example, Devadatta, who, though the window is open, does not see because he is not attending due to being distracted by something else, is distinct from those [windows].

Alternatively, this is an inference: the living soul (jīva) exists as distinct from the sense organs, because one perceives a transformation through another. In this world, whoever perceives a transformation through another is seen to be distinct from that [other]; just as Devadatta, having observed the beautiful [sight] above Pravaraprasāda through the eastern window, demonstrates a transformation such as the touching of the breasts with his hand to her who has arrived through the other window.

Likewise, this self, upon seeing someone eating *āmlīkā* (tamarind) with the eye, undergoes transformations such as a "leap" (*hṛllāsa*) and the flow of saliva through the sense of taste. Therefore, it is distinct from those two.

Alternatively, the self is distinct from the senses because one [sense] perceives and another grasps; for in this world, whoever perceives a jar or the like with one [sense] and grasps it with another is seen to be distinct from those two—just as Devadatta, who perceives a jar through the eastern window and grasps it through the western window, is distinct from those two.
Furthermore, the living being (*jīva*) grasps with its hand or other limbs an object such as a jar that has been perceived by the eye; therefore, [the self] is distinct from those two.

In this regard, many inferences and numerous logical arguments should be formulated by oneself based on the *Viśeṣāvaśyaka-ṭīkā* and other sources. Thus, the first principle, the *jīva-tattva*, has been explained in detail.
Now, desiring to explain the second principle, the *ajīva-tattva*, he says: "That which is the opposite of this," and so forth.

Furthermore, that which possesses characteristics contrary to these is declared to be the non-living (*ajīva*). In the reading "that which possesses the opposite of this," however, that which possesses the opposite—that is, otherness—compared to that living being (*jīva*) is declared to be the non-living.

The meaning is that the non-living is distinct from and yet not different from qualities such as ignorance and those such as form, taste, smell, and touch; it undergoes various states of existence such as human or celestial; it is not the agent of *jñānāvaraṇa* and other karmas, nor the enjoyer of their fruit, and its nature is insentient (*jaḍa*).

And that [space] is said to be of five kinds, distinguished by dharma, adharma, ether (ākāśa), time (kāla), and person (pudgala). Among these, *dharma* is all-pervading (*lokavyāpī*), eternal (*nitya*), stable (*avasthita*), formless (*arūpī*), a substance (*dravya*), an existent aggregate (*astikāya*), consisting of innumerable spatial points (*asaṃkhyapradeśa*), and it acts as an auxiliary for motion (*gaty-upagraha-kārī*). In this context, by the word "eternal" (*nitya*), it is declared not to deviate from its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). By the word "stable" (*avasthita*), it is revealed as being neither deficient nor excessive. Furthermore, being neither deficient nor excessive, and because it is without beginning or end, it does not deviate from its independence. Likewise, by the exclusion of form (*arūpi-prahaṇāt*), it is called immaterial (*amūrta*).

And that which is formless (*amūrta*) is said to exist externally apart from the transformations of color, taste, smell, and touch. Indeed, touch and the other qualities do not deviate from form, because they are concomitant.
For wherever there is a transformation of color, there must also be touch, taste, and smell; therefore, this quartet is concomitant and exists even in the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*).

Likewise, because it is grasped as a substance (*dravya*), it is declared to possess qualities (*guṇa*) and modes (*paryāya*), according to the statement: "Substance possesses qualities and modes" (Tattvārtha Sūtra 5.38).
ñ165: *Tathāstayaḥ* (the existents): "pradeśāḥ" means excellent spaces; "pradeśāḥ" refers to indivisible portions (*nirvibhāgāni khaṇḍāni*). Their "kāya" is said to be their collection (*samudāya*).

ñ166: By the expressions "pervading the world" (*lokavyāpī*) and "having innumerable portions" (*asaṃkhyapradeśa*), that which possesses as many portions as there are portions of the space of the world (*lokākāśa*) is indicated. Likewise, it means that it acts as an auxiliary cause (*apekṣā-kāraṇa*) for living beings (*jīva*) and matter (*pudgala*) that have themselves undergone the transformation of motion (*gati-pariṇata*).

Indeed, the cause is said to be threefold: for example, clay is the transformative cause (*pariṇāmi-kāraṇa*) of a jar; the staff and so forth, as well as the supporting factors, are the instrumental causes (*nimitta-kāraṇa*); and the potter is the productive cause (*nirvartaka-kāraṇa*). As it has been said:
"The cause is held to be threefold: the productive, the instrumental, and the transformative.
For a jar, the potter is the supporter, and the clay is [the transformative cause]—thus they are equal in number. (Verse 1)

The efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) is twofold: the efficient cause and the dependent cause (*apekṣā-kāraṇa*). Those things such as sticks, in which there is both an applied (*prāyogikī*) and a natural (*vaisrasikī*) action, are efficient causes. However, those substances such as the category of merit (*dharma-astikāya*) and so forth, in which there is only a natural action, are called dependent causes in order to indicate their status as specific causes, even though they are also efficient causes.

Considering that it fosters the transformation into activities such as motion in souls and other substances by depending upon the transformation into activity inherent in substances such as *dharma*, *dharma* is therefore the auxiliary cause (*apekṣā-kāraṇa*) in this regard.

Likewise, *adharma*—though characterized by all the same specific attributes such as pervading the world and so forth—should be understood as being without distinction from *dharma*; however, it should be stated that its function is to assist in stability (*sthiti-upagraha*), serving as the auxiliary cause for the stability of souls and matter that have themselves undergone the transformation of stability.

In this way, space (*ākāśa*) also exists as a substance (*dravya*) that pervades the world and the non-world (*lokāloka*), consisting of infinite points (*anantapradeśa*), eternal, stable, and formless (*arūpi*). It should be described as having the function of providing accommodation (*avagāha*). The only difference is that it pervades both the world and the non-world. Regarding this, some teachers do not accept time (*kāla*) as a substance; rather, they consider it to be merely a mode (*paryāya*) of substances such as *dharma* and so forth. According to their view, the world (*loka*) consists of the five bodies (*pañcāstikāya*) known as *dharma*, *adharma*, *ākāśa*, *pudgala*, and *jīva*.

However, for those who maintain that time (*kāla*) is a substance, these six substances constitute the world (*loka*), because the five substances beginning with *dharma* and the substance of time exist therein. Space (*ākāśa*) is a single substance where that [world] is located; it is the pervader of both the world and the non-world (*aloka*) and is the benefactor of accommodation (*avagāha*). Thus, it provides accommodation to those substances that are inherently capable of being accommodated; it does not, however, forcibly cause non-accommodating entities such as *pudgala* to be accommodated.

Therefore, space is the instrumental cause for [beings] like sea-monsters, just as water is for them. If it is asked how the non-world-space (*alokākāśa*) can be helpful for immersion (*avagāha*), since it is not something that can be immersed in, it is said in reply: That [non-world-space] would indeed function by providing room if the two astikāyas of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), which are the causes of motion and stability, were present there; however, those two do not exist there. And because of their absence, the quality of immersion (*avagāhana-guṇa*), even though it exists [in the non-world-space], is not manifested—so it is said. Thus ends the section on non-world-space.

Time (kāla) exists within the two and a half continents, is extremely subtle, partless, and singular; it is called a *samaya*. It is not, however, designated as an *astikāya* (an ontological category), because that which consists of a single *samaya* lacks spatial divisions (*niḥpradeśatva*). And it has been said:
"Therefore, there exists here a single time-unit (*samaya*) pervading the human world.
Because of its oneness, it is not a *kāya*; for a *kāya* is indeed a collection. (Verse 1)

And according to the view of one school, that [substance] is designated as a *dravya* (substance) because it is manifested by activities such as the rising and setting of the sun, planets, and constellations.

It consists of both substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*), existing as a single moment. While it possesses the nature of arising and passing away with every mode, it is—by way of its substantial aspect—inseparable from its own nature, characterized by sequential and non-sequential manifestation, and possesses an infinite number and magnitude that are beginningless and endless. For this very reason, it is said to be eternal by virtue of its substantial self, pervading the flow of its own modes.

Even in the states of past, future, and present, time is without distinction, because it is heard [in scripture] simply as "time. For just as a single atom, although impermanent through its changing modes (*paryāya*), is always existent by virtue of being a substance (*dravya*) and never undergoes non-existence; so too is a single moment (*samaya*).

Furthermore, this time is neither an efficient cause (*nirvartaka-kāraṇa*) nor a transformative cause (*pariṇāmi-kāraṇa*); rather, it is a conditional cause (*apekṣā-kāraṇa*), in that for entities that arise of their own accord, they must exist at this particular time and not at another.

The functions such as *vartanā* (persistence) are the benefits for entities, or alternatively, the functions such as *vartanā* are the marks (*liṅga*) of time; therefore, he states them: "Persistence (*vartanā*), transformation (*pariṇāma*), action (*kriyā*), and priority and posteriority (*paratvāparatve*)" (Tattvārtha-sūtra 5.22). In this context, entities persist by themselves; the function (*vṛtti*) based on time that causes those persisting entities to persist is *vartanā*; the meaning is that it is the state of existence based on the first moment. Transformation (*pariṇāma*) is the nature of a substance (*dravya*) which, without abandoning its own genus (*svajāti*), consists of either motion (*parispanda*) or that which is produced by other applications. This is transformation.

For example: the states of a tree, such as its sprout, root, and so forth, are its transformation (*pariṇāma*); [one says] "there was a sprout," "now it has a trunk," and "it will flourish this year. The states of a person-substance (*puruṣa-dravya*), such as childhood, youth, old age, and so forth, are its transformation. It is the same in other cases as well.

Transformation is of two kinds: beginningless, as in the case of formless things like *dharma* and so forth; and with a beginning, as in the case of material things like clouds, rainbows, pillars, jars, lotuses, and so forth.

The transformation (*pariṇāma*) of things belonging to the same genus, such as trees and so forth, which is produced by the division of seasons and the division of time, becomes manifold even at a single moment. (2) The activity of the transformation of living beings (*jīva*), generated by both application (*prayoga*) and natural decay (*visrasā*), is "action" (*kriyā*); time (*kāla*) is that which assists this action. For example—such expressions as "the jar is destroyed," "I see the sun," and "it will rain"—which refer to the past and so forth and proceed without mutual confusion, depend upon that [time] which is called *kāla*. (3)
Ñ176: "This is prior" and "this is posterior"—such designations of cognition are based on time as their cause.

Ñ177: Thus, time is a substance (dravya) inferable from its auxiliary functions such as *vartanā* (persistence), and it exists within the human realm (*mānuṣa-kṣetra*). Outside the human world, there is no substance called time. For existing entities (*bhāva*) therein arise, perish, and endure by themselves alone; and the existence of entities is inherent to them, not dependent upon time.

Furthermore, the functions of the vital breaths (prāṇa), the downward breath (apāna), the closing and opening of the eyes, and the measure of lifespan in that [state] do not depend on time; for all beings of the same class do not arise simultaneously.
Indeed, objects dependent on time occur for those of the same class at one and the same time, but not for those of different classes.
And those functions, such as the vital breaths, belonging to those [beings], neither arise nor cease at one and the same time.

Therefore, those [qualities] do not depend on time. Priority and posteriority also depend thereon upon duration that is long or short; duration, in turn, depends upon existence; and existence exists by its own nature alone.

As for those who do not consider time to be a substance, in their view, all substances possess only modifications such as "vartanā" (duration/activity), and there is no such thing as time as a causal factor of dependence. 4/

Now, regarding persons (*pudgala*): "Persons possess touch, taste, smell, and color" (Tattvasūtra 5.23). Here, the mention of "touch" at the beginning is for the purpose of making known that when touch exists, taste and the other qualities are also present.

Therefore, water and the other [elements] possess four qualities because they possess touch, just like earth. Likewise, the argument—"the mind possesses touch and the rest, because it is a substance that is not all-pervading, like an atom of earth"—is established as a formal proof (*prayoga*).

In that regard, tangibility (*sparśa*) consists of soft, hard, heavy, light, cold, hot, smooth (*snigdha*), and rough (*rūkṣa*). Among these, only four—smooth, rough, cold, and hot—are possible in atoms (*aṇu*); however, all eight should be stated as applicable to the aggregates (*skandha*) according to their occurrence. Tastes (*rasa*) are bitter, pungent, astringent, sour, and sweet.

Some say that salty is included within the sweet, while others say it arises from a combination [of other tastes]. Odors (*gandha*) are fragrant and foul. Colors (*varṇa*) are black and so forth. Those possessing these qualities reside in the particles (*pudgala*).

It is shown that not only do persons (pudgala) possess qualities such as touch and so forth, but also sound and so forth. "Pudgalas possess sound, cohesion, subtlety, grossness, shape, division, darkness, shadow, heat, and light" (Tattvārthasūtra 5.24). Here, the possessive suffix *matup* is prescribed to indicate a constant connection (*nityayoga*) that reveals the transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the pudgala. Among these, "sound" (*śabda*) refers to resonance (*dhvani*). "Cohesion" (*bandha*) is characterized by mutual adhesion; it is produced by effort (*prayoga*), natural decay (*visrasā*), and so on, like the joining of lacquer and wood in physical bodies, or like the conjunction of atoms (*paramāṇu*).

Subtlety (*saukṣmya*) is the state of being subtle (*sūkṣmatā*); coarseness (*sthaulya*) is the state of being coarse (*sthūlatā*); configuration (*saṃsthāna*) is shape (*ākṛti*); division (*bheda*) is the state of being broken into pieces; darkness, shadow, and so forth are well known. All these—beginning with tangibility and ending with sound—exist only in *pudgalas*. (Ñ 181) *Pudgalas* are of two kinds: atoms (*paramāṇu*) and aggregates (*skandha*). Among them, this is the definition of an atom:
"The atom is that which is the ultimate cause; it is subtle and eternal. (Ñ)
[The atom] has a single taste, color, and smell, two [kinds of] touch, and is characterized by its effects.

(1) Commentary: Because it exists at the limit of all divisions, that alone is the cause, and not anything else such as the dyad (*dvy-aṇuka*) and so forth. Why is that very thing [the cause]? He says: "subtle"—meaning it is accessible through scripture (*āgama*), because it transcends the operation of the senses of people like us.

And it is "eternal"—this is from the perspective of the substantialist standpoint (*dravyārthika-naya*); however, from the perspective of its forms such as blue and so forth, it is indeed impermanent.

There is no substance smaller than that; therefore it is called an atom (*paramāṇu*). Likewise, among the five tastes and two odors, it is endowed with one [type] of taste and so forth, as well as one of the five kinds of color.
Likewise, among the four tangibles, it is endowed with two non-contradictory tangibles—either the smooth and hot, the smooth and cold, or the rough and cold, or the rough and hot.
Likewise, its mark (*liṅga*) is the effect, ranging from the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) up to the great insentient aggregates (*mahā-skandha*).

Thus, atoms (paramāṇu) possess such characteristics as being partless and not joined with one another. On the other hand, aggregates (skandha)—beginning with dyads (dvyaṇuka) and extending up to those consisting of infinite atoms—are possessed of parts. Because of the use of the term "generally" (prāyas), they are capable of activities such as grasping; they are thus collections of atoms. These—dharma, adharma, space (ākāśa), time (kāla), matter (pudgala), and souls (jīva)—are the six substances (dravya). Among these, the first four are single substances; souls and matter are multiple substances. Excluding matter, those five are formless (amūrta); matter, however, is exclusively possessed of form (mūrta).

[Objection: Surely, even though the substance of the soul (*jīva-dravya*) is formless, its existence can be brought within the scope of faith because it is cognizable through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), owing to its nature as consciousness (*upayoga*). However, the categories of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharmāstikāya*), etc., are never at any time cognizable through self-awareness, because they are insentient (*acetana*).

Nor is there knowability through the cognition of another, because [the self] is eternally formless (*arūpitva*). If it is asked, "How then can the existence of those categories such as *dharmāstikāya* be accepted as real? it is said in reply: One must not think with absolute certainty that whatever object is not perceived by direct perception does not exist at all, like the horn of a hare.

For in this world, non-apprehension is of two kinds: therein, one is the non-apprehension of a non-existent object, such as the horn [supposedly] resulting from the contact with the head of a horse; the second, however, is the non-apprehension of objects that do exist.

And this non-apprehension of existing things, despite their presence, is divided here into eight types: namely—due to excessive distance, due to extreme proximity, due to impairment of the sense organs, due to the mind’s lack of stability, due to subtlety, due to obstruction, due to being overwhelmed, and due to being mixed with similar things.

In that regard, there are three kinds of non-apprehension due to extreme distance of place, time, and intrinsic nature. Among these, due to distance of place, for example, when someone like Devadatta has gone to another village and is not seen, how can it be said that he does not exist? He certainly exists; he is simply not apprehended because of the distance of place. Likewise, the far shore of the ocean or Mount Meru and the like, though they exist, are not apprehended.

Similarly, due to distance of time, beings such as one's own ancestors who have passed away, or future Victors such as Padmanābha and others, are not apprehended; yet they have existed and they will exist.
Likewise, due to the remoteness of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-viprakarṣāt*), space, living beings, piśācas, and so forth, are not perceived; yet it is not the case that they do not exist.

(ñ185) Similarly, due to extreme proximity (*atisāmīpyāt*), just as the water in one's own eye is not perceived—how could it be that it does not exist? It certainly exists; it is simply not perceived because of extreme proximity.

(ñ186) Likewise, due to the impairment of the sense faculties (*indriya-ghātāt*), just as those who are blind, deaf, and so forth, do not perceive forms, sounds, and so on—how could it be that forms and the rest do not exist? They certainly exist; they are simply not perceived because of the impairment of the sense faculties.
Likewise, because the mind is unstable, one does not see, just as one whose mind is unsettled does not see. And it has been said:

"Just as a certain arrow-maker does not notice the king passing before him with his retinue, so too one should practice meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). (See Tokunaga’s paper, "The Six Teachers of Bodhya," in the *Festschrift for Professor Mikogami*)

[Question: Why did the king not go? [Answer: He indeed went; however, because his mind was unstable, he did not see [it]. Or rather, for those whose minds are lost, there is no perception of an object even though it exists.

Likewise, due to their subtlety, just as motes of dust, heat, mist, and so forth passing through a window-lattice are not perceived; or as atoms, dyads, and so on, or subtle *nigoda* organisms and the like are not perceived—does it follow that they do not exist? They certainly do exist; however, they are not perceived because of their subtlety. (The *nigoda* souls are the living beings belonging to a specific vegetable kingdom.)

Likewise, there is non-perception due to obstruction, such as the intervention of a wall or the like, or due to an obstruction to cognition. In that regard, regarding intervention: for example, an object situated behind a wall is not perceived. Does it therefore not exist? No; rather, it certainly exists, but because of the intervention, it is not perceived. Similarly, one's own ears, neck, head, and back are not perceived; and although the far side of the lunar disc exists, it is not seen because it is obstructed by the near side.

Furthermore, non-apprehension results from the obscuration of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*); for example, due to dullness of intellect, there is non-apprehension of the specific subtle meanings of the scriptures even though they exist; or, there is non-apprehension of the measure of the water in the ocean even though it exists; or, due to forgetfulness, there is non-apprehension of an object previously apprehended; or, due to delusion (*moha*), there is non-apprehension of the existing principles such as the soul (*jīva*) and so forth. Thus it is said.

Because they are thus overwhelmed: the planets and constellations, being overwhelmed by the light of the sun and other luminaries, are not perceived; yet how could they be non-existent? Rather, they certainly exist, but they are not seen due to that overwhelming [light]. In the same way, even in total darkness, jars and other objects are not perceived.

Ñ192: Furthermore, due to being mixed with similar things (*samānābhihāra*), just as when a handful of mung beans is thrown into a heap of mudga beans, or a handful of sesame seeds into a heap of cotton, they are not perceived even though they are clearly present; or as salt and other substances thrown into water are not perceived—how can it be that these do not exist? They certainly exist; however, they are not perceived because of being mixed with similar things.
Ñ193: And so it is said in the *Sāṃkhyasaptati* (verse 7):
"Due to extreme distance, proximity, impairment of the sense organs, or instability of the mind..."
"Because of subtlety, because of obstruction, because of being overwhelmed, and because of being mixed with similar things.

(VS 4.1.6) Just as it has been stated that even entities possessing a real nature may not be perceived due to these eight causes, one should understand that the *dharmāstikāya* and other such categories, although they exist, are not perceived because their intrinsic natures are remote [from our senses].

The opponent says: "As for those [entities] such as Devadatta who have been shown here as having gone to another country—although they are not perceived by us here, they are indeed perceived by certain people who have gone to that other country; therefore, their existence is established. However, the *dharmāstikāya* and so forth are never perceived by anyone at any time; how, then, can their existence be ascertained?"

To this it is replied: Just as Devadatta and others are determined to exist because they are perceived by some, why then should the *dharmāstikāya* and so forth not likewise be understood to exist because they are perceived by the *kevalins*?
Or, just as atoms, though eternally imperceptible, are inferable from their own effects, why should the *dharmāstikāya* and so forth not also be inferable from their own effects?

Furthermore, these are the effects of the categories beginning with *dharmāstikāya*: therein, *dharma* is inferred from its effect, which is the assistance of motion (*gaty-upagraha*); *adharma* is inferred from its effect, which is the assistance of stability (*sthity-upagraha*); space (*ākāśa*) is inferred from its service of providing accommodation (*avagāha*); time (*kāla*) is inferred from its services such as duration (*vartanā*); and *pudgala*s are determined through both direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).
[Objection: Let it be that space and the others are inferred from their own effects; but how is it so for *dharma* and *adharma*?

To this, the reasoning is stated as follows: Indeed, merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) assist substances that are already characterized by motion (*gati*) or rest (*sthiti*) through their own nature, acting merely as auxiliary causes (*apekṣā-kāraṇa*), just like space (*ākāśa*), time (*kāla*), and so forth; they do not, however, act as productive causes (*nirvartaka-kāraṇa*). For the productive cause is precisely that substance—whether the soul-substance (*jīva-dravya*) or matter-substance (*pudgala-dravya*)—which is distinguished by the effects of motion or rest.

Merit and demerit, moreover, are merely benefactors (*upakāraka*) to substances already characterized by the activities of motion or rest; they do not, however, forcibly characterize them with the activities of motion or rest.

And just as water assists a fish—which, though possessing the power to move swiftly on its own, desires to go here and there—by acting as the medium for its movement, such as rivers, ponds, lakes, and oceans; so too does [the material cause] assist the clay, which is undergoing transformation, with respect to the potter who is the agent, like a staff or other tools.

Furthermore, water is merely a contributory cause (*apekṣā-kāraṇa*) for those moving through the sky, such as birds; it does not, however, forcibly impel a fish—which has entered that water—to go, even if the fish itself is not moving. Nor does the earth itself become the locus of stability for a substance that is already stationary; nor does the earth cause a substance that is not stationary to remain still.

Space, as it is being penetrated by a substance, becomes the cause for that penetration by its very nature; it does not, however, cause that which was not being penetrated to penetrate, owing to its own inherent stability.

Just as rain is observed to be the causal condition for farmers who themselves undertake the labor of plowing, yet the rain-god, though pleased, does not instigate them to begin that work on their behalf.

Or, during the rainy season, the female crane (*balākā*), her womb conditioned by the perception of the sound of new clouds, brings forth [her young] spontaneously; yet the roar of the fresh cloud does not forcibly cause her to give birth if she is not about to do so. Or, a person, having awakened, is seen to abide in abstinence from faults based on the cause of that awakening; yet awakening does not forcibly cause a man who is not abstinent to desist.

Furthermore, the assistance of motion is not applicable to space, which is characterized by providing room (*avagāha*); rather, that assistance is observed to belong to *dharma* alone. Likewise, the assistance of stability belongs to *adharma*, and not to the sky (*vyoman*) characterized by providing room. Indeed, one must necessarily admit some unique quality (*guṇa*) belonging to a substance (*dravya*) that arises from another substance. Whether this status of being a distinct substance is determined through reasoning (*yukti*) or scripture (*āgama*), the reasoning will be explained immediately hereafter.

This scriptural authority (*āgama*) states: "How many, venerable sir, are the substances (*dravya*) declared? O Gautama, six substances are declared. They are as follows: the category of motion (*dharmāstikāya*), the category of rest (*adharmāstikāya*), the category of space (*ākāśāstikāya*), the category of the person (*pudgalāstikāya*), the category of the soul (*jīvāstikāya*), and time (*addhāsamaya*)."
[The categories are] the *jīvāstikāya* (the category of living beings) and *addhāsamaya*, that is, time. [Anuyogadvāra-dravyaguṇasūtra 124].

Now, an objection is raised: "Is it not the case that the upward flight of birds, the upward flaming of fire, and the horizontal blowing of the wind occur solely due to the assistance provided by the substance *dharma*, and that these arise from their own nature (*svabhāva*) which is beginningless? To this, it is replied:

This is a mere assertion; for the reason and example [adduced] against the Arhat are not faultless, because they are unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to him, since his movement is inherent and independent of the assistance of the substance of *dharma*. For the proponents of non-absolutism (*anekāntavādin*) maintain that all living beings (*jīva*) and matter (*pudgala*), having attained the transformation of motion, conform to the *dharma* which assists them; and for those undergoing the transformation of rest, there is *adharma*. Furthermore, movement and rest are not produced by these two [substances].
[The motion and rest of the soul] are helpful merely by way of being auxiliary causes (*sācivyamātreṇa*); for example, "alms provide lodging" or "fire made of cow-dung teaches.

[Objection: But even for you, who assert the existence of the substances *dharma* and *adharma* which pervade the world, the statement that "they assist through motion and rest" is merely a matter of terminology (*saṃjñāmātra*).

Here, the following reasoning is set forth; may you attend: the motion and stationing of souls (*jīva*) and matter (*pudgala*) depend, for their own acquisition [of these states], upon another neutral cause distinct from the three causes—the transformative agent (*pariṇāmin*), the doer (*kartṛ*), and the instrumental cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*)—because they are occasional occurrences despite being non-inherent and ultimate [in nature], like the movement of a fish which acquires its state by depending on water as a neutral cause. Thus is the proof of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).
(196) Space (*ākāśa*) is inferred through its service of providing room for those things that occupy space, such as merit and the rest.

Furthermore, providing space (*avakāśa-dāyitva*) is the assistance (*upakāra*), and that penetration (*avagāha*) is said to be its essential characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). In this case as well, the analogies of water and so forth—which provide assistance for the movement of crocodiles and other creatures—should be applied.

[Objection: But surely this penetration relates to both the person (*pudgala*) and so forth, as well as to space (*ākāśa*); therefore, since it is a property of both, how can it be the characteristic of space alone? [For] it is produced by both, like the conjunction of two fingers.
"It is indeed true that a conjunction produced by two substances cannot be designated by means of a single substance, and it must possess the defining characteristic of being unitary."

Even though [space] is produced by conjunction (*saṃyoga*), the object to be defined (*lakṣya*) is space, which is the primary factor; therefore, "pervasion" (*avagāhana*) refers to that space wherein there is entry or penetration—that is, space as the object of pervasion (*avagāhya*) characterized by the act of pervading (*avagāha*)—whereas other things, such as *pudgala* and so forth, are the pervaders (*avagāhaka*). Since space alone, by virtue of being the unique cause, assists [other things] through its capacity as the object of pervasion, space is to be inferred—even though it is beyond the senses—by means of its own specific assistance which does not occur in other substances, just like the self (*ātman*) or like *dharma* and so forth.

Just as sound produced by the causes of the conjunction between a person’s hand and a stick and a drum is designated as "the sound of the drum," and a sprout produced by the causes of earth, water, wind, and barley is called a "barley-sprout"; for the very same reason—that it is the specific (asādhāraṇa) cause—it should be understood that immersion (*avagāha*) also belongs to space (*ākāśa*). However, the Vaiśeṣikas maintain that space has sound as its mark (*liṅga*), on the grounds that [sound] is established as a quality (*guṇa*) and space as the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*); this is incorrect, because sound possesses color-form (*rūpa*) and other qualities. And the possession of color-form and so forth is to be determined through resistance (*pratighāta*) and obscuration (*abhibhava*).

Time, however, is inferred from such marks as "subsistence" (vartanā) and so forth. For subsistence consists of the experience of its own existence for a single moment within each successive modification (paryāya) of every substance; and since this [subsistence], which rests upon all things, would be impossible at every moment without time, time exists as that which is to be inferred from its effects and is the cause of the transformation of entities. Furthermore, there exist words commonly used in the world that denote time as a substance, and not merely those denoting the movement of the sun. As it has been said:
"Simultaneously or non-simultaneously, quickly, slowly, after a long time, or later than this;
'it will happen' or 'it will not happen,' 'it has happened' or 'that has not happened either. (1)
When all people say, "This is occurring," or "It is occurring," they do so with reference to time alone; therefore, is time not accepted by everyone? //2//

"How are expressions denoting time—such as *ñ: hyaḥ* (yesterday), *śvaḥ* (tomorrow), *adya* (today), *samprati* (now), *parut* (last year), *parāri* (the year before last), *naktam* (at night), *divā* (by day), *eṣamaḥ* (this month), *prātaḥ* (in the morning), and *sāyam* (in the evening)—appropriate if time does not exist? [Objection:

Even transformation (*pariṇāma*) among things of the same class, such as trees and so forth—which is diverse, produced by the divisions of seasons and determined by specific times—is impossible without a regulating cause; therefore, it is concluded that this cause, which exists, is Time (*kāla*).

Likewise, verbal designations of action such as "the jar has been destroyed," "is being destroyed," and "will be destroyed"—which are based on the distinction between the three times of past, present, and future, which are mutually non-confused, and which follow worldly convention—would not be possible without time; therefore, time exists.

Furthermore, that for which there arise the notions and designations "this is prior" and "this is posterior" exists as time. (202) Individuals (*pudgala*) are to be understood through perception, inference, and scripture. Among these, items such as mats, jars, cloths, water-jars, and carts are established by direct perception.

Thus, they are accessible through inference: the existence of subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*), dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), and so forth, is determined by the fact that gross objects could not otherwise be explained. They are also accessible through scripture, as in the passage beginning with "the substance of the person" (*pudgalatthikāe*).

Furthermore, all atoms exist in a single uniform nature; they do not possess four types of forms due to differences in genus—such as the earthy, watery, fiery, and airy atoms—which, according to the Vaiśeṣikas, are endowed with qualities such as the four, three, or two types of touch.

Just as salt and asafoetida, although they have become dissolved in water—which is otherwise fit for perception by touch, sight, taste, and smell—cannot be apprehended by the eyes or the sense of touch because they possess a specific transformation (*pariṇāmaviśeṣa*); so too, the atoms of earth and the other elements, though belonging to the same class, do not become perceptible by all the senses due to their specific transformations, and not because of a difference in their genus (*tajjātibheda*).

The material nature (*paudgalikatā*) of sound and the other sense objects should be understood as follows: sound is a transformation of the substance *pudgala*; its being such a transformation is due to its having form (*mūrtatva*); and it has form because it possesses the capacity to produce modifications in other substances, such as the palate, throat, head, root of the tongue, and teeth, like long pepper (*pippalī*) and similar things.

Likewise, [sound is material] because it causes the vibration of drums, kettledrums, cymbals, and wooden clappers when they are struck. Furthermore, sounds from conch shells and the like, when intensified to an extreme degree, possess the power to deafen the ears; and this power does not exist in formless entities (*amūrta*) such as space (*ākāśa*).

Therefore, sound is not a quality of that [ether], because it moves in opposition to it, like a stream obstructed by a mountain. Likewise, sound is not a quality of space, because it conforms to doors, like sunlight.

In that very same position, the fivefold proof with demonstration (*sanidarśana*) is elaborated as follows: sound is not a quality of space (*ākāśa*), because it possesses the capacity for cessation, like the smoke of *aguru*; likewise, because it is impelled by wind, like grass, leaves, and so forth; because it is perceivable in all directions, like a lamp; because it is capable of being overwhelmed, like a cluster of stars and so forth; and because it is itself an overcomer, like the light of the solar disc.
Indeed, it is well known that a smaller sound is overwhelmed by a larger one; therefore, sound is a transformation of the person (*pudgala*).

Now, if it is asked: "Just as form is perceived in a conch shell, in its destruction, and in its fragments because they consist of *pudgala* (matter), why is it not so in the case of sound?"—it is replied: Because of its subtlety (*sūkṣmatva*), like the form of a lamp-flame that has been extinguished by the intellect, or like the form situated within the atoms of fragrance (*gandhaparamāṇu*). Indeed, the fact that fragrance and the like are transformations of *pudgala* is already well-established.

Regarding darkness, shadow, and so forth: Darkness is a transformation of *pudgala* because it obstructs vision, since it acts as a screen just like a wall, or because it covers things just like a cloth.

Even shadow, because it is cool and refreshing like water, wind, and so forth, is composed of *pudgala*. Furthermore, a reflection—which transforms into the form of a shadow—is also composed of *pudgala* because it possesses a specific form.

Now, if it is asked: "How is it that *pudgala*s, having pierced through the hard mirror and emerged from the face, take on the form of a reflection? It is said in reply: That piercing should be explained by analogy with water flowing through a hard stone surface, the entry of fiery *pudgala*s into a mass of iron, and the emergence of minute drops of perspiration from the body.

Heat (*ātapa*) is also a substance because it causes heating; due to being the cause of perspiration and because of its heat, it is like fire. And light (*udyota*), such as moonlight and the like, is a substance because it provides refreshment; because of its illuminating nature, it is like fire. Likewise, rubies (*padmarāga*) and other gems possess a light that is neither hot nor cold. Therefore, darkness, shadow, and so forth, are transformations of material substances. Thus, the *pudgalas* are established. In this way, the principle of the non-living (*ajīva-tattva*) is well-explained.

Now, he explains the reality of merit (*puṇyatattva*): "Merit consists of the existing *karma*-pudgalas. Merit refers to those existing *karma*-pudgalas—meaning the *karma*-aggregates (*karmavargaṇā*) bound to the soul—which are praiseworthy because they bring about fruits such as the state of a Tīrthaṅkara or rebirth in heaven. (Verses 48–49)
Now, he explains the reality of the influx of evil (pāpāsrava-tattva):

"Evil is the opposite of that [virtue]; however, the causes such as false belief (mithyātva) and so forth—whatever constitutes bondage—is to be known as 'influx' (āsrava) in the teaching of the Jina. (50)

Commentary: The word "tu" (but) indicates a change in the sequence [of the topics]. "Pāpa" (sin), however, is the opposite of that merit (*puṇya*); the meaning is that *pāpa* refers to those unwholesome (*apraśasta*) karmic matter-particles (*karmapudgala*) associated with the soul, which bring about results such as rebirth in hell.

Furthermore, although merit and sin are included within the other principles of bondage (*bandhatattva*) that will be discussed here, they are mentioned separately for the purpose of refuting various divergent views regarding the nature of merit and sin held by others.
These divergent views are as follows: some non-Buddhist outsiders (*tairthika*) maintain this proclamation: "Only merit exists; there is no sin."

Others, however, say that there is only evil and no merit; yet others maintain that both are of an interpenetrating nature, like a variegated gem, and that there is a single common entity called "merit-and-evil" which is the cause of the mixed fruits known as pleasure and pain.

Others, however, say: "In its very root, action itself does not exist; this entire manifold of the world is established by way of its own intrinsic nature. All these various views must be considered incorrect. For both pleasure and pain are experienced by everyone as distinct entities; therefore, their causes—merit and demerit—must also be recognized as two independent factors, and not as either one of those two, nor as a mixture of the two.

Now, the nihilists who deny the existence of karma and the Vedāntins say: "Indeed, merit and demerit should be regarded as being like a lotus in the sky; they are not, however, real entities. For what reason, then, could there be the experience of their fruits in the places of heaven and hell?"

It is said: In the absence of merit and demerit, happiness and suffering would simply not arise, as they would lack a cause; yet this contradicts direct perception. For instance—even while being equal in their human status—some are seen experiencing lordship, while others bear the condition of being his servants; some fill their bellies with hundreds of thousands [of coins], while others are incapable even of filling the cavity of their own stomachs.

Some were like gods, constantly endowed with the bliss of the play of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*); others, however, were like hell-beings, their mental states withered by wakeful suffering (*unnidra-duḥkha-vidrāṇa-cittavṛtti*). (The word *vidrāṇa* here means "roused from sleep" [according to the *Amarakośa*]).

Therefore, since merit and demerit must be accepted as the basis for the pleasure and pain currently being experienced, and since one must also accept heaven and hell as the places of enjoyment for their specific results when those [merits and demerits] are activated; otherwise, there would be the fallacy of the "half-old woman" argument (*ardha-jaratīya-nyāya*).

And the formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: pleasure and pain are preceded by causes, because they are effects, like a sprout; and those which are their causes should be understood as merit and demerit, just as the seed is the cause of a sprout.

Now, if it is argued: "Just as a material object such as blue and so forth becomes the cause of an immaterial cognition that appears as its own reflection, so too shall visible material things such as food, garlands, sandalwood, and women be the causes of immaterial pleasure, while snakes, poison, thorns, and the like will be the causes of suffering. Therefore, what is the use of postulating invisible merit and demerit (*puṇya* and *pāpa*)?"—

That is incorrect, because it is inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*). For instance, even between two persons who possess identical means such as food, garlands, and so forth, a great difference is observed in the results characterized by pleasure and pain. Indeed, even when the same food and other things have been consumed, one person experiences delight while another suffers the onset of disease and the like. This difference in result must necessarily have a cause; for if it were causeless, it would follow that it must either exist eternally or not exist at all.

And that which is the cause is the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) action consisting of merit and demerit. As it has been said: "Whatever distinction there is in the fruit for those who possess equal means, that cannot exist without a cause; because it is an effect, like a jar made from cow dung, that cause is karma. (1) (That distinction in the fruit for those with equal means does not exist without a cause; being of the nature of an effect, like a jar [made from] cow dung, it arises from a cause—that cause is karma.)

Alternatively, merit and demerit are understood through inference from causes and inference from effects. In this regard, the inference from causes is as follows: virtuous actions such as giving and non-virtuous actions such as violence possess an effect that consists of their fruit; because they are causes, just like the actions of agriculture and so forth.

And that which is the effect consisting of the fruit of these [actions] should be understood as merit and demerit, just as rice, barley, wheat, and so forth are the fruits of the actions of agriculture and so forth.

[Objection: Is it not the case that just as activities such as agriculture have their application completed by the mere visible fruit of rice and so forth, so too all activities—such as giving and the like, as well as animal slaughter and the like—should have their purpose fulfilled by the mere visible fruit of praise and so forth, or the consumption of meat and so forth? What is the use of postulating invisible fruits in the form of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*)?

For almost the entire world engages in activities such as agriculture, trade, and violence, which have only visible results; however, very few people engage in activities such as giving, which have invisible results, rather than many.
If it is argued that because virtuous acts like agriculture and violence lack invisible results, virtuous acts like giving will likewise lack invisible results—that is not so.

Precisely because many people engage in impure actions such as agriculture which have visible results, whereas only a very few people engage in pure actions such as giving which have invisible results, it must be understood that actions like agriculture and violence, though having visible results, also possess invisible results in the form of demerit (*adṛṣṭa-pāpa*); for otherwise, the existence of infinite transmigrating living beings would be inexplicable.

For they, having bound for themselves an undesirable result characterized by sin—which is the unseen (adṛṣṭa) fruit caused by actions such as agriculture and violence—remain here in this world as infinite beings, wandering through an endless cycle of existence (saṃsāra).

For if the unseen fruit in the form of sin were not admitted for unwholesome actions such as agriculture and violence, then all those who perform them would, in the absence of such an unseen fruit, attain liberation effortlessly immediately after death.
Therefore, saṃsāra would for the most part be entirely empty, and consequently, no one suffering in saṃsāra would be found at all.
Instead, everywhere only those who perform virtuous deeds such as giving and so forth, and who experience the ripening of those very virtuous fruits, would be found.

Yet, here many who are suffering are seen, while those who are happy are indeed few. From this it is known that the ripening of the fruit of the unseen (adṛṣṭa) in the form of sin—which consists of bondage resulting from actions such as agriculture, trade, and violence—is the cause of suffering; whereas for others, the ripening of the fruit of the unseen in the form of merit (dharma), caused by actions such as giving and so forth, is the cause of happiness.

If it is asked why there is no reversal [of this order], it is said: it is an inference based on the cause, namely that those who initiate unwholesome actions are numerous, whereas those who practice wholesome actions are very few.

(ñ220) Now, the inference based on the effect: although living beings are indistinguishable in their nature as selves (*ātman*), there must be a cause for the diversity of bodies and so forth among humans, cattle, and others; because they are effects, just as a potter is the cause of a jar produced by the assembly of clay, staff, wheel, and cloth.

Nor should it be said that parents and the like, who are indeed perceived, are its cause; for even when the perceived causes are identical, a diversity of bodies and so forth is observed through their being beautiful or otherwise. And this [diversity] cannot exist without the cause known as unseen merit and demerit (adṛṣṭa-śubhāśubha-karma). Therefore, by means of the inference from effect to cause, it follows that beautiful bodies and the like are the effects of merit, while others are the effects of demerit.

Alternatively, the existence of both merit and demerit is to be understood through the authority of the words of the Omniscient One. However, one seeking specific details should consult the *Viśeṣāvaśyaka-ṭīkā*.

Now, he explains the influx (*āsrava*) with the verse beginning, "But the causes are false belief (*mithyātva*) and so forth. False belief (*mithyātva*) is the notion that what are not true deities, teachers, or doctrines are indeed true deities and so forth. Non-restraint (*avirati*) is the failure to abstain from violence and other such acts. Negligence (*pramāda*) consists of intoxicants, sensual objects, and the like. The passions (*kaṣāya*) are anger and the rest. Activities (*yoga*) are the operations of mind, speech, and body. Here, the construction of the words is as follows:

Furthermore, false belief, lack of restraint, and so forth are the causes of bondage—that is, the bondage of karma such as the obscuration of knowledge (jñānāvaraṇīya). That is to be understood as "influx" (āsrava) in the teaching of the Jina.
