Among these, conventional direct perception—such as that of people like us—is non-ultimate because it depends on the causal complex of external sense organs and so forth. Ultimate direct perception, however, depends solely upon the presence of the self (*ātman*), such as the direct perception of clairvoyance (*avadhi*) and the rest.

Empirical cognition (*sāmvyavahārika*) is twofold: that caused by the sense organs such as the eye, and that caused by the mind. Each of these two types is further fourfold, through the distinctions of apprehension (*avagraha*), inquiry (*īhā*), judgment (*avāya*), and retention (*dhāraṇā*).

Among these, *avagraha* is the initial grasping of an object characterized by a subordinate generality, which arises from a perception whose scope is mere existence, occurring immediately after the contact between the object and the sense organ.

The meaning of this is as follows: the *viṣaya* (object) is the thing (*artha*) consisting of substance and mode; the *viṣayin* (subject) is the eye and so forth. The "proper contact" (*samīcīna-nipāta*) between these two is their favorable conjunction, which does not produce error and so on, and consists in their being situated in a suitable place and so forth. Immediately following that, there arises—that is, is produced—a perception (*darśana*) whose scope is mere existence (*sattāmātra*), which is cognition devoid of mental forms (*nirākāra-bodha*). From that [perception] arises the first [stage], which is the grasping (*grahaṇa*)—that is, knowledge (*jñāna*)—of an object qualified by its specific attributes (*viśeṣa*), such as "human-ness" and so forth, while it is still characterized by the general attribute of "existence" (*sattā-sāmānya*) and others.
That is *avagraha*.

Furthermore, *īhā* is the desire for the specific qualities of an object immediately following doubt regarding that apprehended object. Immediately after that, *avāya* is the determination of those desired specific qualities. *Dhāraṇā* follows immediately after that as the cause of memory regarding the object already known.

In this context, each preceding stage is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and each succeeding stage is the result (*phala*). Thus, although it is a single instance of sensory-cognition (*mati-jñāna*), its fourfold nature and the distinction between the means of cognition and its result are established in some way.

Likewise, although there is a distinction between the successive stages such as *avagraha* (perception) and so forth—which are established as cause and effect—from the perspective of their modal aspect (*paryāyārtha*), nevertheless, their unity is in some way non-contradictory from the perspective of the substantial aspect (*dravyārthādeśa*) due to their identity with a single soul (*eka-jīva-tādātmya*). Otherwise, it should be understood that the consequence would follow that the relationship of cause and effect itself would not exist.

Retention (*dhāraṇā*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is the cause of the fruit, which is memory characterized by non-discrepancy with the object of cognition; memory (*smṛti*) likewise [is a means of valid cognition] because it generates the fruit, which is recognition (*saṃjñā*) whose nature is the reflective awareness of that which has been thus experienced; recognition (*saṃjñā*) also [is a means of valid cognition] because it generates the fruit, which is reflection (*cintā*) whose nature is reasoning (*tarka*) regarding that which has been thus recognized; reflection (*cintā*) also [is a means of valid cognition] because it generates the fruit, which is right discernment (*abhinibodha*) characterized as inference (*anumāna*); and that [inference] also [is a means of valid cognition] because it generates the cognitions of avoidance (*hāna*) and so forth.

Thus it has been said: "Cognition (mati), memory (smṛti), recognition (saṃjñā), deliberation (cintā), and discernment (abhinibodha) are not different in meaning" (Tattvārtha Sūtra 1.13). Regarding the phrase "not different in meaning": prior to the association with words, this is cognition (mati-jñāna), having for its object a single entity in some way or another.
Others maintain that the remainder—knowledge arising from the association with words, which is indistinct and possesses many subdivisions—is called scriptural knowledge (śruta).

The followers of the Siddhānta, however, maintain that *mati*, *smṛti*, *saṃjñā*, *cintā*, and *abhinibodha* are synonymous terms denoting cognition (*mati*) which consists of the divisions of apprehension (*avagraha*), inquiry (*īhā*), judgment (*avāya*), and retention (*dhāraṇā*).

Furthermore, although memory (*smṛti*), recognition (*saṃjñā*), reflection (*cintā*), and so forth, apprehend objects already grasped in some way, they must be accepted as valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because they are non-contradictory (*avisamvādaka*), just like inference (*anumāna*). Otherwise, inference would result in being invalid, as its object would be one already grasped by the means of knowledge that establishes the pervasion (*vyāpti*).

In this context, the distinction is as follows: that which exists prior to the association with words—such as memory (*smṛti*) and so forth—which is non-erroneous and capable of accomplishing worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), is *mati*; however, everything that arises from the association with words is *śruta*.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the mention here, within the section on direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), of memory, conceptualization (*saṃjñā*), and so forth—which are types of indirect cognition (*parokṣa*) consisting of recollection, deliberation (*tarka*), and inference—is for the purpose of understanding the distinction between *mati* and *śruta*, occurring by way of incidental discussion (*prasaṅga*).

Now, indirect [perception] (*parokṣa*): indirect perception is cognition that is indistinct yet non-contradictory. It is fivefold, distinguished as recollection (*smaraṇa*), recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), reasoning (*tarka*), inference (*anumāna*), and scripture (*āgama*).

Recollection is a cognition produced by the awakening of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), having as its object a previously experienced thing, and taking the form "that"; for example, "That is the image of the Tīrthaṅkara."

Recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is a synthesis (*saṅkalana*) caused by both experience and memory; it takes such forms as "this is that very same thing," "this is similar to that," "this is distinct from that," or "this is the counter-correlative of that. Examples include: "This is that very Devadatta," "A gavaya is similar to a cow," "An ox is distinct from a cow," "This is longer than that," "shorter," "finer," "larger," "farther," or "closer"; or "This fire over there is intense," and "This sandalwood is fragrant," and so forth.

Here, by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one should cite examples such as the synthesis (*saṃkalana*) produced by inference, scripture, and so forth, which are accompanied by memory—such as [the thought] that "that very same fire is being inferred here," or "that very same object is being expressed by this [word]," and so on.

*Tarka* (reasoning) is a cognition whose possibility arises from perception and non-perception, which takes as its object the relationship between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) as determined across the three times, and which has the form: "This occurs only when that exists," and so forth; for example: "Smoke occurs only when fire exists, and it certainly does not occur in its absence."

Inference is of two kinds: for oneself (*svārtha*) and for others (*parārtha*). Inference for oneself is the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*) which has as its cause the apprehension of the reason (*hetu*) and the recollection of the [invariable] connection (*sambandha*). The reason (*hetu*) is characterized by the single mark of being ascertained and otherwise impossible (*anyathānupapatti*). The probandum (*sādhya*) is that which is intended, uncontradicted, and not yet established. The subject (*dharmin*) is the locus (*pakṣa*) that is well-known and qualified by the probandum.

Inference for others consists essentially of the statement of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*), though it is so called by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). However, in order to instruct those of dull intellect, the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), application (*upanaya*), and conclusion (*nigamana*) should also be employed.

The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is of two kinds, distinguished by positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). That in which the existence of the probandum (*sādhya*) is necessarily demonstrated when there is the existence of the probans (*sādhana*) is the example of positive concomitance. That in which the absence of the probans is stated through the absence of the probandum is the example of negative concomitance.

The application (*upanaya*) is the subsumption of the reason (*hetu*); the conclusion (*nigamana*) is the subsumption of the proposition (*pratijñā*). These five members, beginning with the thesis (*pakṣa*), are thus proclaimed, and so forth.

An example here is as follows: "Sound is subject to transformation because it is produced; whatever is produced is seen to be subject to transformation, just like a jar; and this [sound] is produced, therefore it is subject to transformation. Furthermore: "That which is not subject to transformation is not seen to be produced, such as the breast-milk of a barren woman; and this [sound] is produced, therefore it is subject to transformation," and so forth.

If it is asked: "Why was only 'the necessity of the reason being otherwise impossible' (*anyathānupapatti*) declared here as the single definition of a logical reason (*hetu*), and not the three-fold nature consisting of 'being a property of the subject' (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth?"—it is replied: Because even when the three-fold nature such as *pakṣadharmatva* is present, we do not observe that [a reason] such as "being the son of that man" (*tatputratva*) functions as a means of cognition (*gamaka*); and because we do observe that a reason functions as a means of cognition even in the absence of the three-fold nature. For instance: from the moon in the water [one infers] the moon in the sky; from the rising of the Kṛttikā constellation [one infers] the rising of the Rohiṇī constellation (*śakaṭa*).

From a single blossoming mango tree, all remaining mango trees are inferred to be in bloom; from the rising of the moon, the swelling of the ocean is inferred; and from the rising of the sun, the awakening of the lotus pond is inferred. Furthermore, shade is inferred from a tree—even in the absence of the "property of the subject" (pakṣadharmatā)—these are all inferred by everyone.

If it is argued that in these cases the subject (dharmin), such as time and so forth, certainly exists there, we say no; for this would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). For in that case, when the impermanence of sound is to be proven, even the blackness of a crow and the like would result in being a probans (gamaka), since it would be possible to imagine a subject such as "the world" in those instances.

"Sound is impermanent because it is audible; this is like my brother, because a voice of such a kind would otherwise be impossible; and because in cases such as 'everything is permanent' or 'everything is impermanent because it exists,' we observe that [the reason] is a means of cognition even in the absence of presence in similar instances (sapakṣa).

Knowledge of an object arising from the words of a reliable person (āpta) is scripture (āgama); and by metaphorical extension, the words of a reliable person themselves are so called, as in: "There is a treasure here," or "Mount Meru and others exist."

One who knows the object to be expressed as it truly exists, and expresses it according to that knowledge, is an authoritative person (*āpta*), such as a progenitor or a Tīrthaṅkara. Thus has the indirect means of knowledge (*parokṣa*) been described. By this [it is said]:
"Clear cognition that accords with reality through primary conventional usage is direct perception (*adhyakṣa*); other [cognition] is indeed indirect (*parokṣa*). This is the summary. (Verse 1)

Whatever is non-contradictory is considered a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in that respect, and that which is contradictory is not a valid means of knowledge; this applies to both perception (*adhyakṣa*) and the indirect (*parokṣa*). [Sanmatitarkaṭīkā, p.

59] Therefore, for a single cognition, validity (*pramāṇatā*) exists where there is non-contradiction, while in other cases it is merely a semblance thereof (*tadābhāsatā*). For example, a cognition impaired by cataracts or similar defects is a valid means of knowledge regarding the moon and so forth because it is non-contradictory in that regard, yet that very same cognition is not a valid means of knowledge regarding its number and so forth because it is contradictory in those respects.

It is established that the definition of the determination of one means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as distinct from another consists in non-discrepancy (*avisamvāda*). Thus, there are only two means of valid cognition: direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and indirect cognition (*parokṣa*).

Among these, within the five types of knowledge—sensory cognition (*mati*), scriptural cognition (*śruta*), clairvoyance (*avadhi*), mental cognition (*manahparyāya*), and omniscience (*kevalajñāna*)—sensory and scriptural cognition are, in the ultimate sense, the indirect means of valid cognition; whereas clairvoyance, mental cognition, and omniscience are the direct means of valid cognition.

Now the latter half [of the verse] is explained: "The object possesses infinite properties," and so forth. Here, in the section on the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the object of both direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and indirect cognition (*parokṣa*)—that is, the apprehended—is the object that possesses infinite properties. Because they have the three times as their domain, the properties (*dharma*) are infinite—that is, immeasurable.

These are the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), whether co-existent or sequential, and the modes (*paryāya*) pertaining to self and other. That which possesses such infinite properties is "possessing infinite properties" (*ananta-dharmaka*); by adding the suffix *ka* in its own sense, the meaning is that it is manifold-natured (*anekāntātmaka*).
"Anekāntātmakam" (of manifold nature) is derived from the etymology: that which has many ends (*aneka-anta*), parts (*aṃśa*), or properties (*dharma*) as its essence (*svarūpa*).

"Vastu" refers to every substance (*dravya*), whether conscious or unconscious. Here, the thesis (*pakṣa*) is: "A real entity possesses infinite properties. By the phrase "the object of a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇaviṣaya*), the purely negative reason (*kevalavyatirekī hetu*)—namely, "because of being an object of knowledge" (*prameyatvāt*)—is indicated. Since a reason is defined solely by the condition of being otherwise impossible (*anyathānupapatti*), the probandum is established through internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*) alone; therefore, there is no need for examples (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the like.

That which does not consist of infinite properties is not an object of cognition (*prameya*), just like a sky-flower; this is a purely negative (*kevala-vyatireka*) inference, because positive examples (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) are included within the subject (*pakṣa*) itself and thus cannot serve for a positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

Furthermore, there is absolutely no room for defects such as being unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), or inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) in this reason (*hetu*), because everything is cognized through means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as consisting precisely of infinite properties.

If it is asked, "How can infinite attributes (dharmas) be perceived in a single entity?", it is said in reply: Just as there exists for all cognizers at all times and in all places a cognition of a single-natured entity—which consists of both means of knowledge and objects of knowledge, and which is pervaded by infinite attributes produced either successively or simultaneously—so too do we demonstrate this in detail through the example of a golden jar.

When an object intended for discussion is considered through properties such as existence (*sattva*), knowability (*jñeyatva*), and cognizability (*prameyatva*), then it possesses only its own modes (*svaparyāya*); it does not possess any modes belonging to others (*paraparyāya*).

Since every entity is homogeneous with respect to properties such as existence and so forth, and because there is an absolute absence of anything heterogeneous, there is no exclusion from any [of these properties].

However, when a jar is intended to be discussed in terms of substance (*dravyataḥ*) as being composed of matter (*paudgalika*), then it exists as a substance consisting of matter; it does not exist, however, as substances such as dharma, adharma, or space.

In this context, "pudgala-nature" (paudgalikatva) is its own mode (svaparyāya); because it is distinguished from the infinite [categories] such as dharma and so forth, its other modes (paraparyāya) are infinite, since the substances of *jīva* are infinite. That same jar, though of the nature of *pudgala*, exists by way of being earthen (*pārthivatva*), but not by way of being watery and so forth. Here, "earthen-ness" is its own mode; however, because it is distinguished from many substances such as water and so forth, its other modes are infinite. In the same way, the manifestation of one's own and other modes is to be understood in what follows as well. Even in that which is earthen, it exists by way of being a mineral element (*dhātu-rūpatā*), but not by way of being clay and so forth.
Even though it has the nature of an element (*dhātu*), it exists as gold and not as silver and so forth; even though it is gold, it exists as wrought gold and not as unwrought gold and so forth;
even though it is wrought gold, it exists as being fashioned by Devadatta and not as being fashioned by Yajñadatta and so forth;
even though it is fashioned by Devadatta, it exists in the form of a broad-based vessel and not as a crown and so forth. (In the middle, becoming wide.)

Even the form of a wide base and belly exists as a circular form, not as a non-circular form. Even the circular form exists as its own form, and not again as the form of another jar or the like. Even its own form exists by means of its own constituent parts (*dalika*), and not by the constituent parts of others. In this manner, whatever mode (*paryāya*) it is intended to be described by another, that is its own mode; all others, however, are modes of others. Thus, in terms of substance (*dravyataḥ*), its own modes are few, whereas the modes of others—which consist of exclusions (*vyāvṛtti-rūpa*)—are infinite, because it is excluded from infinite substances.

Regarding its location, it is intended to exist within the three worlds (*tri-lokī*), yet it does not deviate from anything whatsoever. Therefore, it possesses its own nature (*sva-paryāya*) and lacks the nature of another (*para-paryāya*).

Although it exists within the three worlds, it exists by way of being situated in the horizontal world (*tiryag-loka*) and not by way of being situated in the upper or lower worlds. Although it exists within the horizontal world, it exists by way of being situated in Jambūdvīpa and not by way of being situated in other continents (*apara-dvīpa*) and so forth.

He exists as being located in Bharata, but not by virtue of being located in Videha and so forth. Even within Bharata, he exists as being located in Pāṭaliputra, but not by virtue of being in another place.

Even in Pāṭaliputra, he exists as being located in Devadatta’s house, but not otherwise. Even in the house, he exists by being situated in one part of the house, but not in another part. Even in that one part of the house, he exists by being situated in those specific points of space where he lies, but not by being situated in other points of space.

In this way, it should also be stated according to other possible modes as the case may be. Thus, from the perspective of the locus (*kṣetra*), its own modes (*svaparyāya*) are few, whereas the modes of others (*paraparyāya*) are innumerable, because the world consists of innumerable spatial points (*pradeśa*). Alternatively, for a jar situated in the human world, there are infinite modes of others because it is distinguished from the infinite substances situated in other locations. The same applies to Devadatta’s house and so forth. Therefore, the modes of others are infinite.

In terms of time, however, by virtue of its permanence, it existed, exists, and will exist within its own substance; therefore, it does not deviate from that [substance] in any way. When it is being conceptualized as belonging to this present age, it exists as having that specific form, but not as existing in past, future, or other ages.
Even within this age, it exists as belonging to the current year, but not by way of belonging to past years and so forth.

Even that which belongs to the present exists as being vernal, but not as having been produced in another season. Even therein it exists as something new, but not as something old. Even therein it exists as belonging to the current day, but not as belonging to a non-current day. Even therein it exists as the present moment, but not as another moment.
Thus, in terms of time, there are innumerable internal modes, because a single substance persists for an incalculable duration of time.

However, if one intends to express their existence throughout infinite time, then those [substances] are also infinite in number. But as for the "other modes" (*paraparyāya*), they are indeed infinite because they consist in the exclusion of the infinite substances that do not exist at the time in question.

Furthermore, in terms of its actual nature (*bhāva*), it exists as yellow in color, but not with colors such as blue and so forth. Even that yellow [substance] is "one-fold yellow" (*ekaguṇapīta*) in relation to another yellow substance; that same [yellow] is "two-fold yellow" (*dviguṇapīta*) in relation to yet another; and that same [yellow] is "three-fold yellow" (*triguṇapīta*) in relation to something else. In this manner, it should be stated up to the point where, in relation to some yellow substance, it is "infinite-fold yellow" (*anantaguṇapīta*).

Likewise, that very same [substance], in relation to another, is deficient by one quality; in relation to yet another, it is deficient by two qualities, and so on, until—in relation to some [other substance]—it becomes even infinitely deficient in its yellowness. Thus, through its yellowness, infinite internal modes (*svaparyāya*) are obtained. Furthermore, through the application of the degrees of being "more yellow" or "most yellow," there are also infinite external modes (*paraparyāya*), which consist in its differentiation from infinite other colors such as blue and the like.

Thus, even from the perspective of taste, one's own infinite modes (svaparyāyas) are to be understood as being like its own sweetness and so forth, in relation to its own sweet and other tastes; likewise, its infinite foreign modes (paraparyāyas) are to be discerned as being like its blueness and so forth, in relation to other tastes such as the salty and so on.

In this way, by means of fragrant odor (*surabhigandha*) alone, the infinite self- and other-modifications (*svapara-paryāya*) are to be understood. Likewise, with respect to the eightfold touch (*sparśa*)—heavy, light, soft, hard, cold, hot, smooth, and rough—one should understand that there are infinite self- and other-modifications for each, according to the application of degrees of intensity (*tara-tama-yoga*). For it is stated in the Siddhānta that even in a single aggregate (*skandha*) consisting of infinite space-points (*anantapradeśaka*), all eight types of touch are found; therefore, all eight are mentioned here in relation to the jar (*kalaśa*).

Alternatively, even in the substance gold, over an infinite period of time, all five colors, both types of fragrance, six tastes, and eight tactile qualities arise infinitely through varying degrees of intensity; furthermore, there is a differentiation from each of those various other colors and so forth. In relation to that as well, one must understand that one's own and others' properties (*svapara-dharma*) are infinite.

Furthermore, with respect to words, there are multiple intrinsic properties (*svadharma*) of a jar, because it is denotable by various words such as "jar" and so forth in relation to different locations; and there are infinite extrinsic properties (*paradharma*), because it is excluded from other substances that are not denoted by those respective words such as "jar.

Alternatively, whatever sounds (*dhvani*) have been mentioned or will be mentioned as the denoters of all those intrinsic and extrinsic properties of that jar, that many are the jar's intrinsic properties; and those which denote things other than that are the extrinsic properties.

Furthermore, with respect to the enumeration of a jar in relation to its various preceding and succeeding substances, there would be firstness, secondness, thirdness, up to infiniteness; thus, there are infinite own-attributes (*sva-dharma*). There are also infinite other-attributes (*para-dharma*) by virtue of being excluded from those things denoted by those respective enumerations.

Alternatively, whatever enumeration of atoms or enumeration of weights such as *pala* exists in that jar constitutes its own-attribute; there are infinite other-modes (*para-paryāya*) by virtue of being excluded from those things devoid of that enumeration.

With respect to time, that jar has infinite intrinsic properties (*sva-dharma*) by virtue of its infinite states of conjunction and disjunction with all substances; and it also has infinite extrinsic properties (*para-dharma*) which are distinguished from those [substances] that have not been made objects of its conjunction and disjunction.
Furthermore, with respect to dimension, its intrinsic properties would be infinitely diverse—consisting of minuteness, largeness, shortness, and length—in relation to this or that substance.
Those other modes (*paraparyāya*) which arise for it through its distinction from all substances are all to be understood as its distinctness (*pṛthaktva*).

In terms of direction and location, through the notions of priority and posteriority (*paratva-aparatva*), that jar has infinite internal modes (*svaparyāya*) consisting of its proximity, greater proximity, and closest proximity, as well as its distance, greater distance, and remotest distance, in relation to other infinite substances. Furthermore, there is proximity and distance measured by one, two, and so on, up to an incalculable number of *yojanas*. Alternatively, in dependence upon another object, it is "east" in relation to that, and "west" in relation to something else; thus, based on the cardinal and intermediate directions, its internal modes such as distance and proximity are incalculable.

Ñ329: From the perspective of time (*kāla*), due to priority (*paratva*) and posteriority (*aparatva*), there are infinite internal attributes (*svadharma*) of a jar through infinite distinctions such as prior and posterior in terms of moments (*kṣaṇa*), lava, ghaṭī, day, month, year, yuga, and so forth.

Ñ330: Even from the perspective of cognition (*jñāna*), because the jar is apprehended by the infinite cognitions—such as sensory perception (*mati*) and others—of all living beings, as well as by their ignorance (*ajñāna*) regarding its specific divisions and so on, through the distinction between clear and unclear natures, a distinction in the nature of the object of apprehension (*grāhya*) is necessarily possible.

Otherwise, there would be no difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of those [cognitions] that apprehend it either; and thus they would become one. Furthermore, when there is a difference in the intrinsic nature of the object of apprehension (*grāhya*), those [natures] are its own properties (*svadharma*).

With respect to all living beings, a jar possesses infinite attributes (*ananta-dharmatva*) by virtue of being the cause of—whether as causes of pleasure and so forth, or as non-causes thereof—the following: distinctions such as small, large, or very large; infinite varieties of pleasure, pain, abandonment, acquisition, and indifference; the objects of desire; merit (*puṇya*), demerit (*apuṇya*), karmic bondage, mental formations (*citta-saṃskāra*), and so on; the adventitious qualities (*upādhi*) such as anger, pride, deceit, greed, passion, hatred, and delusion; substantiality (*dravyatva*); rolling, falling, and other such motions; and velocity (*vega*).
As for viscidity (*sneha*) and heaviness (*gurutva*), they were already perceived previously through their specific types of touch (*sparśa-bheda*).

Furthermore, with respect to action (*karman*), there are the infinite intrinsic properties (*svadharma*) of a jar consisting of its infinite forms of activity—such as lifting, lowering, contracting, expanding, rotating, flowing, pouring out, filling, moving, shaking, transporting to another place, fetching water, and holding water—which serve as causes for these actions at various times, according to their specific distinctions or degrees of intensity. Moreover, there are infinite extrinsic properties (*paradharma*) of those actions, defined by their exclusion from other things that are not the causes of those actions.

Ñ333: Furthermore, in general, according to the principle previously stated, regarding all the infinite self- and other-modifications (*paryāya*) of universal objects that exist in the past and other times, there are infinite own-natures (*svadharma*) due to the state of infinite differentiation and infinite similarity, based on the similarity of a jar [to itself] through one, two, three, up to an infinite number of properties (*dharma*). Ñ334: And specifically, among the infinite substances of jars, there are infinite own-natures caused by infinite modes of differentiation, because [the jar] is differentiated from each successive [substance] by one, two, three, or even up to an infinite number of properties.

And with respect to its infinite constituent substances, the jar would possess each of the following infinite varieties: thickness, thinness, evenness, unevenness, subtlety, grossness, intensity, brilliance (or shimmering), gentleness, breadth, compactness, lowness, height, and broad-mouthedness, and so forth.

Furthermore, there are infinite properties by way of [attributes] such as grossness and so forth. However, in terms of relations, the relationship of support and supported between the aforementioned jar and its infinite other entities over infinite time becomes infinitely manifold; therefore, in relation to those as well, its own properties are infinite.

Thus, by means of relationships that transcend enumeration—such as those of self and owner, produced and producer, cause and effect, the sixfold modes of agency, the illuminated and the illuminator, the enjoyed and the enjoyer, the carried and the carrier, the locus and the located, the slain and the slayer, the opposed and the non-opposed, the knowable and the knower, and so forth—one must understand that there are infinite attributes for each [entity].

ñ335: Likewise, whatever infinite-infinite modes (paryāyas) of the pot—both its own and those of others—have been described here, their births, destructions, and durations, occurring through repeated manifestation over infinite time, have been, are being, and will be infinite; with respect to those as well, the properties (dharmas) are infinite. ñ336: Thus, beginning from the yellow color, there are infinitely many properties by way of their actual existence.

ñ337: Similarly, when both the self-attributes and other-attributes that have been explained through categories such as substance (dravya), location (kṣetra), and so forth, are predicated simultaneously, the pot would be "inexpressible" (avaktavya).

For there exists no such word by which both the intrinsic properties (*svadharma*) and extrinsic properties (*paradharma*) of a jar, being expressed, could be stated simultaneously; for those things denoted by a word are understood only in a sequential manner.

Even a conventionalized word conveys its own and others' properties only sequentially, not simultaneously, just as in the case of the word *sat* (being), which is conventionally assigned to both the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* according to the rule "the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* [occur] when *sat* [is present]."

Therefore, the "inexpressibility" (*avaktavyatā*) of a jar, according to each specific substance, location, and so forth, would also be its own property (*svadharma*). And since it is distinguished from infinite expressible properties as well as from other substances, there are also infinite "inexpressibles" that are extrinsic properties (*paradharma*). Thus, just as the nature of consisting of infinite properties has been demonstrated in the case of a jar, it should be meditated upon in the same way for every entity, such as the self (*ātman*) and so forth.

In that regard, within the self (*ātman*), there are first these co-existent attributes (*sahabhāvino dharmāḥ*): consciousness (*caitanya*), agency (*kartṛtva*), enjoyership (*bhoktṛtva*), the state of being a knower (*pramātṛtva*), the state of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*), incorporeality (*amūrtatva*), having innumerable spatial points (*asaṃkhyātapradeśatva*), the state of having eight immobile spatial points (*niścalāṣṭapradeśatva*), the state of having spatial points equal in measure to the universe (*lokapramāṇapradeśatva*), the state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*), the state of being incapable of liberation (*abhavyatva*), the state of being capable of liberation (*bhavyatva*), the state of undergoing transformation (*pariṇāmitva*), and pervasiveness of one's own body (*svaśarīravyāpitva*).

Joy and dejection, pleasure and pain, the cognitive and perceptual functions (*upayoga*) of knowledge such as mati and vision, the states of being a god, hell-being, animal, or human; the state of all *pudgala* matter having been transformed into the form of the body and so forth; beginninglessness and endlessness; the state of possessing all possible relations with all living beings; the state of being in *saṃsāra*; the possession of innumerable mental dispositions (*adhyavasāya*) such as anger and the rest; the sixfold group beginning with laughter; the states of being female, male, or neuter; dullness, blindness, and so forth—these and others are the attributes that occur in succession.

In the liberated soul (muktātman), however, there is perfection consisting of the following: beginninglessness and endlessness; knowledge, perception, right conviction, bliss, and vigor; infinite cognition and vision of all substances, locations, times, and all modifications; bodilessness; freedom from old age and death; the absence of form, taste, smell, touch, and sound; immobility; freedom from disease; inexhaustibility; invulnerability; and the various inherent attributes of its own soul as experienced during its previous state in saṃsāra, and so forth.

In the case of *dharma*, *adharma*, space (*ākāśa*), and time (*kāla*), there is the state of having innumerable, non-innumerable, and infinite points (*pradeśa*) and non-points (*apradeśa*) respectively; the quality of assisting all souls (*jīva*) and matter (*pudgala*) in their motion (*gati*), stability (*sthiti*), spatial occupation (*avagāha*), and temporal duration (*vartanā*); the state of being delimited by various delimiters and of being that which is delimited; the state of being stationary; the state of being without beginning or end; the state of being formless (*arūpitva*); the state of being neither heavy nor light and constituting a single aggregate (*ekaskandhatva*); the state of being an object of knowledge such as sensory cognition (*matijñāna*) and so forth; existence (*sattva*); substantiality (*dravyatva*); and so on.

Regarding individual substances (paudgalika-dravya), there are self- and other-modes (sva- and para-paryāya) according to the method explained by the example of the jar. In the case of sounds, these include: acute, grave, and circumflex accents; open and closed articulation; voiced and unvoiced quality; breathy and non-breathy quality; the capacity to express or not express meanings that are expressible or inexpressible; and the various powers to convey infinite meanings based on differences in factors such as location (kṣetra) and time (kāla).

Regarding the self and all other things, one must ascertain their nature as consisting of the universal and particular aspects of permanence and impermanence, existence and non-existence, and the expressible and inexpressible, as well as their properties of exclusion from other entities. (The description of the entity as it can be expressed in words.

An objection is raised: Let those modes (*paryāyas*) which belong to its own nature be related to it; however, how can those modes which belong to other things be designated as related to it, since they have distinct entities as their substrata?

It is said: here, relation is twofold, by way of existence and by way of non-existence. Among these, there is a relation by way of existence with its own modes (*paryāya*), as, for example, a jar [is related] to its form and other qualities. However, there is a relation by way of non-existence with the modes of others, because those [modes] are impossible therein; for example, in the state of a jar, [it is related] to the mode of the nature of clay. Precisely because they do not exist in it, they are connected through the relation of non-existence; and for that very reason, they are designated as "the modes of others."

[Objection: But how can things that do not exist in a certain place be designated as belonging to it? Indeed, it is not possible to designate wealth as belonging to a poor man simply because "wealth does not exist for the poor man. Let there be no transgression of worldly convention! [Response: This statement indeed indicates a mind deluded by great ignorance. It is not the case that wealth does not exist for the poor man, such that it could be designated as his property; let there be no overstepping of worldly usage. Therefore, this is merely a sign of a mind stupefied by profound delusion.

If, indeed, those [entities] are not designated as "belonging to that" with reference to their connection with non-existence, then it follows that they do not exist even in other entities in a general sense.

And in that case, they would not exist even by way of their own nature, which is neither observed nor accepted. Therefore, they must necessarily be designated as "belonging to that" with reference to their connection with non-existence.
Furthermore, wealth is indeed designated as belonging to a poor person with reference to its connection to non-existence; thus people in the world say, "This poor man has no wealth.

As for what was also said—that "it cannot be designated as 'belonging to him'"—even there, it cannot be designated as "his" by way of its existence, but not even by way of its non-existence; therefore, there is no transgression of worldly convention whatsoever.

[Objection: Is it not the case that non-existence (*nāstitva*) is an absence (*abhāva*), and absence is of a void nature (*tuccharūpa*); and how can there be a relation with that which is void? For the void, being devoid of all causal capacities (*śakti*), lacks even the capacity for relation. Furthermore: if non-existence consists in the absence of other modes (*paraparyāya*) therein, then let there be a relation with that non-existence; but how can there be a relation with those other modes themselves? Indeed, a jar that is related to the absence of a cloth cannot also be related to the cloth itself, because such a cognition does not occur.

This is incorrect, because it results from a failure to understand the true reality of things (*vastutattva*). For instance: what is called "non-existence" is simply the non-occurrence of a thing in this or that form, and it occurs only in relation to a particular state (*paryāya*), not otherwise. To illustrate: when a jar thinks, "I must not exist in the form of whatever state belongs to a cloth or the like," it follows by implication that the jar depends upon those respective states; this is well-established.

Therefore, since by various modes [of existence] there is the non-becoming of this or that [thing] in dependence upon this or that mode, those other modes are also useful for it, and thus they are designated as "belonging to it" (*tasya*). And when such an intention is expressed, even a cloth is indeed related to a jar; for in dependence upon the cloth, there exists the non-becoming of the jar in the form of the cloth. And likewise, even worldly people employ the term "related" with respect to jars, cloths, and so forth, on the basis of their mutual reciprocal non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*); this is beyond dispute.

Furthermore, these are designated as its "modes" (*paryāya*), because they function as qualifiers of its own modes. In this context, those things which serve as qualifiers of a thing's own modes are its modes; for example, color and other qualities are the modes of a jar, acting as mutual qualifiers.

Furthermore, the modes (*paryāya*) of cloth and so forth are utilized for the sake of the specific [modes] of a jar; for without them, those [modes of the jar] would lack the designation of their own modes. To explain: if those were not the modes of another, then the modes of the jar would not be designated as "its own modes. Since the designation of "own" exists only in relation to "other," those other modes are also useful to it by virtue of being the cause for the designation of its own modes; therefore, they are designated as "its" [modes]. (kkk)

Furthermore, every entity possesses a specific nature (*pratiniyatasvabhāva*), and that specific nature is dependent upon the absence of its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). Therefore, as long as there is no cognition of the counter-correlate, it is impossible to know the entity in its true reality as being of the nature of that absence. This being the case, since modalities such as cloth and so forth are also counter-correlates of a jar, if they are not fully understood, the jar cannot be apprehended according to its true nature; thus, modalities such as cloth and so forth are also modalities of the jar.

And thus, the formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: That which is not perceived when another is not perceived is related to that other; for example, the color and other qualities of a jar. And since the jar is not perceived in its true nature when the states (*paryāya*) such as the cloth are not perceived, those [states] are related to it. Nor is this reason (*hetu*) unestablished (*asiddha*); for if the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), whose form consists of the states such as the cloth, is not fully known, it is impossible to truly know the jar, which consists in the absence of that [counter-correlate]. And the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakṛt*) has said:
"That [jar] is not known when those [states] are unknown, and it is known when they are known."
"Whence are those [other] properties not [properties] of that [substance], like the properties of color and so forth belonging to a jar?

(1)" [That is: "Since [the substance] is not known when they are unknown, and it is known when they are known, how can those not be its properties, just as color and other properties belong to a jar? Therefore, even the modes (*paryāya*) such as cloth and the like are related to the jar; and the modes of others are infinite-fold compared to one's own modes. Both—namely, one's own and the modes of others—are equal in measure to the total number of modes of all substances. And this is not unscriptural, since it is stated in the *Ācārāṅga*:
"Whoever knows one thing, he knows all; whoever knows all, he knows one.

This is its meaning: whoever perceives a single object through all its modes (*paryāya*) necessarily perceives everything; for without the perception of all, it is impossible to comprehend a single intended object in its entirety, as it is differentiated by the distinctions between its own and other modes. And whoever directly perceives everything in its entirety knows that one [object] which is differentiated by the distinctions between its own and other modes. It has also been stated elsewhere:
"By whom a single entity is seen in every way, by him all entities are seen in every way;
by whom all entities are seen in every way, by him a single entity is seen in every way.
(1) Therefore, it is established that because of its knowability (*prameyatva*), every real thing consists of infinite properties (*anantadharmātmaka*). (55)
Then the author of the Sūtra himself defines the characteristics of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and indirect perception (*parokṣa*):

"Such knowledge as apprehends an object through its immediacy (*aparokṣatā*) is direct perception; the other is to be known as indirect perception by virtue of the observation of its apprehension. (56)

Commentary: In this context, "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) is the designation of the object to be defined; "the cognition that apprehends an object through its immediacy" (*aparokṣatayā*) is the designation of its definition.

*Parokṣa* (indirect) is that which has transcended the range of the senses; other than that is *aparokṣa* (direct). Its state (*tadbhāva*) is "that-ness" (*tattā*), by which [it is characterized], namely by directness, by way of immediate perception (*sākṣātkāritayā*). It is not, however, by way of being indistinct, doubtful, and so forth. [It is the cognition] that grasps an internal object—the nature of the self—and an external thing—such as a jar, a mat, a cloth, a cart, or a hut—by means of its determinate nature (*vyavasāyātmakatayā*), [thereby] directly discerning it. Because a qualifier functions as an exclusion, only such [cognition] is perception (*pratyakṣa*), and not any other kind.
By the phrase "by way of being non-mediately perceived" (*aparokṣatayā*), he eliminates the confusion of perception with the definition of the mediately perceived.
By this, it should be understood that the refutation is made of the definitions of perception postulated by others, such as "freedom from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and so forth.

The proponents of knowledge (*jñānavādins*) said: "O Ārhatas! Let it be explained here simply that perception (*pratyakṣa*) is that which apprehends the object (*artha*), which is the very nature of the self (*ātmasvarūpa*); why is the word *artha* explained as an external object? For there is no such thing as an external object. In response to this doubt, the phrase "by means of the observation of the apprehension" (*grahaṇekṣayā*), which will be stated later, should be connected even to the expression "that which apprehends the object. This is because the application of the phrase "by means of the observation of the apprehension" is intended specifically for those, such as the Yogācāras, who are intent on refuting external objects. — (Yogācāra)

Therefore, this is the meaning: perception (*pratyakṣa*) is that which, by depending upon the observation of the apprehension—that is, the cognition—of an external object as distinct from the knowledge itself, serves as the grasper (*grāhaka*) of that object. (This is the definition of perception.)

Nor should it be said that by the mere phrase "and not the apprehender of an object," it is established—relative to an external object—that whatever is an apprehender [of an object] is perception; for even by the phrase "the apprehender of an object which is the nature of the self," it indeed becomes an apprehender of an object. Therefore, by the expression "by means of the observation of apprehension," [the author] refutes those such as the Yogācāras who prattle that all cognition is devoid of any determination of an external object.

For just as internal self-awareness (*antah-samvedana*) functions in the apprehension of its own part, so too does it function in the apprehension of external objects; otherwise, in the absence of the apprehension of external objects, there would not be a uniform appearance of blue and so forth for all cognizers restricted to specific locations. Yet, such [an appearance] exists for everyone as restricted to specific locations; therefore, it is concluded that the object exists.

Now, if it is argued that there is no apprehension of external objects because it is simply the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) that appears in such and such a manner, then other mental continua (*santānāntara*), like external objects, would also be dissolved [into non-existence].

If, however, there exists an inference that establishes other mental continua—for instance: "The activity and speech of Yajñadatta and others, who are distinct from the intended Devadatta and so forth, are preceded by cognition, because they are activity and speech, just like the activity and speech of those [persons] currently agreed upon"—then [the existence of other continua is established].

If it is argued that the inference proving another mental continuum is established because the connection between one's own activity and speech and their being effects of cognition is ascertained, we say no; for by means of the dream-example, this very object of the inference would result in being erroneous.

For instance: "All cognitions are without an objective basis (nirālambana), because they are cognitions, like a dream-cognition. With this intention [it is argued]: just as there is an absence of external objects because the apprehension of external objects is without an objective basis, so too there would be an absence of other mental continua because the proof of other continua is itself without an objective basis. "Other than that, the object of knowledge is indirect (parokṣa)": other than the aforementioned direct perception (pratyakṣa), that which apprehends and determines its own or another's object in an indistinct manner is to be understood as indirect (parokṣa) knowledge.

Showing that even though this is indirect (*parokṣa*) with respect to external objects, it is indeed direct (*pratyakṣa*) with respect to self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), he says: "by the observation of its apprehension."

Here, "grasping" (grahaṇa) refers to the operation of cognition toward an external object that is not immediately present (*aparokṣa*), occurring by virtue of the context; it does not, however, mean the grasping of itself. For, if it were with respect to the grasping of itself, then since all cognitions would be perceptual (*pratyakṣa*) due to their clarity, there would be no [cognition] to be excluded, and thus the qualification would be redundant. Therefore, [the term *apekṣā*] means "by way of the requirement for the observation (*īkṣā*) of grasping—that is, of the outward-directed operation"; in other words, it means "by way of the consideration of the outward-directed activity."

Now, this is the meaning here: although [cognition] is direct (*pratyakṣa*) with respect to self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), nevertheless, because it functions by way of signs (*liṅga*), words (*śabda*), and so forth, in the apprehension of external objects through non-immediate perception, it is called "indirect" (*parokṣa*). //56//
Then, in order to further strengthen the previously stated fact that a real entity consists of infinite attributes, he says:
"That which is endowed with origination, destruction, and persistence is held to be existent;
therefore, a real entity possessing infinite attributes is said to be within the scope of valid cognition. (57)

Commentary: The word "yena" (by which) will be explained later. Because the sentence is restrictive (*sāvadhāraṇatvāt*), only that entity which is endowed with the combination of arising, passing away, and persistence is accepted as being existent (*sat*) or real. The meaning is that the very conjunction with arising, destruction, and stability is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of an existent entity.

[Objection: But if an entity that was previously non-existent becomes existent later through its conjunction with arising, passing away, and persistence, then even things such as a rabbit’s horn would possess existence, since they too could be joined with those [three characteristics].

If it exists previously, then its existence by way of its own nature (*svarūpasattva*) has already been attained; what, then, is the use of imagined [factors] such as arising? Likewise, if the existence of arising, passing away, and persistence were also due to their connection with another triad of arising and so forth, then an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result.

If, on the other hand, existence is intrinsic (*svataḥ*), then that will belong to the entity itself by its very nature; thus, the postulation of arising and so forth is useless. To this, it is replied:

For we do not maintain that an entity possesses existence merely through its connection with distinct arising, passing away, and persistence; rather, it is accepted that what is existent has as its very nature the connection with arising, passing away, and persistence.
To explain: every object, such as the earth, mountains, trees, and so forth, does not arise or perish in its substantial essence (*dravyātman*), because a clear continuity (*anvaya*) is observed.

It should not be argued that there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) due to the observation of continuity (anvaya) in cases such as nails that have been cut and grown back again; for the continuity that is sublated by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is not clearly established. Nor is the continuity under discussion contradicted by a means of valid cognition, because it is characterized by true recognition (pratyabhijñāna).
This is according to the statement: "In all individual manifestations, there is certainly a difference from moment to moment, yet there is no distinction [in their nature];
for the arrangement of form and genus is based on the reality of capacity and incapacity. (Vākyapadīya 3.1.40)

Therefore, by way of its substantial nature (*dravyātman*), every entity simply persists; however, by way of its modal nature (*paryāyātman*), every entity arises or perishes, because there exists the experience of modes that is unerring. Nor is there any deviation [from this rule] in the case of a white conch shell being experienced through yellow and other modes, for that experience is of a faltering nature. Indeed, it is not of an unfaltering nature such that the destruction of the previous form would be inseparable from the assumption of a subsequent form while not abandoning its function.

Furthermore, the experience of successive states such as joy, aversion, and indifference regarding a real entity like the *jīva* is not of a faltering nature, because there is no subverting factor [to contradict it].

If it is objected: "Are arising and the other [characteristics] mutually distinct, or not? If they are distinct, how can one thing possess a threefold nature? If they are not distinct, even so, how can one thing possess a threefold nature?"—that is incorrect; for we accept their distinction in some respect, since they possess characteristics that are distinct in some respect.
For instance: origination, destruction, and persistence would indeed be distinct, because they possess distinct characteristics, like color and other [sensory qualities].

Nor is the possession of distinct characteristics unestablished; for origination is the manifestation of the self-nature of what was non-existent, destruction is the separation from existence of what was existent, and persistence is the continuation in the form of a substance—since these are perceived by everyone as having such unmixed characteristics.
Furthermore, these are not distinct solely by virtue of being independent of one another; for things that are mutually independent would result in non-existence, like a barren woman’s son.
For instance: arising alone does not exist, because it is devoid of persistence and cessation, like a tortoise’s hair.

Likewise, destruction alone does not exist, because it is devoid of persistence and arising; it is just like that. Similarly, persistence alone does not exist, because it is empty of destruction and arising; it is exactly like that. Thus, one must understand that arising and the other [phases] exist in a thing only through their mutual dependence. And so, how could that which is threefold not be one? As it has been said:
"When the jar was destroyed, she grieved; when the crown was produced for her son..."
The son spoke words of affection, yet the king maintained an attitude of neutrality;
for it is established that reality consists of these three aspects— the cessation of the previous form, the arising of another form, and the maintenance of both— because such is our cognition.

One who desires a jar, a crown, or gold undergoes grief, joy, or indifference according to the cause, based on their destruction, production, or persistence. One observing a milk-vow does not eat curd, nor does one observing a curd-vow drink milk.
"Neither [of these two alternatives] is possible for one who maintains the vow of non-duality; therefore, the object consists of three natures.

[Āptamīmāṃsā 59–60] For the opponent must be asked this: when a jar perishes, does it perish partially (deśena) or in its entirety (sāmastyena)? If the position is that it perishes partially, then only one part of the jar would perish, not the whole; yet it is observed that the entire jar has perished. Furthermore, no one would have the perception that "only one part of the jar is broken. Therefore, the position that it perishes partially is not worthy of acceptance.

Nor is the position that [the pot] perishes in its entirety tenable. For if the pot were to perish in its entirety, then once the pot has perished, there would be no perception of the shards or the nature of the clay, because the pot would have perished in all its parts. Yet, at that time, the shards and the nature of the clay are indeed perceived, for there is the cognition: "These are shards made of clay, not of gold. Therefore, the position that it perishes in its entirety is also not logical.
Therefore, this must necessarily be accepted: a jar perishes in its nature as a jar, it arises in its nature as shards, but it remains constant in its nature as the substance of clay.
Likewise, when a jar arises, the opponent must also be asked: does it arise in part, or does it arise in its entirety?
If he says "in part," then the jar would be perceived as having arisen only in part, and not as being whole.
Furthermore, a jar is perceived as "full" and "produced"; therefore, the position that [the jar is produced] by way of its location is not able to withstand scrutiny.

Nor is the position that it is produced in its entirety tenable. If it were produced in its entirety, then at that time there would be no perception of the clay; yet such is not the case, for there is indeed the perception: "This is made of clay, and not of gold. Consequently, one must necessarily admit that when the jar arises, it arises in the form of a jar, it perishes in the form of a lump of clay, and it remains constant in the form of clay.
For if a thing were not accepted as it is perceived by everyone, then the determination of all things would never be possible. Therefore, a thing must exist exactly as it is perceived.

For this very reason, that which has perished is precisely what has perished and will somehow perish; that which has arisen is precisely what has arisen and will somehow arise; and that which thus remains is precisely what remains and will somehow remain.

Likewise, that very thing which has perished in one form has arisen in another form and persists in yet another; for thus, everything—whether internal or external—is at all times experienced by uncontradicted direct perception as consisting precisely of these three states, such as arising and so forth. And since contradiction cannot be established regarding the intrinsic nature of a thing as it is being experienced, otherwise there would follow the absurdity of contradiction even among a thing's own color, taste, and other qualities.

And the formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: Every entity consists of origination, destruction, and persistence; because it exists. Whatever does not consist of origination, destruction, and persistence does not exist, even if it were [supposedly] existent; for example, a donkey’s horn. And this [subject] is like that; therefore, it is so. This is a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekānumāna*).

By this definition of existence (*sal-lakṣaṇa*), both the "connection with Being" (*sattā-yoga*) postulated by the Naiyāyikas and others, as well as the "existence characterized by causal efficiency" (*arthakriyā-lakṣaṇa-sattva*) favored by the Buddhists, should be understood as refuted. The manner of that refutation is to be understood from other texts.

Now, the word "by which" (*yena*) is to be applied [to the following]: for the reason that "existent" (*sat*) is held to be endowed with origination, destruction, and persistence; for that reason, it is the object (*gocara* or *viṣaya*) of the two means of valid cognition (*māna*), namely perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*parokṣa*).

"Endowed with infinite attributes" (*anantadharmaka*) means that in which there are infinite attributes—such as existence, knowability, measurability, substantiality, and so forth—which consist of infinite modes (*paryāya*), that is to say, which are of a non-absolutist (*anekānta*) nature. "Entity" (*vastu*) refers to the categories of the living (*jīva*), the non-living (*ajīva*), and so on; this has been stated or declared. The underlying point is this: since an entity is ultimately real precisely because it consists of the triad of origination and the rest (*utpādāditraya*), for that very reason every entity is an object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it consists of infinite attributes; for it is only when there is the state of consisting of infinite attributes that the state of consisting of origination, destruction, and persistence arises, since otherwise that [state] would be untenable.

In this context, the repeated use of the term "possessing infinite attributes" (*anantadharmaka*) is intended solely to demonstrate that it is precisely for that which consists of infinite attributes that the nature of arising, passing away, and persistence is logically established; one should not suspect tautology here with the term "possessing infinite attributes" mentioned in the subsequent verse.

And thus the formal argument (*prayoga*): An entity consists of infinite properties (*anantadharmātmaka*), because it consists of origination, destruction, and persistence (*utpādavyayadhrauvyātmakatvāt*). Whatever does not consist of infinite properties also does not consist of origination, destruction, and persistence; for example, a sky-lotus (*viyadindīvaram*). This is a negative inference (*vyatireky-anumāna*). Furthermore, as has already been shown, infinite properties exist within a single entity. Properties arise and perish, while the substratum (*dharmī*), in its form as substance (*dravya*), remains eternally constant.

If the substratum (*dharmin*) exists eternally as something distinct from its properties (*dharmas*) in some way, then those properties existing throughout the three times must also exist eternally in some way, by virtue of their nature as potentialities (*śakti*); otherwise, if the properties were non-existent, it would follow that the substratum—which is in some way non-different from them—would also be non-existent.

Furthermore, properties are neither absolutely different nor absolutely non-different from the substratum, because they are not perceived as such, and because they are perceived as being in some way non-different from it.

Nor should it be said that there is simply the non-existence of another substratum (dharmin) apart from the existence of this or that phenomenon (dharma) as it arises or perishes; for phenomena devoid of a substratum are never perceived, and they are always cognized only as having a single substratum.

Even though phenomena that arise and perish are manifold, it is impossible to deny the substratum (*dharmin*) which, though single, consists of those various manifold properties and exists as a substance (*dravya*) that is constant, being the object of uncontradicted perception; for if one were to deny the substratum—even though it is the object of uncontradicted perception—it would follow that all its properties must likewise be denied.

And thus, since it would follow that all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) would be abolished, it is established that an entity consists of infinite properties (*anantadharmātmaka*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: the subject of dispute is an entity whose nature consists of properties such as unity and multiplicity, permanence and impermanence, existence and non-existence, generality and particularity, the expressible and the inexpressible, and so forth; because it is perceived by a clear cognition in exactly that way.

Whatever is perceived by a non-erroneous cognition must be accepted as being within the scope of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) exactly in that way; just as a jar, being perceived in its form as a jar, is accepted as being within the scope of valid cognition precisely as a jar, and not as a cloth.
In the same way, an object perceived by a non-erroneous cognition must therefore be accepted as being within the scope of valid cognition as having a nature that is both one and many.
Nor is the reason here unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*); for the property of being perceived by an unerring cognition exists in every entity whatsoever.

Indeed, it is not unestablished for anyone that every category of object—consisting of substance and mode, of the nature of one and many, and of the nature of eternal and non-eternal; consisting of existence and non-existence by way of its own form and the forms of others; consisting of the universal and the particular by way of the forms of inclusion and exclusion from homogeneous and heterogeneous things; and consisting of the expressible and inexpressible because its own and other modes are respectively apprehended sequentially and are inexpressible simultaneously—is cognized through unerring cognition.

For that very reason, it is not "unestablished due to doubt" (*samdigdhāsiddha*); for indeed, there is no such thing as "doubt" regarding an entity that is perceived as being non-sublating. Nor is it "contradictory" (*viruddha*), because it lacks the capacity to establish a contradictory object.

For there is no such thing as the unswerving perception—by means of which it would be contradictory—of either the absolute substance (*dravya*) or the absolute mode (*paryāya*) favored by the Sāṃkhyas and Buddhists, or of the mutually distinct substance and mode accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas and Naiyāyikas.
Nor is there any sublation of the thesis by perception or other means of valid cognition, which would render the reason ineffective.

Nor is there any deficiency of the probandum or the probans in the example; for it has already been demonstrated that the pot's nature as possessing properties such as unity and plurality, as well as its being perceived by non-erroneous cognition, are not unestablished. Therefore, having heard this faultless formal argument, why is it not accepted that [the reason] is not inconclusive?

[Objection: But surely, how can the non-absolutism (anekānta) regarding existence, non-existence, permanence, impermanence, and so forth, maintain its steadfastness in order to sustain its own life, given that it is bitten by the venomous serpents of defects such as insurmountable contradiction?

[Response: For instance, how can that very entity which is existent be nonexistent? And if it is nonexistent, how can there be a contradiction? This is because existence and nonexistence are established through mutual exclusion, like the sensations of cold and heat.

Furthermore, if existence were established through the nature of non-existence, and non-existence through the nature of existence, then, due to the lack of distinction between existence and non-existence, there would be the abolition of determinate conventional usage. The same should be said regarding permanence, impermanence, and so forth.

Likewise, if a thing were accepted as consisting of both existence and non-existence, there would be doubt because there would be no determination by way of the restrictive judgment, "This thing is existent" or "It is non-existent.
Similarly, by whichever part it is existent, is it existent *only* by that part, or is it [both] existent and non-existent even by that?

If the first position is held, then there would be a loss of the *syād-vāda* (the doctrine of manifoldness). In the second case, however, one must ask: is that aspect by which it exists simply existence, or is there non-existence even in that? This leads to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Likewise, regarding the aspect by which there is difference: is that simply difference, or is there non-difference even in that? In the first case, there is a destruction of your own doctrine; in the second, there is again an infinite regress. The same should be stated regarding permanence and impermanence, universals and particulars, and so forth.

Likewise, there would be a lack of common locus (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), because the locus of existence would be one thing and the locus of non-existence another. Furthermore, there would be a confusion (*saṃkara*) such that by the very form in which something exists, it would simultaneously be both existent and non-existent; for it is said: "Confusion is the simultaneous occurrence of both. Moreover, there would be a mutual perversion (*vyatikara*), such that by the form in which something exists, it would also be non-existent, and by the form in which it is non-existent, it would also be existent; for it is said: "Perversion is the entering into each other's domains."

Likewise, if it is accepted that everything possesses a nature of manifoldness (anekāntātmatva), then even water and other substances would possess the form of fire and so forth, and fire and other substances would also possess the form of water and so forth. Consequently, one seeking water would act toward fire and the like, and one seeking fire would act toward water and the like. Thus, there would be the loss of determinate worldly practice (vyavahāra). Furthermore, this would contradict valid means of knowledge such as direct perception (pratyakṣa) and others. Therefore, such a thing is simply impossible.

To this it is replied: That which was stated by the preeminent among the hosts of disputants—namely, "How can that which is existent be non-existent," and so forth—is merely a fabrication of words; for there is no possibility of a contradiction between existence and non-existence when they are perceived [as distinct]. This is because such a contradiction is defined by non-perception [of the two together], like a suckling infant in the womb of a barren woman.

Furthermore, while a thing exists by way of its own nature (*svarūpa*) and so forth, there is no non-perception of its non-existence by way of another nature (*pararūpa*) at that very same time, such that there would be a contradiction characterized by non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*), as in the case of cold and heat.

However, contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion could only occur between existence and non-existence when both are possible in a single locus, such as a mango fruit, just as color and taste [coexist]; it cannot occur between two things that are impossible, nor between those that are respectively possible and impossible.

By this, even in the case of contradiction consisting in the relationship of predator and prey—as observed between a snake and a mongoose, which are respectively strong and weak—the coexistence of existence and non-existence is not to be suspected; for those two possess equal strength, like the various colors in the fluid of a peacock's egg.

Furthermore, is this contradiction caused by the mere existence of their own essential natures (*svarūpa*); or by the impossibility of [their] coexistence at one time; or by the impossibility of [their] subsisting in a single substance; or by the absence of both one time and one substance; or by the impossibility of [their] existing at one time, in one substance, and in one location?

Regarding these, the first [option] is not tenable. For it is not the case that the sensation of cold, by its very existence as such without depending on any other cause, is contradictory with the sensation of heat; nor is the sensation of heat so with the other. Otherwise, there would be an absence of these two even throughout the three worlds.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable; for even at a single time, both [qualities] are perceived separately.
Nor is the third; for even in a single metal vessel, a cold touch is perceived at night and a hot touch during the day, yet there is no contradiction therein.
Nor is the fourth; for both are perceived together in things such as an incense-ladle (*kaḍucchaka*).

The fifth [alternative] is also untenable; for in a single heated iron vessel, there is heat in a particular location relative to touch, yet in that very same location there is coldness relative to color. For if there were heat even relative to color, it would follow that the eyes would be burned.

If it is asked, "How can a single entity possess two mutually exclusive forms simultaneously?", we say no; for just as in the case of a single person, through the force of relative dependence (*apekṣā*), qualities such as lightness and heaviness, childhood, old age, youth, sonship, fatherhood, teacherhood, and pupilship—which are mutually contradictory—are nonetheless non-contradictory simultaneously, so too are existence, non-existence, and the like.
Therefore, absolute contradiction among entities is not tenable; rather, a contradiction that exists only in some respect is common to all entities and does not constitute a sublation.

Likewise, doubt is also not tenable, because existence and non-existence are perceived in their distinct forms. Doubt arises only when there is an unstable perception, as in the case of a post and a person in a certain place.

Furthermore, that which was stated regarding "infinite regress" is the speech of one who has not served a guru; for existence, non-existence, and so forth, are properties (*dharma*) of the entity (*vastu*) itself, and not properties of properties, according to the statement: "There are no properties of properties."

Nor does the acceptance of this [non-absolutism] entail the loss of non-absolutism (anekānta) through the admission of absolutism (ekānta), because non-absolutism is correctly inseparable from absolutism; otherwise, non-absolutism itself could not be established. This is because absolutism is presented as a perspective (naya), while non-absolutism alone is taught as the valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa); thus, it is established as being consistent with both what is observed and what is accepted. Furthermore, even if existence is established by the presentation of the means of knowledge, let there also be the conceptualization of both existence and non-existence; there is no fault whatsoever in that regard.

If it is argued that "an infinite regress (anavasthā) has already been mentioned," we say no; for even that is an ornament of non-absolutism (anekānta), not a defect, because it actually serves to illuminate non-absolutism by preventing its total destruction. Indeed, an infinite regress is a defect only when it causes the destruction of the root. As it has been said: "An infinite regress is indeed called a defect when it causes the destruction of the root.
Even when there is an infinity of entities or an incapacity [to reach them], an infinite regress is not to be avoided. (1)

Therefore, in whatever manner the conceptualization of existence or non-existence is applied even to a sentient being, in that very same manner it serves only to illuminate the doctrine of non-absolutism (anekānta), and not to destroy the fundamental reality.

For instance: here, all categories of existence possess existence by their own nature (*svarūpa*) and non-existence by the nature of others (*pararūpa*). In this regard, for the soul (*jīva*), its general capacity for cognition (*upayoga*) is its own nature, because that is its defining characteristic; anything other than that, namely non-cognition, is the nature of others. Through these two, its existence and non-existence are perceived.

Furthermore, regarding their application: the specific nature of cognition (*jñāna*) is the determination of its own object’s form, while the nature of vision (*darśana*) is the apprehension of the formless. That which is contrary to these is the "other-nature" (*pararūpa*). Consequently, through these two [natures], existence and non-existence are established even in that case.

Furthermore, for knowledge as well, the nature of indirect cognition is lack of clarity (*avaiśadya*), while the nature of direct perception is clarity (*vaiśadya*); for vision (*darśana*) as well, the nature caused by the eye and non-eye [senses] is the visual apprehension (*ālocana*) of the eye and so forth, and the nature of limited vision (*avadhi-darśana*) is the apprehension by means of the limited [clairvoyance]. Anything else is the "other-nature" (*pararūpa*). Therefore, by means of these two [natures], existence and non-existence are established even in that case.

Even for indirect (*parokṣa*) sensory-cognition (*mati-jñāna*), its nature consists in the apprehension of its own object through the instrumentality of the senses and the non-senses (*anindriya*); the nature of scriptural-cognition (*śruta*) consists in being caused by the non-sense alone; even for direct (*pratyakṣa*) cognition that is partial—namely, limited vision (*avadhi*) and mind-reading (*manah-paryāya*)—its nature consists in the clear apprehension of an object without dependence on the mind or the senses; the nature of complete direct perception (*kevala-pratyakṣa*) consists in the direct realization of all substances and all their modes (*paryāya*); anything other than these is the "other-nature" (*pararūpa*).

Furthermore, existence and non-existence must be understood in relation to those two [aspects] as well.
