In this manner, the knowers of reality should infer the subsequent distinctions regarding both the intrinsic and extrinsic natures of things, for the distinctions among those specific attributes are infinite.
Likewise, the delineation of the intrinsic and extrinsic natures of objects such as pots and cloths should be performed; and based on that, their existence and non-existence are to be established.
Thus, even when a thing exists, the conceptualization of its existence and non-existence serves only to illuminate non-absolutism (anekānta); it does not lead to any other conclusion whatsoever.

[Objection: But surely, even if one conceives of existence as another property of existence, the statement that "the properties of a property do not exist" would be contradicted. [Response: Do not speak thus. You are still unacquainted with the nectar-like secrets of the doctrine of non-absolutism (syādvāda); for a property such as existence, which is a property in relation to its own substratum (dharmin), becomes the substratum itself in relation to another property of its own. It is precisely in this way that the establishment of a manifold nature (anekāntātmaka) is logically consistent.

Furthermore, even when one conceives of another existent (*sattva*) within an existent, the former existent possesses the status of the subject (*dharmin*), while the other existent possesses the status of the property (*dharma*). Since it is precisely the subject that is accepted as having properties, there is no room for the previously mentioned fault. Nor does this lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) because the subject itself would acquire the status of a subject in relation to yet another property; for the conventional usage of "property" and "subject" is beginningless and endless—like the continuous flow of day and night, like the sequence of seed and sprout, or like the cycle of *saṃsāra* which cannot be transcended. This same principle should be stated regarding the distinctions of permanence and impermanence, difference and non-difference, and so forth.

Likewise, even the lack of a common substratum (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) is non-existent; for in uncontradicted perceptual cognition, existence and non-existence appear as having a single substratum. Indeed, there is no lack of a common substratum between two things appearing in such a manner, because otherwise it would follow that color and taste—even though they reside in a single fruit—would also lack a common substratum. Furthermore, both confusion (*saṃkara*) and intermixture (*vyatikara*) are to be refuted by the example of variegated cognition (*mecaka-jñāna*); just as variegated cognition, though unitary, possesses multiple natures, yet neither confusion nor intermixture occurs therein, so it is here as well.

Furthermore, just as when the middle and little fingers of the ring finger are joined simultaneously, there is neither shortness nor length, and no fault such as confusion arises therein; so it is here as well.

Likewise, as for what was stated—that "even water and the like possess the nature of fire and the like"—that too is for the most part like the ravings of one intoxicated by great delusion. For instance, water and the like possess the nature of water and so forth with respect to their own nature (*svarūpa*), not with respect to the nature of another (*pararūpa*). Consequently, there is no logical consequence that those seeking water would engage with fire and the like. This is because we accept that everything consists of the essence of all things through its own and other modes (*sva-para-paryāya*); otherwise, the very nature of a real entity (*vastu-svarūpa*) would be untenable.
Furthermore, by way of their past and future states, even water-atoms possess the nature of fire in relation to the dimensions of fire that have existed or will exist.

Likewise, in the case of heated water, the nature of fire is indeed admitted to belong to the water in some sense. What possible sublation by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) could there be against existence and non-existence as they appear in cognitions such as direct perception?
For there is no such thing as "the impossible in what is observed"; otherwise, that [charge of impossibility] would follow everywhere.

Furthermore, it is not possible to conceive of the non-existence of that which is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) and result in the total collapse of conventional discourse regarding valid cognition and so forth.

By this, even that which is said—namely, "In the case of non-absolutism (anekānta), valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is also invalid, the omniscient one (*sarvajña*) is also not omniscient, and what is established is also unestablished," and so forth—is merely a stringing together of syllables; for the proponents of the doctrine of manifoldness (*syād-vāda*) certainly maintain that even a valid cognition is valid with respect to its own object and invalid with respect to the objects of others. Likewise, even an omniscient one is omniscient with respect to his own perfect knowledge (*kevala-jñāna*), but not omniscient with respect to the knowledge of transmigrating souls (*saṃsārika-jīva*).

If he were omniscient even in relation to that [other being], then it would follow that all living beings are omniscient, or else it would follow that omniscience itself is merely a form of knowledge belonging to those still in the state of spiritual development (chādmasthika).

Even one who has attained perfection (siddha) is considered perfected only in relation to the destruction of the conjunction of his own karmic atoms; however, in relation to the conjunction of the karma of other living beings, he is not yet perfected.

If [the soul] were established even in dependence upon that [action], then it would follow that all living beings are already liberated (*siddha*). Thus, everything that others assert—such as "even what has been done is not done," "even what has been said is not said," or "even what has been experienced is not experienced"—is to be understood as refuted. Now, is the destruction of karma for the liberated (*siddhas*) absolute or partial? In the first case, there is the loss of non-absolutism (*anekānta*).
In the second case, since there would be no total destruction of karma even for the liberated, it follows that they are not liberated at all, just like transmigrating souls (*saṃsārin*).

To this it is replied: Even the exhaustion (*kṣaya*) of one's own karmas occurs in the wheel [of existence] with respect to their duration (*sthiti*), intensity (*anubhāga*), and nature (*prakṛti*), but not with respect to the atoms (*paramāṇu*).

For indeed, the destruction of atoms cannot be brought about by anyone; otherwise, if things such as jars were reduced to atoms by Mudgala and others, it would follow that all things would cease to exist after some period of time. Therefore, even in that case, there is only non-absolutism (*anekānta*); thus it is established that the teaching of non-absolutism is not contradicted by what is perceived or what is accepted.
(All doctrines can be subsumed within *syādvāda*.)

For these Buddhists and others, although they themselves accept the doctrine of *syād-vāda* through reasoning, they nevertheless refute it with mere words; they surely imitate the conduct of a man who, proud of his noble lineage, declares his own mother to have been unchaste since birth.
To illustrate this: first, the non-absolutism (*anekānta*) accepted by the Sugatas is set forth.

Since perception apprehends an object that is common to both the momentary and the non-momentary, even if the non-momentariness is superimposed due to some cause of error, perception is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding non-momentariness; on the contrary, it is invalid, because it is overcome by a contrary conceptual determination (*viparītādhyavasāya*).

Even if [the object] were momentary, that [perception] would not be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it does not produce a corresponding determinate judgment (*adhyavasāya*); whereas in the case of the form "blue," it is a means of valid cognition because it produces such a certainty. Thus, for those Buddhists who argue in this way, the non-validity of a single perception regarding both its momentariness and non-momentariness follows, while its validity regarding blue and so forth is established; consequently, the acceptance of the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*) follows by necessity.

Likewise, for those who accept two forms for a single conceptual cognition—one which, arising after the act of perception, determines its own internal aspect as being the external object (thus possessing conceptualization), and another which, regarding its own nature, is non-conceptual according to the statement that "all minds and mental factors are direct perception with respect to self-awareness"—how can they avoid falling into the doctrine of manifoldness (*anekāntavāda*)?

Likewise, that very same cognition—such as the mind [directed toward] abstaining from violence, giving, and so forth—which is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to the nature of consciousness and pleasure as they are experienced through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), is precisely that which is not a valid means of knowledge with respect to such qualities as momentary destruction or the capacity to attain heaven. Thus, there is indeed an inconclusiveness (*anekānta*).

Similarly, how could there not be an inconclusiveness in the case where an object is a knowable (*prameya*) by way of its form as blue, quadrangular, vertical, and so on, yet is not a knowable by way of its middle part, its momentary transformation, and so forth?

Likewise, the Buddhists maintain that even a conceptual cognition, such as the perception of dreams and the like, which is erroneous with respect to external objects, is nonetheless non-erroneous with respect to its own nature. Similarly, they accept that while a pair of moons and so forth is false in its duality, it is not false with respect to its whiteness, its fixed location, and its movement.

And how could an erroneous cognition, not perceiving itself as having the nature of error yet apprehending itself as having the nature of cognition, fail to establish two contradictory intrinsic natures within its own self?
Likewise, with respect to preceding and succeeding moments, they have accepted that a single moment possesses both the state of being produced and the state of being a producer.

Similarly, thinking that cognition bearing the form of the object alone is the grasper of the object and not otherwise, they have maintained that even a single cognition grasping a variegated cloth does not possess multiple forms.
Likewise, how could the wisdom of the Sugata not be manifold, having all things as its object and assuming all possible forms?

Similarly, [the Vaibhāṣikas] accepted that from a single logical reason there arises both positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—by virtue of its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and its presence in similar instances (*sapakṣasattva*)—and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—by virtue of its absence in dissimilar instances (*vipakṣe 'vidyamānatvāt*)—even though these two are mutually contradictory.

Thus, those Buddhists such as the Vaibhāṣikas, who, despite personally adopting the doctrine of manifoldness (*syādvāda*), point out contradictions therein, become nothing but objects to be ignored by the discerning; for their capacity for discrimination has been rendered vast yet obscured by the mass of darkness born from their blindness toward their own teachings.
Furthermore, according to the Sautrāntika view, a single cause exists which, by being included within a successive series of causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), produces multiple effects.

For example, a form (*rūpa*) contained within a complex consisting of color, taste, odor, and so forth, produces its own subsequent moment of form by way of being the substantial cause (*upādāna-bhāva*), while it produces the moments of taste and so forth by way of being a cooperative cause (*sahakāri-tva*). And that very same form, when included within another complex consisting of form, light, mental attention (*manasikāra*), the eye, and so forth, produces the cognition of a person by way of being a cooperative cause.

Furthermore, regarding the subsequent moments such as illumination and so forth: if a single cause thus produces multiple effects simultaneously, does it do so by means of a single intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or by means of multiple intrinsic natures?

If it were by means of a single intrinsic nature, then because the effects would be produced by a single intrinsic nature, there could be no distinction between them. Alternatively, why is it that even an eternal entity, while producing various effects by means of a single intrinsic nature, is not [likewise] refuted?

Now, if it is argued that because a permanent entity possesses a single nature, the production of diverse effects is not possible, then how could an impermanent entity produce them either? For [it too] possesses a partless, single nature.

If you say that it produces them due to a difference in auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*), then let that same [production] occur for the permanent entity as well, due to a difference in auxiliary conditions.
If you say that the impermanent entity produces them by means of diverse natures, then let the permanent entity likewise be the cause of those [effects].

Now, if various intrinsic natures are not possible for that which is eternal—because that which is eternally immutable possesses a single intrinsic nature—then likewise, various intrinsic natures do not exist for that which is non-eternal either, because it possesses a single partless intrinsic nature.
Thus, since the same fault applies equally to both the eternal and the non-eternal, it is better to accept that a real entity consists of both the eternal and the non-eternal.
In this way, the entire web of faults arising from the positions of absolute eternity or absolute non-eternity is avoided. (Sautrāntika)

Even the followers of the Tathāgata who profess [the existence of] cognition (*jñānavādin*), while themselves experiencing that the single consciousness which is undivided from the forms of the self and the object is distinct from the forms of the apprehended and the apprehender, how could they possibly refute the *syād-vāda*? Likewise, you do not experience the state of consciousness being devoid of the forms of the apprehended and the apprehender even in a dream; for if such a state were experienced, it would follow that all living beings are now liberated, according to the statement: "Liberation is the arising of the knowledge of reality."

And we also perceive that there is a perception; for even if one were to argue that it is a mere appearance, since there is a perception of the perception itself, the manifestation of multiplicity—arising from the fact that [the object] has been experienced by means of that experience—is difficult to deny. 2.

Likewise, the cognition of everything, by being apprehended through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) as empty of the forms of subject and object, while not cognizing itself [as such], yet experiencing its own nature as consciousness, would indeed reject the doctrine of absolute existence (*sad-ekāntavāda*), because it is of a nature other than conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Similarly, even the form of the object (*grāhyākāra*), which simultaneously manifests multiple objects, rejects the doctrine of absolute unity by virtue of its variegated singular nature (*citraikarūpatā*); thus, it rejects the doctrine of absolutism. (The Buddhist Cognitivist).
Now, it is demonstrated how the doctrine of manifoldness (*syād-vāda*) was accepted by the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas.

From the contact of the sense organs with their objects and so forth, the cognition of smoke arises; from that, the cognition of fire arises. In this context, the contact of the sense organs and so forth is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); its fruit is the cognition of smoke; and the cognition of smoke, in relation to the cognition of fire, is the means of valid cognition known as inference (*anumāna*).

However, the cognition of fire is the fruit of inference. Thus, they accept that the cognition of smoke possesses a dual nature, being both the fruit of perception and a means of valid cognition through inference.

In the same way, in other cases of cognition as well, the status of being a result (*phalatā*) and the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*) should be understood as appropriate, depending on the preceding and the subsequent.

In this very manner, [the Vaiśeṣikas] accept that the form of a composite whole (*avayavin*), such as a variegated cloth, possesses a manifold aspect (*vicitrākāra*), and they do not declare this to be contradictory. As it is stated in the *Kandalī*: "If it is argued that it is untenable for one thing to have a manifold nature because of contradiction, we say no. For there is a common saying among the learned: 'If it is one, how can it be variegated? If it is variegated, whence is its unity?'"
"And likewise, that which is variegated (*citra*)—this is considered even more variegated. "What contradiction is there? and so forth.

There is no irrationality regarding a form whose nature is variegated (*citratman*); for that [form], which arises through the efficacy of diverse causes, has been established by perception itself, which is renowned for its universal validity, as stated in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya* (p.
30) and elsewhere: "In one part of a single incense-spoon (*dhūpakaḍucchuka*), there is a cold touch, while in another part, there is a hot touch."

Even though the parts are distinct, because the whole is one, those two touches would belong to a single entity and would thus be contradictory. For it has been established that even when a single cloth or similar object is perceived to possess many contradictory properties—such as being moving and stationary, dyed and undyed, covered and uncovered—there is not even a scent of contradiction.

Furthermore, the desire to create and the desire to dissolve belonging to the eternal Lord (Īśvara), which consist of the qualities of *rajas* and *tamas* respectively, as well as His eightfold forms such as Earth, Water, and so forth, which consist of the quality of *sattva*, are mutually contradictory.
5. For a single *āmalaka* fruit, both "largeness" and "smallness" exist in relation respectively to a *kuvala* and a *bilva* fruit; these two [qualities] are contradictory.
6. Likewise, for a sugar cane, both "shortness" and "length" exist in relation respectively to a firewood stick and a bamboo pole.
7. For Devadatta and others, both "remoteness" and "proximity" exist in relation respectively to their father and their son.

Furthermore, there is another [category] called *sāmānya* (generality), which is termed *sāmānyaviśeṣa* (generality-particular). And the *sāmānyaviśeṣa* is characterized by substantiality (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), and action-ness (*karmatva*).

For substantiality is a generality because it exists in the nine substances, and it is a particular because it excludes qualities and actions. In the same way, the status of being both a generality and a particular should be understood for quality-ness and action-ness as well. Thus, it is a "generality-particular" (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) because it is both a generality and a particular. It is contradictory for that single entity to possess both the state of being a generality and the state of being a particular.

Nine: Those who maintain that five forms are attributed to one and the same cause—for instance, that a single earth-atom possesses existence (*sattva*) due to its connection with existence, substantiality (*dravyatva*) due to its connection with substantiality, earthness (*pṛthivītva*) due to its connection with earthness, atomhood (*paramāṇutva*) due to its connection with atomhood, and distinctness from other atoms due to ultimate particularity (*antyaviśeṣa*)—are forced by necessity to admit that the atom consists of both the universal and the particular. This is because if existence and the other properties were distinct from the atom, it would follow that the atom lacks existence, substantiality, earthness, and so forth. Ten.

In this way, that [distinction] should also be understood to apply to space and the other [elements]. For yogins, regarding atoms—which are eternal and possess identical form, quality, and activity—as well as liberated souls, there arises a cognition that "this is distinct from that" with respect to each substrate; those [substrates] from which such a cognition arises are the ultimate particulars (*viśeṣas*). In this regard, if both the identity of form, quality, and activity and the state of being distinct were predicated of each substrate, it would merely establish a logical contradiction (*syād-vāda*).

Thus, how can the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas not become objects of ridicule among the wise, for they strive to refute [the Buddhist position] while simultaneously accepting the inconclusiveness (*anekānta*) of the self?

Furthermore, if non-exclusivity (anekānta) is accepted, this is an advantage: when considering how [entities] such as parts and wholes, which are mutually distinct, subsist in one another, the entire web of objections that descends upon us is thereby avoided.

For instance: the Naiyāyikas and others maintain that there is an absolute mutual difference between the parts (*avayava*) and the whole (*avayavin*), and not merely a partial one. Consequently, they deserve this critical inquiry: when the whole exists in its parts, does it exist by way of a single part (*ekadeśena*) or in its entirety (*sāmastyena*)? If it exists by way of a single part, that is untenable, because the whole is admitted to be partless (*niravayavatva*). Even if it were to have parts, if the whole were non-different from those [parts], then the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anekāntāpatti*) would follow, since a single, partless entity would result in having multiple parts.

Now, if the whole (*avayavin*) is distinct from those parts, then it must be stated how it exists in them: by way of occupying a single part (*ekadeśena*) or in its entirety (*sāmastyena*). If the position is that it occupies a single part, then the same problem recurs for each part, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If, on the other hand, it exists in them in its entirety, that too is untenable; for since the whole would be completely present in each individual part, it would follow that there are as many wholes as there are parts.
Therefore, a whole distinct from those parts cannot withstand logical analysis.

If it is argued: "But even in the case of non-difference (*abheda*), would there not be either only the whole (*avayavin*) or only the parts (*avayava*)," we say no; for non-difference is not admitted as being absolute. Rather, a whole is accepted in relation to its parts as having a nature that is mutually inseparable, yet whose distinctions are to be displayed according to the speaker's intention. This is because in all cases where appearances are uncontradicted, the mutual difference and non-difference of wholes is perceived. Otherwise, if one were to conceptualize things appearing in one way as being otherwise, it would follow that one could likewise conceptualize the monism of Brahman (*brahmādvaita*), nihilism (*śūnyatāvāda*), and so forth.

Thus, when conjunction (*saṃyoga*) among conjoined things, inherence (*samavāya*) among inherent things, a quality-possessor (*guṇin*) among qualities, and a universal (*sāmānya*) among individuals are accepted as being absolutely distinct, they must be refuted by the dilemmas of whether [the relation] subsists in its entirety or in part, when one considers their mode of existence in those substrates.

Therefore, since many refutations descend upon absolute difference (*ekāntabheda*), and since no refutation arises in the case of non-absolutism (*anekānta*), there is no liberation through the acceptance of non-absolutism.

Therefore, it would have been better to abandon parsimony from the very beginning and accept non-absolutism; what is the use of postulating the absolutism of difference? This is merely a self-inflicted affliction at an inappropriate time. (Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika)

Ñ384: How could the Sāṃkhya, who asserts that *pradhāna* is composed of the mutually contradictory qualities (*guṇa*) of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, and who accepts two contradictory properties—activation and cessation—belonging to a single primordial nature (*prakṛti*) during the states of saṃsāra and liberation, be capable of declaring his own aversion to the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*)? Ñ385:

As for the Mīmāṃsakas, they themselves already accept non-absolutism regarding unity, plurality, and so forth through other modes; therefore, they do not deserve to be subjected to any kind of cross-examination regarding their acceptance of that [non-absolutism].

Alternatively, even they should be questioned in this manner regarding the absolute eternality of the word and its relationship [to its meaning]: it is the Mīmāṃsakas' accepted position that "an injunction (*nodanā*) produces a cognition whose object is a thing in the form of an effect that is void of the three times.

In this regard, if the state of being an effect were void of the three times, it would fall within the scope of the means of knowledge consisting in non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*); if, however, it were a real entity (*artha*), it would fall within the scope of perception and the other [means of knowledge]; but if it possessed both forms, then it would fall within the scope of the injunction.

Now, the examples and logical arguments favored by all schools of thought, such as the Buddhists and others, are set forth for the sake of establishing non-absolutism (anekānta). 1. All schools of thought, including the Buddhists and others, acknowledge that doubtful cognition (*saṃśaya-jñāna*) consists of two aspects; they do not reject non-absolutism. 2.

Likewise, how could opponents—who accept inference (*anumāna*) as being characterized by contradictory properties (*viruddha-dharmādhyasta*), serving both to establish their own position and to refute the position of others—ever be able to repudiate non-absolutism?

Just as all colors such as blue and others existing in the fluid of a peacock’s egg are neither of a single form nor of multiple forms, but rather exist as both single and multiple forms according to their actual state, so too is the non-absolutism (anekānta) of one, many, and so forth. As it has been said, relying on the non-absolutism of name, representation, and the rest:
"Just as colors such as blue and others exist in the fluid of a peacock’s egg, all of them mutually intermingled, so too are name and the other [modes] in a jar. (1)
There is no positive concomitance (anvaya), for that [the particular] is differentiated; nor is there differentiation, because it exists through positive concomitance.
A jar is a distinct genus (*jātyantaram*) whose existence consists in the conjunction of two different clay-particles. //2//

For here, the word *hi* signifies a reason, in the sense of "because": that is the jar. When one part is a lion and another part is a man, that object which consists of these two parts is called "Narasimha" (Man-Lion) as a non-part [i.e., a single unified entity] through its indivisibility. (3)

He is not a man because he has the form of a lion, nor is he a lion because he has the form of a man; for, due to the distinction between his sound, cognition, and activity, he is indeed a different species. //4//

Whether they assert that the definition of a logical reason consists of three characteristics or five characteristics, why do all others not consider [the reason] to be existent, non-existent, and so forth? //5//

Just as for a single person, various relationships such as being a father or a son—which have distinct causes—are not contradictory; for example, that same man is a son in relation to his own father, but a father in relation to his own children, and so forth. However, relationships that have non-distinct causes are contradictory; for example, [the claim] that he is both a father and a son in relation to his own father alone. In the same way, even the doctrine of manifoldness (*anekānta*) is not contradictory because its causes are distinct: it is one in terms of its substantial nature (*dravyātman*), but many in terms of its modal nature (*paryāyātman*), and so forth.
Your claim that [the universal] is both one and many by way of its substantial nature (*dravyātmanā*) and so forth is contradicted by the fact that it has a non-different cause (*abhinnanimittatā*).

For the root of contradiction lies in having non-distinct causes, and not in having distinct causes. Thus, even entities such as pleasure and pain, or humans and gods, are not possible for the self without its being manifold (anekānta), characterized by both permanence and impermanence and so forth. Just as, for example, in the case of a serpent—a substance that is stable—the states of having an expanded hood and having a retracted hood are mutually contradictory, yet they are not contradictory with respect to the substance itself; or as, for example, the destruction of straightness and the arising of curvature in a single finger.

Or, just as when cow's milk remains, the destruction of the state of "milk" and the subsequent production of the state of "curd" both occur and are perceived through means of valid cognition such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), so too does every entity consist of both substance and mode (*dravyaparyāyātmakatā*).
Furthermore, in all philosophical systems (*darśana*), even the reasons (*hetu*) stated to establish one's own intended probandum attain correctness only by accepting non-absolutism (*anekānta*).
To illustrate this, here is written a section of debate titled *Para-hetu-tamo-bhāskara* (The Sun for the Darkness of Opponent Reasons), composed by [the author] himself.

For instance: here indeed, those who consider themselves the crest-jewels of the entire circle of logicians, who always forcefully nourish their own pride, who harbor envy toward virtuous scholars, and who proclaim their own vigorous brilliance even within assemblies of simple folk—even while experiencing through their own clearly arisen experience the non-absolutism (*anekānta*) residing in the totality of all things as being free from error, and even while themselves explicitly stating that very non-absolutism through reasoning—[they nevertheless act otherwise].

Not accepting the inconclusiveness [of your argument] based on mere words, failing to see the true nature of things as they actually exist, nurturing only your own attachment to your own view, never asking about the true nature of a valid reason (*samyag-hetu*) in the presence of the learned, and not understanding it through your own intellect, you have now put forward this "proof" (*sādhana*) for the sake of establishing your thesis (*sādhya*). Even in that case, the reason (*hetu*) is the basis for the establishment of the thesis.

Therefore, in order to establish the non-absolute nature [of things], we—who demonstrate the true nature of reality as it exists—first clarify the very nature of the logical reason (*hetu*) itself as being correctly characterized by non-absolutism (*anekānta*).
May you listen for a moment with attentive minds, having set aside pride in your own positions and adopting an impartial stance.

For instance: is your proposed reason intended to prove its own thesis through positive concomitance (*anvaya*), or through negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), or through both positive and negative concomitance?

If [the reason] were first of all based on positive concomitance (*anvaya*), then even the fact of being that person’s son and so forth would be a means of cognition (*gamaka*), because positive concomitance alone exists there as well.
Nor is it based on negative concomitance (*vyatireka*); for that would lead to the undesirable consequence that being that person’s son and so forth would indeed be a means of cognition.

For in the absence of darkness elsewhere—in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) consisting of fair-skinned persons—the probandum would necessarily be established by that very fact of being his son and so forth.

If it is argued that [the reason] possesses both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatirekin*), then even in that case, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the probandum (*sādhya*) is established merely from "being that person's son" and so forth. Nor should one suspect that this [reason] is a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) because it lacks the three characteristics (*trairūpya*); for otherwise, the same consequence would apply even to "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and other such reasons when proving impermanence.
Furthermore, according to your own view, the three characteristics do indeed exist in the case of "being that person's son" and the like.

[Opponent: "Let this fault apply to their [the Naiyāyikas'] view, according to which the three-fold nature (*trairūpya*)—consisting of being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), presence in the similar class (*sapakṣasattva*), and absence from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣāsattva*)—is the complete definition of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*). But it does not apply to us, who maintain that the logical reason has five characteristics (*pañcalakṣaṇahetu*), because we also accept two further characteristics: the absence of a counter-argument (*asatpratipakṣatva*) and the fact that the object is not sublated by perception or scripture (*pratyakṣāgamābādhitaviṣayatva*). [Proponent: "In that case, since it is impossible for purely positive (*kevalānvaya*) or purely negative (*kevalavyatireka*) inferences to possess these five characteristics, it would follow that they lack probative force (*āgamakatva*)."

Furthermore, the Yogins do not accept that those two [the son of a blacksmith and the son of a Brahmin] lack probative force; for this reason, since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to ascertain an invariable connection (*pratibandha*), the fact that [the reason] cannot be established otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*) is precisely what constitutes the basis for the lack of probative force in cases such as "being the son of that [man]" (*tatputratva*). [Objection: But is it not the case that the three characteristics (*trailakṣaṇya*) and so forth are absent?

[Response: If it is argued that here [in the case of the son of a blacksmith], the certainty of absence from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣe 'sattva*) does not exist, then the Buddhist replies: "In that case, there is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the point that, in the absence of dark complexion (*śyāmatva*), one must necessarily be excluded from being the son of that man. Thus says the Buddhist.

But the *yoga* (conjunction) roars: "The transformation of food such as vegetables is co-extensive with blackness, but not with being that person's son; thus, because of the existence of this *upādhi*, it is impossible for [the reason] to be absent from the heterologous instances (*vipakṣa*) in the case of 'being that person's son'. [Response:

These two [opponents] thus take refuge in nothing other than "the impossibility of the reason otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*) under a different name. Therefore, let that alone be the definition of a logical reason (*hetu*).

Moreover, in cases such as "The moon in the sky exists because of the moon in the water," "The sun will rise tomorrow because of today’s sunrise of the sun," and so forth, even though there is an absence of the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), [the inference still occurs] because otherwise the specific tone of my mother's voice would be inexplicable.

Furthermore, in cases such as "Everything is momentary or non-momentary because of its existence," the reason is seen to be indicative of the probandum even in the absence of a similar instance (*sapakṣa*); so what is the use of the three features (*trairūpya*) and so on?

If it is argued that "the single, flawless definition of a logical mark (*liṅga*) is simply the certainty of its being otherwise impossible (*anyathānupapatti*); this alone is the reality, while this elaborate [list of criteria] is merely a proliferation," then the Buddhist must state that the definition consists of having an uncontradicted object (*abādhitaviṣayatva*), having no counter-argument (*asatpratipakṣa*), and being known (*jñātatva*), while the follower of the Nyāya school must state that the definition is simply being known (*jñātatva*).

[Objection: "Now, since we are dealing with a probans (*jñāpaka-hetu*), it is already established that [the reason] possesses an uncontradicted objective domain (*abādhitaviṣayatva*) and lacks a counter-probans (*asatpratipakṣatva*) by virtue of the mere certainty of its exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*); and it is also established that it is known. Therefore, since everything is already established by virtue of dealing with a probative probans (*gamaka-hetu*), what is the use of this further elaboration regarding the remaining [criteria]?

[Response: Precisely for this reason, a probans is not a prover by positive concomitance (*anvaya*) alone; rather, it is so by means of a specific form of positive concomitance that implies negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

Nor [is it established] by mere absence (*vyatirekamātra*), but rather from a specific absence accompanied by presence (*anvaya*)—that is, from a qualified absence. Nor is it established by those two alone when they are not mutually interpenetrated; rather, it is because presence and absence function without abandoning each other's nature. For a logical reason (*hetu*) is defined solely by the characteristic of "the impossibility of being otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*) once it is ascertained, and it possesses the form of presence and absence exactly as demonstrated. Furthermore, it should not be said that the Jains' assertion that a reason has only one characteristic contradicts the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekānta*); for what is meant is that the reason has only one characteristic in terms of the rule governing its formal application (*prayoga*).

But [if you argue that] in the case of a restriction by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-niyama*), there is no lack of certainty in the reason because that which is restricted to a single intrinsic nature is devoid of intrinsic nature—like the horn of a hare—then how is it not the case that the reason possesses the character of being inconclusive? O you who possess ears! You must understand this: all reasons whatsoever, when presented by others—whether they be great ones whose intellects are opposed to the non-absolutism (*anekānta*) established by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) well-known to every living being, or the disciples of Kaṇabhuj, Akṣapāda, Buddha, and so forth—must be accepted as possessing the states of being unestablished, contradictory, or inconclusive according to the speaker’s intention. Thus it should be understood.

For instance: first of all, their contradiction is stated. For if one were to admit that three or five aspects of a single reason (*hetu*) are real, then that [reason] would establish an entity that consists of multiple properties. Thus, how is it not a case of proving the opposite? Because one has admitted that a single reason possesses multiple properties.

Nor should it be said that the very existence of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) is identical to its exclusion from all dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*); for it is impossible for presence and absence—the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—to be identical in every respect. Alternatively, every logical reason (*hetu*) would become either purely positive (*kevalānvayin*) or purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*), rather than possessing three or five characteristics (*trirūpa* or *pañcarūpa*). And in that case, even the absence of a means of proof (*sādhanābhāva*) would be a communicator [of the probandum].

Now, if the existence [of the reason] is not accepted as being based on the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), but rather its mere presence when the probandum (*sādhya*) exists is admitted, and its non-existence when the probandum is absent is what is expressed—and if that [non-existence] is not something distinct from the existent—then it is non-existent (*asat*).

For in this way, because there is no absence of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), the three characteristics (*trairūpya*) and so forth of the logical reason (*hetu*) would not exist. If, on the other hand, that [reason] were a different property (*dharmāntara*) from those two, then how could all the reasons proposed by others not be contradictory? For a reason that possesses a single form yet has a manifold nature, when ascertained as being invariably concomitant (*avinābhūta*) with such a probandum (*sādhya*), establishes a non-exclusive entity (*anekāntavastu*); thus, it is pervaded by a non-exclusivity that is itself contradictory to exclusivity.

In the same way, the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of all probans-attributes (*sādhana-dharma*) should be inferred; for the reason (*hetu*) may be either a universal (*sāmānya*), or a particular (*viśeṣa*), or both, or an experience (*anubhava*).

First of all, the universal is not the reason. For if that [universal], which pervades everything or pervades its own entire substratum, were to be employed as a reason, it would have to be established either by perception (*pratyakṣa*) or by inference (*anumāna*).
It is first of all not established by perception; for perception functions by following the sense-faculties (*akṣa*), and the sense-faculty is restricted precisely by a fixed location and so forth.
Therefore, knowledge following from the senses is capable of operating only with respect to a specific place and so forth, but not with respect to that which pervades all times and places.

If it is argued that because [the universal] is not distinct from the nature of the specific place, when that [place] is ascertained, there is also the ascertainment of that [universal], we say no; for if it were not distinct from the nature of the specific place, it would simply be something restricted to a specific place, and not something pervasive.

Thus, a cause in the form of a pervasive universal is not established by perception. If its establishment were through inference, the demoness of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would be difficult to avoid.

For inference, proceeding as it does preceded by the apprehension of a mark (*liṅga*), establishes only a universal (*sāmānya*); and the mark is not admitted to have a particular form, because [particulars] do not possess the property of concomitance (*ananugama*).

Now, the mark, being of a universal form, must be either apprehended or unapprehended. It cannot be unapprehended, because that is undesirable and because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If it is apprehended, then its apprehension must occur either through perception (*pratyakṣa*) or through inference. It cannot be through perception, because perception grasps only what is in close proximity (*saṃnikṛṣṭa*).

Nor can it be established by inference (*anumāna*). For in that case as well, if the apprehension of the mark (*liṅga*) occurs without [prior] inference, the same difficulty recurs. Furthermore, because inferences would be infinite, the apprehension of even a single mark would not occur even in a thousand aeons. Moreover, a universal (*sāmānya*), whose own nature is to be supported by all its individual instances (*vyakti*), when ascertained through perception and inference, would produce the ascertainment of its own substrata. And since the ascertainment of its own substratum would likewise require the ascertainment of its own substrata, it follows that every person would be omniscient.

Furthermore: since a universal (*sāmānya*) does not produce its own cognition prior to its conjunction with the sense organ that is its own substrate, it would not produce it even later, because its nature is unchanging. Moreover, if it were to change or if excellence were to be imparted to it by others, it would follow that it is momentary (*kṣaṇika*). Furthermore: that universal must be either different from the individuals (*vyakti*), non-different, or both different and non-different to be a cause [of cognition]. It cannot first be different, because it is not perceived separately from the individuals.

If it is argued that the universal is not perceived separately because it is related to individuals through inherence (*samavāya*), we say no; for inherence is defined as the cause of the cognition "it is here. Furthermore, such a cognition—"this is here"—cannot occur without the perception of difference.
Moreover, on this basis, is the universal such as "horseness" held to be omnipresent within its own substrata, or is it held to be omnipresent throughout all things?

If [the universal] were present in all its own substrata, then a universal such as "horseness" would not be connected with an individual that is first arising in a place devoid of individuals such as white horses (*karka*), because the universal cannot abide in a place devoid of individuals and does not come from another individual. If, on the other hand, it is accepted that it is omnipresent in everything, then it would be manifested by white horses just as well as by brindled cows (*śābaleya*).

Nor should it be said that only white horses (*karka*) and the like have the capacity to manifest that [universal], while brindled horses (*śābaleya*) and the like do not; for what kind of capacity do those white horses possess?

If you say it is "the state of having a common form" (*sādhāraṇarūpatva*), we say no: if individual instances (*vyakti*) are inherently common in form, then they will by themselves produce the recurring cognition "horse, horse. What, then, is the use of postulating a universal distinct from them?

Furthermore, if individuals (*vyakti*) possess an inherently unique form (*asādhāraṇarūpa*), then they could not become common even through connection with another universal (*sāmānya*), because they would remain inherently unique by nature. Thus, since a universal distinct from the individual does not exist, the reason characterized by that [universal] is unestablished (*asiddha*). How, then, can the probandum (*sādhya*) be established on its basis?

Now, if it is argued that the universal is non-different from the individual and thus serves as the reason (*hetu*), that too is incorrect. For that which is non-different from the individual cannot follow after other individuals—just like the specific nature of the individual itself—and thus its status as a universal is untenable; there is a mutual contradiction between being non-different from the individual and having the nature of a universal. If it is argued that it is both different and non-different, no; because of the contradiction. If it is argued that it is different in some respect and non-different in another, that too is not tenable, because a universal is partless (*niraṃśa*). Therefore, a reason that is exclusively of the nature of a universal is not established in its entirety.

Nor is it the particular form (*viśeṣarūpa*); because that is unique (*asādhāraṇa*), it is unfit to be a prover (*gamaka*), for positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is only possible when there is commonality (*sādhāraṇatva*). Nor is the combination of both the universal and the particular a reason (*hetu*) when they are not mutually interpenetrated, because the faults of both would then follow. Nor is it "neither" (*anubhaya*); since things defined by mutual exclusion (*anyonyavyavacchedarūpa*) entail the presence of the second when the first is absent, "neither" is non-existent and thus unfit to be a reason.

Furthermore, a universal (*sāmānya*) constructed by the intellect (*buddhi-prakalpita*) cannot be a logical reason (*hetu*), because it lacks the nature of a real entity (*avastu-rūpatva*), because it is not invariably concomitant (*apratibaddhatva*) with the probandum (*sādhya*), and because it is unestablished (*asiddhatva*). Thus, since universals and the like are unestablished, all reasons characterized by them are likewise unestablished.

Likewise, all reasons put forward by others that lack an invariable connection (*pratibandha*) should be understood as inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Moreover, an invariable connection between the probandum and the probans—whether they be absolute universals or particulars—is not logically tenable.

For instance: what connection (*pratibandha*) could there be between two universals (*sāmānya*) that are absolutely eternal and stand in a relationship of neither being assisted nor assisting one another? If they were to assist one another through a mutual relationship such as cause and effect, it would follow that they are impermanent.

As for two particulars (*viśeṣa*), even if a connection is grasped when they are restricted to a specific place and time, since those two perish at that very spot, how could another particular—whose connection has not been grasped in the subject (*dharmin*) where the probandum resides—be taken as a reason (*hetu*) without being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)?

Furthermore, a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is possible only when the characteristics of a logical mark (*liṅga-lakṣaṇa*), such as its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), are established. Now, if there were an absolute difference or non-difference between the probandum (*sādhya*), the probans (*sādhana*), and the subject (*dharmin*), the application of properties such as *pakṣadharmatva* to the logical mark would be untenable, because no relationship could be established. For what kind of relationship could exist between the probandum, the probans, and the subject? Would it be inherence (*samavāya*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), opposition (*virodha*), the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), identity (*tādātmya*), or origination from that (*tadutpatti*)?

First of all, inherence (*samavāya*) is not [the relation]; for that which is distinct from both the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) is not apprehended by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is because the cognition that establishes it—such as "the cloth is here in the threads"—is not common experience; for even those with feet covered in dust are seen to have the perception, "the threads are here in the cloth. Furthermore, it would follow that inherence exists even in such cases as "the absence of a jar here on the ground."

Alternatively, if one accepts that inherence (*samavāya*) exists by its own nature within the subject (*dharmin*) and the property (*dharma*), and so forth, then likewise the properties to be proven (*sādhya*) and others should also exist by their own nature within the subject; what is the point of the useless postulation of inherence?

Furthermore, if one accepts that inherence exists through another inherence, then in that case too, if one postulates yet another inherence, there arises an insurmountable river of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Let it be granted that inherence (samavāya) has an occurrence either intrinsically or extrinsically; nevertheless, it would not possess the quality of being the connector only for specific related entities, but rather for others as well, because it is equally present everywhere and possesses a single nature.
Nor is it conjunction (saṃyoga); for if such [conjunction] were to exist between the probandum, the probans, and so forth, would it be distinct from them or non-distinct?

In the first case, why is this [inference] intended for these specific things and not for others as well? For there is no difference in their distinctness (*bheda*). Nor can inherence (*samavāya*) be the regulator here, because it is identical everywhere.

In the second case, however, only the probandum (*sādhya*) and so forth would exist; there would be nothing called "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) that is in any way distinct. If one were to accept a distinct conjunction, one would be resorting to the position of an opponent. Furthermore, contradiction (*virodha*) should not be asserted, because it is impossible under the doctrine of absolute unity (*ekāntavāda*); for that [contradiction] must be either non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*) or mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihāra*).
In this regard, as for the first [alternative], does it mean that there is never a simultaneous dwelling in one place, or that after staying for some time, there is subsequently no dwelling?
If the first position is held, there would be no contradiction regarding snakes, mongooses, and so forth; otherwise, there would be an absence of serpents and the like even within the three worlds.

If the second [position] is held, however, there would be a contradiction even regarding human beings and women, since they too, after staying together for some time, eventually depart from one another.
Furthermore, how can there be this contradiction between the submarine fire and the waters of the ocean, or between lightning and rainwater, given that they have coexisted for a long time?
Moreover, mutual exclusion is common to all entities; why then should it belong only to these specific ones?

Nor does the relation of qualifier and qualified hold together, because that [relation] is absent when conjunction and the like are impossible, and that [conjunction] has already been refuted previously.

Nor is identity (*tādātmya*) between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) tenable; for since the probandum and the probans are respectively unestablished and established, their difference must be admitted, making identity impossible. Furthermore, if there were identity, either the probandum or the probans would alone exist, and not both; if they were somehow identical, one would be forced into the Jaina doctrine. As for origination from that (*tadutpatti*), it is possible only if there is a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), and a causal relationship is established only upon the establishment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).

However, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) for an eternal entity is not possible through either successive or simultaneous action, because one cannot admit two distinct natures—one productive and one non-productive—regardless of whether auxiliary causes are present or absent.
For an impermanent entity, moreover, such efficiency is untenable whether it is existent or non-existent; for if it is existent, its operation upon that which exists at the same time is impossible.

Alternatively, if [the cause] were active, there would follow the consequence that all subsequent moments, having arisen precisely at the time of their respective causes, would exist simultaneously in a single moment; and there would follow the consequence that all entities would stand in a mutual relationship of cause and effect. Furthermore, because [an entity existing in a single moment] would be devoid of all causal capacities, the relation of cause and effect would be impossible; otherwise, even things such as a rabbit's horn would entail that same consequence.

Thus, since a connection between the probandum and so forth is untenable under the doctrine of absolute [momentary] existence, the definition of a logical reason—such as its being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*)—would be entirely inconsistent; and likewise, a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) would be impossible to establish.

Likewise, for those who maintain an extremist position (*ekāntavādin*), even the apprehension of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is untenable. This is because, in the case of a self whose nature is unchanging, there is no sequence of prior and subsequent cognitions; and even in the case of that which perishes at every moment, there is an absence of a single consciousness (*caitanya*) persisting through the apprehension of both cause and effect.

Nor should it be said that the connection, such as the relation of cause and effect, is synthesized by a memory occurring immediately after the experience of the effect and so forth, because memory arises only with respect to what has already been experienced.

Furthermore, no connection (*pratibandha*) has ever been experienced, because such a connection must reside in both [terms], and since neither the earlier nor the later of the two can be apprehended by a single [cognition], there is no determination of a connection either. Thus, in this way, under the view of absolute [one-sidedness], every reason (*hetu*) propounded by others would be exclusively inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), due to the absence of a connection and the resulting lack of certainty.

Thus, since neither a universal alone, nor a particular alone, nor those two mutually distinct entities together can function as a logical reason (*hetu*), one must accept that the capacity to prove a probandum consisting of multiple aspects resides in a reason whose nature is a combination of both universal and particular, which serves as the basis for the cognitions of continuity and exclusion.

Furthermore, it must be explained how that very form which is excluded from other forms can also attain persistence, and how that which persists can also rely upon exclusion; for no contradiction is established regarding the nature of an object as it is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in its dual aspect of both persisting and being excluded—just like the case of the universal and the particular, or variegated cognition, or the single variegated color of a multicolored cloth.

Furthermore, regarding the reason (hetu) put forward by the proponent of an extreme position (ekāntavādin), there are these alternatives: is the probandum (sādhya) a universal (sāmānya), or a particular (viśeṣa), or both mutually distinct, or neither?
First, it is not a universal, because such a thing alone is impossible and lacks causal efficiency (arthakriyākāritva).
Nor is it a particular, because it cannot be proven due to its non-continuity (ananuyāyitva). Nor is it both, because it does not escape the defects of both.

Nor can it be neither [of the two]; for that which is non-existent cannot be a probandum (*sādhya*) because it lacks both the nature of being a reason (*hetu*) and the nature of pervading [the subject]. Therefore, when demonstrating a single reason—consisting of a dual nature of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) that are mutually interpenetrating—for the sake of proving a property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*) that is the object of dispute and possesses the nature of both universal and particular, within the locus of the probandum (*sādhya-dharmin*), there is not even the slightest possibility for the faults mentioned regarding the positions of exclusivity (*ekānta*). Consequently, one must necessarily accept that the essential nature of a reason is of a non-exclusive (*anekānta*) character.
Otherwise, in all inferences, there would be the total annihilation of the probandum and the probans according to the logic already stated.

Therefore, O partisan of an extremist view: by abandoning pride in your own position, with a mind free from despondency, closing your physical eyes and opening the eye of intelligence, and proceeding solely in accordance with reason through an impartial disposition, may you investigate the desirable non-absolutism (anekānta) while desiring to know its true nature;
and may you realize that reality which is endowed with all logical arguments rooted in the single foundation of valid cognition and is entirely free from the faults previously mentioned.
Thus ends the section on debate titled *Para-hetu-tamo-bhāskara*. From this, the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*), which is accepted by all philosophical systems, is established.
(Siddhānta) Now, stating the Jaina doctrine in brief, he says:
"O sinless one, this summary of the Jaina system has been declared."
Nowhere is there any obstruction from the front, the back, or from any other direction. //58//

Regarding the commentary on the Jaina philosophy: because its full extent is unfathomable and thus impossible to express in detail, it is stated in this very manner—"the essence of the application" (*upayogasāra*) is a summary (*samāsa*). It is "directly perceived" (*pratyakṣa*), meaning it has been declared and expressed as faultless (*anagha*), being free from defects; for when everything that can be said is rooted in the Omniscient One, there is no room for the impurity of error.

In this Jaina philosophy, there is no contradiction—that is, no mutual inconsistency—between what was stated previously and what was stated subsequently, even within the subtle mental processes involved in investigating the nature of the categories such as the living (*jīva*) and the non-living (*ajīva*).

The underlying meaning is this: while mutual contradiction exists between what was said first and what was said later even in the foundational scriptures (*mūla-śāstra*) of other philosophical systems, let alone in the compositions of later deceitful authors.

Likewise, in the Jaina philosophy, because the meanings are perfectly coherent within the twelvefold canon (*dvādaśāṅga*) composed by the Kevalins and in the traditional treatises (*pāramparya-grantha*), even when examined with subtle scrutiny, that [contradiction] does not exist.

As for those few words heard here and there in other philosophical systems that touch the hearts of the sensitive, even they have emerged from the nectar-ocean of the well-spoken teachings of the Jina; yet, having merely gathered them, people vainly consider themselves to be great. As the venerable Siddhasena said: [The verse follows.]

"Whatever wealth of elegant sayings flashes forth in our well-ascertained systems of dependent reasoning (*paratantra-yukti*), those are yours alone—drops from the words of the Jina that emerged from the primordial great ocean and serve as the authority for the world.

(32) Regarding this, others say: "Aha! You Jains; you who profess devotion to the reality taught by the Arhat have manifested something utterly incoherent, namely, that even in your own systems there is a contradiction between what precedes and what follows."

If it is argued: "In our system, even when examined by those with subtle vision, not even a trace of contradiction is observed anywhere—just as there is no blackness in the rays of the moon"; this is what is said.

O friends, if you listen with impartiality, setting aside partiality for your own views, free from pride, and with attentive ears—paying heed with your wits open (*pratibhāvadbhiḥ*)—then we shall demonstrate everything to you.
For instance, first of all, a contradiction between the earlier and later [statements] is pointed out within the doctrine accepted by the Tathāgatas.

Having previously stated that everything is fragile and momentary, he later asserted: "That which does not follow the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) is not a cause; that which is not a cause is not an object.

This is the meaning of this: cognition arises only when the object exists, and not when it is absent; thus, the object, by following the positive and negative concomitance, is the cause of cognition. And since cognition arises from that very object, it takes that alone as its object.

By asserting this, the existence of the object for two moments has been stated. For instance: knowledge, which is the effect arising from the object as its cause, arises in the second moment, but not at the same time as the cause, because it is impossible for cause and effect to exist simultaneously.

Furthermore, that knowledge perceives only the very object that produced it and nothing else, according to the dictum: "That which is not the cause is not the object. Thus, the existence of the object for two moments follows by necessity; and since this contradicts the doctrine of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇakṣaya*), there is a contradiction between what was previously asserted and what follows logically.
Likewise, having stated that what is not a cause cannot be an object, [the author] further asserted that even objects such as the past and future are the objects of yogic perception.

Now, since the past and future are respectively destroyed and unarisen, they could not serve as causes for that [perception]. Furthermore, for one who asserts that which is not a cause to be an object, there would be a contradiction between what precedes and what follows.

Ñ423: Even if there is no causality for the cognition that grasps the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*), how could there not be a contradiction between what precedes and what follows for one who expresses an object existing in the three times? For it is not accepted that what lacks a cause can be the object of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Ñ424: Likewise, if the momentary destruction [of things] is accepted, the apprehension of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) occurring at different times becomes possible. Therefore, for one who considers the grasping of pervasion between the probandum and the probans to have the three times as its object, how could there be a contradiction between what precedes and what follows?
Likewise, the doctrine of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇakṣaya*) has been established.

However, in this verse: "In the ninety-first eon from now, I killed a man with a spear; by the ripening of that karma, O monks, I am pierced in the foot," how can there not be a contradiction between what precedes and what follows for the Buddha, who speaks the words *me* and *asmi* regarding a past life in a manner inconsistent with momentary destruction?

In that way, having previously stated that every entity is partless (*niraṃśa*), how could the statement of the Buddhist—who later asserts that it possesses parts—not be self-contradictory? For [he claims that] while the self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) of the mind of non-violence, abstention, and generosity grasps its own internal qualities such as being a real substance (*sad-dravya*), consciousness (*cetanatva*), and the capacity to attain heaven (*svarga-prāpaṇa-śakti*), it nevertheless produces a definitive determination (*nirṇaya*) regarding only one part of those internal qualities—namely, its being a real substance—and not the second part, such as the capacity to attain heaven, even though that too is internal.
How, then, could his speech not be internally inconsistent?

Thus, although non-conceptual perception grasps an object such as "blue" in its entirety, it does not produce a definitive determination regarding the aspect of the momentary destruction inherent in that blue object. Therefore, for the Buddhist who asserts that objects possess parts (*sāmśatā*), the contradiction between his earlier and later statements is indeed easily perceived.

(427) Likewise, even while asserting that the three characteristics of a logical reason (*hetu*) and the dual nature of doubt consist in their having distinct aspects, he who does not accept that an object has parts is also guilty of a contradiction between his earlier and later positions. (428)

Thus, according to the Buddhist doctrine, atoms that are not mutually conjoined, yet possess proximity and aggregate, appear in the form of jars and so forth; they do not, however, produce an effect in the form of a composite whole (*skandha*) through a relationship of mutual contact like fire and fuel.

In this regard, there are these faults: because the individual atoms are not conjoined with one another, if a jar were held by the hand at a single location, the entire jar would not be held; likewise, lifting, lowering, and moving [the object] would not occur.

Furthermore, the Buddhists, who accept that the defining characteristic of existence for a jar consists in its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) such as supporting [water] and so forth, have indeed admitted those very properties; yet those [properties] are untenable according to their own tenets. Consequently, there is a contradiction between their earlier and later positions.

(ñ430) Now, the internal inconsistency between the systems of the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas is demonstrated: having stated that "existence" (*sattva*) is the connection with the universal "Being" (*sattā*), how could their statement not be contradictory when they assert the real existence (*sad-bhāva*) of universals, particulars, and inherence even in the absence of a connection with "Being"?

Having stated that "cognition does not know itself because of the contradiction of an action [acting] upon itself," how is there no contradiction with one's own words for those who maintain that the cognition of God is self-cognized due to the absence of such a contradiction of an action upon itself? Even a lamp, while illuminating itself by itself alone, dispels the contradiction of an action [acting] upon itself.

Ñ432: How is it not a contradiction to describe the dispassion of the sage Akṣapāda—who taught that even *chala*, *jāti*, and *nigrahasthāna*, which consist of fallacious arguments, possess the nature of reality—as being like proclaiming that darkness has the nature of light?

Ñ433: Having accepted the partlessness (*niravayavatva*) of space, how is there no contradiction for one who asserts its quality, sound, is heard only in a single part of it and not everywhere, thereby implying that space possesses parts?

§434: Existence (*sattā*) and conjunction (*yoga*) exist only when all things possess parts (*sāṃśatā*). Yet, a universal (*sāmānya*) is admitted to be partless and unitary; therefore, how is there not a contradiction between what precedes and what follows?

§435: Inherence (*samavāya*) is held to be eternal and of a single nature, yet its relation with all the inherent substrates (*samavāyin*) occurs necessarily only when [the relata] possess a manifold nature. Thus, a contradiction between what precedes and what follows is easily understood.

Regarding the statement "a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which possesses an object" (*arthavat*), if one explains this as "a means of valid cognition is that for which an object is a cooperative cause" (*sahakārī*), then for one who asserts that yogic perception has past and other such objects as its domain, there would be a contradiction between what precedes and what follows; for it is impossible for a past [object] and so forth to function as a cooperative cause.

(436) Likewise, memory is not accepted as a means of valid cognition either because it apprehends what has already been apprehended (*gṛhītagrāhitva*) or because it is not produced by an [external] object (*anarthajanyatva*). If memory were invalid due to apprehending what has already been apprehended, then it would follow that even those cognitions occurring in a continuous stream (*dhārāvāhijñāna*) would be invalid, since they too apprehend what has already been apprehended. (437)

Furthermore, the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas do not accept that cognitions occurring in a continuous stream (*dhārāvāhi-jñāna*) lack validity. If memory were invalid simply because it does not arise from an external object (*anarthajanya*), then inference (*anumāna*)—which has objects such as the past and future—would also be invalid for the same reason of not arising from an external object. For they maintain that inference has objects belonging to all three times, just like verbal testimony (*śabda*): indeed, by means of smoke, present fire is inferred; by the rising of clouds, future rain; and by the swelling of a river, that [rain] which has already occurred.

Thus, since there is a similarity between memory and continuous streams of cognition as well as inference, the claim that memory lacks authority while continuous streams of cognition and the like possess it involves a contradiction between what precedes and what follows.
Furthermore, regarding the Lord’s perception whose object is all things—is it held to be independent of the contact between sense-faculties and objects, or is it produced by such contact?

If [perception] were independent of the contact between the sense-faculty and its object, then the inclusion of the term "contact" in the sūtra—"perceptual knowledge produced by the contact of the sense-faculty and the object is non-verbal"—would be purposeless; for divine perception exists even without such contact.
If it is argued that divine perception is intended to be produced precisely by the contact of the sense-faculty and the object, it is said in reply:

No, for since the mind associated with Īśvara has an atomic dimension (*aṇuparimāṇa*), it cannot simultaneously come into contact with all objects; consequently, when he cognizes one object, he does not [cognize] others even though they exist. Therefore, like us and others, he could never possess omniscience.

Because simultaneous contact [with all objects] is impossible, there is no simultaneous cognition of all things. If it is argued that he is omniscient because he cognizes all things sequentially, this is not so; for since the sequential cognition of all things over a long period of time is possible even for people like us—just as it is for Śiva (Khaṇḍaparaśu)—it would follow that we too are omniscient. Furthermore, because past and future objects have already perished or have not yet arisen, there can be no contact with them by means of the mind; for contact is only possible between existing things, and those [past and future objects] do not exist at that time.

In that case, how could the knowledge of the Great Lord (Maheśvara) be a grasper of past and future objects? Since that knowledge is held to be a grasper of all objects, the contradiction between the former [claim] and the latter is easily understood. Likewise, it should be understood that even for yogis, the perception of all objects is obstructed by insurmountable contradictions.

Having previously stated that when the effect-substance (*kārya-dravya*) has arisen, its form (*rūpa*) arises later because a form without a substrate cannot arise due to its being a quality (*guṇa*), it would be contradictory to state later that when the effect-substance has perished, its form perishes; for in that case, the form would have to remain without a substrate once the effect has perished and only then perish later.
For the Sāṃkhya, however, there is thus a contradiction with his own words: *prakṛti* (primordial nature) is held to be eternal, unitary, partless, inactive, and unmanifest;

yet it is also asserted that this very same [nature] transforms through modifications such as the Great One (*mahat*) and so forth, which are impermanent and so on. This is inconsistent from beginning to end.

Furthermore, since the determination of an object is the function of the intellect (*buddhi*), to say that [the intellect] does not perceive an object because it lacks the discernment of a conscious subject contradicts the common experience of all the world.

Furthermore, to claim that the intellect (*buddhi*), though called "great" (*mahat*), is insentient (*jaḍa*) and does not perceive anything at all, is contradicted by both one's own and others' experience. Moreover, as for the assertion that the five elements, such as space, are produced from the subtle essences (*tanmātra*) known as the primary sounds and so forth—this too is internally inconsistent within the doctrine of absolute permanence; how can it be accepted with faith?

Just as for the Puruṣa, because of his immutable eternity, neither transformation nor bondage and liberation occur, so too for Prakṛti these do not occur precisely because of her immutable eternity. And since that which is immutably eternal is held to have a single nature, therefore those [qualities]—transformation, bondage, and liberation—which are accepted by others for Prakṛti, as well as her eternity, are mutually contradictory.

Furthermore, for the Mīmāṃsaka, there is thus a contradiction with his own position: having stated, "One should not harm any living beings" and "One should certainly not be a harmer," how can there be no contradiction between the earlier and later parts of the Veda when it declares, "One should offer a large bull or a large goat to a learned Brahmin"? Likewise, having first said, "One should not harm any living beings," it is subsequently recited in that very scripture as follows:
"Six hundred animals are employed on the middle day of the Aśvamedha, according to the scriptural injunction, being fewer by three animals. Likewise,

how could such scriptural statements as "One should sacrifice the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma" (AitĀr 6.13) and "One should sacrifice fifteen animals dedicated to Prajāpati" (TĀ 1.4), and so forth, not entail a contradiction between what precedes and what follows?
Having first prohibited false speech in general, he subsequently stated: "One may speak a falsehood for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa," and so forth. Likewise:
"O King, a word joined with jest does not cause harm, nor among women, nor at the time of marriage;
they say that five kinds of falsehoods are non-fatal: when life is at stake, and when all one's wealth is being seized. [MBh 1.77.16, etc.]

Likewise, after having rejected in various ways the taking of what is not given, it was later stated: "Even if a Brāhmaṇa takes what belongs to another by force or by power, even so there is no 'taking of what is not given' for him; because all this has been given to the Brāhmaṇas, and it is only due to the weakness of the Brāhmaṇas that the Śūdras enjoy it. Therefore, when a Brāhmaṇa seizes it, he takes his own; a Brāhmaṇa eats his own, wears his own, and gives away his own. (Ñ444) Similarly, after having declared, "There is no destiny for one who has no son," it was said: (Ñ445)
"Many thousands of young celibate brahmins have gone to heaven, O brahmins, without having produced offspring," and so forth; likewise:
"There is no fault in eating meat, nor in liquor, nor in sexual intercourse."

Regarding the verse found in the Smṛti: "This is the course of beings; however, withdrawal from it yields great fruit" (Manu 5.56): if worldly engagement (*pravṛtti*) were faultless, then how could it be said that "withdrawal from it yields great fruit"? This would be a contradiction.

Regarding the claim that "violence prescribed by the Vedas is a cause of *dharma*," there is an evident contradiction with one's own words. For instance: if violence is a cause of *dharma*, how can it be violence? And if it is violence, how can it be a cause of *dharma*? Indeed, it cannot be both a mother and barren.
